disputedCircuits.note: The Tulja Bhavani Temple article calls it one of the 51 Shakta pithas, while Wikipedia's combined table lists it at entry 64 and the Shakta Pithas in Maharashtra article counts it instead within Maharashtra's regional 'three and a half' set (as of 2026).

name: Mahalakshmi Temple, Kolhapur
significance: A major goddess temple where Mahalakshmi is worshipped locally as Ambabai, reckoned one of the three-and-a-half Shakti seats of the Shakta tradition in Maharashtra.
story: The goddess is said to have manifested here to destroy the demon Kolhasur, from whom Kolhapur takes its name.

disputedCircuits.note: Wikipedia describes Kolhapur as one of the 18 Maha Shakta pithas, as one of 52 Shakta pithas, and as a member of Maharashtra's 'three and a half' peethas, and it does not appear anywhere in Wikipedia's combined Shakta pithas table (as of 2026).

name: Renuka Devi Temple, Mahur
significance: A hill shrine to Renuka, mother of Parashurama, counted among the three-and-a-half Shakta pithas of Maharashtra; the surrounding town is also revered as the birthplace of Dattatreya.
story: Renuka was mortally wounded by Sahasrarjuna when she refused to surrender the cow Kamadhenu, and her son Parashurama performed her last rites at Mahur, where she then manifested on the hill.

disputedCircuits.note: Wikipedia describes Mahur as one of the 18 Maha Shakta pithas and as a pitha 'among 108 peethas' and a member of Maharashtra's 'three and a half' peethas, and it does not appear in Wikipedia's combined Shakta pithas table (as of 2026).

name: Saptashrungi Temple
deity: Goddess Saptashrungi Nivasini (a form of Durga)
significance: A hill shrine where the goddess is carved into a cave in a sheer rock face, counted among Maharashtra's three-and-a-half Shakta pithas and among the wider set of 51 Shakta pithas.
story: The right arm of Sati is said to have fallen here as Shiva carried her body across the world.

name: Shani Shingnapur Temple
deity: Shani, worshipped as a swayambhu black stone
significance: An open-air shrine to Shani built around a self-manifested black stone. The surrounding village is known for houses and shops built without doors or locks, in the belief that the god himself punishes theft.
story: Shepherds are said to have struck a black stone that bled, after which Shani appeared in a shepherd's dream, claimed the stone as his own and promised the village protection from theft.

name: Khandoba Temple, Jejuri
deity: Khandoba (Malhari Martand, a form of Shiva)
significance: One of the foremost pilgrimage centres of Maharashtra, this hilltop temple to Khandoba is the family deity shrine of farming, Brahmin and Dhangar communities across the Deccan.
story: Khandoba is said to have descended as an avatar of Shiva to subdue the demon brothers Mani and Malla, killing one and pardoning the other when he vowed to serve people.

name: Bhuleshwar Temple
significance: A hilltop Shiva temple about 45 km from Pune, protected as a monument and known for its dense figural stone carving worked in black basalt.
story: Devotees say that sweets offered before the linga sometimes disappear from the offering bowl.

name: Dagadusheth Halwai Ganapati Temple
significance: Pune's best-known Ganesha temple, visited by well over a hundred thousand devotees a year and the focus of a prominent ten-day Ganeshotsav celebration.
story: The sweet-seller Dagadusheth Halwai and his wife Laxmibai are said to have founded the shrine on a sage's advice after losing their only son in a plague.

name: Chintamani Temple, Theur
significance: One of the larger and better-known Ashtavinayaka shrines, about 25 km from Pune near the confluence of the Bhima and Mula-Mutha. It was a major Ganapatya centre that drew royal patronage under the Peshwa Madhavrao I.
story: Ganesha is said to have recovered the wish-granting Chintamani jewel from the greedy king Gana for the sage Kapila and then stayed on at Theur.

name: Mayureshwar (Moreshwar) Temple, Morgaon
builtDisplay: not earlier than 17th c.; Peshwa-era patronage
significance: The starting and finishing point of the eight-temple Ashtavinayaka pilgrimage and the principal centre of the Ganapatya sect, enclosed by a tall stone wall with minarets at its corners.
story: Ganesha is said to have incarnated as Mayuresvara, riding a peacock, to defeat the demon Sindhu.

name: Siddhivinayak Temple, Siddhatek
style: black stone, north-facing sanctum under a domed ceiling
significance: The third of the eight Ashtavinayaka shrines and the only one in the Ahilyanagar (Ahmednagar) district; its image is unusual in having a right-turned trunk.
story: Vishnu is said to have performed penance here invoking Ganesha, receiving the siddhis with which he overcame the demons Madhu and Kaitabha.

name: Ballaleshwar Temple, Pali
style: east-facing stone temple laid out in the shape of the letter 'shri'
significance: One of the eight Ashtavinayaka shrines and the only Ganesha temple known by the name of a devotee rather than of the god.
story: A boy named Ballal worshipped a stone as Ganesha despite his father's beatings; the god appeared, healed him and agreed to remain there under the boy's name.

name: Varadvinayak Temple, Mahad
significance: One of the eight Ashtavinayaka shrines, in Mahad village of Khalapur taluka; the present temple was raised in 1725 by the Peshwa general Ramji Mahadev Biwalkar around an image reported found in 1690.
story: The sage Gritsamada's prayers are said to have won Ganesha's promise to dwell here permanently as Varadavinayaka, the granter of boons.

name: Girijatmaj Temple, Lenyadri
builtDisplay: 1st–3rd c. Buddhist cave, later given to Ganesha worship
style: rock-cut Buddhist vihara adapted as a Hindu shrine
significance: The only Ashtavinayaka shrine set on a mountain and inside a Buddhist cave group, occupying cells of Cave 7 of the Lenyadri excavations.
story: Parvati is said to have meditated here for twelve years, after which Ganesha granted that he would be born as her son.

name: Vigneshwara (Vighnahar) Temple, Ozar
deity: Ganesha as Vigneshwara, remover of obstacles
style: walled courtyard temple with a gold-foiled shikhara and lamp towers
significance: One of the eight Ashtavinayaka shrines, believed to house a self-existent image; it was renovated by Chimaji Appa after his capture of Vasai Fort and again in 1967.
story: Ganesha subdued the demon Vignasura, sent by Indra to wreck a king's sacrifice, and at the demon's request took the title Vigneshwara.

name: Mahaganapati Temple, Ranjangaon
significance: An east-facing Ashtavinayaka shrine whose main structure dates from the Peshwa period and was later renovated by Madhavrao I and Sardar Kibe of Indore.
story: The presiding image, gifted by the local Khollam family of goldsmiths, is described as having ten trunks and twenty arms.

name: Mumba Devi Temple
deity: Goddess Mumba, a local form of the mother goddess
builtDisplay: rebuilt at Bhuleshwar after 1739–1770; shrine about six centuries old
significance: The temple of the goddess from whom Mumbai takes its name, first built by Koli fishermen at Bori Bunder and re-established at Bhuleshwar after the original was destroyed in the mid-18th century.
story: Parvati is said to have taken birth as the fisherwoman Mumba among the Koli people, and to have stayed on as their village deity at their request.

name: Mahalakshmi Temple, Mumbai
significance: One of Mumbai's most visited temples, built in 1831 by the merchant Dhakji Dadaji and housing the three goddesses of the Tridevi.

name: Walkeshwar Temple
significance: An old Shiva temple on Malabar Hill in South Mumbai, associated with the adjoining Banganga freshwater tank and used as a venue for Hindustani classical music festivals.
story: Rama is said to have paused here on his way to Lanka, fashioning a linga of sand and shooting an arrow into the ground to bring up the Ganga as the Banganga tank.

name: Kanheri Caves
deity: Buddhist monastic complex of viharas and chaityas
significance: A group of 109 caves cut into a basalt outcrop inside Sanjay Gandhi National Park, forming a long-lived Buddhist monastic and teaching centre on the Konkan coast with elaborate water-management works.

name: Karla Caves
builtDisplay: 2nd c. BCE–5th c. CE; Great Chaitya c. 50–70 CE
style: rock-cut chaitya hall with apsidal plan and wooden roof ribs
significance: A rock-cut Buddhist cave complex near Lonavala containing the Great Chaitya, the largest rock-cut chaitya hall in India, funded by rulers, merchants and Yavana donors.

name: Bhaja Caves
builtDisplay: 2nd c. BCE, with inscriptions to the 2nd c. CE
style: rock-cut Buddhist architecture imitating timber construction
significance: A group of 22 rock-cut caves near Lonavala whose barrel-vaulted chaitya and reliefs document the early development of Buddhist architecture; one carving is cited as evidence that drums of the tabla type were in use over two millennia ago.

name: Global Vipassana Pagoda
deity: Vipassana meditation dome dedicated to the teaching of Sayagyi U Ba Khin
style: Burmese, modelled on the Shwedagon Pagoda
significance: A donation-funded meditation hall at Gorai seating roughly 8,000 practitioners beneath what is described as the world's largest stone dome built without supporting pillars; it was inaugurated in 2009 as a monument to Vipassana practice.

name: Deekshabhoomi
style: modelled on the Great Stupa at Sanchi
significance: The Nagpur site where B. R. Ambedkar and some 400,000 followers embraced Buddhism on 14 October 1956, the largest mass religious conversion on record; its hollow stupa is central to Ambedkarite Buddhism and draws millions of pilgrims.

name: Ganpatipule Temple
significance: A shrine on the Konkan shore in Ratnagiri district whose west-facing image, said to have risen from the soil, makes it one of coastal Maharashtra's busiest pilgrimage and tourist destinations.
story: Local tradition holds that Ganpati moved here from nearby Gule after taking offence at a villager's remark, the name Pule meaning that he came forward.

name: Shiv Mandir, Ambarnath (Ambreshwar Temple)
significance: An 11th-century Shilahara temple on the Waldhuni river near Mumbai, likely raised by King Chhittaraja. It is a well-known example of Bhumija architecture, with a sanctum set below floor level and a shikhara left unfinished.

name: Kopeshwar Temple
significance: A 12th-century Shiva temple on the bank of the Krishna, built under the Shilahara king Gandaraditya and known for its open Swargamandapa and dense carving; it is noted as a Shiva temple that also enshrines an image of Vishnu.
story: Vishnu is said to have brought Shiva here to calm his rage after Sati's death at Daksha's sacrifice, which is why the god is called Kopeshwar, the wrathful one.

name: Shri Gajanan Maharaj Sansthan, Shegaon
deity: Samadhi shrine of Sant Gajanan Maharaj
significance: The samadhi temple of the saint Gajanan Maharaj, who died in 1910, administered by a trust formed in 1908. It has made Shegaon one of the largest pilgrimage centres of Vidarbha, drawing hundreds of thousands of visitors a year.
story: A dhuni fire lit by the saint is said to have burned continuously beside his samadhi ever since.

name: Shree Swami Samarth Math, Akkalkot
deity: Samadhi shrine of Swami Samarth of Akkalkot
significance: The shrine of Swami Samarth, a 19th-century master of the Dattatreya tradition who came to Akkalkot around 1856 and took samadhi in 1878; his large following across Maharashtra keeps the ashram a busy pilgrimage centre.
story: The Swami said that he had emerged from a banyan tree and had earlier borne the name Nrusimha Bhan, and devotees regard him as an incarnation of Dattatreya.

name: Mangueshi Temple
deity: Shiva as Manguesh, worshipped as a linga
builtDisplay: linga moved here 1560; present structure Maratha era, renovated 1890 and 1973
style: Goan Saraswat, with a seven-storey deepastambha
significance: One of the largest and most visited temples in Goa and the family deity shrine of many Gaud Saraswat Brahmins; the linga was carried here from Kushasthali in 1560 to escape Portuguese conversions.
story: Shiva is said to have fled Kailash after losing at dice and to have taken the form of a tiger to frighten Parvati, whose cry of Mam Girisha became the name Manguesh.

name: Shanta Durga Temple
style: Goan Saraswat, with pyramidal shikhara and a balustraded dome
significance: A Goud Saraswat Brahmin temple about 30 km from Panaji, patronised by Baji Rao I in 1738 and serving as the family deity shrine for many Saraswat households.
story: Shantadurga is said to have stepped between Shiva and Vishnu in a destructive quarrel, holding one on each hand until peace was restored.

name: Mahalasa Narayani Temple, Mardol
deity: Mahalasa Narayani, a form of Vishnu as Mohini
significance: The chief temple of Mahalasa, a major pilgrimage centre in Ponda taluka and the family goddess shrine of Gaud Saraswat and Daivajnya Brahmin and Vaishnava households across Goa and the Konkan.
story: Folk tradition makes Mhalsa the daughter of the merchant Timmaseth, married to Khandoba at his command in a dream, at which two Shiva lingas are said to have appeared.

name: Mahadev Temple, Tambdi Surla
significance: A 13th-century basalt temple deep in the forest of the Western Ghats, protected as a Monument of National Importance and the only well-preserved example of Kadamba temple architecture surviving in Goa.
story: Local tradition holds that a large king cobra lives permanently in the dim sanctum beside the linga.

name: Saptakoteshwar Temple
style: Kadamba plan with a shallow Mughal-style dome, European-style mandapa and a deepastamba
significance: One of the six great Shiva sites of the Konkan and the family deity shrine of the Kadamba kings; the present structure was commissioned by Shivaji in 1668 after the linga had been rescued and moved during Portuguese rule.
story: The Skanda Purana relates that seven sages made a linga of seven metals here, and that Shiva agreed to remain as Saptakoteshwar, lord of the seven.

name: Bhojeshwar Temple
significance: An unfinished 11th-century Shiva temple attributed to the Paramara king Bhoja, housing a 7.5-foot linga. Because work stopped, the site preserves architectural drawings, mason marks and quarry remains that document medieval temple construction in unusual detail.
story: Merutunga's Prabandha-Chintamani has King Bhoja describing to the poet Magha the Bhojasvamin temple he intended to raise in Malwa, though the two men lived centuries apart.

name: Sharda Devi Temple, Maihar
significance: A hilltop temple on Trikut hill counted among the Shakti Pithas and one of the busiest goddess shrines of Madhya Pradesh, especially during Navaratri.
story: Sati's necklace is said to have fallen here, giving Maihar its name, and the warriors Alha and Udal are remembered as the first to worship the goddess in the forest.

name: Pitambara Peeth
deity: Goddess Bagalamukhi, one of the ten Mahavidyas
significance: A temple complex and ashram at Datia founded in the 1920s by Shree Swami Ji, among the best known shrines of Bagalamukhi, with further temples to Dhumavati, Parashurama, Hanuman and Kal Bhairav and a Sanskrit library.
story: The Vankhandeswar linga within the complex is held by tradition to date from the time of the Mahabharata.

name: Bijasan Mata Temple, Salkanpur
deity: Bijasan Devi (Vindhyavasini, a form of Durga)
significance: A Siddhapeeth of Vindhyavasini Bijasan Devi standing about 800 feet above the plain near Rehti in Sehore district, and one of the most frequented goddess shrines in Madhya Pradesh.

name: Ram Raja Temple
deity: Rama, worshipped as a reigning king
significance: The only temple where Rama is worshipped as a king, and in a palace rather than a purpose-built shrine; it was established by Madhukar Shah of Orchha and his queen and receives hundreds of thousands of visitors a year.
story: Queen Ganesh Kunwari is said to have received the child Rama in her lap at the Sarayu in Ayodhya and to have brought him to Orchha on three conditions, after which the image refused to be moved from her palace.

name: Chaturbhuj Temple, Orchha
deity: Vishnu; intended for Rama and now serving Radha Krishna
style: Nagara with Maru-Gurjara elements, combining temple, fort and palace forms
significance: A towering Bundela temple at Orchha with one of the tallest vimanas of any Indian temple, begun by Madhukar Shah and completed by his son Vir Singh Deo during Akbar's reign.
story: It was raised for the Rama image the queen brought from Ayodhya, but the image would not be moved from her palace, which became the Ram Raja temple instead.

name: Chausath Yogini Temple, Mitaoli
deity: The 64 Yoginis, with Shiva in the central shrine
style: circular hypaethral yogini temple with 65 chambers
significance: An 11th-century circular yogini temple, also called the Ekattarso Mahadeva temple, built under King Devapala and protected by the ASI; its ring plan is often cited as an inspiration for the design of India's parliament building.
story: The yoginis were believed able to fly, which is given as the reason the central courtyard is left open to the sky.

name: Bateshwar Hindu Temples
style: post-Gupta and early Gurjara-Pratihara North Indian, including mandapika shrines
significance: A group of nearly 200 sandstone temples and ruins spread over about 25 acres north of Gwalior, forming an unusually dense record of experimentation in early medieval temple design in central India.

name: Kakanmath Temple
style: North Indian, with a shikhara about 30 m high
significance: A ruined 11th-century Shiva temple at Sihoniya commissioned by the Kachchhapaghata ruler Kirttiraja, now a Monument of National Importance under the ASI.
story: The name is popularly explained as honouring Kakanavati, said to have been the queen of one Surajpala.

name: Udayagiri Caves
deity: Vishnu and Shiva, with one cave dedicated to the Jain tirthankara Parshvanatha
builtDisplay: early 3rd–5th c.; principal caves consecrated 401 CE
significance: A hillside of rock-cut sanctuaries near Vidisha holding some of the oldest surviving Hindu temple architecture and iconography in India, including the great Varaha panel, and the only Gupta site with securely dated royal inscriptions.
story: The Varaha panel shows Vishnu in boar form lifting the earth goddess Bhudevi clear of the demon Hiranyaksha.

name: Chausath Yogini Temple, Bhedaghat (Golaki Math)
deity: Eighty-one yoginis around a central Shiva-Bhairava shrine
style: circular yogini temple about 125 ft across with 81 cells
significance: The largest of the circular yogini temples, set on a hilltop above the Narmada near Jabalpur and built under Yuvaraja II of the Kalachuris; unusually it holds 81 shrine cells rather than the customary 64.

name: Narmada Udgam Temple, Amarkantak
significance: The principal temple of the pilgrim town of Amarkantak, enclosing the kund accepted as the source of the Narmada. It was raised by the Kalachuris of Tripuri and later renovated by the Holkar queen Ahilyabai.
story: Adi Shankaracharya is said to have declared this stream the true source of the Narmada while searching for its origin.

name: Ahilyeshwar Temple and Maheshwar Ghats
significance: Maheshwar was the Narmada-bank capital of the Holkar queen Ahilyabai, who endowed the town with temples, a fort-palace and the broad stone ghats that still define its riverfront.

name: Kundalpur Jain Temples
style: Square shrines with domed roofs and pinnacles
significance: A Digambar Jain pilgrimage complex of roughly fifty temples on and around a hill northeast of Damoh, centred on the colossal Rishabhanatha image known as Bade Baba. The shrine was renovated around 1700 with help from the Bundela ruler Chhatrasal.
story: Jain tradition holds that Shridhar Kevali, the last of the omniscient ones, attained liberation here.

name: Bawangaja
style: Monolithic Kayotsarga colossus in brown stone
significance: A Digambar Jain pilgrimage centre in the Satpura range of south-western Madhya Pradesh whose 84-foot rock-cut standing image of Rishabhadeva is among the largest monolithic Jain statues in the world, set among a group of eleven temples.
story: Indrajit, Kumbhakarna and other ascetics are said to have attained emancipation here through self-meditation, and their ancient footprint images are preserved at the Chulgiri shrine.

name: Maladevi Temple, Gyaraspur
significance: The largest and finest surviving temple at Gyaraspur, cut partly into the hillside and dedicated to Adinatha, with a dense sculptural programme of tirthankaras, yakshas and yakshis and a foundation inscription of the reign of Valleka.

name: Pashupatinath Temple, Mandsaur
style: Western school of early Indian art
significance: A Shiva temple at Mandsaur, ancient Dashapura, housing a rare 4.5 m eight-faced linga of about the early 6th century that names eight aspects of Shiva. Inscriptions of 404–487 CE record Gupta kings and local donors including silk weavers from Gujarat.

name: Bhoramdeo Temple
significance: A group of four Shiva temples in Kabirdham district whose 11th-century stone temple is covered in figural and erotic sculpture, earning it the name 'the Khajuraho of Chhattisgarh'. Its brick shrine is far older, and the complex was added to between the 7th and 12th centuries.
story: Local lore says the Gond people of the area worshipped Shiva as Bhoramdeo, and that a Naga chief raised the temple.

name: Rajiv Lochan Temple
significance: A temple of four-armed Vishnu at the confluence town of Rajim, ascribed by inscription to Vilasatunga of the Nala dynasty and dated on palaeographic grounds to the 8th century. It is celebrated for its carved doorways and pillars and for the annual Rajim mela.
story: One legend says king Ratnakar built the temple after Vishnu appeared before him as the lotus-eyed Rajiva-Lochana; another that the mythical king Jagat Pal raised it in a single day.

name: Lakshmana Temple, Sirpur
style: Brick temple on a stone jagati with carved stone sanctum doorway
significance: The earliest dated monument at Sirpur, a brick Vishnu temple of about 600 CE whose stone doorway carries Anantasayana Vishnu, the ten avatars and scenes of daily life, and which set a pattern for later building in the Mahanadi valley.

name: Mahamaya Temple, Ratanpur
significance: A goddess temple at the old Kalachuri capital of Ratanpur, counted among the fifty-two Shakti Peethas and revered as Kosaleswari, presiding deity of ancient Dakshina Kosala and family deity of the Ratanpur rulers.
story: Tradition says the temple stands where king Ratnadeva was granted a vision of the goddess.

disputedCircuits.note: The Mahamaya Temple article describes Ratanpur as one of the 52 Shakta pithas, an enumeration outside the commonly cited 51, with no citation attached and no body part named (as of 2026).

name: Rajarani Temple
significance: An 11th-century Kalinga temple in Bhubaneswar with an 18 m clustered spire and some of the finest figure sculpture in Odisha; its empty sanctum means it is kept as a monument rather than a working shrine, and its design influenced later central Indian temples.
story: Local belief derives the name from the Naga and Nagini figures at the entrance, read as a king and queen.

name: Brahmeswara Temple
significance: A Shiva temple with four subsidiary shrines, richly carved inside and out, recorded by inscription as the foundation of the Somavamshi queen Kolavati Devi in the eighteenth regnal year of Udyotakesari.

name: Ananta Vasudeva Temple
significance: The principal Vaishnava temple of old Bhubaneswar, founded in the 13th century by the Eastern Ganga princess Chandrika Devi and unusual in worshipping Krishna, Balarama and Subhadra as complete stone images.

name: Dhauli Shanti Stupa
significance: A white peace pagoda on Dhauli hill above the Daya river, built by the Japan Buddha Sangha and the Kalinga Nippon Buddha Sangha beside Ashoka's rock edicts, at a site long central to Odisha's Buddhist heritage.
story: The hill is widely believed to be where the Kalinga War was fought, the carnage that turned Ashoka to Buddhism.

name: Ratnagiri Mahavihara
builtDisplay: 5th–13th c.; main phase under the Bhauma-Karas
style: Post-Gupta brick with chlorite and khondalite carving
significance: A ruined mahavihara on a hill between the Brahmani and Birupa rivers, the major Buddhist monastery of Odisha and a centre of Tantric and Vajrayana practice, with three main monuments, over seven hundred votive stupas and colossal Buddha heads recovered by excavation.
story: Villagers long took the mounds for the palace of a mythical king and called the site the queen's mound.

name: Udayagiri Buddhist Complex
style: Brick and stone stupas, viharas and chaitya-grihas
significance: The largest Buddhist complex in Odisha, known from inscriptions as Madhavapura Mahavihara, forming with Lalitgiri and Ratnagiri the 'Diamond Triangle' of Odishan Buddhism.

name: Lalitgiri
style: Apsidal brick chaitya-griha; Gandhara and Mathura influence
significance: The oldest Buddhist site in Odisha and part of the Diamond Triangle, with an apsidal chaitya-griha, four monasteries and a stupa that yielded relic caskets, showing occupation from the 3rd century BCE through the Tantric period.
story: The site was once identified with the Pushpagiri Vihara described by Xuanzang, though excavation later placed Pushpagiri at Langudi hill.

name: Biraja Temple
significance: The principal temple of Jajpur and a Shakti Peetha, housing a two-armed Durga slaying Mahishasura; it gives the town its names Viraja Kshetra and Viraja Pitha.
story: The Tantra Chudamani says Sati's navel fell here in the Utkala country.

name: Tara Tarini Temple
significance: A hilltop shrine of the twin goddesses Tara and Tarini on the Kumari hills above the Rushikulya river, counted among the four principal Adi Shakti Pithas of India.
story: It is said to mark the place where Sati's breasts fell.

disputedCircuits.note: Tara Tarini is named as one of the four Adi Shakta pithas (breast) in Wikipedia's Shakta pithas article, where it appears at entry 54 of the combined table rather than within the first 51 (as of 2026).

name: Samaleswari Temple
style: Sandhara order, with a pillared circumambulatory gallery
significance: The presiding goddess temple of Sambalpur on the bank of the Mahanadi, whose square sanctum is ringed by a covered pillared passage; it is the leading pilgrimage centre of western Odisha and the neighbouring parts of Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand.

name: Sakshi Gopal Temple
significance: A medieval Krishna temple between Puri and Bhubaneswar, counted among the sixteen Krishna shrines traditionally ascribed to king Vajranabha; it is known for the Anla Navami festival and for offering wheat-based rather than rice prasada.
story: Krishna is said to have walked from Vrindavan to stand witness to a promise made to a poor young man, turning to stone when the youth looked back to check that the god was following.

name: Nrusinghanath Temple
significance: A 45-foot Kalinga-style temple at the foot of the Gandhamardan hills in western Odisha, built by Baijal Singh Dev of Patna State, where Vishnu is worshipped in the rare feline form of Marjara Kesari.
story: The deity is said to have taken cat form to chase the demon-mouse Musika Daitya into a tunnel beneath the hill, and to guard it still.

name: Mundeshwari Temple
builtDisplay: 6th–7th c.; ASI dates it to 108 CE
significance: A hilltop temple on the Kaimur plateau claimed by the Archaeological Survey of India as one of the oldest continuously worshipped Hindu temples in the country, and the earliest surviving Nagara-style shrine in Bihar, unusual for its octagonal plan.
story: Xuanzang is said to have described a hilltop shrine flashing with light in this area during his travels of 636–638 CE.

name: Jal Mandir, Pawapuri
style: Marble water temple in a lotus tank
significance: A white marble Jain temple standing in the middle of a lotus tank at Pawapuri, built on the spot traditionally identified as the cremation place of Mahavira, who attained nirvana here.
story: The fish of the tank are said to wear gold nose rings, and catching or harming them is forbidden.

name: Vishwa Shanti Stupa, Rajgir
significance: A 120-foot white peace pagoda on Ratnagiri hill at Rajgir, founded by Nichidatsu Fujii and completed in 1969, carrying four gilded Buddha statues for four events of the Buddha's life; it is one of some eighty peace pagodas built worldwide by Nipponzan Myohoji.

name: Relic Stupa and Ashokan Pillar, Vaishali
style: Brick stupa; polished sandstone pillar with lion capital
significance: At Vaishali the Licchavis enshrined one of the eight shares of the Buddha's relics in a brick stupa, among the earliest archaeologically known; nearby at Kolhua stands one of the best-preserved Ashokan pillars, 11 m tall and topped by a single lion.
story: Tradition says the Buddha gave the Licchavis his alms bowl here and conjured the illusion of a river in spate to turn them back.

name: Kesaria Stupa
builtDisplay: present structure Pala, 8th–12th c.; origin c. 250 BCE
significance: One of the tallest and largest Buddhist stupas in India, a terraced mandala-form mound about 32 m high whose visible fabric is of the Pala period over a core attributed to Ashoka; its plan invites comparison with Borobudur.
story: Local tradition connects the stupa with the alms bowl the Buddha gave the Licchavis of Vaishali.

name: Shikharji
builtDisplay: present temples 1768 (Jagat Seth); shrines from the 14th c.
style: Hilltop tonks with marble footprint shrines
significance: The most important Jain tirtha, a 1,365 m hill in Giridih district where twenty of the twenty-four tirthankaras are believed to have attained moksha; its summit shrines are held equally sacred by Digambara and Svetambara Jains.
story: Parshvanatha is said to have attained liberation at the Suvarnabhadra kuta, whose footprint shrine is marked by a chatra.

name: Chhinnamasta Temple, Rajrappa
significance: A tantric shrine of the headless goddess Chhinnamasta at Rajrappa in Ramgarh district, drawing two to three thousand pilgrims a day and known for its distinctive tantric design and animal sacrifice.
story: The goddess is shown standing on the bodies of Kamadeva and Rati on a bed of lotus.

disputedCircuits.note: The Rajrappa article describes the Chhinnamasta temple's tantric character but makes no Shakta pitha or Siddha Pitha claim, and the site does not appear in Wikipedia's combined Shakta pithas table, while the goddess Chhinnamasta is also the presiding deity at Chintpurni in Himachal Pradesh (as of 2026).

name: Maluti Temples
deity: Moulakshi (Mauliksha), with Shiva, Durga, Kali and Vishnu shrines
significance: A village holding 72 surviving terracotta temples of an original 108, built by the Baj Basanta rajas between the 17th and 19th centuries; the Global Heritage Fund has listed them among the world's most endangered cultural heritage sites.
story: The family goddess Mauliksha is said to be the elder sister of the goddess Tara of Tarapith.

name: Tarapith Temple
significance: A tantric temple of the goddess Tara in Birbhum district with an adjoining cremation ground, revered as a mahapitha and among the busiest pilgrimage sites in West Bengal.
story: The temple is inseparable from the tantric saint Bamakhepa, who worshipped here and lived in the cremation ground beside the Dwarka river.

disputedCircuits.note: Tarapith appears at entry 60 of Wikipedia's combined Shakta pithas table (third eye), outside the first 51, and the Tarapith article itself makes no Shakta pitha claim at all (as of 2026).

name: Taraknath Temple, Tarakeswar
significance: An 18th-century atchala Shiva temple in Hooghly district housing a swayambhu linga, one of the busiest Shaiva pilgrimage sites in West Bengal, especially at Shivaratri and the Gajan festival.
story: Local legend says Raja Bharamalla Rao built the temple after a linga was discovered in the nearby jungle.

name: Temple of the Vedic Planetarium, Mayapur
deity: Radha Madhava, with the Pancha Tattva and Narasimha
style: Modern temple with a large dome and Vedic cosmological interior
significance: ISKCON's flagship temple at Mayapur, under construction since 2009 and chaired by Alfred Ford, built around a planetarium presenting Vedic cosmology and intended to serve as the movement's global headquarters.
story: Bhaktivinoda Thakur identified this spot in 1894 as the true birthplace of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

name: Hangseshwari Temple
style: Ratna temple with thirteen lotus-bud spires
significance: A five-storeyed ratna temple at Bansberia whose thirteen spires and internal plan were conceived around tantric ideas of the channels of the subtle body. Begun by Raja Nrisinhadeb Roy in 1799, it was completed by his widow Rani Sankari in 1814.
story: The deity is named for Rani Hanseswari, the raja's mother, venerated as a manifestation of Kali.

name: 108 Shiva Temples, Kalna
significance: Also called Nabakailash, a complex of 108 Shiva temples at Ambika Kalna set in two concentric circles of 74 and 34 shrines, built in 1809 by the Maharajas of Bardhaman and planned so that every linga is visible from the centre.

name: Jalpesh Temple
deity: Shiva as Jalpesh, Bhairava of the Bhramari Shakti Pitha
dynasty: Koch of Cooch Behar; Raikats of Baikunthapur
significance: A Shiva temple on the Jarda river near Maynaguri housing the linga called Anadi, founded by Bishwa Singha and rebuilt by Raja Pran Narayan in 1653. Its Shivratri fair is among the oldest in northern West Bengal and draws pilgrims from neighbouring countries.

name: Yiga Choeling (Ghum) Monastery
significance: The best known of the Ghum monasteries near Darjeeling, a Gelug foundation of 1875 housing a 4.6 m Maitreya Buddha and 108 volumes of the Kangyur, and a refuge for Tibetan monks since 1959.

name: Chausathi Yogini Temple, Hirapur
deity: The sixty-four yoginis, with Kali at the centre
significance: A roofless circular shrine some 25 feet across, built in 864 CE by the Bhauma-Kara queen Hiradevi, its inner wall set with niches for sixty-four yoginis around a central Kali. It is the earliest of India's yogini temples and the model for those that followed.
story: Priests relate that Durga took sixty-four forms to defeat a demon, and that the victorious yoginis asked to be remembered in a temple of this shape.

name: Sonagiri Jain Temples
style: White hilltop temples with tall spires and a 43-foot manastambha
significance: A Digambar Jain tirtha of 103 temples across a 132-acre hill site near Datia, centred on an 11-foot image of Chandraprabhu known as Bade Baba; the temples date from the 9th century onwards over a much older rock-cut image.
story: Jain tradition holds that since the time of Chandraprabhu five and a half crore ascetics have attained moksha here, among them king Nanganang and half a million followers.

name: Griddhakuta (Vulture Peak)
builtDisplay: associated with the Buddha's lifetime; structures undated
significance: A hill above Rajgir, ancient Rajagaha, that was the Buddha's favourite retreat and the setting given for major discourses including the Heart Sutra, the Lotus Sutra and much of the Prajnaparamita literature. Its name comes from a profile said to resemble a sitting vulture with folded wings.
story: In the Lotus Sutra the Buddha declares that through countless eons he has always lived on Holy Eagle Peak.

name: Umananda Temple
significance: A brick Shiva shrine raised in 1694 on the Brahmaputra river island at Guwahati by order of the Ahom king Gadadhar Singha, standing on a site that also preserves traces of an earlier post-Gupta stone temple. Badly damaged in the 1897 Assam earthquake, it was rebuilt afterwards by a local merchant.
story: Shiva is said to have burnt Kamadeva to ashes here for disturbing his meditation, which is why the hillock is called Bhasmachala.

name: Navagraha Mandir
significance: An astronomy-linked shrine on Chitrachal Hill whose sanctum holds nine lingams for the nine celestial bodies, each draped in a colour assigned to its planet. Wrecked by the earthquake of 1697, it was rebuilt in full by the Ahom ruler Rajeswara Singha in 1752.

name: Basistha Temple
significance: An octagonal brick temple with a polygonal sikhara raised in 1764 under the Ahom king Rajeswar Singha on the remains of a stone temple of about the 11th century. It sits where three hill streams meet to form the Basistha and Bharalu rivers of Guwahati.
story: The site is held to be the ashrama of the sage Vasistha, and its sunken chamber is said to keep his footprint.

name: Hayagriva Madhava Temple
significance: A stone temple of 1583 on Manikut hill at Hajo, built by Raghudeva Narayan of the Koch dynasty, whose lowest wall course carries an unbroken frieze of elephants. Its outer walls are carved with the ten avatars of Vishnu and with scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.

name: Sivadol
significance: A group of three temples to Shiva, Vishnu and Durga built in 1734 by Bar Raja Ambika, queen of the Ahom king Siva Singha, on the bank of the Sivasagar tank dug between 1731 and 1738. The main Sivadol rises about 104 feet under a gilded dome and is among the tallest temples in Assam.

name: Mahabhairav Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on a hillock in northern Tezpur, endowed during Ahom rule when Tungkhungia kings granted it land and appointed its priests and attendants. The old stone shrine has since been rebuilt in concrete, and the temple is now run by a committee under the Government of Assam.
story: The lingam is believed to be of living stone that slowly grows, and King Bana is said to have gained his prosperity by worshipping Shiva here.

name: Madan Kamdev
significance: A ruined temple complex of the Kamarupa Pala period, first noticed by Edward Dalton around 1855 and excavated from 1977, which uncovered a main temple and the remains of about a dozen more. Its sculpture, dated by the excavators to the 10th-12th centuries, includes Bhairava, Vishnu, Saraswati and celebrated Uma-Maheshwara couples.
story: Puranic tradition holds that Kamadeva, burnt to cinders by an angry Shiva, was reborn at this spot.

name: Sri Surya Pahar
significance: A hillside archaeological site near Goalpara where Hindu, Buddhist and Jain remains lie together, including hundreds of rock-cut Shiva lingas, about 25 rock-cut stupas of the early centuries CE and temple foundations excavated between 1992 and 2001. Some scholars have proposed it, rather than Guwahati, as the ancient capital Pragjyotishpura.
story: Local tradition says the sage Vyasa carved 99,999 lingas here in an attempt to raise a second Kashi.

name: Unakoti
significance: A Shaiva rock-cut site in northern Tripura carved with colossal reliefs, chief among them a Shiva head some thirty feet high with an elaborate headdress, along with a giant Ganesha and several Nandi figures. An inscription of the 11th-12th century records a pilgrim named Sri Jayadeva; the site is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India and was added to UNESCO's tentative list in December 2022.
story: Shiva is said to have travelled towards Kashi with one crore companions who overslept, and on waking alone he cursed them into stone, leaving one short of a crore.

name: Chaturdasha Temple
significance: Built in 1760 by King Krishna Manikya when the Tripura capital moved to Agartala, this temple enshrines the royal house's fourteen deities and is the focus of the Kharchi puja. Its dome copies the roof form of Tripuri village huts and is topped by a stupa-like finial suggesting Buddhist influence.

name: Rumtek Monastery
deity: Karma Kagyu lineage; seat of the Gyalwang Karmapa
significance: The Dharmachakra Centre, seat in exile of the Karmapa and principal monastery of the Karma Kagyu school, first built in the mid-18th century under the 12th Karmapa. The 16th Karmapa found it ruined after leaving Tibet in 1959 and had it rebuilt over four years, inaugurating it at Losar in 1966; it holds his relics in a golden stupa and houses the Karma Shri Nalanda Institute.

name: Pemayangtse Monastery
significance: One of Sikkim's oldest and most senior Nyingma monasteries, begun as a small lhakhang by Lama Lhatsun Chempo in 1647 and enlarged under the third Chogyal Chakdor Namgyal in 1705. Reserved for monks of pure lineage, its head lama held the privilege of anointing the Chogyals of Sikkim; the three-storey building has been repaired after the earthquakes of 1913 and 1960.

name: Tashiding Monastery
significance: A Nyingma monastery founded in West Sikkim in 1641 by Ngadak Sempa Chenpo Phunshok Rigzing and expanded in 1717 under the third Chogyal. Regarded as the spiritual centre of Sikkim, it keeps 41 chortens and stones carved with mantras.
story: A vase of holy water consecrated by Guru Padmasambhava is said to be kept here, and at the yearly Bhumchu festival the change in its water level is read as an omen for Sikkim's coming year.

name: Enchey Monastery
deity: Buddha and Padmasambhava; protectors Khangchendzonga and Yabdean
significance: A Nyingma monastery above Gangtok, first raised in the 1840s under the eighth Chogyal and rebuilt in its present form in 1909 during the regency of Sikyong Tulku. Gutted by fire in 1947 and restored the following year, it houses about ninety monks and remains under the authority of Pemayangtse.
story: The site is said to have been chosen by the tantric adept Lama Druptab Karpo, who flew here from Maenam Hill and set up a small gompa.

name: Parshuram Kund
deity: Parashurama, with a shrine to Devi Renuka
significance: A bathing pool on the Lohit river that is one of the best-known Hindu pilgrimage sites in Arunachal Pradesh, drawing large crowds at Makar Sankranti. The original kund was buried by the 1950 Assam earthquake, after which boulders settled into a ring in the riverbed and sadhus re-established the site in the 1970s.
story: Parashurama, his axe stuck fast to his hand after killing his mother Renuka, is said to have dipped his hands here, whereupon the axe fell away and his sin was washed off.

name: Malinithan
significance: A ruined temple site on the north bank of the Brahmaputra in Lower Siang district, where excavation exposed a carved stone plinth about eight feet high with sculptures of deities, animals and floral work. Masons' marks here match those at other Chutia-period sites such as the Tamreswari temple, and its absence from 10th-11th century texts places its construction later.
story: Sankardev's retelling has Krishna and Rukmini break their journey to Dwarka here, where Durga garlanded them with flowers, giving the place its name.

name: Shree Govindajee Temple
significance: The royal temple of Manipur adjoining the Imphal palace, commissioned by Maharaja Nara Singh in 1846 and rebuilt by Maharaja Chandrakriti after the earthquake of 1868, being reconsecrated in 1876. Its images were removed to Kongma during the Anglo-Manipur war of 1891 and reinstalled in 1908 beside the new palace.
story: Maharaja Jai Singh is said to have been told in a vision to carve Krishna's image from a jackfruit tree, work he began in 1776 and consecrated in 1779.

name: Sringeri Sharada Peetham
builtDisplay: 14th c. (Vijayanagara); tradition ascribes it to Adi Shankara
significance: One of the four cardinal mathas of the Advaita Vedanta tradition, on the bank of the Tunga, traditionally founded by Adi Shankara though its documented record begins in the 14th century. Vijayanagara rulers became its patrons after 1336 and financed the Vidyashankara temple completed in 1338, and its 12th acharya Vidyaranya advised the empire's founders; it has directed Smarta religious life across south India for six centuries.
story: Adi Shankara is said to have chosen the spot after seeing a cobra spread its hood to shade a pregnant frog from the sun.

name: Annapoorneshwari Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Horanadu in the Western Ghats of Chikkamagaluru district, on the bank of the Bhadra, known as Sri Kshetra Horanadu and celebrated for feeding every pilgrim who comes. It is a leading Devi shrine of Karnataka, though its founding date is not documented.
story: Its establishment is traditionally credited to the sage Agastya.

name: Kollur Mookambika Temple
style: Dravidian with Vijayanagara and Hoysala elements
significance: A major Shakta temple at the foot of the Kodachadri hills on the Souparnika river in Udupi district, dated to about 800 CE and associated with the patron Halugallu Veera Sangayya. Its sanctum holds a self-manifested linga together with a four-armed panchaloha image of the goddess, whose installation is ascribed to Adi Shankara.
story: The goddess is said to have struck the demon Mookasura dumb so that he could not ask Shiva for a boon, and then killed him when he harassed the sage Kola Maharshi.

name: Dharmasthala Temple
deity: Manjunatha (Shiva), with Ammanavaru and Jain guardian deities
significance: A temple of about 800 years' standing founded by the Jain chieftain Birmanna Pergade and his wife Ammu Ballalthi, and reconsecrated in the 16th century by the Madhva saint Vadiraja Tirtha. It is unusual in being administered for some twenty generations by a Jain Bunt family, the Heggades, while Madhva Brahmin priests conduct its worship.
story: Guardian spirits are said to have come to Birmanna Pergade seeking a home where dharma was kept, and told him to raise shrines for four protective deities.

name: Kukke Subramanya Temple
deity: Kartikeya as Subramanya, lord of serpents
significance: A serpent-worship centre on the Kumaradhara river in Dakshina Kannada, resorted to by devotees seeking relief from doshas connected with snakes. Sthanika Brahmins were its founding priests until the early 20th century, when the office passed to Shivalli Madhva Brahmins; worship now follows Madhvacharya's Tantrasara Sangraha.
story: The serpent king Vasuki is said to have hidden here from Garuda and to be worshipped alongside Kumaraswamy, who slew the demons Taraka and Shurapadmasura on the nearby Kumara Parvatha.

name: Kateel Durgaparameshwari Temple
significance: A Shakta temple standing on an islet in the middle of the Nandini river about 20 km from Mangalore, and one of the busiest temple towns of Tulu Nadu. Its founding date is not documented.

name: Mangaladevi Temple
significance: The temple at Bolar from which the city of Mangalore takes its name, built in the 9th century under the Alupa king Kundavarman with the encouragement of the Nath teacher Matsyendranath. It has a two-storeyed gateway tower in the Kerala manner and keeps a standing link with the Kadri Yogirajmutt, whose ascetics attend its festivals.
story: A Malabar princess named Parimala is said to have renounced her kingdom for Matsyendranath, who initiated her into the Nath order and renamed her Mangaladevi.

name: Chamundeshwari Temple
significance: The hilltop shrine of the tutelary goddess of the Mysore royal house, its original structure Hoysala work of the 12th century and its tower added under the Vijayanagara rulers. A stairway of a thousand steps was cut in 1659, and in 1664 Dodda Devaraja Wodeyar set a monolithic granite Nandi on the 700th step; the temple is counted among the eighteen Shakta pithas as Krauncha Pitha.
story: Durga is said to have killed the buffalo-demon Mahishasura on this hill, from which the town took the name Mahishuru, now Mysuru.

disputedCircuits.note: The Chamundeshwari Temple article calls it one of the 18 Shakta pithas, known as Krouncha Pitha and associated with Sati's hair, citing a Times of India travel page, and it does not appear in Wikipedia's combined Shakta pithas table (as of 2026).

name: Srikanteshwara Temple, Nanjangud
significance: A large Shiva temple on the Kapila river whose origins go back to the Gangas, with the sanctum built in the Chola period around the 11th century and the front mandapa added under the Hoysalas. The seven-storey gopura, 120 feet high, was raised in 1845 by Devarajammanni, queen of Krishnaraja Wadiyar III; the 50,000 square foot complex holds 122 images of Shiva, 65 lingas and a stone Nandi installed in 1644.
story: Tipu Sultan's elephant is said to have recovered its sight after being bathed in the temple's sacred water for forty-eight days.

name: Biligiri Ranganatha Swamy Temple
significance: A hilltop shrine to Vishnu that gives the Biligiri Rangana Hills their name, set within a wildlife sanctuary declared in 1974 and made a tiger reserve in 2011. Its April festival draws pilgrims from across the region, and every second year the Soliga community presents the deity a hide slipper about one foot nine inches long.

name: Ghati Subramanya
significance: A temple about 60 km from Bengaluru, unusual in housing Subramanya and Narasimha together in one sanctum, and developed by the Ghorpade rulers of Sandur. It is one of the principal south Indian centres for the propitiation of Ketu.
story: Both images are believed to have risen out of the earth of their own accord, and childless couples who make vows here are held to be granted children.

name: Banashankari Amma Temple
significance: A goddess temple in Bagalkot district first raised under the Badami Chalukyas, with epigraphic evidence pointing to about 603 CE in the reign of Jagadekamalla I, whose house took the goddess as its tutelary deity. After the old Dravidian structure decayed, the Maratha chieftain Parusharam Agale rebuilt it in Vijayanagara style in 1750.
story: The Skanda and Padma Puranas tell of the goddess Shakambhari rising from the sacrificial fire to kill the demon Durgamasura, and of her feeding the country with vegetables during a famine, which gave her that name.

name: Mahakuta group of temples
significance: A Shaiva monastic complex of early Chalukya shrines gathered round the spring-fed Vishnu Pushkarni tank near Badami. The Mahakuta pillar inscription of 595-602 CE records a queen's grant of ten villages, Pattadakal and Aihole among them, and a later inscription of Vinapoti, a consort of King Vijayaditya, records gifts of rubies and silver; the shrines mix dravida tiered towers with nagara curvilinear ones in an early experiment towards vesara.

name: Lad Khan Temple
significance: One of the oldest surviving Hindu temples in India, at Aihole in Bagalkot district, now dated to about the 5th century rather than the 7th-8th as once thought. Its shrine, pillared mandapa of twelve carved columns, lattice windows and circumambulatory path translate timber building forms into stone; it was rededicated from Vishnu to Shiva, and takes its popular name from a man called Lad Khan who once lodged in it.

name: Bhoga Nandeeshwara Temple
significance: A twin-shrine complex at the foot of Nandi Hills, the northern Bhoganandishwara being the older and the Arunachaleswara added soon after, and described as the oldest surviving temple in the Nolambavadi manner of Dravidian architecture. Ganga, Hoysala and Vijayanagara rulers each added to it, and it is now a nationally protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Kotilingeshwara
significance: A modern temple founded in 1980 by Swami Sambha Shiva Murthy at Kammasandra in Kolar district, whose 15 acres hold a main Shivalinga 108 feet high, an 11-metre Nandi and roughly 650,000 smaller lingas donated by devotees and inscribed with their names. Eleven subsidiary shrines and pilgrim facilities stand on the site, which fills with visitors at Maha Shivaratri.
story: The first lingas are said to have been set up by a former atheist who became a devotee of Shiva, a story retold in the 2001 film Sri Manjunatha.

name: ISKCON Temple Bangalore
significance: One of the largest Krishna temples in the world, opened in May 1997 by President Shankar Dayal Sharma, with a gold-plated dhwaja-stambha 17 m high and a gilded kalasha shikhara of 8.5 m. Besides daily worship and free prasadam it runs the Akshaya Patra Foundation, which provides school meals across India.

name: Bull Temple (Dodda Basavana Gudi)
significance: Commissioned in 1537 by Kempe Gowda, the founder of Bengaluru, under Vijayanagara rule, this shrine holds one of the largest Nandi images anywhere, a granite monolith about 15 feet high and 20 feet long, blackened by generations of charcoal and oil. Its tower was added in the early 20th century, and the temple hosts the Kadalekaayi Parishe groundnut fair each Karthika month.

name: Gavi Gangadhareshwara Temple
significance: A monolithic cave temple in Bengaluru substantially renovated in the 16th century by Kempe Gowda I after his release from five years' imprisonment by Rama Raya. Its forecourt carries four monolithic pillars representing the damaru, trishula and two great discs, and each Makar Sankranti the setting sun passes between the horns of the Nandi outside to light the linga within the cave.
story: A tunnel inside the temple is said to lead all the way to Kashi.

name: Lakshmi Narasimha Temple, Nuggehalli
deity: Lakshmi Narasimha, with Keshava and Venugopala
significance: A trikuta Vaishnava temple in soapstone built in 1246 by the commander Bommanna Dandanayaka during the reign of the Hoysala king Vira Someshwara, in a town then called Vijaya Somanathapura and endowed as an agrahara. Its walls carry about 120 sculpted panels of deities and epic scenes, work attributed to the Hoysala sculptors Baichoja and Mallitamma.

name: Ishvara Temple, Arasikere
significance: A Hoysala-period Shiva temple raised around 1220 under Narasimha II, notable for an unusually complex plan in which a sixteen-pointed star-shaped hall is joined to a five-storeyed vimana. Its outer walls carry roughly 120 relief panels drawing on Shaiva, Vaishnava, Shakta and Vedic subject matter.

name: Amrutesvara Temple, Amruthapura
significance: Built in 1196 during the reign of the Hoysala king Veera Ballala II by his commander Amrutheshwara Dandanayaka, this medium-sized ekakuta shrine is valued for its wide open hall and finely worked Hoysala sculpture.
story: The tower over the vestibule carries the Hoysala emblem of Sala fighting a lion, the mythical founding episode from which the dynasty took its name.

name: Veera Narayana Temple, Belavadi
deity: Vishnu as Veeranarayana, with Yoga-Narasimha and Venugopala
significance: A three-shrined Hoysala temple completed around 1200 under Veera Ballala II, with the central sanctum holding Veeranarayana and flanking shrines for Yoga-Narasimha and Venugopala. Its stellate plan and Vesara superstructures make it one of the larger surviving Hoysala trikuta layouts.
story: Local tradition traces the village to the Mahabharata, holding that the Pandava prince Bhima killed the demon Bakasura here and delivered the settlement.

name: Doddabasappa Temple
significance: A twelfth-century Shiva temple of the Western Chalukya period, distinguished by an unusually elaborate twenty-four-pointed star-shaped plan carried without interruption through a seven-tiered dravida superstructure.

name: Trikuteshwara Temple, Gadag
deity: Shiva (three lingas on a single stone)
significance: A Shiva temple of the Kalyani Chalukya era, named for the three lingas set on one stone in its sanctum, and known for its lathe-turned ornate pillars and pierced stone screens. The complex also contains a much-visited shrine to Saraswati.

name: Mahadeva Temple, Itagi
significance: Raised around 1112 by Mahadeva, a commander under the Western Chalukya emperor Vikramaditya VI, this temple pairs dravida wall articulation with a nagara superstructure and is ringed by thirteen subsidiary linga shrines. A contemporary inscription calls it Devalaya Chakravarti, emperor among temples.

name: Kalleshvara Temple, Bagali
deity: Shiva, with shrines to Surya and Narasimha
builtDisplay: 10th c. (Rashtrakuta, completed c. 987 under Tailapa II)
significance: A rare temple whose fabric spans two Kannada dynasties: a late Rashtrakuta vimana and closed hall of the mid-tenth century, fronted by an open hall added around 987 under the founding Western Chalukya king Tailapa II. Its shrines to Surya and Narasimha sit alongside the main Shiva sanctum.

name: Yellamma Temple, Saundatti
significance: A hilltop shrine to the goddess Yellamma, identified with Renuka and revered as a deity of fertility, drawing very large pilgrim gatherings from Karnataka and neighbouring states. The present structure was built in 1514 by Bomappa Nayaka of Raybag on a site that had held a temple since the Rashtrakuta and later Chalukya centuries.
story: The katha tells how Renuka, wife of the sage Jamadagni, broke her vow of chastity and was beheaded by her son Parashurama at his father's command, only to be restored to life by the sage; some versions say she was revived with another woman's head, which is why she is also called Yellamma.

name: Saavira Kambada Basadi (Thousand Pillar Temple), Moodabidri
significance: The principal Jain basadi of Moodabidri, begun in 1430 by the local chieftain Devaraya Wodeyar and named for the many carved pillars of its sequence of halls. Its sanctum holds an eight-foot panchadhatu image of the Tirthankara Chandraprabha.

name: Namdroling Monastery
significance: The largest teaching centre of the Nyingma school of Tibetan Buddhism outside Tibet, founded in 1963 at the Bylakuppe Tibetan settlement by Penor Rinpoche, eleventh throneholder of the Palyul lineage. It remains the seat of that lineage, now led by its twelfth throneholder, Karma Kuchen.

name: Attukal Bhagavathy Temple
deity: Bhagavathy, identified with Bhadrakali and with Kannagi
significance: A goddess temple close to the centre of Thiruvananthapuram whose deity is understood both as Bhadrakali and as Kannagi, the heroine of the Tamil epic Cilappatikaram. It is best known for the Attukal Pongala, a mass offering cooked by women that draws enormous crowds each year.
story: Tradition holds that the goddess appeared as a radiant girl to the head of the Mulluveettil family at the Killi river, vanished, and then came to him in a dream directing him to consecrate her in a sacred grove at a spot she marked with three lines.

name: Chottanikkara Temple
significance: One of Kerala's most visited goddess temples, where the same deity is worshipped in three aspects through the day: Saraswati in the morning, Lakshmi at noon and Durga in the evening. It has a long reputation as a place of healing for the mentally distressed.
story: A tribal named Kannappan who sacrificed buffaloes to the goddess found a divine calf embodying Vishnu and Lakshmi, and after his daughter's death was read as punishment for his cruelty, his altar became the sacred shrine.

name: Vaikom Mahadeva Temple
significance: A major Shiva temple of central Kerala whose lingam is venerated as Vaikathappan, set in a large walled compound with an unusual oval sanctum that reads as circular from outside.
story: The demon Khara received three lingams from Shiva at Chidambaram, and on his southward journey one of them would not be moved again, fixing the temple's site, where the sage Vyaghrapada later became its custodian.

name: Ettumanoor Mahadevar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in Kottayam district rebuilt in its present form in 1542, celebrated for its murals and for the seven and a half golden elephants displayed during its annual festival.
story: Temple tradition holds that the Pandavas and the sage Vyasa worshipped here.

name: Kadampuzha Devi Temple
deity: Parvati as a huntress, worshipped in a pit rather than as an image
significance: An unusual Kerala goddess shrine with no installed image: the deity is worshipped in a pit, in her form as a huntress. It is known for the offering of muttarukkal, made by devotees seeking the removal of obstacles.
story: During the Pandavas' exile Arjuna performed severe penance here to obtain the Pashupatastra, and Shiva, disguised as a hunter alongside Parvati, tested his pride before granting it.

name: Kodungallur Sree Kurumba Bhagavathy Temple
significance: One of the oldest and most important Bhadrakali temples in Kerala and a principal centre of the state's goddess worship, best known for the Bharani festival. Its date of foundation is not established, though tradition ties it to the Sangam age.
story: It is told that after Parashurama raised Kerala from the sea the demon Darikan terrorised the land until Bhadrakali sprang from Shiva's three eyes and destroyed him; another tradition identifies the goddess here with Kannaki of the Tamil epic.

name: Mannarasala Sree Nagaraja Temple
significance: The foremost serpent shrine of Kerala, set in a wooded grove filled with thousands of votive serpent images and unusual in being led by a priestess of the resident family.
story: Parashurama is said to have installed Nagaraja here so that the serpents would sweeten the salt-poisoned soil of newly raised Kerala and spare its people.

name: Ambalappuzha Sree Krishna Swamy Temple
deity: Krishna, shown as Parthasarathy with whip and conch
significance: A Krishna temple in Alappuzha district believed to have been built in the fifteenth century by the Chembakasserry ruler Pooradam Thirunal Devanarayanan Thampuran, where the deity is worshipped in the charioteer form of Parthasarathy. It is famous throughout Kerala for its daily palpayasam offering.
story: A sage who was Krishna in disguise beat the local king at chess and claimed rice doubled on each square of the board, a debt no granary could settle, which is why the temple has served payasam to devotees ever since.

name: Chettikulangara Devi Temple
significance: A large Bhadrakali temple in Alappuzha district, reckoned to be around twelve hundred years old, with its present sreekovil dating to about 1540. It is best known for Kettukazhcha, in which the surrounding villages bring towering decorated effigies and chariots to the temple ground.
story: A boatman is said to have ferried a mysterious old woman to Chettikulangara who then vanished, and the people took this as the goddess herself arriving to claim the place for her temple.

name: Parassinikadavu Sree Muthappan Temple
deity: Sree Muthappan, a manifestation of Shiva
significance: A shrine on the Valapattanam river where worship is conducted not through image ritual but through the theyyam performances Thiruvappan and Vellattam, enacted daily. It is unusual among Kerala temples in being open to all castes and communities.
story: A divine boy who appeared as Shiva in the guise of a hunter turned the toddy-tapper Chantan to stone in a quarrel over palm toddy, and after propitiatory rites was honoured as Muthappan and worshipped as a deity.

name: Rajarajeshwara Temple, Taliparamba
significance: A leading Shiva temple of north Kerala, rebuilt into its present form in the early eleventh century after earlier work by the Mushika or Kolathiri rulers, with a square sanctum under a two-tiered pyramidal roof. It was attacked and partly destroyed by Mysorean forces in the late eighteenth century before being repaired.
story: The sage Maandhata is said to have been given a Shiva linga to install where no cremation ground lay, finally setting it at Taliparamba, after which the linga repeatedly vanished and reappeared to later devotees.

name: Thirunelli Temple
significance: A Vishnu temple set among the Brahmagiri hills of Wayanad, reached through forest and long resorted to for ancestral rites performed at the nearby Papanasini stream.
story: Brahma is said to have found an image of Vishnu inside an amla tree at this spot and recognised the place as the god's own heavenly abode.

name: Lokanarkavu Temple
significance: A Durga temple near Vatakara in Kozhikode district, held by its records to be about fifteen hundred years old, and closely bound to the martial culture of northern Malabar.
story: The temple is inseparable from the ballads of the warrior Thacholi Othenan, and practitioners of Kalaripayattu still seek the goddess's blessing here before their first public performance.

name: Sree Poornathrayeesa Temple
significance: The chief temple of Tripunithura and long the tutelary shrine of the Cochin royal family, where Vishnu is worshipped as Poornathrayeesa in the Santhana Gopala form. The present structure was raised after a fire destroyed the earlier building around 1920.
story: It is told that Vishnu gave the image of Poornathrayeesa to Arjuna after restoring to life the ten lost children of a Brahmin, and the sanctum was built in the shape of a chariot to mark that event.

name: Ernakulam Shiva Temple
deity: Shiva in the Gowrisankara form, the lingam held to be swayambhu
significance: The principal Shiva temple of Ernakulam city, from which the place takes its name, referred to in Sangam literature as existing under the Cheras. Its present buildings were put up between 1843 and 1846 under the patronage of Sankara Warrier of Edakkunni.
story: The Mahabharata episode attached to the site tells of Arjuna's severe penance to Shiva, who came disguised as a tribal hunter before granting him the Pashupata weapon.

name: Kaviyoor Mahadevar Temple
deity: Shiva with Parvati, worshipped as Thrikkaviyoorappan
significance: One of the older Shiva temples of central Travancore, its present sanctum dated to the tenth century and carrying two inscriptions of AD 951-952. The Hanuman shrine within the complex is as widely visited as the main sanctum.
story: Rama is said to have installed the Shiva image here on his return from Lanka, and when Hanuman could not replace it with a lingam fetched from the Himalayas the ground rose into a hillock, making Kaviyoor his permanent abode.

name: Oachira Temple (Parabrahma Temple)
significance: An ancient temple in Kollam district dedicated to Parabrahma and remarkable for having neither an image nor a sanctum: worship is offered in the open, under a stand of carefully preserved trees.

name: Janardanaswamy Temple, Varkala
significance: A cliff-top Vishnu temple above the Varkala beach, whose restoration is credited to a Pandya king around the first century BC with further renovation during the reign of Umayamma Rani in 1677-84. Its circular sanctum under a conical copper dome is characteristic of Kerala building.
story: Brahma is said to have cursed the devas to be born as mortals, and they performed penance at Varkala, the place where the sage Narada's cloth fell, building a Vishnu temple there to free themselves.

name: Kamakshi Amman Temple
deity: Kamakshi, an aspect of Adi Shakti
builtDisplay: attributed to the 5th-8th c. (Pallava), with later work
significance: The principal goddess temple of Kanchipuram and one of the foremost centres of Shakta worship in the south, where Kamakshi is seated in padmasana rather than standing. Its origins have been variously placed with the Pallavas between the fifth and eighth centuries and with later Chola-period work.
story: It is told that the goddess Tripura Sundari destroyed the demon Bhandasura and then settled at Kanchipuram; another account says a golden image of Kamakshi was brought here in 1783 after the collapse of Vijayanagara.

disputedCircuits.note: Wikipedia's combined Shakta pithas table assigns the Kanchipuram pitha at entry 49 to the Adi Kamakshi Amman Temple 'behind Kamakshi Amman Temple', while its list of 18 Maha Shakta pithas names the Kamakshi Amman Temple itself, so two distinct temples in the same town are named for the same pitha (as of 2026).

name: Samayapuram Mariamman Temple
deity: Samayapuram Mariamman, a form of Adi Parashakti
significance: One of the wealthiest and busiest Mariamman temples in Tamil Nadu, north of Tiruchirappalli, whose present structure was raised in the early eighteenth century by Vijayaraya Chakravarti II. Its deity is sought above all for relief from disease.
story: Tradition says the image once stood at Srirangam and was removed after it was blamed for the presiding deity's illness, then found by passers-by who raised a shrine, the Kannanur Mariamman temple, which grew into the present one.

name: Swaminathaswamy Temple, Swamimalai
significance: The fourth of the six war-camp abodes of Murugan, built on a sixty-foot mound reached by a long stair, with three gopurams and three enclosures and shrines to Sundareswarar and Meenakshi at the foot of the hill.
story: Here the child Murugan is said to have expounded the meaning of the syllable Om to his father Shiva, and so earned the name Swaminatha, teacher of the lord.

name: Subramaniya Swamy Temple, Tiruttani
significance: The fifth of Murugan's six principal abodes, standing on a hill approached by a flight of stone steps and among the most visited pilgrimage temples of northern Tamil Nadu.
story: After destroying the demon Surapadman, Murugan is said to have come to Tiruttani to let his anger subside, and it was here that he married Valli.

name: Pazhamudircholai Murugan Temple
significance: The last of the six war-camp abodes of Murugan, set in dense hill forest north of Madurai, with subsidiary shrines to Ganesha and to Murugan's consorts Valli and Deivanai.
story: The Kanda Puranam relates that Murugan withdrew as a hermit after the fruit of knowledge was awarded to his brother Ganesha, and that when the poet Avvaiyar came to him he shook a naaval tree to offer her its fruit, giving the place its name.

name: Nagaraja Temple, Nagercoil
significance: The serpent temple that gives Nagercoil its name, with a sanctum for the five-headed Nagaraja and further shrines to Ananthakrishna with Rukmini and Satyabhama, and to Shiva. Sixteenth-century inscriptions describe it as a Jain temple, and its pillar carving resembles work of the ninth to twelfth centuries.
story: A Nambudiri Brahmin returning from a Pandyan king's court is said to have rediscovered a Naga image here and begun its worship, later installing Vishnu and Shiva after a vision.

name: Mahamaham Tank
deity: Shiva; focus of the Mahamaham festival
significance: The great bathing tank at the centre of Kumbakonam, dating at least to the sixteenth century, whose sixteen surrounding mandapas and stone ghats were built by Govinda Dikshitar, minister to the Thanjavur Nayak ruler Ragunatha. Its Mahamaham festival, held once every twelve years, is regarded as the southern counterpart of the Kumbh Mela.
story: It is told that Shiva gathered the seeds of all creation into a cosmic pot before the great flood, and when the pot broke its contents formed this tank, to which the nine river goddesses of India come during the festival to renew their waters.

name: Suryanar Kovil
deity: Surya (Suryanar), with consorts Ushadevi and Pratyusha Devi
significance: The one Navagraha temple of Tamil Nadu whose principal shrine belongs to the Sun rather than to Shiva, raised under Kulothunga Chola I as the Kulottungachola-Marttandalaya and enlarged in the Vijayanagara period. It carries a five-tiered rajagopuram and is now run by the state Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
story: Legend holds that the nine planetary deities, struck with leprosy by Brahma's curse and banished to Vellurukku Vanam, were allowed by Shiva to bless devotees from this spot.

name: Kailasanathar Temple, Thingalur
deity: Shiva as Kailasanathar; Navagraha shrine of Chandra (the Moon)
builtDisplay: 16th c. Nayak structure on a Chola foundation
significance: One of the nine Navagraha temples of Tamil Nadu, assigned to the Moon, standing between Thanjavur and Kumbakonam. The site is praised in the 7th-century Tevaram as a Vaippu Sthalam, and its present masonry was built by the Nayaks over an earlier Chola complex.
story: The moon god Chandra is said to have worshipped Kailasanathar here after a curse dimmed him, and to have regained his powers in return.

name: Nagannathaswamy Temple, Keelaperumpallam
deity: Shiva as Naganatha Swamy; Navagraha shrine of Ketu
builtDisplay: 16th c. Nayak structure on a Chola foundation
significance: Known as the Ketu Sthalam, this is the Navagraha temple of Tamil Nadu tied to the shadow planet Ketu, about two kilometres from Poompuhar in Mayiladuthurai district. A flat rajagopuram and two prakarams enclose the Nayak-period masonry raised over a Chola foundation.
story: After the churning of the ocean of milk loosed the poison Halahala, the serpent Vasuki is said to have prayed here and Shiva appeared as Naganathar to grant redemption.

name: Sri Lakshmi Narayani Golden Temple (Sripuram)
significance: A modern gold-sheathed shrine at Thirumalaikodi near Vellore, completed in August 2007 by the Sri Narayani Peedam trust led by Sakthi Amma. It sits on about forty hectares of the Thirupuram spiritual park and is approached along a star-shaped Sri Chakra path more than 1.8 km long.

name: Vadapalani Andavar Temple
significance: A major Murugan shrine in western Chennai that began in 1865 as a thatched hut where Annaswami Nayakar worshipped a painted image of the god, with the masonry temple following around 1890 and renovation in 1920. Its rajagopuram carries stucco panels of episodes from the Skanda Purana.
story: A sage of Palani is said to have appeared in Annaswami Nayakar's dream and told him to worship Murugan at home, which is how the shrine began.

name: Ashtalakshmi Temple, Chennai
deity: Lakshmi in her eight forms (Ashta Lakshmi)
significance: A seaside temple at Besant Nagar begun in 1974 and consecrated in April 1976 at the wish of the Kanchi seer Chandrashekarendra Saraswati. Modelled on the Sundara Varadaraja Perumal temple at Uthiramerur, it stacks nine sanctums across four levels so pilgrims can visit every shrine without walking above another sanctum.

name: Adhiparasakthi Siddhar Peetam, Melmaruvathur
significance: A goddess shrine on the Chennai–Tiruvannamalai road that grew around a swayambhu stone exposed when a storm uprooted a neem tree in 1966. Villagers first raised a hut over the stone, and the image of Adi Parashakti was installed in November 1977.
story: The neem tree that stood here is said to have dripped a healing nectar, and the Mother is believed to dwell in the snake mound as a cobra so as to keep blessing devotees.

name: Sittanavasal Cave
builtDisplay: 7th c. Pandya renovation; ascetic use from c. 2nd c. BCE
significance: A rock-cut Jain monastery and cave temple in Pudukkottai district, used by Shramana ascetics from about the 2nd century BCE. An inscription credits its renovation to a Pandya king of the 7th century, and the Archaeological Survey of India now maintains it as a ticketed monument.

name: Kalugumalai Jain Beds
deity: Jain Tirthankaras, including Parshvanatha and Gomateshwara
significance: About 150 rock-cut niches of Tirthankaras carved into the Kalugumalai hill under the Pandya king Parantaka Nedunjadaiya in the late 8th century, left unfinished. Its 98 inscriptions form the largest single concentration of Jain epigraphs in the far south, a fifth of them naming women mendicants.

name: Ranganathaswamy Temple, Srirangapatna
dynasty: Western Ganga, with Hoysala and Vijayanagara additions
significance: The upstream shrine of the three Ranganatha temples on the Kaveri, recorded by inscription as founded in 894 CE by the chief Tirumalaiah under Western Ganga rule. It was enlarged by the Hoysalas under Vishnuvardhana, renovated in 1210 under Veera Ballala II, and extended again in the Vijayanagara and Wodeyar periods.

name: Satyanarayana Swamy Temple, Annavaram
significance: A hilltop shrine on Ratnagiri in Kakinada district, first built in 1891 and rebuilt in stone in 1933–34. It is one of the busiest pilgrimage centres in Andhra Pradesh, visited above all for the collective performance of the Satyanarayana Vratam, especially in the month of Karthika.
story: The hill is said to be a son of the mountain Meru and his wife Menaka, blessed by Vishnu, on whom Satyanarayana chose to manifest.

name: Dwaraka Tirumala Temple
significance: A Venkateswara temple in Eluru district that draws pilgrims from across coastal Andhra and is known locally as Chinna Tirupati, or little Tirupati.

name: Varasidhi Vinayaka Swamy Temple, Kanipakam
significance: A Ganesha temple in Chittoor district built in the early 11th century under the Chola emperor Kulottunga I and expanded in 1336 under the Vijayanagara rulers. The image stands in a well that never runs dry and is administered today by the Andhra Pradesh endowments department through a trust board.
story: Three disabled brothers digging a well are said to have struck a hard object from which blood gushed; they were healed on the spot, and the self-manifested Ganesha has stayed in the water ever since, the image reportedly growing so that its old silver armour no longer fits.

name: Srikurmam Temple
deity: Vishnu as Kurmanatha, the tortoise avatar
significance: One of very few temples in India where Vishnu is worshipped in his Kurma or tortoise form. A temple inscription of 1281 CE records the restoration of Kurmakshetra by Ramanuja under the Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva, and the complex carries inscriptions running from the 11th to the 19th century.

name: Arasavalli Sun Temple
dynasty: Eastern Ganga; rebuilt in the 18th c.
significance: One of the very few Indian temples where Surya remains the presiding deity, founded in the 7th century under the Eastern Ganga king Devendra Varma a kilometre east of Srikakulam. The building standing today is largely the result of 18th-century work, reconstructed in 1778 by Elamanchili Pullaji Panthulu.
story: The Padma Purana holds that the sage Kasyapa installed the image of Surya here for the welfare of mankind.

name: Madhukeswara Temple, Mukhalingam
significance: The principal Shaiva temple of Mukhalingam, the town that served as Kalinganagari, capital of the Eastern Gangas, and built under Kamarnava Deva II around the turn of the 9th century. Two further Shaiva temples stand in the village, the latest dating to the early 11th century, and the group was renovated by the Maharaja of Paralakhemundi in the 17th century.

name: Yaganti Uma Maheswara Temple
deity: Shiva with Parvati as Uma Maheswara
significance: A hill temple in Nandyal district built in the 15th century by Harihara Bukka Raya of the Sangama dynasty of Vijayanagara, where Shiva and Parvati are worshipped together as Uma Maheswara. Its pushkarini is fed through a carved bull, and the hillside holds the Agastya, Venkateswara and Veera Brahmam caves.
story: Tradition says the sage Agastya meant to raise a Venkateswara temple here, but the image's toe broke, so he did penance and Shiva granted the shrine instead.

name: Mahanandiswara Swamy Temple, Mahanandi
style: Badami Chalukya gopuram with Vijayanagara additions
significance: The chief shrine of the Nava Nandi group of nine Nandi temples near Nandyal, its original structure built by the Badami Chalukyas in the 7th century with further work in the 10th and 15th centuries. Tenth-century inscriptions record repairs made under the local Nanda rulers.
story: Local tradition traces the name to the Nanda rulers of the region, who worshipped Nandi as their ancestral deity.

name: Trikoteswara Swamy Temple, Kotappakonda
deity: Shiva as Trikoteswara, lord of the three peaks
significance: A three-peaked hill shrine in Palnadu district whose exact foundation date is unknown but which received land and cattle grants from the Eastern Chalukyas and Kakatiyas between the 9th and 14th centuries. Vijayanagara rulers added Dravidian mandapams and gopurams, and the temple is now administered by Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams.
story: The god is linked to Anandavalli, a cowherd woman whose fierce devotion is said to have drawn Shiva from Rudra Shikharam to Brahma Shikharam, where he settled as the lingam of the present temple.

name: Amaralingeswara Temple, Amaravati
deity: Shiva as Amareswara, with Bala Chamundika
dynasty: Kota chiefs, with Reddi and Vijayanagara patronage
