significance: A goddess temple in the Woraiyur neighbourhood of Tiruchirappalli, known since early Chola times though no records fix its date, and now run by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Endowment Board. Its defining feature is that the sanctum has no roof.
story: Devotees hold that a roof once raised over the sanctum was burnt away by the goddess's own power, and that unlike Nataraja she never changed her raised leg, keeping the stance that shows her force.

name: Nimishamba Temple
significance: A goddess shrine on the bank of the Kaveri about two kilometres from Srirangapatna on the road to Sangam, raised some three to four centuries ago under Wodeyar rule and fronted by a seven-tiered rajagopuram.
story: Her name joins nimisha, a minute, to amba, mother, from the belief that she grants boons within a minute; she is said to have helped King Muktharaja against demons.

name: Baba Bhusandeswar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Kumbhirgadi in the Bhograi block of Balasore district, whose black granite lingam measures twelve feet by fourteen with only half of it above ground and an octagonal middle section, and is claimed to be the largest in Asia. Maha Shivaratri is the main observance.
story: Ravana is said to have received the lingam from Shiva with a warning never to set it down, and to have planted it here in desperation while carrying it in the Pushpaka Vimana.

name: Thindal Murugan Temple
significance: A Murugan temple on the Thindalmalai hillock a few kilometres from Erode, known for the golden temple car in which the images are carried in procession.

name: Thiruppudaimarudur Temple
significance: A Shiva temple near Veeravanallur in Tirunelveli district, one of only three shrines to have the marudhu tree as its sthala vriksham. In a sacred triad it represents Shiva's foot, with Srisailam as the head and Thiruvidaimarudur as the body, and its Theerthavaari festival falls at Thaipoosam in the month of Thai.
story: King Surendra is said to have built the temple after Shiva granted him the Brahmadand, still kept inside, and sent him to the Himalayas in search of an image of Gomathi.

name: Pachala Someswara Temple
deity: Shiva, as a lingam of green onyx
significance: A Shaiva complex at Panagal in Nalgonda district dating to the eleventh or twelfth century, probably built under the Kunduru Chodas and the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra I. Four shrines open off a large rectangular mandapam carried on seventy carved pillars illustrating stories of Shiva and Vishnu, and the Panagal Museum, opened on the premises in 1982, holds around 640 antiquities.
story: Legend says a large and brilliant emerald once lay beneath the lingam and was carried off during raids on the region.

name: Adat Shiva Temple
deity: Shiva as Sri Parameswara, with a separate Maha Vishnu shrine
significance: A Kerala-style temple in Adat village, Thrissur district, unusual in having two separate complexes, one for Sri Parameswara and one for Maha Vishnu. It is counted among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, and celebrates Maha Shivaratri and Ashtamirohini.
story: The shrine is believed to have been established by the sage Parasurama.

name: Suyambulingaswamy Temple, Uvari
deity: Shiva as Swayambunathar, a self-manifested lingam, with Brahma Sakthi
significance: A Shiva temple in the coastal village of Uvari on the Tiruchendur–Kanyakumari road in Tirunelveli district, where the sun's rays fall on the swayambhu lingam throughout the Tamil month of Marghazhi.
story: Devotees believe illness disappears if one bathes in the sea for forty-one days while praying to the deity, and give thanks with baskets of sea sand or images of nagas.

name: Narasimhaswamy Temple, Namakkal
significance: A cave temple cut into the rock below Namakkal Fort, enshrining a seated Narasimha with his consort Namagiri Tayar. Its panels of Trivikrama, Narasimha slaying Hiranyakashipu and the reclining Vishnu make it an important example of early South Indian rock-cut sculpture.
story: Lakshmi is said to have performed penance here after Narasimha refused to forgive Hiranyakashipu; the shaligrama image Hanuman carried for her grew into the hill on which Narasimha then made his abode.

name: Thirukondeeswaram Pasupatheeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in Tiruvarur district counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams, the shrines praised in the Tamil Saiva canon. It was sung by the Nayanar saint Tirunavukkarasar (Appar) in his Tevaram hymns.

name: Thiruvallam Sree Parasurama Temple
significance: Standing on the bank of the Karamana River, this is the only Kerala temple with Parasurama as the presiding deity and is counted among the 108 Abhimana Kshetrams. It is a protected monument of the Kerala Department of Archaeology and carries sub-shrines for Brahma, Matsya, Murugan, Veda Vyasa, Ayyappa, Krishna and Ganesha.
story: Parasurama is said to have raised Kerala from the sea with his axe and then called on the serpent king Vasuki to sweeten the salt-laden soil, after which serpents became guardians of the land.

name: Thrissilery Shiva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in Wayanad attributed to the Chera kings and reckoned about a thousand years old. It is ritually bound to the nearby Thirunelly Vishnu Temple: ancestral rites performed at Thirunelly are held to be incomplete until the pilgrim also visits here.
story: The separate Jala Durga shrine within the compound is said to have been consecrated by the sage Parashurama.

name: Punnainallur Kothandaramar Temple
deity: Rama as Kothandaramar (with Sita and Lakshmana)
significance: An 18th-century Rama temple near Thanjavur, one of the 88 shrines of the Thanjavur Palace Devasthanam administered by the Tamil Nadu HR&CE department. It preserves shaligrama sculptures presented to the ruler of Thanjavur by a king of Nepal, and its walls carry painted episodes from the Ramayana.

name: Trithala Maha Siva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the southern bank of the Bharathappuzha, probably raised in the 9th–10th centuries and noted for marking the transition from Chola to Pandya temple architecture. It is one of the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, and its lingam, formed of river sand, is never anointed.
story: Agnihotri, eldest of the twelve children of Vararuchi in the Parayi petta panthirukulam legend, is said to have heaped river sand into a mound that hardened into a Shiva lingam when his mother tried to remove it.

name: Tiruppaatrurai Adhimooleswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple carrying several Chola-period inscriptions and counted a Paadal Petra Sthalam, praised by the 7th-century Nayanar saint Tirugnanasambandar in the Tevaram. It is run by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Board and keeps six daily rituals and three annual festivals.
story: A Chola king hunting here loosed an arrow at a bird and struck an anthill that began to ooze milk; Shiva then appeared in his dream to reveal his presence, and the king built the temple on the spot.

name: Thrikkadavoor Sree Mahadeva Temple
significance: One of the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, situated in Kollam district and administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board. It is known for its golden flagstaff and a ten-day Srattu festival held in the Malayalam month of Kumbham.
story: The sage Mrikandu and his wife Marudmati are said to have obtained the short-lived son Markandeya here; when Yama cast his noose it fell instead around the lingam, and Shiva overcame him and granted the boy deathlessness.

name: Nalukulangara Maha Devi Temple
significance: A goddess temple in Kuthiathode panchayat, Alappuzha district, whose presiding Bhadrakali is known locally as Nalukulangara Amma. Its outer shrines carry Shiva, Murugan and Saraswati.

name: Padanilam Parabrahma Temple
significance: An unusual Kerala shrine with no enclosing wall or roof and no conventional idol, where a stone Om symbol beneath open tree cover is worshipped as Parabrahma. It was one of the major temples of the former Travancore state and served as the administrative centre of the Nooranad region.
story: The name Padanilam is traced to pada, battle, after the fighting between local chieftains over control of the temple and its villages, which is said to have ended when Pazhoor Panamana Thampuran intervened by fasting.

name: Vedapureeswarar Temple, Cheyyar
significance: A Shiva temple at Thiruvadhipuram in Cheyyar, formerly known as Thiruvothur, counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Tamil Saiva canon. Tradition at the site records the saint Tirugnanasambandar turning a male palm tree into a female one, and Arunagirinathar worshipping Murugan here.
story: When Sambandar could not tell this temple apart from the neighbouring Devadi Raja Perumal temple, Ganesha is said to have appeared before him and pointed out the Shiva shrine.

name: Thirumangalam Sree Maha Vishnu Siva Temple
significance: A temple at Engandiyur in Thrissur district housing Maha Vishnu and Shiva in separate east-facing sanctums. It is one of the 108 famous Shiva temples of Kerala and is managed by the Kattumadam Devaswam Trust.
story: The Shiva lingam is held to be swayambhu, self-manifested, and installed by the sage Parashurama.

name: Thiruvatta Mahadeva Temple
significance: One of the earliest temples in Kerala and among its 108 famous Shiva shrines, built under the Kulasekhara Perumals of the second Chera dynasty. The Vazhappally copper-plate inscription issued in the reign of the Chera king Rama Rajasekhara refers to this Shiva temple.
story: Folklore holds that the sage Parashurama installed the Shiva idol here in the Treta Yuga.

name: Anthikad Karthyayani Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Anthikad in Thrissur district, counted among the 108 Durga temples of Kerala. It is administered by the Cochin Devaswom Board.

name: Padayanivettom Devi Temple
significance: A twin-goddess temple at Vallikunnam in Mavelikkara taluk, which records indicate has stood for at least 1,200 years. It preserved older ritual forms of worship such as Padayani, Thottam pattu and Kalamezhuthu pattu, and a Devaprashna inquiry confirmed the presence of its two goddesses.
story: The place is said to be named for a Padayani performance during which villagers glimpsed two radiant women by torchlight, taken to be the two goddesses, for whom temples were then founded.

name: Tirukkandalam Sivanandeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Tirukkandalam, formerly Tirukkallil, in Tiruvallur district, counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams. It was sung by the Nayanar saint Sambandar in the early medieval Tevaram hymns.

name: Tiruchopuram Mangalapureeswarar Temple
significance: A coastal Shiva temple in Cuddalore district, one of the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams glorified in the early medieval Tevaram. Its hymns are attributed to the Nayanar saint Sambandar.

name: Nadapuram Iringannur Siva Temple
significance: One of the 108 famous Shiva temples of Kerala and among the oldest in Kozhikode district, with a two-tiered rectangular tiled sanctum. It is reckoned one of the three Thrikkapaleeswaram shrines of that list.
story: Tradition credits the sage Parashurama with installing the idol, and the village name Iringannur is explained as 'place of the two-eyed one' from the deity's distinctive two-eyed Sadashiva form.

name: Kasi Viswanathar Temple, Tenkasi
significance: Founded in the 13th century by the Pandya ruler Parakrama Pandyan and enlarged by the Madurai Nayaks from the 16th century, this granite-walled complex gives Tenkasi its name as the 'Kasi of the south'. Inscriptions of 1384 record grants of houses and villages to Brahmins for Vedic recitation, and its long-flat tower was rebuilt as a 180-foot seven-tiered gopuram completed in 1990.
story: Shiva is said to have appeared to the king in a dream and told him to follow a column of ants; the temple was raised where the trail ended, sparing his people the journey to Varanasi.

name: Thrippalur Mahadeva Temple
significance: A temple on the bank of the Gayatri river at Alathur, one of the 108 famous Shiva temples of Kerala, with three shrines: square sanctums for Shiva and Krishna and a circular one for Narasimha. It was once held by the Kavalappara Swarupam of the Palakkad rulers and is referred to in several Malayalam classics.
story: Folklore holds that the sage Parashurama installed the Shiva idol in the Treta Yuga, the temple being raised to calm the god's power.

name: Thiruvambadi Sri Krishna Temple
significance: A Thrissur city temple where Krishna in child form and Bhadrakali are worshipped with equal standing, with sub-shrines for Ganesha, Sastha and Brahmarakshasa. It leads one of the two rival contingents of the annual Thrissur Pooram festival.
story: The goddess here is regarded as the younger sister of the Bhagavathi of the Paramekkavu temple, the Pooram's other contingent.

name: Paippad Puthenkavu Bhagavathi Temple
significance: An old Bhagavathi shrine on the Changanassery–Kaviyoor road about five kilometres from Changanassery. It is run by an elected Devaswom board drawn from two NSS Karayogams, and its annual festival falls on the Bharani day of the Malayalam month of Meenam.

name: Sivalokanathar Temple, Gramam
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam in Viluppuram district whose original Chola complex was rebuilt in masonry by Vijayanagara kings in the 16th century. It was converted into a stone temple under Parantaka I around 940 CE and carries inscriptions of the medieval Cholas, the Pandyas and the Rashtrakutas.
story: Local legend explains the older name Thirumundeeswaram from the gatekeepers Thindi and Mundi who worshipped Shiva here; another account has King Chokkalingam find a lingam beneath a lotus while hunting and raise the temple over it.

name: Annappanpettai Sundareswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the Sirkazhi block of Mayiladuthurai district, at a place historically called Kalikamoor, counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams. It was sung by Tirugnanasambandar in the Tevaram, and the sage Parasara is held to have worshipped here.

name: Mallinathaswamy Jain Temple, Mannargudi
significance: One of the best known of the old Jain tirthas of Tamil Nadu, raised at Mannargudi under Chola rule in the 12th century. It has a three-tiered rajagopura, a two-tiered vimana and a mahamandapa built in Maratha style; the present 56 cm image of the presiding Tirthankara was made in 1986.

name: Shri Vishwanath Mandir, BHU
significance: Planned by Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya and funded by the Birla family, this marble temple on the Banaras Hindu University campus took from 1931 to 1966 to build and is modelled on the Kashi Vishwanath temple. Its shikhara rises about 77 m, nine shrines are gathered into one structure, and the full text of the Bhagavad Gita is inscribed on its inner walls.

name: Chennakeshava Temple, Hullekere
significance: A soapstone ekakuta shrine built in 1163 CE by a minister of the Hoysala king Narasimha I, with lathe-turned pillars, tiers of miniature vimanas and the Hoysala royal emblem on its sukhanasi. It is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.
story: The emblem carried on the tower shows Sala, the legendary founder of the Hoysala line, stabbing a lion.

name: Mrityunjay Mahadev Mandir
significance: A Shiva temple at Daranagar in Varanasi whose present building dates to the 18th century, though the smaller shrines it contains are held to be far older. It is the principal place in the city for the recitation of the Mrityunjaya mantra, and its compound holds a celebrated well.
story: Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods, is said to have emptied all his medicines into the temple well, so that its water heals illness and guards devotees against untimely death.

name: Eachanari Vinayagar Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple about 12 km from Coimbatore city on the Palakkad road, known for its very large stone image of Vinayagar and administered by the Tamil Nadu HR&CE department.
story: Local tradition says the huge Vinayagar image was being carted from Madurai to the Perur Pateeswarar Temple when the cart's axle broke here, and the deity was installed on the spot.

name: Tiruneelakkudi Neelakandeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the Kaveri in Thanjavur district counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams, praised in the Tevaram hymns of the Nayanar saints Tirunavukkarasar and Sambandar. Its lingam is unusual, with square projections and a rough surface.
story: The name recalls the churning of the ocean of milk: Shiva swallowed the poison, Parvati held his throat to make him Neelakanta, and she then soothed him with oil here, a rite the temple still performs.

name: Panamukkumpally Sastha Temple
significance: A Sastha temple in Thrissur city that takes part every year in the Thrissur Pooram, the state's best-known temple festival.

name: Mukthi Natheshwara Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Binnamangala near Nelamangala outside Bengaluru, which the article dates to the Chola period around 1110 CE.

name: Pazhoor Perumthrikkovil
significance: A 12th-century sandhara-type Kerala temple with doors on all four sides, a granite plinth and a circular vimana, protected by the Kerala State Archaeology Department since 1994 and notable for its old woodwork and murals of Puranic scenes.

name: Palayoor Mahadeva Temple
significance: An ancient Shiva temple site at Palayoor near Chavakkad; the temple no longer stands, the site having been converted into a Christian church in the traditional account of St Thomas's arrival in Malabar.
story: It is counted among the 108 Shiva temples said to have been founded by Parasurama, who is held to have installed the deity himself.

name: Kilimarathukavu Temple
builtDisplay: present temple rebuilt in the 21st c.
significance: A Shiva-Parvati temple at Kadakkal that also houses Dharma Sastha and Ayyappan; the original structure was destroyed and the present temple built in the 21st century, with the Travancore Devaswom Board taking over administration in 2011.
story: Temple lore holds that Shiva and Parvati came here disguised as forest dwellers to test Arjuna, and that Shiva revealed himself, granted him the Pashupatastra and then remained on the spot as a lingam.

name: Bhimeswar Dham
significance: A Shiva shrine on Dakini Hill about 13 km from Guwahati where a hill stream runs continuously over the lingam; devotees hold it to be one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, an identification scholars dispute. Maha Shivaratri is its principal observance.
story: The Shiva Purana account told here has Shiva destroying the demon Bhimasura when he attacked King Priyadharman at worship, the stream over the lingam being Shiva's perspiration from that fight.

name: Thirumalida Swayambhoo Shiva Temple
significance: A swayambhu Shiva temple on the bank of the Manimala river at Mallappally, described as the only west-facing swayambhu Shiva shrine in Kerala; Maha Shivaratri draws thousands of pilgrims.

name: Ashtamsa Varadha Anjaneyar Temple
significance: A Hanuman temple at Peelamedu in Coimbatore completed in 2004, whose salagrama-stone west-facing image shows Lakshmi in the deity's right palm and is dressed in a different alankaram each day.

name: Lakshminarasimha Temple, Vignasante
deity: Narasimha, with Venugopala and Lakshmi Narayana
significance: A soapstone trikuta temple of about 1286 CE with a three-storey Vesara vimana, built by the brothers Appayya, Gopala and Madhava under Hoysala king Narasimha III; it is one of the last Hoysala temples raised before the Delhi Sultanate invasions, and is an ASI-protected monument.

name: Veerateeswarar Temple, Thirukovilur
significance: A 10th-century Chola temple on the Then Pennai river at Thirukoilur, built as two parallel enclosures each with a three-tiered rajagopuram. It is a Paadal Petra Sthalam sung by three Nayanmars in the Tevaram and one of the Ashta Veerattanam shrines marking Shiva's eight victories over demons.

name: Karpaka Vinayakar Temple
significance: A rock-cut cave shrine at Pillayarpatti holding carvings of Ganesha, a Shiva lingam and a figure read as Ardhanarishvara or Harihara, attributed to about 650 CE and enlarged with mandapams in later centuries. It is one of the nine ancestral temples of the Nagarathar (Chettiar) community, and 11th-century panchaloha images were recovered during 19th-century restoration.

name: Masilamaniswara Temple, Thirumullaivoyal
significance: A 9th-century Chola foundation near Chennai, extended by later Cholas, Pandyas and the Vijayanagara rulers, with an unusual Gaja Prishtam (elephant-back) vimana. It is a Paadal Petra Sthalam revered in the 7th-century Tevaram and belongs to the Shakti triad of Tondaimandalam.
story: The temple's tradition tells of King Thondaiman striking a lingam hidden in dense mullai thickets during a campaign; Shiva and Parvati appeared, helped him defeat two brothers, and he raised the temple on the spot.

name: Akshayapureeswarar Temple
deity: Shiva (Akshayapureeswarar), with a principal shrine to Shani
significance: A 13th-century Shiva temple whose inscriptions credit Parakrama Pandyan I, best known as one of the 27 Nakshatra temples of Tamil Nadu, linked to the Pushya asterism and holding a Shani shrine with his consorts Jyestha and Mandha.
story: The legend here has Shani, lamed by Yama, tripping over the roots of a vila tree at this spot on Akshaya Tritiya, whereupon Shiva appeared as Akshayapureeswarar, healed him and blessed him with marriage.

name: Bata Mangala Temple
significance: A Shakta shrine on the Jagannath Sadak about 7 km from Puri, where pilgrims customarily stop to pray to the goddess before continuing to the Jagannath Temple.
story: It is told that when Brahma stood bewildered before the void, Bata Mangala appeared and directed him to Jagannath, allowing creation to begin.

name: Bharat Mata Mandir
deity: Bharat Mata (the nation personified as a goddess)
significance: A temple on the Mahatma Gandhi Kashi Vidyapith campus founded by Babu Shiv Prasad Gupta and inaugurated in 1936, which holds no image at all: its object of veneration is a to-scale marble relief map of undivided India. Gandhi opened it, remarking that the only thing enshrined there was the map.

name: Kolanjiappar Temple
significance: A Murugan temple on the outskirts of Virudhachalam with a five-tiered rajagopuram, pillared hall and sanctum, administered by the Tamil Nadu HR&CE department; Panguni Uthiram, a ten-day Vasantha Utsavam and the Adi festival are its main celebrations.
story: Tradition holds that Shiva sent his son Murugan as a hunter into the Kolanji forest to test the saint Sundarar, and that Murugan afterwards settled there as Kolanjiappar; another account says a cow was found mysteriously giving milk beneath a kolanji bush at the site.

name: Thalakodu Sree Krishna Temple
significance: An old Krishna temple at Cheriyoor near Taliparamba in north Kerala, belonging to the Mullappally illam and open to all Hindus.

name: Pallikonda Perumal Temple, Malayadippatti
deity: Vishnu (Pallikonda Perumal, reclining), with Mahalakshmi and Bhudevi
significance: A rock-cut cave temple about 33 km from Pudukkottai, dated by its inscriptions to the 7th–8th century and housing a reclining Vishnu; it is paired at the same site with a Shiva cave temple and is maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India. Its dvarapalas are unusual in having only two arms.
story: The sage Dhivakara Maharishi is said to have done penance here for Vishnu's grace, and the deity, called Kan Thirantha Perumal, is believed to cure ailments of the eyes.

name: Amaravila Rameswaram Sri Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple about a kilometre from Neyyattinkara whose sreekovil holds an east-facing lingam together with a west-facing Parvati; Maha Shivaratri with its Pongala offering and a ten-day festival in December–January are the main observances.
story: The temple's name comes from the belief that Rama himself installed the image here, and it is counted among the 108 Shiva temples ascribed to the sage Parasurama.

name: Kaalikaamba Kamatheshwara Temple
significance: A temple in the old Nagarathpet quarter of Bengaluru dedicated jointly to Kaalikaamba and Kamatheshwara, described as roughly eight centuries old and dating to the Chola period.

name: Kashi Vishweshwar Temple, Kadugodi
builtDisplay: Chola period, reign of Rajendra Chola
significance: A Chola-period Shiva temple in Kadugodi on the eastern edge of Bengaluru, assigned to the reign of Rajendra Chola and showing design carried over from the earlier Western Ganga dynasty. The locality's name comes from the temple standing in forest — kadu (forest) and gudi (temple) — and the original lingam, once stolen, was replaced with one brought from Varanasi.

name: Thirukolakka Sapthapureeswarar Temple
deity: Shiva (Sapthapureeswarar), with consort Osai Kodutha Nayaki
significance: A Shiva temple at Keezhai Thirukolakka, historically called Sapthapuri, counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams and sung in the Tevaram by Tirugnanasambandar and Sundarar.
story: It is at this shrine that the child saint Sambandar is said to have miraculously received his golden cymbals.

name: Eshwara Temple, Kengeri
significance: An 11th-century Shiva temple at Kengeri assigned to the reign of Rajendra Chola I, one of the small group of Chola-era shrines surviving in the Bengaluru area; it stands close to the Kote Anjaneya Swamy Temple.

name: Tirunaarayur Soundaryeswarar Temple
significance: One of the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams, sung by Tirugnanasambandar in the Tevaram; the temple is known for a swayambhu Ganesha worshipped as Polla Pillaiyar.
story: Tradition holds that the deity revealed himself here to the boy Nambiyandar Nambi, sent by his father to make the ritual offerings.

name: Mathur Shiva Temple
deity: Shiva, with Parvati in the same sanctum
significance: One of the 108 celebrated Shiva temples of Kerala, at Kunnamkulam, where the west-facing Shiva shares the sanctum with an east-facing Parvati and the lingam is held to be an unshaped reddish rudrakshasila. Maha Shivaratri is the chief festival.
story: The image is said to have been installed by the sage Parashurama.

name: Maragathambikai Chandrachoodesvarar Temple
deity: Shiva (Chandra Choodeswarar), with Parvati as Maragathambal
significance: A hill temple at Hosur with 13th-century inscriptions, credited to the Hoysala chief Thirupuvanamalla Barvatharaja Anthiyazhvar around 1260 and enlarged under the Cholas, Hoysalas and Vijayanagara rulers; the surrounding region is treated in the Bhadragiri Mahatmyam of the Brahmanda Purana.

name: Thirumanangeeswarar Temple
deity: Thiruvudai Amman (chief goddess), with Shiva as Thirumanangeeswarar
significance: A goddess-led Shiva temple near Minjur north of Chennai, forming with the Kodiyidai Amman temple at Thirumullaivoyal and the Vadivudai Amman temple at Tiruvottiyur the Shakti triad of Tondaimandalam.

name: Arakeshvara Temple, Hole Alur
significance: A mid-10th-century temple raised by the Western Ganga king Butuga II to mark his defeat of the Cholas at the Battle of Takkolam, with a plain plan of sanctum, vestibule, closed hall and detached open mantapa. Its rounded pillars carry bas-reliefs of that victory over the Chola prince Rajaditya. It is a monument of national importance under the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Bhairavakona
deity: Shiva in eight forms (Shashinaga, Rudra, Visweswara, Nagarikeswara, Bhargeswara, Rameswara, Mallikarjuna and Pakshamalika), with a separate Kala Bhairava shrine
significance: A group of eight inscribed rock-cut cave shrines cut from a single formation in the Nallamala Hills, dated to the 7th–8th century and compared with the rock-cut work at Mahabalipuram; each cave carries a Brahma-Vishnu-Shiva grouping, alongside life-size dvarapalas, carved lions and Harihara figures, with a 200 m waterfall beside the site. Mahasivaratri and Kartika Purnima draw large pilgrim crowds.
story: Local tradition traces the name to a shepherd, Kalabhairava Kondayya, who made a vow to the deity during a drought.

name: Someshwara Swamy Temple
significance: A Chola-period Shiva temple at Agara on Sarjapura Road in Bengaluru, described in the article as roughly 1,200 years old.

name: Lakhamandal Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the Jaunsar-Bawar hills above the Yamuna, whose surviving shikhara is dated to the 12th–13th century while brick remains on the site go back several centuries earlier. A sixth-century inscription found here records that a princess named Ishwara of Singhpura raised a shrine in memory of her husband Chandragupta, and Archaeological Survey excavations have recovered a large quantity of sculpture around it.
story: Local tradition ties the site to the Mahabharata, holding that this is where Duryodhana built the lac house in which he meant to burn the Pandavas alive.

name: Muringamangalam Sreemahadevar Temple
significance: The largest Shiva temple in Pathanamthitta district, with an east-facing Mahadeva sanctum and subsidiary shrines to Ganapathi, Ayyappa, the nagas and Krishna. It was historically held by the Pandalam royal family.

name: Kailasanathar Temple, Nedungudi
deity: Shiva as Kailasanathar (also Kasinathar), with the goddess Prasannanayaki
significance: A Shiva temple on the Karaikkudi–Aranthangi road holding two lingas, whose goddess shrine to Prasannanayaki is dated to the 13th century. The complex has the usual sequence of garbhagriha, artha mandapa and maha mandapa.
story: Two asura brothers, Perunjeevi and Siranjeevi, were told by Vishnu to worship Shiva together here; the deity is also called Padikkasunathar after a tale of abhisheka milk poured here appearing on the steps at Kashi.

name: Lakshmi Narayan Temple, Bhopal
significance: A hilltop Birla temple in Bhopal whose foundation stone was laid in 1960 by Madhya Pradesh chief minister Kailashnath Katju and which was inaugurated in 1964 by Dwarka Prasad Mishra. Besides the Lakshmi Narayan sanctum it houses images of Shiva, Jagdamba and Hanuman.

name: Vedapureeswarar Temple, Thiruverkadu
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of about 1.5 acres with two gopurams, praised in the 7th-century Tevaram hymns; the original complex is held to predate that century and is attributed to the Cholas. The present structure was rebuilt in 1973 and the temple is run by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
story: Sage Agastya, kept from seeing Shiva's wedding at Kailasa by the crowd, prayed here and was granted the sight of Shiva and Parvati in their wedding dress.

name: Sikri Mata Temple
deity: Sikri Mata, held to be a form of Durga
significance: A goddess temple founded in 1532 by Jalim Giri Baba of the Goswami community, according to Bhaat records. During the 1857 rebellion more than 130 rebels were hanged from an old banyan tree on its grounds; the shrine passed from the founder's descendants to the gram panchayat in 1977 and to the Modinagar municipal body in 2024.
story: Jalim Giri Baba is said to have built the shrine after a darshan of Durga told him to raise it on that spot.

name: Madhya Kailash Temple
significance: A busy Vinayakar temple at the junction of Sardar Patel Road and Rajiv Gandhi Salai in Adyar, with the main deity ringed by shrines to Shiva, Surya, Devi and Vishnu as well as Anjaneya and Swarna Bhairavar.
story: Its best-known image is the Adhyantha Prabhu, half Ganesha and half Hanuman, said to have been made after a temple official saw that combined form in a vision.

name: Nileshwar Muthappan Madappura
deity: Muthappan, worshipped in theyyam form as Vishnu
significance: A madappura in the north Kerala town of Nileshwar dedicated to Muthappan, the folk deity of the Malabar coast whose worship centres on theyyam performance.

name: Nageshvara Temple, Begur
significance: A temple complex on the southern edge of Bengaluru whose two principal shrines were raised under the Western Ganga kings Nitimarga I and Ereyappa Nitimarga II, with later additions in Chola, Hoysala and Vijayanagara idiom. An Old Kannada inscription of about 890 found here carries the earliest known mention of the name Bengaluru.
story: Ravana is said to have worshipped Nageshvara here on his way back to Lanka after losing the atma linga at Gokarna.

name: Mudikondan Kothandaramar Temple
deity: Vishnu as Kothandaramar (Rama), with Yogasayana Perumal and Ranganathar
significance: A Vishnu temple in Nannilam taluk held to predate the age of the Alvars, with sanctums for Rama as Kothandaramar, Yogasayana Perumal and Ranganathar.
story: Returning from Lanka, Rama is said to have halted at sage Bharadwaja's hermitage here and shown himself in coronation form before the actual crowning at Ayodhya, which is how the village got the name Mudikondan.

name: Tirttanakiri Sivakozhundeesvarar Temple
deity: Shiva as Shivakozhundhu Easwarar, with Oppila Nayaki
significance: One of the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams, the Shiva shrines sung in the Tamil Tevaram canon; this one was praised by the Nayanar Sundarar in the early medieval period.

name: Sri Sri Nilakantheswar Temple
deity: Shiva, as a lingam set in a circular laterite yoni
significance: A west-facing twentieth-century Shiva temple in the Bhimatangi neighbourhood of western Bhubaneswar, built in the Kalinga manner of the older temples of the city.

name: Tholudur Madhurantaka Choleswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the village of Tholudur in Cuddalore district, Tamil Nadu, where the presiding deity is worshipped as Madhurantaka Choleswarar.

name: Kokarneswarar Temple, Thirukokarnam
significance: A rock-cut temple excavated for the Pallava king Mahendravarman I around the middle of the 7th century, with Chola and Pandya additions early in the second millennium. Its goddess Brihadambal was the family deity of the Thondaiman rulers of Pudukkottai, and the shrine is reckoned among the oldest accurately datable stone temples still in worship.

name: Mukteshwar Mahadev Temple
deity: Shiva, as a white marble lingam in a copper yoni
significance: A cave temple on a hilltop above the Ravi about 22 km from Pathankot, on the Shahpur Kandi dam road, holding a marble lingam along with images of Ganesha, Brahma, Vishnu, Hanuman and Parvati. It is among the most visited shrines in the Pathankot area.
story: The name is explained by a tale that Shiva killed a demon here and granted him mukti, and the caves are said to have sheltered the Pandavas during their exile.

name: Srinivasa Perumal Temple, Egmore
significance: A Vishnu temple in the Egmore quarter of Chennai, formerly called the Lakshmi Narayana Perumal temple, with a three-tiered gopuram and an Anantha Vimanam over the sanctum; it is administered by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
story: Sages including Visvamitra and Gautama are said to have worshipped at this spot.

name: Ezhava Siva, Aruvippuram
significance: The Shiva installed at Aruvippuram in 1888 by the social reformer Sree Narayana Guru, who as a non-Brahmin of the Ezhava community was challenged over his right to consecrate a temple and answered that he had installed an 'Ezhava Siva'. The act became a landmark in Kerala's fight against caste exclusion from temples, and the Guru inscribed there his vision of a place where all live in brotherhood regardless of caste or religion.

name: Shree Dwadasha Jyotirlinga Temple
deity: Omkareshwara (Shiva), with replicas of the twelve Jyotirlingas
style: Mixed South Indian and North Indian
significance: A modern Shaiva complex on Omkar Hills in Bengaluru, begun in 2002 under Sri Shivapuri Mahaswamiji and consecrated in February 2011, that gathers shrines representing all twelve Jyotirlingas in one place so pilgrims can circuit them without travelling across India.

name: Tapkeshwari Temple
significance: A goddess shrine set in a valley of the Tapkeshwari hill range south of Bhuj in Kachchh, a cave-riddled range noted for its indigenous plant and animal life.

name: Vadakkan Koyikkal Devi Temple, Puthiyavila
significance: A Devi temple near Kayamkulam whose unusual two-storey sreekovil places the goddess on the ground floor and Shiva above; Bhadrakali and Ayyappan are also worshipped here, and the ten-day Kumbha Bharani with its kettukazhcha displays is the principal festival.

name: Thandu Mariamman Temple
significance: A Mariamman temple at Uppilipalayam in Coimbatore whose annual April car festival is among the larger religious gatherings of the Kongu region.
story: The goddess is said to have cured the soldiers of a Kongu Nadu ruler of chicken pox.

name: Papanasanathar Temple, Papanasam
deity: Shiva as Papanasanathar, with Parvati as Ulagammai
significance: A three-precinct Shiva temple at the foot of the Western Ghats in Tirunelveli district, founded by the Pandya king Chandrakula and enlarged by Vijayanagara and Nayak rulers in the 16th century, with a seven-tiered gateway tower within granite walls; it is run by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Endowment Board.
story: Sage Agastya, unable to reach Kailash for Shiva's wedding, is said to have been granted the sight here, Shiva appearing before him and Lopamudra in the marriage posture.

name: Penneswaraar Temple
significance: Built in 1188 by Kulottunga Chola III after his victory over the Hoysalas, this Krishnagiri-district Shiva temple carries the district's tallest rajagopuram, some forty-two inscribed stones from successive dynasties, and the largest concentration of Navakandam sculptures in Tamil Nadu.
story: Parashurama is said to have prayed to Shiva at Penneswaramadam after destroying the wicked Kshatriyas twenty-one times.

name: Vyagrapurisvarar Temple, Thiruvengaivasal
significance: A Shiva temple in Pudukkottai district whose sanctum faces west so that the evening sun falls on the deity, and which holds an unusual octagonal prakara shrine for Murugan alongside several subsidiary shrines.
story: Guided by the sage Kapila, the divine cow Kamadhenu is said to have worshipped Shiva here by pouring water from her ears and won his blessing.

name: Peddintlamma Temple, Kolletikota
significance: A 13th-century shrine on the shore of Kolleru Lake, raised by an Eastern Ganga army general in the reign of Narasingha Deva I and built in a Kalinga idiom mixed with southern design; it remains a local pilgrimage centre.
story: The general is said to have sacrificed his daughter to win a battle against a rival encampment at Kolleru, and to have built the temple over her memory when the victory came.

name: Bohra Ganesh Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple about two kilometres from central Udaipur, its east-facing image shown dancing; the name records a local practice of leaving written requests for money before the deity, the Bohra community having been the town's traditional moneylenders.

name: Raviswarapuram Siva Temple
significance: An east-facing Shiva temple at Kodungallur counted among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, recorded in Sangam literature as one of the major temples of the Chera realm; Maha Shivaratri is its main festival.
story: Local tradition holds that the sage Parashurama installed the image here.

name: Varadaraja Perumal Temple, Shoolagiri
deity: Prasanna Varadaraja Perumal (Vishnu), with Perundevi Mahalakshmi
builtDisplay: Chola sanctum; mandapa added by Krishnadevaraya (16th c.)
significance: A Vishnu temple at Shoolagiri in Krishnagiri district whose inner sanctum dates to Chola rule and whose front mandapa was added by Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara, with later contributions from Hoysala rulers and local palayakkarars.
story: The Pandavas are said to have halted here during their forest exile, Arjuna consecrating Varadaraja Perumal, with five great boulders marking their stay.

name: Valiya Koonambaikulam Temple
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; described as very ancient
significance: One of Kerala's older Bhadrakali temples, at Vadakkevila in Kollam, whose Kumbha Bharani festival draws thousands of women for the Chandra Pongal offering; the temple trust also runs an engineering college in the district.

name: Hasanamba Temple
significance: The tutelary goddess temple of Hassan, which takes its name from her, built by the local chieftain Sanjeeva Krishnappa Nayaka in Hoysala times; it is opened only once a year around Deepavali, a ghee lamp left burning inside for the months it stays shut.
story: Seven Matrikas are said to have travelled from Varanasi and stayed on for the beauty of the place, three of them — Maheshwari, Kaumari and Vaishnavi — dwelling in the anthills within the temple.

name: Badrakali Amman Temple, Sivakasi
deity: Badrakali Amman (Bhadrakali, fierce form of Parvati)
significance: The principal temple of Sivakasi, with a five-tiered gopuram some 110 feet high and a gold-plated vimana over the north-facing sanctum; its ten-day Panguni and Chithirai Pongal festivals are the town's largest, and the temple figures in accounts of the 1899 Sivakasi riots.

name: Tadkeshwar Mahadev Temple
builtDisplay: traditionally found in 1215; over 800 years old
significance: A Shiva temple on the bank of the Wanki river near Abrama in Valsad district, remarkable for a roof left deliberately open with a hole about 22 feet across so that the midday sun falls on the six-to-eight-foot semicircular lingam; fairs are held at Maha Shivaratri and through Shravan.
story: The ceiling is said to have been raised twice and lost twice, to fire and then collapse, until Shiva appeared in a devotee's dream saying 'I am Tadkeshwar Mahadev, I need the rays of the sun' — and the temple was left open to the sky.

name: Parumala Valiya Panayannarkavu Devi Temple
deity: Bhadrakali (with the Sapta Matrikas) and Shiva
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; described as very ancient
significance: Set on an island in the Pamba at Parumala, this is reckoned one of the three foremost Bhadrakali temples of Kerala and also counts among the 108 Shiva temples of the state; it is referred to in classical Malayalam literature.
story: Tradition holds that Parashurama installed the Shiva image here, and that the sages Durvasa and Narada installed the goddess in the Treta Yuga.

name: Mundayur Mahadeva Temple
significance: An east-facing Shiva temple at Anjur in Thrissur district, counted among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala; the Zamorin of Kozhikode's army is recorded as having meditated on Shiva here before going into battle. Laksharchana and Shivaratri are its main observances.
story: The image is said to have been installed by the sage Parashurama.

name: Valisvarar Temple, Sevur
deity: Shiva as Valisvarar, with Aram Valartha Nayaki
significance: A Shiva temple at Sevur in Tiruppur district, counted among the Vaippu Sthalams — shrines named in the hymns of the Tamil Saiva saints Sambandar and Sundarar; Maha Shivaratri is its main festival.
story: The site is said to have been worshipped by Vali of the Ramayana, from whom the deity takes his name.

name: Trilinga Sanghameshwara Temple
deity: Sanghameshwara Swamy (Shiva) with Parvati; three lingams
significance: A Kakatiya-period temple at Vilasagar near Vemulawada raised under Prola II, with three lingams in separate sanctums facing east, north and south beneath stepped pyramidal shikharas; it is treated as a HariHara kshetram, serving both Shaiva and Vaishnava worship.

name: Amunthirathu Devi Temple
builtDisplay: temple built 1988; worship at the site far older
style: Pandya kovil blended with Kerala tradition
significance: A Bhadrakali temple at Mudakkal north of Attingal, holding a black stone image of Amunthirathamma; the community's presence here traces to 1727, when Marthanda Varma brought Vanjipuzha madam Brahmin families from Chengannur to Thiruvananthapuram, and the present temple was built in 1988 and registered as a trust in 2005.

name: Shri Keshavraiji Temple, Bet Dwarka
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; temple registers run back some 250 years
significance: A Krishna temple on Bet Dwarka island beside the Shankh Sarovar tank, built and maintained by the Pushkarna Brahmin community, whose ishtadeva he is; its handwritten registers of visiting devotees go back roughly 250 years.

name: Makaliyam Sreeramaswamy Temple
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; attributed to the Cheras
significance: A Rama temple at Irumpanam near Kochi, attributed to Chera patronage, where Rama is venerated in his form after the slaying of Khara; largely destroyed by fire, it was rebuilt by devotees with copper-plated roofs and panchaloha Dashavatara panels and is now run by the Cochin Devaswom Board.

name: Perumparampu Sri Mahadeva Temple
significance: A centuries-old Shiva temple near Edappal in Malappuram district, counted among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, with a west-facing sanctum of the square Kukkudakruthy form; it was rebuilt in 2010 and keeps Maha Shivaratri as its chief festival.
story: The lingam is said to have been installed by the sage Parashurama.

name: Krimchi Temples
deity: Shiva, Vishnu, Ganesha and Parvati (group of shrines)
significance: A group of stone temples about 12 km from Udhampur, dated by the Archaeological Survey of India to the 8th–9th centuries and built in the Nagara idiom with rekha shikharas, panchratha plans, gavaksha ornament and pillared mandapas — among the oldest surviving temple architecture in the Jammu region.
story: Locally the group is called the Pandava Temples: Raja Kichak is said to have founded the town, and the Pandavas to have stayed here at length during their exile.

name: Ratangarh Mata Temple
significance: A goddess shrine in the forests of Datia district in Bundelkhand that draws very large Navratri crowds; a stampede on the approach during the 2013 festival killed 115 people and injured more than a hundred.
story: Local tradition holds that Samarth Ramdas, guru of Shivaji, camped here in 1666 to plan the Maratha king's escape from Agra Fort, and that Shivaji was sheltered in this jungle afterwards.

name: Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, Tithal
builtDisplay: begun 1991 (BAPS); inaugurated by Pramukh Swami Maharaj
significance: A BAPS Swaminarayan mandir standing directly on the beach at Tithal in Valsad district, begun in 1991 and inaugurated by Pramukh Swami Maharaj, with carved images of Swaminarayan alongside Shiva, Parvati, Ganesha, Krishna and Hanuman; it has become a fixture of visits to the beach.

name: Kalinka Temple
builtDisplay: present structure c. 2010; shrine centuries old
significance: A Kali shrine on a 2,090 m ridge in the Bironkhal block of Pauri Garhwal, rebuilt around 2010 with a lotus-bud shikhara and run by the Garhwal-Almora Kali Mandir Vikas Samiti, a cooperative of about a dozen surrounding villages.
story: A Badiyaari shepherd is said to have been told in a vision to raise a shrine, and to have piled up rocks into a mound on the mountain top.

name: Karkodeswarar Temple, Kamarasavalli
significance: A Shiva temple at Kamarasavalli near Thirumanur in Ariyalur district, with an east-facing sanctum, a south-facing shrine for Balambika, and the usual rajagopura, prakaram, vimana and kosta niches.
story: The serpent Karkotaka is shown in sculpture worshipping Shiva here with Vinayaka and Nandi, and those born under the sign of Cancer are said to find relief by praying at this shrine.

name: Puramundekkadu Shri Mahadeva Temple
significance: An east-facing Shiva temple at Vattamkulam near Edappal, counted both among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala and among the five Shiva temples ringing Guruvayoor; Maha Shivaratri is its main festival.
story: The image is said to have been installed by the sage Parashurama.

name: Kalamassery Mahaganapathy Temple
significance: A modern Ganesha temple founded in 1981 by N. Reghunatha Menon and rebuilt in traditional Kerala form in 2000, now run by a family trust; it is known for its Ashta Dravya Maha Ganapathy Havana and the Aanayoottu elephant feeding held at the start of Karkkidakam.

name: Javari Temple, Khajuraho
deity: Vishnu, whose broken image stands in the sanctum; the temple is also described as dedicated to Shiva
significance: A small, finely proportioned Chandela temple in the eastern group at Khajuraho, part of the UNESCO World Heritage site; it is entered through an elaborate makara torana arch, and its principal image survives only as a headless torso.

name: Irumkulangara Durga Devi Temple
significance: An old Devi temple less than two kilometres from the Padmanabhaswamy temple in Thiruvananthapuram, sharing its thanthri and historically linked to it by priests who came across the backwater by country boat; it was rebuilt in Kerala vastu form and reconsecrated in December 2009.

name: Agroha Dham
deity: Mahalakshmi, with shrines to Saraswati and Maharaja Agrasena
significance: A modern pilgrimage complex at Agroha, the town the Agrawal community holds to be its place of origin, built between 1976 and 1984 by the Agroha Vikas Trust after a national Aggarwal convention resolved on it; the historic settlement declined after its capture in 1194.

name: Jarai-ka-Math
significance: A red sandstone panchayatana temple at Barua Sagar near Jhansi, ascribed to the Gurjara-Pratihara emperor Mihira Bhoja around 860 and protected by the Archaeological Survey of India since 1928; its main image is lost, leaving only the pedestal and a jewelled stone foot, and its walls carry sculpture often compared with Khajuraho.

name: Kalikambal Temple
significance: A temple on Thambu Chetty Street in old George Town, moved to its present site on 1 March 1640 when the English East India Company built Fort St George over its original seashore location, with construction continuing to 1678; Shivaji is recorded as having worshipped here on 3 October 1677, and its rajagopuram was added between 1976 and 1983.
story: The goddess is said to have been worshipped here first in a fierce form, which Adi Shankara replaced with the serene Kamakshi.

name: Kalikamba Temple
significance: A temple on Lower Car Street in Mangalore closely associated with the Vishwakarma Brahmana community of smiths and carpenters; its sanctums were rebuilt in granite in 2000, and it holds a ten-day Ugadi festival and a mass upanayana every five years.

name: Kalika Siva Temple
deity: Shiva, as a lingam in a circular yonipitha
significance: A small medieval sandstone shrine of about four metres beside the Manikarnika tank embankment just outside the Kapilesvara temple compound in Bhubaneswar; still in worship, it was repaired by Odisha State Archaeology and is looked after by the Kapilesvara Trust Board.

name: Hanuman Tok
significance: A hilltop Hanuman shrine about 11 km above Gangtok at some 2,195 m, raised over a sacred stone by the administrator Appaji Pant in 1950 and completed in 1952; the Indian Army later took over the surrounding land and maintains it, and it commands a wide view of the Kangchenjunga range.
story: Hanuman is said to have set down to rest at this spot while carrying the Sanjeevani herb from Dunagiri to revive Lakshmana.

name: Kadeshwari Devi Temple
deity: Kadeshwari, the mother goddess as Shakti
significance: A goddess temple on the headland behind Bandra Fort at Land's End in Mumbai; the municipal corporation moved in 2006 to build a protective bund after the sea began eating away its foundations and boundary walls.

name: Kalabhairavi Temple
deity: Chamunda, four-armed and seated on a corpse
significance: A twelfth-century shrine inside the Jaleswar Siva temple precinct at Kalarahanga in Bhubaneswar, attributed to King Madhusudhan Deva and guarded by Shaiva dvarapalas; still in worship, it was repaired by the state archaeology department.

name: Jyotir Math
deity: Narayana, with the goddess as Purnagiri
significance: The northern of the four cardinal pithams traditionally established by Adi Shankara, seat of the Shankaracharya of the north at Joshimath in Garhwal; it stood vacant for some 165 years until Brahmananda Saraswati was installed on 11 May 1941 and built the present thirty-room monastery and the Purnagiri Devi shrine.

name: Harihara Deula
deity: Shiva and Vishnu, as the twin Siddhesvara and Nilamadhava shrines
significance: A pair of twin temples at Gandharadi on the Mahanadi in Boudh district, built by the Somavamshi kings in the late tenth century, one holding a shivalinga and the other a four-armed chlorite Vishnu; the pairing is read as a statement of Shaiva-Vaishnava accord and marks a formative stage of Kalinga architecture.

name: Kadampanad Bhagavathy Temple
significance: A Bhagavathy temple at Kadampanad about 12 km from Adoor, managed by karayogam unit 232 of the Nair Service Society; its ten-day festival in Meenam ends with an aaraattu procession accompanied by caparisoned elephants.

name: Kadri Manjunath Temple
builtDisplay: 10th-11th c. origin; rebuilt in stone 14th c.
significance: A major Mangalore temple that grew out of the Buddhist Kadarika Vihara, keeping a metre-and-a-half bronze Lokeshwara installed by the Alupa king Kundavarma and dated by inscription to 968; the shrine was rebuilt entirely in stone in the 14th century and carries inscriptions in Tulu, Kannada and Malayalam.
story: Parashurama is said to have done penance at Kadali Kshetra, where Shiva appeared to him as Manjunatha with Parvati.

name: Perakam Mahadeva Temple
significance: One of the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala and among the oldest in Thrissur district, at Perakam village, with a round sreekovil set within a nalambalam alongside a thidappalli and mandapam. Maha Shivaratri is its chief festival.
story: Folklore holds that the sage Parashurama installed the Shiva image at Perakam.

name: Deulajhari
significance: An old Shaiva centre in Athmallik subdivision, Angul district, where the Siddheswar Baba temple stands within some 24 acres of native pandanus forest. Twenty-four hot springs survive on the site, out of eighty-four recorded there in the past.

name: EME Temple
significance: A temple built in February 1966 on the Indian Army's EME School campus at Vadodara under its first commandant, Brigadier A. F. Eugene, its aluminium geodesic dome following Buckminster Fuller's design. It draws architectural motifs from six faiths as a statement of Indian secularism and holds 108 stone sculptures dated between about 600 and 1600 CE.

name: Madhav Govind Rameshwar Temple
significance: A trikutachala shrine at Agapur in Ponda taluka, Goa, whose three sanctums hold Vaishnava and Shaiva deities together.

name: Ramnathi Temple
significance: A Goud Saraswat Brahmin temple at Bandora in Ponda, moved here from Loutolim in 1566 to save it from destruction under Portuguese rule and largely rebuilt in 1905. It follows the panchayatana arrangement with five shrines, the older Betal and Kalbhairav structures having been kept from before the rebuilding; the temple marked 450 years on the site in May 2011.
story: The lineage of the deity is traced to Rama, who is said to have installed a Shivalinga at Rameswaram in expiation for the killing of the brahmin Ravana.

name: Kandiyoor Sree Mahadeva Temple
significance: Completed in 823 under Rajasekhara Varman and rebuilt in 1218 by Rama Kotha Varma of Odanad, this is the earliest Kerala temple whose origin is fixed by an epigraph. It is one of the 108 great Shiva temples of Kerala and has a two-tiered rectangular sanctum.
story: The sage Mrikandu is said to have found an image of Shiva in his Kiratamurthy form while bathing in the Ganga, and to have installed it on the bank of the Achankovil.

name: Poonkunnam Siva Temple
deity: Shiva (as Paramasivan), with Parvati in the same sanctum
significance: A small Shiva temple in the Punkunnam suburb of Thrissur, unusual in housing Parvati within the same sanctum, with further shrines to Ganapathi, Ayyappan, Krishna and the nagas. It is administered by the Cochin Devaswom Board and keeps Maha Shivaratri as its main festival.

name: Chittaranjan Park Kali Mandir
significance: Begun in 1973 as a Shiva shrine on a hillock at the edge of Delhi's Bengali colony, with the Kali temple added in 1984 and terracotta ornament worked between 2006 and 2009. Its Durga Puja, held since 1977, is among the largest in Delhi, and the complex also runs a Bengali library, language classes and an idol-making atelier.

name: Bannari Mariamman Temple
significance: One of the most prominent Mariamman temples in South India, at Bannari near Sathyamangalam in the Erode district foothills. Its Kundam festival in Panguni draws hundreds of thousands of pilgrims and is marked by a local holiday across the district.
story: Herders are said to have noticed a cow letting down her milk each day beneath a vengai tree, and on digging there found a self-manifested form of the goddess.

name: Choorakkottukavu Bhagavathy Temple
significance: A goddess temple in Thrissur that takes part in the Thrissur Pooram each year, its deity setting out for the Vadakkumnathan temple with a single elephant and nadaswaram and building to a procession of fourteen elephants with pandi melam.

name: Sirsi Marikamba Temple
deity: Marikamba, a fierce form of Durga
significance: Built by the townspeople of Sirsi in 1688 and decorated with kaavi murals, a now-vanished coastal Konkan technique. Gandhi's refusal to enter it in 1934 over animal sacrifice led to a local campaign that ended the practice, and its biennial Sirsi Jathre is reckoned South India's largest fair.
story: The seven-foot image of the goddess is said to have been recovered from a pond on the road to Hangal.

name: Siddha Bhairavi Temple
significance: A Shakta temple near Berhampur built in 1937 around a roughly carved one-legged, four-armed image of Bhairavi turned up by a plough in a nearby field. Its precinct holds 108 subsidiary shrines, including the twelve jyotirlingas, Vaishno Devi, the Dashavatara and Jagannath with his siblings.
story: Devotees hold that Bhairavi will ride out with the Kalki avatar at the close of the Kali Yuga to restore dharma.

name: Patnadevi Temple
significance: A Yadava-period complex in the Gautala Autramghat sanctuary, with the Chandika Devi shrine built in 1128 and the group finished by 1150 under Yadavrao Kheunchandra and Govindraj Mourya. The goddess is the kuladevata of many communities, and the mathematician Bhaskara II is said to have written the Siddhanta Shiromani at an ashram here.

name: Cherai Gowreeshwara Temple
significance: A Murugan temple in the coastal village of Cherai on Vypin island, north of Kochi, built in the traditional Kerala manner.

name: Khatu Shyam Temple
significance: One of Rajasthan's busiest pilgrimage centres, drawing millions each year and especially at the Falgun Mela; tradition credits its founding in 1027 to the local ruler Roop Singh Chauhan. Durga Das Mathur composed the devotional Shyam Pacchisi here in 1675, and the Battle of Khatu Shyamji was fought nearby in 1779.
story: Barbarika, grandson of Bhima, is said to have given up his head before the Mahabharata war, and Krishna blessed him to be worshipped under his own name Shyam through the Kali Yuga.

name: Parasuramalingeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the Ayanavaram neighbourhood of Chennai, where the god is worshipped in lingam form with the goddess Parvathambigai.

name: Sreekanteswaram Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the heart of Thiruvananthapuram, reckoned more than seven centuries old and run by the Travancore Devaswom Board; the older Pazhaya Sreekanteswaram temple is held to be the deity's original seat. Its ten-day festival falls in Dhanu, with the arattu on Thiruvathira day.
story: An elderly sweeper from the old Sreekanteswaram temple is said to have rested at this spot, received a vision of Shiva, and found the self-manifested lingam there.

name: Marudhamalai Temple
significance: A hilltop Murugan temple northwest of Coimbatore, regarded as the god's seventh abode and reached by a ghat road or some 837 steps. The medieval saint Arunagirinathar sang of it in the Thiruppugal, and a cave shrine to Pambatti Siddhar adjoins it.

name: Padanayarkulangara Mahadeva Temple
significance: One of the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, standing on the Pallikkal river at Karunagappally, a town once held by the Ay dynasty and later by Odanad and Travancore. Maha Shivaratri is its principal festival.
story: Shiva and Krishna are said to have passed through this forest together; Krishna was taken with the spot and settled there, and Shiva, finding him, sat down beside him and hallowed the place.

name: Shree Kaleshwara Temple
significance: A Konkan Shiva temple at Nerur in Sindhudurg district, built around a naturally formed lingam in its sanctum. Its five-day Mahashivaratri festival, when the deity is drawn in a chariot, brings visitors from well beyond the district.
story: A brahmin is said to have found the natural lingam buried at this spot, and the temple was raised to enshrine it.

name: Somabara Mandapa
deity: Vishnu (with Jagannath, Balabhadra, Subhadra and Buddha)
significance: A 15th-century laterite Vishnu shrine with vimana and frontal porch, standing inside the Kapilesvara temple precinct at Bhubaneswar. It was restored by Odisha State Archaeology and is kept by the Kapilesvara Temple Trust Board, observing Janmashtami, Radhashtami and Dola Purnima.

name: Evoor Major Sri Krishnaswamy Temple
deity: Krishna in the Prayoga Chakra form
significance: A Krishna temple near Haripad whose four-armed image, holding conch, discus and butter, is worshipped in the rare Prayoga Chakra form. The sanctum burned down and the present structure was raised in the 19th century under Moolam Thirunal; its raktha-pushpanjali offering is not made at other Vishnu temples.
story: The site is traced to the burning of the Khandava forest, when Arjuna's arrow fell here - giving the place its name Eythoor, later Evoor - and Krishna is said to have consecrated the image while Arjuna made the first offering.

name: Ghuisarnath Temple
significance: A Shaiva temple on the bank of the Sai river in Pratapgarh district, about 45 km from the district town, which its devotees identify with the Ghushmeshwar jyotirlinga named in the Koti Rudra Samhita of the Shiva Purana.
story: The Shiva Purana tells of Ghushma, who made and immersed a hundred and one lingas daily; when her jealous sister-in-law killed her son and Shiva restored him, the god stayed on as a jyotirlinga bearing her name.

name: Anna Nagar Ayyappan Koil
significance: Founded by the Sri Ayyappa Seva Samajam, formed in 1976 out of the vilakku pooja gatherings of Shanti Colony, and consecrated on 13 May 1984 by a former chief priest of Sabarimala. Built to shastraic rule in Kerala style with a west-facing sanctum, it won the Mylapore Academy award for best-maintained temple in Chennai in 1998.

name: Shantadurga Kalangutkarin Temple
significance: The goddess was carried from Calangute to Nanoda in the 17th century to escape the forced conversions of Portuguese Goa; the present temple was finished in 1905 and rebuilt in marble in the 1990s. She is the patron deity of ninety-six Kulee families of Marathas, Kalavants, Bhandaris and Rajapur Saraswat Brahmins.
story: When Shiva and Vishnu fought, Brahma is said to have appealed to Parvati, who came between them as Shantadurga with Vishnu at her right hand and Shiva at her left, and is shown holding two serpents for the two gods.

name: Swaminarayan Mandir, Vadtal
deity: Lakshmi Narayan (with Radha-Krishna, and Vasudev, Dharma and Bhakti)
significance: Built in fifteen months on land given by the devotee Joban Pagi, at Swaminarayan's own direction and under the architect Brahmanand Swami, and finished on 3 November 1824. Its nine-domed lotus plan and carved wooden pillars house the Laxminarayan Dev Gadi, the southern seat of the Swaminarayan movement; Gandhi spoke here in January 1921.
story: Swaminarayan is remembered as having played Holi in the eastern garden and swung on a twelve-door swing here, and as having had the Gomati lake dug, preaching the Vachanamrit on its bank.

name: Sarkaradevi Temple
significance: A Bhadrakali temple in Chirayinkeezhu that became one of South India's best-known goddess shrines after Marthanda Varma instituted its Kaliyoot festival in 1748. The nine-day Kaliyoot enacts the birth of Bhadrakali and her fight with the demon Darika, and the Ponnara family still oversees the festival.
story: Marthanda Varma is said to have vowed the Kaliyoot to the goddess if she granted him victory over Kayamkulam, and to have kept the promise after winning the war.

name: New Swaminarayan Temple, Bhuj
significance: Raised by the Nar Narayan Dev Gadi on five acres after the 1824 temple was destroyed in the 2001 Gujarat earthquake, at a cost of about a billion rupees. Its throne, domes and doors are of gold and its pillars and ceilings of carved marble; the nine-day inauguration in May 2010 drew some half a million visitors.

name: Puthiyakavu Devi Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Ponkunnam in Kottayam district that serves as a resting place for pilgrims on their way to Sabarimala.

name: Saraswathi Kshetramu, Ananthasagar
significance: Founded on 2 May 1980 by the ashtavadhani scholar Astakala Narasimha Rama Sharma in the Shivaru hills near Siddipet, and reckoned the third major Saraswati temple in India after those at Vaishno Devi and Basar. It is said to be the first to show the goddess standing.

name: Prathyangira Devi Temple, Sholinganallur
deity: Maha Prathyangira Devi in her Shanta (peaceful) form
significance: One of the few temples anywhere dedicated to Prathyangira, and said to be the only one enshrining her peaceful Shanta form; it stands between the Buckingham Canal and the Bay of Bengal in south Chennai. Devotees seek the goddess as a counter to witchcraft, and free homas are performed on special occasions.

name: Kuttankulangara Sri Krishna Temple
significance: A Thrissur temple more than three centuries old whose Krishna, in the Santanagopala form, is petitioned by couples seeking children. Its January-February utsavam includes the Pannivetta, in which a model pig is shot down at the foot of the banyan tree.

name: Mayannur Kavu Sri Kurumba Bagavathy Temple
significance: A kavu, or sacred grove shrine, at Mayannur in Thrissur district dedicated to the goddess Sri Kurumba Bhagavathi.

name: Sharana Basaveshwara Temple
significance: The principal shrine of Kalaburagi in north-eastern Karnataka, honouring the Lingayat teacher Sharana Basavappa and the Virashaiva ideals of dasoha (giving as earning) and kayaka (labour as worship).

name: Pariyur Kondathu Kaliamman Temple
significance: A well-known Amman temple at Pariyur near Gobichettipalayam whose present structure, with a five-tier main gopuram, was raised in the mid-1950s; its foundation date is unknown. The place takes its name from the Tamil chieftain Vel Pari.
story: The goddess is credited with the prosperity of Vel Pari's reign, one of the seven legendary patrons of Tamil tradition.

name: Nagsankar Mandir
significance: A Shiva temple east of Tezpur said to have been founded in the 4th century by King Narasankar of Nagakha. Its tank shelters more than 500 rare soft-shell turtles of vulnerable and endangered species.

name: Pataleshwar Cave Temple, Pune
significance: An 8th-century monolithic rock-cut Shaiva temple of the Rashtrakuta period in northern Pune, completed around 750 CE. Its three sanctums, probably first meant for Brahma, Shiva and Vishnu, now hold Parvati, the original Shiva linga and Ganesha.

name: Velloor Perunthatta Siva Temple
significance: A Shaiva temple at Velloor near Thalayolaparambu in Kottayam district, with the east-facing Shiva shrine in its own sanctum; it is counted among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala.
story: Tradition holds that the sage Parashurama installed the deity here.

name: Belha Devi Temple
deity: Belha Mata (local form of the Devi)
significance: A living Shakta shrine on the bank of the Sai river in Bela Pratapgarh, from which the town takes its name. The present main temple was built between 1811 and 1815 by Raja Pratap Bahadur Singh of Awadh.
story: Rama is said to have worshipped the goddess here during his forest exile.

name: Anandeshwaram Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Pandanad in Chengannur taluk, Alappuzha district. The original shrine stood on the bank of the Pampa and was destroyed when the river shifted course, after which the deity was moved to the present site nearby.

name: Bhuteshwar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Jind built by Raghbir Singh, set beside a large tank that gives it the local name Rani Talab. It is one of the stations on the 48 kos parikrama of Kurukshetra.

name: Nageshvara-Chennakeshava Temple complex, Mosale
significance: A twin temple complex about 10 km south of Hassan pairing a Shiva shrine with a Vishnu shrine of matching design. Its style places it before 1250 CE, and one scholar dates it to about 1200, in the reign of the Hoysala king Veera Ballala II.

name: Mannanthala Anandavaleeswaram Temple
significance: A temple in the Mannanthala suburb of Thiruvananthapuram whose goddess was formerly worshipped as Bhadrakali with animal sacrifice. Sree Narayana Guru ended the practice and reconsecrated the shrine, directing that the deity be worshipped as Parvati; Vinayaka, Subramanya and Nagaraja have subsidiary shrines.

name: Mailar Mallanna Temple
deity: Khandoba (Mailar Mallanna, a form of Shiva)
significance: A 15th-century Vijayanagara-period temple at Khanapur, about 15 km from Bidar on the Udgir road, dedicated to Khandoba in his Kannada form Mailar Mallanna.
story: Khandoba as Martanda Bhairava is said to have slain the demons Mallasura and Manikasura; the dying Malla gave up his white horse and asked that his spirit abide in every shrine of the god.

name: Mazhuvannur Maha Siva Kshethram
significance: A Shiva temple at Tharuvana in the Wayanad hills, some 800 m above sea level, which also houses Arayil Bhagavathy, Durga, Nandi, Ayyappa and Ganapathi. Its name means the place where the axe fell.
story: Shiva is said to have hurled his axe at Krishna during their quarrel over Banasura's kingdom; where it fell, Parashurama built this temple.

name: Meenkulathi Temple
significance: A Meenakshi temple at Pallassana in Palakkad district, whose present shrine and adjoining tank took shape over some four centuries. Its walls are set so that their shadow never falls on the ground.
story: A stone carried from Chidambaram by the Veerasaiva Mannadiar clan is said to have become immovable when set down under a palm-leaf umbrella here, taken as a sign that Meenakshi had chosen the spot.

name: Thanjavur Nisumbasuthani Temple
significance: A Shakta temple on Poomal Ravuthan Kovil Street in the East Gate quarter of Thanjavur, whose goddess Nisumbasuthani is also called Vada Badrakali. The Thiruvalangadu copper plates record its establishment in the Chola period, and it is among the temples of the Thanjavur Palace Devasthanam.

name: Pasupatheesvarar Temple, Pasupathikovil
significance: A Shaiva temple 14 km from Thanjavur on the Kumbakonam road, its foundation attributed to the early Chola king Kochchenganan and its sculpture including work of the Thanjavur Nayak period.
story: Varahi is said to have worshipped here for deliverance from the asuras and Kamadhenu to have done penance at the shrine, which is why the goddess is called Palvalanayaki, worshipped by the cow.

name: Kotasattemma Temple, Nidadavolu
significance: A pilgrimage temple at Nidadavolu whose image dates from the Chalukya period and is attributed to Chalukya Veerabadhra. Lost and buried after upheavals in the Reddy period, the idol was recovered in 1934 by Devulapalli Rama Murthy Sastri, who built the present temple on his land.

name: Sri Ramakrishna Math, Lucknow
deity: Sri Ramakrishna, with Sarada Devi and Vivekananda
style: Eclectic (Hindu, Buddhist, Rajput and Christian elements)
significance: The Lucknow centre of the Ramakrishna Mission, opened on 2 February 1987 on 4.86 acres granted by Chandrabhanu Gupta, the first chief minister of Uttar Pradesh. Its shrine holds images of Ramakrishna, Sarada Devi and Vivekananda, and its design blends several Indian and European idioms.
story: During a period of communal tension devotees hurriedly raised a small Shiva shrine on the grounds, which came to be regarded as a remover of obstacles.

name: Thirumeignanam Gnanaparameswarar Temple
significance: A Shaiva temple at Thirumeignanam in Thanjavur district, also known as Tirunallur Mayaanam, whose deity Gnanaparameswarar is praised in a hymn of Tirugnanasambandar.

name: Thrikkunnathu Mahadeva Temple
significance: An old Shiva temple at Kanjany in Thrissur district, on the Thrissur-Triprayar road, with a separate Vishnu shrine in the same complex. It is counted among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala.
story: Folklore credits the sage Parashurama with installing the temple's image.

name: Chinakkathoor Temple
significance: A Bhagavathi temple at Palappuram near Ottapalam with two shrines, the Thazhekavu below and the older Melakavu above, and a Ganapati shrine beside a great banyan. The upper shrine is served by priests of the Kulangara Nair family while Namboothiris officiate below and during the ten-day pooram.

name: Ketakeshwar Dewal
significance: A Shiva temple at Ketakibari near Tezpur said to hold one of the largest Shiva lingams anywhere. The site falls into two parts, the lingam where it now stands and its original base a little away.
story: An earthquake is said to have torn the lingam from its base and set it down where it rests today.

name: Chandramauleshwara Temple, Unkal
significance: An 11th-century temple at Unkal in Hubballi built by Bommanna Dandanayaka in the Kalyana Chalukya period, laid out on a square cross plan of the sandhara type described in the Sanskrit architectural texts. Now a monument of national importance under the Archaeological Survey of India, it carries sculpture drawn from Shaiva, Vaishnava and Shakta traditions.

name: Chari Sambhu Temple
deity: Nilamadhava (Vishnu) and Sidheswar (Shiva), in twin shrines
builtDisplay: 8th c. (ASI); extended under the Bhanjas in the 9th
significance: Twin temples of black granite on the bank of the Mahanadi at Gandharadi in Boudh district, dated by the Archaeological Survey of India to the 8th century and enlarged in the 9th under the Bhanja rulers of Khinjali mandala. One shrine holds Nilamadhava and the other Sidheswar, an unusual Vishnu-Shiva pairing, and the pair is protected by the ASI.

name: Baba Keenaram Sthal
deity: Baba Keenaram, founder of the Aghori order of Shaivism
significance: The headquarters and principal pilgrimage centre of the Aghori order of Shaivism, at Ravindrapuri in Varanasi, built around the seat of Baba Keenaram who founded the sect. Maha Shivaratri is its chief observance.

name: Chaturbhuj Temple, Khajuraho
deity: Vishnu, as a four-armed image 2.7 m high
significance: A Chandela temple of about 1100 CE in the village of Jatakari, south of the main Khajuraho group and also called the Jatakari temple, part of the Khajuraho Group of Monuments inscribed by UNESCO in 1986. Built as a sanctum without ambulatory with vestibule, mandapa and entrance porch, it is the one Khajuraho temple with no erotic sculpture, and its 2.7-metre four-armed Vishnu is among the finest images at the site.

name: Ayikudi Balasubramanya Swami Temple
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; roofed in stone c. 1931
significance: A Murugan temple on the bank of the Hanumannathi at Ayikudi, raised over the samadhi of the Brahmin ascetic Mugura Bhakthar. The area lay under Travancore until 1947 and the temple has been managed by the Thiruvadhankur royal family for about a century and a half; its roof of coconut and palm leaf was replaced around 1931.
story: The image is said to have been found in the Mallam river by a devotee named Mallan, and the child Murugan is believed to come down to the river steps to share payasam with the other children.

name: Chenraya Perumal Temple
significance: A Vishnu temple at Adhiyamankottam, about 7 km from Dharmapuri on the Salem road, held to have been built by Hoysala and Vijayanagara rulers, most notably Krishnadevaraya. It is a monument of national importance under the Archaeological Survey of India, listed as N-TN-C18.

name: Kodungoor Devi Temple
significance: A Devi temple at Kodungoor in Kottayam district reckoned to be more than two centuries old. Once the private shrine of the Madathil family, it is now administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board, and in March 2023 it held a women's festival with a parade of female elephants.

name: Babulnath Temple
deity: Shiva, as Babulnath, lord of the babul tree
significance: One of the oldest temples in Mumbai, standing on a hillock above Girgaum Chowpatty, where Shiva is worshipped as the lord of the babul tree. The temple banned plastic bags on its premises in 2010.

name: Chirakkadavu Sree Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple about 32 km east of Kottayam and 3 km south of Ponkunnam, reckoned a thousand years old, whose lingam is held to be swayambhu and was found beneath a bilva tree. The village takes its name from the chira, or pond, on its eastern side.
story: A king who built his ashram by the bilva tree and performed austerities there is said to have had the Lord appear to him in a dream; he continued his penance and passed to heaven, remembered as Kuwala Maharshi.

name: Chathannoor Sree Bhoothanatha Temple
significance: A temple to Bhoothanathar at Chathannoor in Kollam district that hosts one of the largest temple festivals in the district. Its Nedum Kuthira, raised jointly with the Meenadu Sastha temple, is among the biggest of its kind in Kollam.

name: Chateshwar Temple
significance: A pancharatha Shiva temple at Kishinapur near Salipur in Cuttack district, built by Vishnu, a minister of the Ganga king Anangabhima Deva III, whose inscription is preserved at the site. Loose Shaiva and Shakta sculptures of the Eastern Ganga period survive in the precinct, and Dola Purnima, Mahashivaratri and Kartik Purnima are among its festivals.

name: Sree Shivashakthi Mahaganapathi Temple
significance: A temple at Keezhammakam in Chenkal panchayat, southern Thiruvananthapuram district, holding Shiva, Parvati and Ganapati together. Ganesh Chaturthi is its chief festival, with further observances from Chithra Pournami and at Maha Shivaratri.

name: Sri Laxmi Venkatesh Temple
significance: A Goud Saraswat Brahmin temple at Kanhangad in Kasaragod district, affiliated to the Kashi Math, whose consecration rites began in 1864 and concluded on Akshaya Tritiya in 1865. It was founded at the instance of Srimad Bhuvanendra Tirtha with the support of the four Chowguli families.
story: The image is said to have come from Innoli, whose community could not sustain the offerings, and the swami is remembered as asking the god to accept whatever naivedya the people of Kanhangad could give and to return four times the blessing.

name: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Temple, Thalassery
significance: A Goud Saraswat Brahmin temple of the Dvaita tradition at Thalassery, built in 1831 on the site of an older shrine after the merchant Devdas Bhandari gave the Lakshmi Narasimha image early in the nineteenth century. It also holds Kodanda Rama and Venkataramana, has a three-tiered simhasana, and unusually faces north; it was consecrated by Sumatheendra Tirtha, fifteenth pontiff of the Kashi Math.

name: Sree Venugopala Krishna Swami Devasthan
significance: A Krishna temple at Chendamangalam in Ernakulam district, founded by settled Goud Saraswat Brahmin families under Chennoth Parambil Dasa Prabhu on land given by the Paliath Valiyachan of the Paliyam house, with the pratishta performed on 30 April 1900.
