It keeps a stone principal image with a separate utsava murti and figures of Garuda and Hanuman, and its six-day festival falls in Vaisakha.

name: Andalurkavu
significance: A very old kavu near Dharmadam by Thalassery in Kannur district, where Rama is worshipped as Daivathaar with Lakshmana as Angakkaran and Hanuman as Bappuran, and which is closely tied to the Thiyya community. A small bow and arrow is offered in the name of every Thiyya boy born in the four surrounding regions, giving it the byname Andalure Aayiram Ville, the thousand bows of Andalur.

name: Vethalan Kavu Mahadeva Temple
significance: A temple near Kayamkulam in Alappuzha district described as one of the very few anywhere in which Shiva is worshipped in the form of Vethala. Its chief observances fall on the last Friday of Makaram, at Shivaratri and at Vishu.

name: Neelkanth Mahadev Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the Garhwal hills about 32 km from Rishikesh whose shikhara is built in a tiered pyramidal Pandya manner unusual for the region, credited to a sadhu named Mekh Chand. Fairs are held at Maha Shivaratri and Shraavana Shivaratri, when kanwariyas walk up from Haridwar.
story: The site is held to be where Shiva swallowed the Halahala poison churned up from the ocean at the Samudra Manthan, which turned his throat blue.

name: Yelahanka Gate Anjaneya Temple
significance: A Hanuman temple built in the 1680s by Kempegowda, the founder of Bangalore, and named for the Yelahanka gate of the Bangalore Fort beside which it stood.

name: Sri Sri Kalika Maharani Temple
significance: A modern Kali temple at Chira Chas in Bokaro raised between July 2010 and July 2012 by Aashiyaan Estate Developers at the initiative of Shivananda Sinha. Laid out on a pentagonal lotus plan with five petal-shaped entrances, it runs over 160 feet long under a 90-foot stupa, with a prayer hall of more than 4,000 square feet in the basement.
story: Devotees hold that the goddess grants the wishes of those who pray here, and a cobra found during the digging of the foundations was taken as an auspicious sign of Shiva.

name: Vijayanatheswarar Temple, Thiruvijayamangai
significance: A Shiva temple 11 km from Kumbakonam in Thanjavur district, built by the medieval Cholas in the architectural idiom of their period and counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams hymned in the Tevaram. The goddess here is Mangalanayaki, with subsidiary shrines to Ganesha, Dakshinamurthy, Surya and Chandra.
story: The temple marks the Mahabharata episode in which Arjuna sought the Pasupata weapon: he and Shiva, disguised as a hunter, both shot the demon Mookasura and quarrelled over the kill until Shiva revealed himself and granted the weapon.

name: Bhavanarayana Temple, Bapatla
builtDisplay: 15th c.; foundation credited to Kubja Vishnuvardhana
significance: The temple that gives Bapatla its name, whose foundation the article credits to the Vengi Chalukya ruler Kubja Vishnuvardhana, who took the title Paramabhagavata for it. It is a centrally protected monument of national importance and carries inscriptions in Telugu, Tamil and Sanskrit.

name: Thalassery Jagannatha Temple
significance: Consecrated by the social reformer Sree Narayana Guru in 1908 at the invitation of Varathoor Kaniyil Kunhikannan of Thalassery, this shrine became a landmark of the movement to open temple worship to the Thiyya community. A statue of the Guru was added to the compound in 1927.
story: The Guru is said to have seen his own statue at Colombo while it was still in transit from Italy to the temple.

name: Baba Garib Sthan Mandir (Garibnath Temple)
significance: The principal Shiva temple of Muzaffarpur, popularly called the Deoghar of Bihar for the crowds it draws during Shravan. Its lingam is said to have come to light when a stand of peepal trees on the site was felled.
story: When the trees were cut a blood-red substance is said to have flowed from them, a great lingam was uncovered, and Baba appeared in the landowner's dream directing that worship continue there.

name: Anandavalleeswaram Temple, Kollam
deity: Shiva as Ananda Swaroopan (with Parvati as Anandavally)
significance: An 11th-century temple in Kollam city, one of the 108 famous Shiva temples of Kerala, whose teak sanctum is reckoned some 1,200 years old. The article notes it as the only Indian temple to hold Krishna, Maha Vishnu, Bhoomi Devi and Lakshmi Devi consecrated together under one roof.
story: Folklore credits the sage Parashurama with installing the Shiva idol, and the name is explained from anandam, joy, the state in which god and goddess are held to dwell here.

name: Vahisvaramudayar Temple, Malayadipatti
significance: A rock-cut cave shrine at Malayadipatti in Kulathur taluk, attributed to Kuvaavan Satthan around 730 CE and carrying an inscription of the Pallava king Nandivarman (775–826 CE). It is one of a twin pair of cave temples at the site, the other dedicated to Vishnu.

name: Panayur Palur Shiva Temple
significance: One of the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, standing near Vaniyamkulam in Palakkad district. Its east-facing square sanctum is built in the kukkudakruthi form, and Maha Shivaratri is its principal festival.
story: Folklore counts it among the shrines whose idol was installed by the sage Parashurama.

name: Anjumoorthy Temple
significance: A temple at Anjumoorthy Mangalam in Palakkad district whose presiding deity is Sudarshana, set in a compound of five structures. Its age is given inconsistently in the sources, from about five hundred to about fifteen hundred years.

name: Tirunettur Mahadeva Temple
deity: Shiva as Sri Parameswara (with Maha Vishnu as Vaikundeswara)
significance: A 5.5-acre temple compound at Vyttila in Ernakulam district holding separate east-facing Shiva and Vishnu shrines. It is reckoned one of the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, and the Vishnu shrine is said to have been added at the suggestion of Vilwamangalam Swamiyar.
story: The Shiva shrine is counted among the 108 that the sage Parashurama is held to have established across Kerala.

name: Pamani Naganathar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Pamani, historically Tiru Padaleswaram, counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams and sung by Sambandar, Sundarar and Appar in the Tevaram. It serves as a Rahu–Ketu parihara sthalam, with its remedial rites performed on Fridays and Sundays.

name: Nagore Naganathaswamy Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Nagore with a rajagopuram and an inner prakaram carrying shrines to Rahu, Dakshinamurti, Vinayaka and Murugan; it is one of the serpent-associated Shiva shrines of the Kaveri delta, and Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham and Karthika Deepam are observed here.
story: The sthala purana holds that Vasuki and other sacred serpents came to worship at this and three other snake temples, and that the deity appeared here as a self-manifested lingam beneath a punnai tree; townspeople say snakes do not bite anyone in Nagore.

name: Sri Pandi Muneeswarar Temple
deity: Pandi Muneeswarar, identified with the Pandya king Nedunchezhiyan
significance: A folk-deity temple at Melamadai in Madurai, popularly known as Pandi Kovil, still maintained by descendants of the Muthuraiyar family who founded it.
story: It is said that Valliammal and Periyasamy unearthed an image eight feet down near Mattuthavani after a bearded sage appeared in a dream declaring himself Pandyan Nedunchezhiyan, doing penance for the injustice done to Kovalan; the temple was raised where the image was found.

name: Patcheeswarar Temple
significance: A Pallava-period Shiva temple at Cheyyar with an east-facing five-tiered rajagopuram, a sanctum with antarala and maha mandapam, a Nataraja Sabha holding bronzes, and shrines to Parvati, Vinayaka, Murugan, Garuda, Gajalakshmi and the Nalvar.
story: The name is explained by the tradition that Garuda, the eagle mount of Vishnu, worshipped Shiva at this spot.

name: Betrayaswamy Temple
deity: Vishnu (Betrayaswamy / Devaperumal), with Lakshmi as Soundaryavalli
significance: A Vishnu temple at Denkanikottai in the Tamil Nadu-Karnataka border country, built in the Hoysala idiom with a five-tiered rajagopuram; the Wodeyars of Mysore endowed its major shrines and pillared halls in the 16th century.
story: The Skanda Purana account here has Venkateswara appearing to the sage Kanva to save him from the yaksha Devandagadagan, taking the form of a hunter and killing the yaksha with a mace called Denkani, from which the town takes its name.

name: Kothandaramar Temple, Thillaivilagam
deity: Rama (Kothandaramar), with Sita, Lakshmana and Hanuman
significance: One of the five Pancha Rama Kshetrams of Tiruvarur district and among the 108 Abhimana Kshetrams of the Vaishnava tradition, noted for a four-foot standing Hanuman and for fine carving on the image of Rama.

name: Kollam Rameswaram Mahadeva Temple
significance: A 12th-century Shiva temple at Thangassery attributed to an order of the Chera ruler Rama Kulasekhara, counted among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala; it has a rectangular sanctum with stone and wood carving, a copper flagstaff, two towers and two recorded inscriptions.
story: The sage Parasurama is held in tradition to be its founder.

name: Talupulamma Temple, Lova
significance: A grama-devata shrine set in a valley between the forested hills of Darakonda and Teegakonda near Tuni, worshipped as a goddess who grants wishes and following the Grama Devata agamas; its fifteen-day Jatara in Chaitra and the Ashada month utsavams draw large crowds.

name: Panchavan Madeviyar Pallippadai Temple
significance: A rare Chola pallippadai, a temple raised over a burial: Rajendra Chola placed the ashes of his stepmother Panchavan Madeviyar, a queen of Rajaraja I, in an urn here and built a Shiva shrine above it, the urn still shown over the lingam. It fell into ruin and was restored by the Tamil Nadu Archaeology Department in 1978.

name: Karni Mata Temple, Udaipur
significance: A hilltop shrine holding a stone image of Karni Mata on the Machla Magra ridge above Doodh Talai in Udaipur, reached on foot or by ropeway and known for its outlook over the city and its lakes.

name: Abaya Hastha Swayambu Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Agaram
significance: A Narasimha temple near Hosur built around a swayambhu stone identified in 1998 during land development and still being extended; the land was made over to the Ahobila Mutt, and Narasimha Jayanti is the principal festival.
story: The shrine recalls Vishnu bursting from the pillar as Narasimha, pleased by the devotion of Prahlada.

name: Kanipura Sri Gopalakrishna Temple
builtDisplay: ancient; renovated 10th c. under Kadamba king Jayasimha
significance: An old Vaishnava temple at Kumbla in Kasaragod district holding a jet-black granite Balagopalakrishna, renovated in the 10th century by the Kadamba king Jayasimha whose capital was Kumbla; it is reckoned an Abhimana Kshetram.
story: Krishna is said to have given the image to the sage Kanva in the Dvapara Yuga; the water that flowed from the sage's rites became the Kumbha Hole river, and the town grew around it.

name: Ayyappan Temple, Coimbatore
significance: An Ayyappan temple at Siddhapudur in Coimbatore, planned from 1942 and consecrated in 1969, where worship follows Sabarimala usage; its gold-covered dhwaja stambha, raised in 1972, is described as the only one of its kind in Tamil Nadu.

name: Andoor Kandan Sree Dharma Sastha Temple, Tholady
builtDisplay: rebuilt 2002; grew from the older Tholadichan Kovil
significance: A Dharma Sastha temple at Tholady east of Neyyattinkara, grown out of a small shrine called Tholadichan Kovil and rebuilt in 2002 with new structures and images; Makaravilakku Mahotsavam on 14 January is its main festival.
story: Travellers on the old Tholady path are said to have cut branches and beaten sticks beside the Ayyappa image, and the place took its name from the practice.

name: Kattakampal Temple
significance: A two-acre west-facing temple complex near Kunnamkulam with an east-facing Shiva sanctum and a separate west-facing sanctum for Kattakampal Bhagavathy; it is counted among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, and the seven-day Kattakampal Pooram in Medam is its great festival.
story: Tradition credits the sage Parashurama with installing the Shiva here, and the festival's high point re-enacts Kali's war with Darika and the demon's killing.

name: Madhava Perumal Temple, Mylapore
significance: A Sri Vaishnava temple in Mylapore, rectangular within ten-foot walls and entered by a five-tier gopuram, held to be the birthplace of Peyalvar, one of the twelve Alvar poet-saints.
story: At the churning of the ocean of milk Vishnu is said to have sent Lakshmi to the hermitage of sage Bhrigu, and to have married his daughter Amritavalli here — whence his other name, Kalyana Perumal.

name: Shree Dev Vyadeshwar Temple
significance: The Shiva temple of Guhagar on the Konkan coast, kuladevata of many Chitpavan families, laid out on the panchayatana plan with the central Shiva shrine ringed by shrines to Surya, Ganesha, Ambika and Vishnu with Lakshmi; three of the shrines were renewed and the east gate restored in 2015.
story: The sage Vyadi is said to have installed the lingam here, and Parashurama — who had raised the Konkan from the sea and settled sixty rishis on it — asked Shiva to meet him daily at the spot, so the god took the name Vyadeshwar, lord of Vyadi.

name: Ajaikapada Bhairava Temple
deity: Ekapada Bhairava, an aspect of Shiva, with a shivalinga in the sanctum
builtDisplay: early 10th c. origin; rebuilt early 20th c.
significance: A shrine near the Alaka branch of the Mahanadi in Jagatsinghpur district traced by archaeological survey to the early 10th century under the Somavamsi kings; ruined by flooding and invasion, it was rebuilt in the early twentieth century around its one-footed Bhairava image.

name: Amaramkavu
significance: A forest-goddess shrine set in what the article calls the largest surviving sacred grove in Idukki district, about three acres of protected biodiversity on the edge of Thodupuzha town.

name: Jaleswar Siva Temple Precinct
deity: Shiva, as a lingam in a circular yonipitha
significance: A walled twelfth-century Shiva precinct at Kalarahanga on the northern edge of Bhubaneswar, once ringed by water on all four sides, whose sanctum lingam sits 1.15 m below the chandrasila; it was repaired by Odisha State Archaeology.
story: A king of Chudangagada devoted to Lingaraja is said to have been told in a dream to raise a temple at the lotus pond where the lord dwelt as Jalasayi, and built it on the pond's western embankment.

name: Indralath Temple
significance: The tallest brick temple in Odisha, standing at Ranipur-Jharial in Balangir district and dated by the Archaeological Survey of India, which maintains it, to the 10th-11th century; its images of Narasimha, Vishnu, Ganesha and Kartikeya point to a site where Shaiva and Vaishnava worship met.
story: The temple takes its name from the belief that Indra himself first worshipped Shiva at this spot and raised a shrine over it.

name: ISKCON Temple, Chennai
deity: Radha and Krishna, with Jagannath, Baladeva and Subhadra
significance: A Gaudiya Vaishnava temple on Hare Krishna Land off the East Coast Road, begun in March 2002 and consecrated on 26 April 2012 at a cost of about 100 million rupees on 45,000 square feet, funded by some 8,000 life patrons; it descends from the Chennai centre ISKCON opened at Kilpauk in 1975.

name: Sethu Kshetram
deity: Ganapathi, with a shrine to Ayyappan
significance: A Ganapati temple on the Mount-Poonamallee Road at Porur, founded in 1964 for the workforce of W. S. Industries and standing within the company campus. Its foundation stone was laid by the Shankaracharya of Sringeri.

name: Shiv Khori
deity: Shiva, as a naturally formed lingam
significance: A cave shrine about 200 m deep in Reasi district, some 80 km from Katra, whose rock formations are read as images of the gods around a self-formed lingam. Pilgrim numbers rose to roughly two million by 2016 after the Shiv Khori Shrine Board was set up in December 2003.
story: One passage inside the cave, now sealed, is said to have run through to the Amarnath cave in Kashmir.

name: Shri Vinayaka Shankaranarayana Durgamba Temple
significance: A three-deity temple on the bank of the Netravathi at Nandavara in Dakshina Kannada, with a sanctum, tirtha mantapa, welcome gopuram and brass-clad flagstaff. Alongside its Jathra Mahotsava it runs midday meals and free medical camps for the surrounding villages.

name: Serugudi Sukshmapureeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Serugudi in Tiruvarur district counted among the Padal Petra Sthalams, its deity sung by the Nayanar saint Sambandar. The precinct also holds shrines to Ganesha, Murugan and the Navagrahas.

name: Semmeninathar Karumbeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple near Vishnampettai in Thanjavur district, one of the Padal Petra Sthalams, praised in the hymns of Sambandar and Thirunavukkarasar. Tradition links its building to the Chola king Karikala.
story: Parasurama is said to have worshipped Shiva here to be freed of the sin of killing the Kshatriyas.

name: Shankaragaurishvara Temple, Pattan
significance: Raised by King Shankaravarman of the Utpala dynasty at Pattan, about 27 km from Srinagar, with deeply carved facades and pedimented entrance columns. It is now ruinous and no longer in worship, and stands beside the smaller Sugandhesha temple that Shankaravarman built for his queen.

name: Siddhanath Temple, Mhaswad
deity: Siddhanath, an incarnation of Shiva and kshetrapal of the region
significance: A Shaiva temple at Mhaswad in Satara district, about 56 km from Pandharpur, attributed to the Badami Chalukyas and completed on its second side in 1738 by their descendant Dubal of Karad. Its Mhaswad Yatra, with a chariot of Siddhanath and crowds smeared in pink gulal, draws devotees from across India.

name: Moteshwar Mahadev
place: Ujjanak, Kashipur, Udham Singh Nagar district
deity: Shiva, worshipped as Bhimashankar in an unusually large lingam
significance: A Shiva temple at Ujjanak near Kashipur named for the sheer girth of its lingam, which cannot be encircled by two hands. The complex also holds shrines of Bhairav Nath, the Shiv Ganga Kund and Maa Jagdamba Bhagwati Balsundari, and holds fairs at Maha Shivaratri, Chaitra and Shravan.
story: Local tradition holds that Dronacharya set Bhima to rebuilding the shrine, after which it came to be called Bheem Shankar.

name: Sharvani Devasthan
place: Salgaonwada, Adavalpal, near Bicholim, North Goa district
deity: Sharvani, with Vetoba (a form of Shiva)
significance: A Goan goddess temple at Salgaonwada near Bicholim, the kuladevata of the Salgaonkar, Prabhu, Naik, Shenoy, Dhond and Petkar families. Its original shrine stood at Saligaon before the deity was moved here.

name: Siruvapuri Sri Balasubrahmanyam Temple
significance: A Murugan temple in Thiruvallur district that temple records place more than five hundred years back. The 14th-century poet Arunagirinathar came here repeatedly and composed Thiruppugal verses on its deity.
story: Lava and Kusha, the sons of Rama, are said to have worshipped at this spot.

name: Paramekkavu Bagavathi Temple
significance: One of the largest Bhagavathi shrines of central Kerala and the head of the Paramekkavu side of the Thrissur Pooram, the division of the city's temples into two competing groups being the work of Sakthan Thampuran. Its devaswom also runs the Paramekkavu Vidya Mandir school.

name: Sri Nellikulangara Bhagavathi Temple
significance: The goddess temple of Nemmara in Palakkad district, whose Nenmara Vallanghi Vela in April is built on a friendly rivalry between the villages of Nemmara and Vallangi. The festival brings Kummattikali, Karivela and a parade of caparisoned elephants.

name: Chembukkavu Bhagavathy Temple
significance: A Thrissur city temple counted among the 108 Durga shrines of Kerala and a participant in the Thrissur Pooram, administered by the Cochin Devaswom Board. Its goddess is reckoned the younger sister of the Bhagavathi at Ayyanthole, and her processions to Vadakkumnathan are timed before the sun grows strong.

name: Pataleshwar Mandir
significance: A Shiva temple on Jadhua Road in Hajipur, Vaishali district, held locally to be of ancient standing and busiest at Shivratri.
story: The lingam here is said to have risen out of the ground of its own accord, making the shrine a swayambhu one.

name: Nuggikeri Hanuman Temple
significance: A Hanuman temple at Nuggikeri near Dharwad whose image was consecrated by Sri Vyasatirtha, a saint of the court of Krishnadevaraya at Hampi, and which also holds shrines to Rama, Shiva, Saraswathi, Durga, Venugopala Swamy and Jagannath. The second Konkanastha Peshwa handed its management to the Nuggikeri Desai family in the eighteenth century, and three branches of that family still take yearly turns running it and organising the Ratha Mahotsav on Hanuman Jayanti.

name: Om Banna
deity: Om Singh Rathore, the folk deity Om Banna or Bullet Baba
significance: A roadside shrine on the Pali–Jodhpur highway near Chotila village, about 20 km from Pali, honouring Om Singh Rathore, who died in a motorcycle crash in 1988, together with the motorcycle itself. Travellers stop to offer incense, flowers, coconut, liquor, red thread and sweets, and an eternal flame is kept burning at the site.
story: After the crash the motorcycle is said to have kept returning to the same ditch however often the police impounded it, and travellers came to believe that Om Banna's spirit watches over those in distress on the road.

name: Udayamperoor Perumthrikovil Temple
significance: A twelfth-century Shiva temple at Udayamperoor in Ernakulam district, set in a courtyard of some four acres with gopurams and a round sanctum, and counted among Kerala's 108 Shiva temples. Three inscriptions of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries are associated with it, one of them still well preserved on the base of the namaskaramandapa.
story: Folklore credits the installation of the idol to the sage Parashurama.

name: New Delhi Kali Bari
significance: A Kali temple on Mandir Marg west of Connaught Place, built in the 1930s after years of demand from New Delhi's growing Bengali community, with an acre of land allotted on the new road and Subhas Chandra Bose as the first president of its committee. Its image follows the one at Kalighat in Kolkata, and the temple has become the centre of Bengali cultural life in the capital; its Durga Puja, first held in 1925, is among the oldest in the city.

name: Thiruvalluvar Temple, Mylapore
deity: Valluvar, the Tamil poet-saint, with his consort Vasuki
significance: A shrine to the poet-saint Valluvar and his consort Vasuki on M. K. Amman Street in Mylapore, Chennai, standing inside the larger Ekambareswarar temple complex. Believed to have been built in the early sixteenth century, it was extensively renovated in the 1970s and has sanctums, a pillared maha mantapam, a shikhara and circumambulatory corridors.
story: Valluvar is traditionally said to have been born beneath the iluppai tree in this compound, where his foster parents found him and took him in.

name: Niranam Thrikkapaleeswaram Dakshinamurthy Temple
deity: Dakshinamurthy, the teaching form of Shiva
significance: A Shiva temple at Niranam in Pathanamthitta district whose presiding form is Dakshinamurthy, Shiva as the guru of knowledge. It came to prominence in the age of the Niranam poets between about 1350 and 1450, and is unusual in giving the Saptamatrikas a sanctum of their own.
story: Local tradition credits the installation of the idol to the sage Parasurama.

name: Thiruthaleeshwarar Temple
significance: A small Shiva temple about 1.5 kilometres southeast of Aranvoyal in Tiruvallur district, resorted to locally as a shrine that relieves naga dosham.

name: Thiruvaloor Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Kerala-style Shiva temple in Thiruvaloor village in Alangad, Ernakulam district, with a shrine to Ganapati and an adjoining subsidiary kavu, Keezhanikavu, holding Vishnu, Bhagavati and the nagas. Shivaratri is its main festival.
story: The idol is held to be an agni pratishta, with Shiva's third eye open, and the pond due east of the sanctum is said to have been dug to cool the fire that would otherwise harm people.

name: Thirupuraikkal Temple
deity: Kannagi (Karnaki), worshipped in full idol form
significance: The only temple in Kerala where Kannagi is worshipped in full idol form, at Moothanthara in Palakkad district, with a Visalakshi Sametha Shiva shrine in the same compound served by Tamil Brahmin priests in the Tamil Shaiva rite. Tipu Sultan is recorded to have sacked and destroyed the temple during his rule at Palakkad, its sacred relics being preserved and shared out among other temples; the three-day Valiya Aarattu is the district's largest annual festival.

name: Kanjilassery Maha Siva Temple
significance: A west-facing Shiva temple at Chemancheri in Kozhikode district, counted among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala and also housing Maha Vishnu.
story: Tradition holds that the sage Parashurama installed the idol, and that Kasi, Kanchipuram, Kanjirangad and Kanjilassery were all founded at the same moment.

name: Kalayat Ancient Bricks Temple Complex
significance: An 8th-century group of red-brick shrines at Kalayat in Kaithal district, laid out as a panchayatana of five temples of which two survive. They are built of locally made bricks laid without mortar or plaster, the Shiva shrine following the pancharatha plan and its shikhara bricks forming a beehive pattern.
story: The place name is traced to Kapilayatana, the abode of the sage Kapila, and the temples are popularly attributed to Raja Salban (Shalivahana).

name: Pananchery Mudikkode Shiva Temple
significance: A west-facing Shiva temple at Mudikkode in Pananchery, about 12 km from Thrissur, counted among the 108 famous Shiva temples of Kerala. Maha Shivaratri in the month of Kumbham is its main festival.
story: Folklore credits the sage Parashurama with installing the idol.

name: Dharmesvara Temple, Kondrahalli
significance: A Shiva temple at Kondrahalli in Hoskote taluk dated to 1065 CE and built in the Chola period. Its temple tank is tied to the Mahabharata, and the site is discussed in the literature on Indian temple architecture.
story: The tank here is held to be where the Yaksha Prashna took place: four Pandava brothers fell dead at its water, and Dharmaraja answered the Yaksha's questions to win their lives back from Yama.

name: Manakkattu Devi Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Pallippad in Karthikappalli taluk, administered through four NSS Karayogams. Kunjekutty Pilla, known as Valyachan and an army chief under Dharma Raja Karthika Thirunal Rama Varma of Travancore, is remembered as its foremost devotee.
story: The idol is said to have been found when a farming woman struck a stone with her curved knife and it bled, centuries after the local shrines burned in the fire Arjuna set to the Khandava forest at Krishna's bidding.

name: Deepanayakaswamy Jain Temple, Deepangudi
significance: A Jain temple at Deepangudi in Tiruvarur district with a three-tiered stucco-figured rajagopura, a vimana on an upapeeta and peeta, and front, artha and maha mandapas. The village takes its name from the presiding Tirthankara, and an inscription of Rajendra Chola II uncovered in 2009 records a donation by a Jain named Nandhian.

name: Kondazhy Thrithamthali Siva-Parvathy Temple
significance: One of the 108 celebrated Shiva temples of Kerala, which under Chera rule served as the central temple for the administration of the surrounding eighteen tiers; besides the Parvati shrine it holds eleven subsidiary deities. Its sculpture was damaged during Tipu Sultan's invasion of Kerala and stayed so for about two centuries.
story: Tradition credits the sage Parashurama with installing the Shiva image on the south bank of the Nila.

name: Kamaleswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the Pudupet neighbourhood of Chennai, best known for its association with the 18th-century dubash and philanthropist Pachaiyappa Mudaliar.

name: Nattatreeswarar Temple
significance: A 10th-century Chola temple standing on a hillock island in the Kaveri on the Erode-Karur road, with an athi tree in the precinct held to be about 3,000 years old; Aadi Perukku and the Tamil New Year draw thousands of pilgrims.
story: Temple lore says the sage Agastya raised a lingam of sand on the hillock and meditated there, and that Shiva appeared and declared the place would bless not only the sage but all his devotees.

name: Singamadai Ayyanar Temple, Nalli
deity: Ayyanar (Singamadai Ayyanar), with consorts Purana and Pushkala
significance: An Ayyanar temple beside Singamadai lake about 18 km from Sattur, built by the Sevalpatti zamindar roughly five centuries ago; it also houses Pechiyamman and several forms of Karuppasamy, and its Masi-month Shivaratri festival draws people from some thirty villages around.
story: It is told that a devotee carrying sacred sand from Srivilliputtur during a drought set it down near Nalli when floods threatened the village, and a voice from the sky declared that Ayyanar had saved the land and crops and would bless the people if a temple were raised for him.

name: Manikandeswaram Uma Maheswara Temple
deity: Shiva and Parvati (Uma Maheswara), sharing one sanctum
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; traditionally over 2,000 years old
significance: A Kerala-style temple at Vadakkekad unusual for housing Shiva and Parvati together in a single sanctum with Ganesha outside; it was attacked in 1790 by Tipu Sultan, who broke sculptures and carried off its valuables, and though land reform cut its holdings from some 800 acres it remains in daily worship under the Malabar Devaswom Board. The poet Vallathol Narayana Menon wrote parts of his work beneath its banyan tree.

name: Moole Shankareshvara Temple, Turuvekere
style: Bhumija Nagara on a semi-stellate base
significance: A soapstone Shiva temple at Turuvekere built about 1260 under the Hoysala king Narasimha III; Adam Hardy classes its tower as Bhumija Nagara raised on a semi-stellate base, joined to the usual Hoysala sanctum, vestibule and closed hall. It is a protected monument under the Karnataka state archaeology division.

name: Tirttapaleeswarar Temple, Triplicane
significance: A Shiva temple on Natesan Street off the Mylapore–Triplicane road in Chennai, counted among the Sapta Sthana — the seven Shiva temples of Mylapore visited together as a set.

name: Peravallur Sundararaja Perumal Temple
significance: A Vishnu temple in the Peravallur neighbourhood of north Chennai, also known after nearby Periyar Nagar, administered by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department; Vaikuntha Ekadashi is its principal festival.

name: Arangulanathar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Thiruvarangulam in Pudukkottai district with a hundred-pillared mandapa and shrines for the three principal Nayanars and all sixty-three; it is one of the Tevaram Vaippu Sthalams named in a hymn of Sambandar.

name: Brahma Temple, Khajuraho
significance: A small Chandela shrine on the bank of the Khajuraho Sagar, part of the UNESCO World Heritage group, built of granite rather than the sandstone of most Khajuraho temples and so read as transitional between the two materials. Only the sanctum and its sandstone shikhara survive; the temple is misnamed, since worshippers took its four-faced Shiva lingam for an image of the four-faced Brahma.

name: Mylara Lingeshwara Temple
deity: Mylara Lingeshwara, a form of Shiva
significance: The temple of Mylara Lingeshwara, a regional form of Shiva, in Mylara village of Hoovina Hadagali taluk in northern Karnataka.

name: Tapkeshwar Temple
deity: Shiva, as a natural cave shivalinga
significance: A cave shrine on the bank of the Tons at Dehradun, built over a natural shivalinga onto which water drips continuously from the rock above — the feature that gives the temple its name.
story: The cave is linked to Dronacharya: when his wife could not nurse their son Ashwatthama and the family could not afford milk, the boy prayed to Shiva, who fed him with milk dripping from the lingam.

name: Narasingam Yoga Narasimha Perumal Temple
significance: A cave temple cut into the Yanaimalai hill 8 km from Madurai, begun in 770 CE by Maran Kari, minister to the Pandya king, and finished by his brother Maran Eyinan; the six-foot Yoga Narasimha is carved from the living rock. Inscriptions record later endowments by Srivallabha Pandya and Sundara Pandya, and there is a separate stone shrine for the goddess Narasingavalli.
story: The Sthala Purana says sage Romasa did penance here for a child and asked to see the Narasimha avatar; the form proved so fierce that Prahlada and Mahalakshmi had to calm it, leaving the seated Yoga Narasimha worshipped today.

name: Nagesvara Temple, Bhubaneswar
deity: Shiva, as a lingam in the garbhagriha
significance: A Shiva temple on the western bank of the Lingaraja west canal in Bhubaneswar, built of ochreous sandstone carved in the Kalinga manner. Local tradition credits it to the Kesari rulers; it remains in worship and in generally sound condition apart from surface decay.

name: Dhenupureeswarar Temple, Madambakkam
significance: A Chola temple of the reign of Parantaka Chola II, later consolidated in stone under Kulothunga Chola I, notable for its apsidal gajaprishta vimana shaped like an elephant's back. It had fallen into ruin before being rediscovered and restored by devotees on the guidance of the Kanchi acharya Maha Periyava, and is now a nationally protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India.
story: Sage Kapila, punished for worshipping a Shiva lingam with his left hand, was reborn as a cow; the cow poured its milk over a buried lingam here, and when it was found Shiva granted the sage release.

name: Mondaicaud Amman Temple
significance: A goddess temple near Colachel on the Kanyakumari coast, so heavily attended by women pilgrims that it is called the women's Sabarimala; its Maasi Kodai festival is the chief annual event. It is noticed in nineteenth-century writing including the Aithiga Mala of 1889 and in district gazetteers.

name: Therazhundur Vedapureeswarar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam on the Kaveri, sung by the Nayanar Tirugnanasambandar and known in older texts as Thirunedungalam. The Archaeological Survey has recorded Tamil inscriptions on its door jambs dated to the 34th and 44th regnal years of Kulottunga Chola I.

name: Kandaswami Temple, George Town
deity: Murugan as Kandhaswami, with Deivanai and Valli
significance: Known as Kandhakottam, this Murugan temple near Parry's Corner was founded in the 1670s by Maari Chettiar around an image brought from a tank near Thiruporur, and rebuilt in stone in the early 1800s. It covers about eight acres, is administered by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department, and is remembered as a place of worship of the saint Ramalinga Swamigal.

name: Navalinga Temple, Kukkanur
significance: A cluster of nine shrines with shikharas raised in the ninth century under the Rashtrakuta kings Amoghavarsha I or Krishna II, built in poor sandstone but richly carved and now much weathered. Old Kannada inscriptions on the site, dated between 1005 and 1186, record grants to shrines of several goddesses and to Mallikarjuna; lintels over the entrances carry Gajalakshmi.

name: Sri Dakshinamukha Nandi Tirtha Kalyani Kshetra
deity: Shiva, as a shivalinga fed by the Nandi's spout
significance: A sunken temple on 2nd Temple Street in Malleswaram, built as a pillared corridor around a stepped tank, in which water runs constantly from the mouth of an unusual south-facing Nandi onto the lingam below. Buried for centuries, it was uncovered in 1997 when residents opposed building work on the plot and the ground was excavated.
story: The spring feeding the tank is held to be the sacred source of the river Vrishabhavati.

name: Thiruthuraipoondi Piravi Marundeeswarar Temple
deity: Shiva as Piravi Marundeeswarar, also worshipped as Gajasamharamurthy
significance: A Shiva temple in Tiruvarur district counted among the Tamil nakshatra temples, this one being the shrine of those born under the Ashvini birth star.

name: Ranganathaswamy Temple, Karamadai
deity: Vishnu as Ranganathaswamy, with Ranganayaki Thayar and Bettadamman
significance: A Vishnu temple 23 km from Coimbatore on the Mettupalayam road, first built under the Cholas and enlarged by Tirumalai Nayakar in the seventeenth century and by Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar in the 1940s; its northern tower dates to 1944 and the seven-tiered eastern rajagopuram was finished in 2013. It is counted among the 108 Abhimana Kshetrams, follows the Tenkalai tradition, and is run by the state endowments department.
story: A herdsman is said to have found the deity's face beneath an anthill after his cow bled into it.

name: Gauthameswarar Temple, Kumbakonam
deity: Shiva as Gauthameswarar, with Soundara Nayaki
significance: A Shiva temple on the eastern bank of the Mahamaham tank at Kumbakonam, one of the twelve Shiva shrines tied to the Mahamaham festival held there every twelve years. Its most recent kumbabhishekam was performed in September 2015.
story: A thread from the primordial kumba is said to have fallen here and taken the form of a linga, and sage Gowthama worshipped it to expiate the killing of a cow.

name: Veemeeswarar Temple, Serapanancheri
significance: A Chola temple near Padappai on the Tambaram–Walajabad road whose earliest inscription belongs to Kulothunga Chola III, placing it around 1180. It is unusual for its very large lingam and for having two Nandis, and was once ringed by the Agni, Brahma and Vishnu theerthams, now dry.
story: Surya is said to come here regularly to worship Shiva, and the deity is held to govern all twenty-seven nakshatras.

name: Sree Madiyan Koolom Temple
deity: Kshetrapalan, with Kalarathri Amma (Bhadrakali) and Nadayil Bhagavathi
significance: One of the oldest temples of north Kerala and the seat of the Allada Swaroopam, dedicated to Kshetrapalan alongside the goddess Kalarathri. It admitted worshippers of the lower castes even before the Temple Entry Proclamation.
story: Kshetrapalakan is said to have come to earth at Mahadeva's command to take the Allada country, but was so taken by the smell of appam being made for Nadayil Bhagavathi that he sat down and stayed — his followers calling him Thampuran Madiya, the lazy lord, from which the name Madiyan comes.

name: Ambamata Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Udaipur completed in Vikram Samvat 1721, corresponding to 1664, by Maharana Raj Singh of Mewar, on the spot where an image of the goddess was dug out of the ground.
story: Raj Singh, suffering from an eye ailment no physician could cure, was preparing to travel to the Ambika Mata shrine in the Arbuda hills when the goddess told him in a dream that she would come to Mewar instead; the image was unearthed where she indicated and his sight was restored.

name: Choleesvarar Temple, Mulanur
significance: A Shiva temple at Mulanur counted among the Vaippu Sthalams named in the hymns of the Nayanar Sundarar, with subsidiary shrines to Vinayaka, Subramanya with Valli and Deivanai, Surya, Bhairava and Nataraja.

name: Elumur Ardhanareeswarar Temple
significance: A Vaippu Sthalam sung by the Nayanar Appar and therefore held to have existed by the seventh century; the name Elumur, 'place of seven', is explained by seven sages said to have worshipped Shiva here. After the temple fell into ruin the lingam and other images were found buried in the silt of a tank, reinstalled first under a thatched roof and later in a permanent shrine, which is why the deity is also called Jalakandeswarar.

name: Mannar Thrikkuratti Mahadeva Temple
deity: Shiva, with a separate srikovil for Krishna
significance: One of the 108 famous Shiva temples of Kerala, standing on the bank of the Pampa at Mannar, with a Shiva sanctum and a separate shrine for Krishna.
story: Folklore credits Parashurama with installing the image, and holds that the temple's enormous compound wall was raised in a single night by a troupe of Shiva's bhutas.

name: Cochin Thirumala Devaswom
deity: Vishnu as Venkatachalapathi, with Sreedevi and Bhoodevi
significance: The principal temple of the Gowda Saraswat Brahmins of Cochin, consecrated in 1599 by Swami Sudhindra Thirtha for a Venkateshwara image brought from Goa by families fleeing Portuguese persecution. The Portuguese destroyed it in 1662 and it was rebuilt the following year under Dutch rule; after further trouble in 1791 the image was kept at Alappuzha until it was brought back in 1853.
story: The image is held to be swayambhu, said to have been shaped by Vishvakarma himself through a sculptor working for the Vijayanagara king Saluva Narasimha Deva Raya.

name: Vanmeekanathar Temple, Tiruvetriyur
significance: A Shiva temple in Sivagangai district counted among the Vaippu Sthalams sung by the Nayanars Sambandar and Sundarar; locally it is known after the goddess as the Bagampiriyal temple.

name: Karapuranathar Temple
significance: A ninth-century Shiva temple near the west bank of the Thirumanimutharu at Uthamacholapuram, its name compounded from karai (riverbank), puram (place) and nathar (lord). Local historical tradition links the village to the Sangam-age story of Vel Pari, the poet Kapilar and the marriage of Pari's daughters.
story: A devotee named Karadhushan is said to have thrown himself into fire to prove his devotion; Shiva put the flames out, and is worshipped here as Karapuranathar in memory of it.

name: Ramalingeswara Swamy Temple
significance: A Shiva temple of the Chola period in Santharavuru, Chinnaganjam mandal, coastal Andhra Pradesh. Its temple authorities claim a bell that rings out 108 times from a single strike, a property they say is matched only by one bell at Varanasi.

name: Mavelikara Maruthakshi Devi Temple
builtDisplay: records go back at least 60 years
significance: A goddess temple near Mavelikkara railway station in Alappuzha district, dedicated to Maruthakshi Devi with Shiva worshipped as Appuppan, and administered by the Maruthakshi Devaswam.

name: Laloor Bhagavathy Temple
significance: One of the 108 Durga temples of Kerala traditionally ascribed to Parashurama, now under the Cochin Devaswom Board. Its goddess takes part in the Thrissur Pooram, arriving with nine elephants to pay respects at the Vadakkunnathan temple, and the place name is explained as a worn form of yagoor, from the yagas once performed there.
story: A mantra inscribed within the temple is said to be the one the gopis used when they worshipped the goddess to gain Krishna as their husband.

name: Shri Vaijnath Temple
significance: Reckoned the fifth of the twelve jyotirlingas of Shiva, this Hemadpanthi temple at Parli in Beed district stands some 75–80 feet high with a brass-plated eastern doorway, and was renovated in 1706 under Ahilyabai Holkar. It draws its largest crowds at Mahashivratri, and male devotees perform the abhisheka bare above the waist.

name: Morkulangara Devi Temple
significance: A Bhagavathi shrine at Vazhappally in Changanassery completed under the Thekkumkur kings and now administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board. Its image stands over six feet tall, unusually large for a Kerala temple, and the three-day Meena Bharani festival is its principal celebration.
story: The goddess is said to have settled at this spot after destroying the demon Darika.

name: Neelkantheshwar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Pali in Lalitpur district built around an unusual three-headed image of the god. It draws a large fair on Maha Shivaratri, when devotees process to the shrine.
story: Local belief holds that the three-headed image emerged from the mountain of its own accord and the temple was raised around it.

name: Mallikarjunar Temple, Dharmapuri
deity: Shiva (Mallikarjunar), with the goddess Kamatchi Ammai
significance: A Shiva temple within the old Athiyaman fort at Dharmapuri, counted among the Vaippu Sthalams praised in the hymns of the Nayanar Sundarar. It also holds the samadhi shrine of Siddhalingesvarar, which receives the first worship of the day, along with shrines to Yoga Narasimha, Virabhadra, Bhairava and Surya.

name: Bhayankavu Bhagavathi Temple
significance: A goddess temple near Tirur whose square sanctum holds a granite image of the Mother Goddess along with subsidiary deities. It is best known for the Thalappoli observance in the Malayalam month of Kumbam, with Kalamezhuthu floor drawings and Poothan and Thira folk performances.

name: Sri Vinayaka Temple, Guddattu
significance: A Ganesha temple near Kundapura established in the 13th century and described as the only Jaladhivasa Ganapathi shrine in India. It is held in the ancestry of the Guddattu Adiga family and observes daily rites including Tailabhyanjana, Panchamrutha and Rudrabhisheka.
story: The three-foot image of Ganesha is believed to have emerged from the rock itself.

name: Dalavanur Cave Temple
significance: A rock-cut cave temple between Gingee and Mandagapattu attributed to the 7th-century Pallava king Mahendravarman I and thought to have been dedicated to Shiva. It is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India and is noted for its unusual inscriptions and for Jain rock beds cut above the cave.

name: Kudroli Bhagavathi Temple
deity: Bhagavathi, worshipped in fourteen forms under three names
significance: A Mangaluru goddess temple with a reported eight centuries of history, ranked as the Koota Kala among eighteen Bhagavathi temples across Karnataka and Kerala. Its precinct holds a Veera Sthambha and a marble statue of Narayana Guru, and the Bharani Utsav is held once every seven years.

name: Sri Madduramma Temple
significance: A village goddess temple at Huskur in Anekal taluk, described as one of the oldest in the Bengaluru area and dating to the Chola period. A grand annual festival is held there in March or April.

name: Cheranalloor Mahadeva Temple
significance: One of the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala and an important shrine of the former Cochin Kingdom, with a circular sanctum and a square namaskara mandapam. Before the agrarian reforms it drew an annual income of roughly 24 tons of paddy from extensive landholdings.
story: The sage Parashurama is said to have installed the Shiva image here in the Treta Yuga.

name: Marikamba Temple, Sagara
significance: Built in 1596 under Venkatappa Nayaka of the Keladi and Ikkeri kingdom, whose family held Marikamba as their tutelary deity. The shrine preserves the goddess's footprints, first consecrated on the town's outskirts and later moved to its centre, and hosts the triennial Marikamba Jathra with a sixteen-foot chariot.
story: Adi Shankaracharya is said to have been told by the goddess in a dream to establish her temple on this spot.

name: Kanimangalam Sastha Temple
significance: One of the temples that take part in the Thrissur Pooram, and the first of the poorams to enter the Vadakkunnathan temple. Its deity is regarded as the protector of the goddesses who join the festival, verifying arrangements for the other participating processions.

name: Kanjiramattam Sree Mahadeva Temple
significance: An old Shiva temple on the bank of the Thodupuzha river, counted among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala. The deity is shown seated in meditation beneath a kalpavriksha with Parvati, and the compound holds subsidiary shrines to Durga, Ganapati and Mookambika.
story: The lingam is traditionally said to have been installed by the sage Parasurama.

name: Pachaimalai Subramanya Swamy Temple
significance: A hill temple to Murugan near Gobichettipalayam, built in 1956 after a devotee reported a divine spark on the hillock in 1954 and enlarged in 1980. It has a five-tier gopuram and a forty-foot statue of the god, and the hill is named in the 17th-century Thirukutrala Kuravanji.
story: The sage Durvasa is said to have installed a chakra on the hillock, after which Murugan appeared there in the form of a serpent to grant darshan.

name: Kadachira Sri Thrikkapalam Siva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the Anjarakandy river that is unusual in housing two images of equal standing in separate sanctums. It is one of three Thrikkapaleeswaram shrines listed among Kerala's 108 Shiva temples, the others being at Niranam and Nadapuram, and its main festival is Maha Shivaratri.
story: Tradition holds that the sage Parasurama installed the image here.

name: Muttichur Kallattupuzha Sri Maha Siva Temple
significance: A west-facing Shiva temple on the bank of the Karuvannur river at Anthikad, counted among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala. It is referred to in the Malayalam poem Koka Sandesam.
story: Local lore credits the sage Parashurama with installing the temple's main image.

name: Ranganathaswamy Temple, Nirthadi
significance: A Vishnu temple rebuilt in 1698 by the Chitradurga chief Baramappa Nayaka after the earlier structure was destroyed by Aurangzeb's armies in 1696, as recorded by a Kannada inscription at the site and documented by Benjamin Lewis Rice. Now an ASI-protected monument, it retains an entrance mukhamantapa, yali pillars and a moulded frieze.

name: Chowara Chidambaraswamy Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Chowara whose east-facing northern sanctum enshrines the god in the dancing form of Nataraja, and which is reckoned among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala. Its main festival is Maha Shivaratri in the Malayalam month of Kumbha.
story: The temple is believed to have been founded by the sage Parasurama.

name: Kudappanakunnu Kunnathu Sri Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the northern edge of Thiruvananthapuram, reckoned among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, with east-facing sanctums and subsidiary worship of Ganapathy and the serpent Vasuki. Its annual festival falls in the Malayalam month of Dhanu.
story: The shrine is believed to have been established by the sage Parasurama.

name: Yoga Nandeeshwara Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at the summit of Nandi Hills in Chikkaballapur district whose fabric is dated to the Chola period. It is the hilltop counterpart of the larger Bhoga Nandeeshwara temple at the foot of the same range.

name: Nilakantheswar Temple
significance: A 7th-century Shiva shrine raised on seven rocks of the Jagamanda hills at Padmapur, where a rock inscription connects the site with the Buddhist logician Dharmakirti. Three further Shiva temples on the same hillock have made Padmapur a local pilgrimage and tourist centre.

name: Shivleni Caves
significance: Rock-cut Shiva caves at Ambajogai carrying an inscription of Saka 1066 associated with the Paramara king Udayaditya of Malwa, with a four-pillared pavilion opening on a hall carried by thirty-two pillars and sculptures of Shiva, the Saptamatrikas and Ganesha. They were described in Fergusson and Burgess's 1880 The Cave Temples of India and are a state-protected monument.
story: Local belief holds that the caves mark a wedding of the goddess Jogaidevi that could not be completed, at which the elephants and structures inside were turned to stone.

name: Shri Kala Bhairava Nath Swami Temple
significance: A temple to Bhairava in the old village of Adegaon in Seoni district, described as one of the better-known Bhairava shrines of the region.

name: Mohajmata Temple, Terahi
significance: A small quadrangular shrine of sanctum and porch at Terahi whose walls carry carved goblin figures, fronted by a well-preserved torana gateway about 18 feet away. It is a centrally protected Monument of National Importance and was conserved by the Gwalior State archaeological department in the 1930s.

name: Neredmet Moodu Gullu
significance: A cluster of three village-goddess shrines in Old Neredmet, Secunderabad, reckoned to be about 120 years old. Daily worship is offered here, and thousands of devotees gather for the Ashada Jathara festival.

name: Madwa Mahal Temple
significance: A stone Shiva temple raised in 1349 by the Phani Nagavanshi Gond king Ramchandra Dev, a kilometre from the Bhoramdeo temple, with a 31-foot-square pillared mandapa and a granite tower carrying erotic sculpture. A state-protected monument, it was used for weddings, which gave it the local name Dulha Rao or bridegroom's temple.

name: Ramachandra Temple, Rajim
significance: A brick-and-plaster temple on a stone plinth at Rajim, which Alexander Cunningham's 1884 report attributed to a merchant named Govind Lal some 250 to 400 years earlier. Its two rows of five mandapa pillars and the older doorframe are far older than the building, probably 7th-century work carried here from the ruins of Sirpur.

name: Om Sri Skandhashramam Temple, Chennai
significance: A modern Murugan temple in suburban Chennai consecrated on 24 June 1999 by Swami Santhananda, who died before it was finished. It is said to be the first temple in India dedicated to the goddess Ugraprathyankira Devi and holds a 9.5-foot Sahasralingam carved with 1,007 lingams.

name: Vettikulangara Devi Temple, Cheppad
significance: One of the older Devi temples of Kerala, administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board, with subsidiary shrines to Mahadeva, Ganesha, Ayyappan, Nagaraja and Nagayakshi. Its principal festivals are the Thrikarthika Maholsavam in Vrischikam and the Thiru Utsavam in Kumbham.
story: A Brahmin scholar called Thampuran is said to have brought a Devi idol here, which the Naluveettil family later found while digging a pond.

name: Chandragutti Renukamba Temple
significance: An old cave shrine of the goddess Renuka set in the hills of Shivamogga district, roughly 19 km from both Soraba and Sirsi. It is one of the better-known Renuka centres of the Malnad-Uttara Kannada borderland.
story: Renuka is said to have been born from the sacrificial fire of a king of Chandragutti, and it was here that her husband Jamadagni had their son Parashurama behead her, only for Parashurama to use his boon to restore her to life.

name: Virbhadra Temple
significance: An ancient Shiva site near Rishikesh where excavation revealed continuous occupation from about the 2nd to the 8th century, including a middle-phase shrine with a linga and plain facade and a later structure of the 7th to 8th centuries. Shivratri and the month of Sawan draw all-night jagran, special pujas and a fair.
story: Virbhadra is remembered as the fierce form Shiva created out of his rage after Sati immolated herself when insulted by her father at a sacrifice.

name: Adi Annamalaiyar Temple, Adi Annamalai
deity: Shiva as Adi Annamalaiyar (Adi Arunachalesvarar), with Adi Abithakujalambal
significance: A Shiva shrine on the girivalam path around Arunachala, held to be older than the great Annamalaiyar temple in Tiruvannamalai town. It is counted among the Vaippu Sthalams praised in the hymns of the Nayanar saint Appar.
story: Its lingam, like that of the big temple, is held to be swayambhu, self-manifested rather than installed.

name: Vadeshwaram Temple
significance: A hilltop Shiva temple on Keecheri hill in Kannur district, credited to Vatukavarma of the Mushika dynasty around 500 CE and counted among Kerala's 108 ancient Shiva shrines. Its eight-petalled ashtadala plan is described as without parallel elsewhere in India, and it is nicknamed the Kailasa of North Malabar.

name: Kuzhanthai Velappar Temple
significance: A hill temple above Poombarai near Kodaikanal, attributed to a Chera king of the 2nd to 5th centuries, with an east-facing sanctum and no tower. Devotees are given the sandalwood paste applied nightly to the idol as medicine, and the annual chariot festival falls on Kettai after Thai Poosam.
story: The idol is said to have been made by the siddha Bogar from navapashanam, an amalgam of nine poisons, as a spiritual medicine, and a Chera king is held to have restored the neglected shrine after being told to in a dream.

name: Asaladeebesvarar Temple, Mohanur
deity: Shiva as Asaladeebesvarar, with the goddess Maduraveni
significance: A Shaiva temple near the Kaveri at Mohanur with a single prakaram, the lingam facing west and the goddess east, and shrines to Vinayaka, Subramania, Nataraja, Kali and the 63 Nayanars. It is one of the Vaippu Sthalams named in the hymns of Appar, and Maha Shivaratri is its chief festival.
story: Local tradition holds that a small spring rises from beneath the feet of the presiding deity and runs to the Kaveri.

name: Kasbeswari Kali Mata Temple
deity: Kasbeswari Kali (image of ten-armed Durga as Mahishasuramardini)
builtDisplay: 17th c. structure; founded under Dhanya Manikya
significance: A hilltop Kali shrine above Kamalasagar lake near the Bangladesh border, about 27 km from Agartala, founded by the Tripura ruler Dhanya Manikya who also had the lake excavated; the present building is of the 17th century. Its sandstone image is 15th-century work, with a Shivalinga carved at the goddess's feet.

name: Dhakeshwari Mata Temple, Kumortuli
significance: Built in 1950 by the businessman Debendranath Chowdhury, who endowed property for its daily services, this Kumortuli shrine houses the image carried from the Dhakeshwari temple in Dhaka at Partition in 1947 and worshipped in Chowdhury's own house for two or three years first. The ten-armed goddess stands a foot and a half tall on her lion, flanked by Lakshmi, Saraswati, Kartik and Ganesha.
story: The name Dhakeshwari means the hidden or covered goddess, from the tale of King Ballal Sen finding Durga concealed in the jungle.

name: Karneshwar Dham
significance: A Shaiva complex at Karon in Deoghar district made up of twenty-eight temples, the principal one holding the Karneshwar Shivalinga and twenty-seven subsidiary shrines around it. Maha Shivaratri and Durga Puja are its main observances.
story: The site is named for Karna, remembered as the ruler of ancient Karon in Angadesh, who is said to have installed the Shivalinga here to worship Shiva.

name: Dandeeswarar Temple, Velachery
significance: A Shaiva temple in the Velachery suburb of Chennai, built in the Pallava period and repaired under the Cholas, with a five-tier vimana and separate shrines for several deities. It is run by the Tamil Nadu HR and CE Department.
story: Temple lore says Yama installed the lingam here after Shiva kicked him, and on praying for pardon was given back his strength along with the staff, the dhandam, that names the shrine.

name: Thakurdwara Bhagwan Narainji (Pandori Dham)
significance: A Vaishnava seat of the Ramanandi order founded by the Dogra Brahmin saint Bhagwanji, counted among the fifty-two dvaras of the subcontinent and controlling thirty-nine branch maths from Jammu to Chennai. It drew patronage under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, and its Baisakhi fair on the first three days of Vaisakha brings processions, Navgraha puja, ritual bathing and charitable distribution.
story: The second mahant, Narainji, is said to have survived an attempt by Emperor Jahangir to poison him, after which the emperor accepted him.

name: Sri Sampath Vinayagar Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple in a busy quarter of Visakhapatnam built in 1962 by the Arcot Mudaliar brothers T. S. Rajeshwaran and T. S. Selvaganesan and now under the Andhra Pradesh Endowments Department. Residents bring newly bought vehicles here for blessing, and Ganesh Chaturthi is kept with great ceremony.
story: The city holds that the temple shielded Visakhapatnam during the 1971 war, sinking the Pakistani submarine PNS Ghazi off its coast.

name: Siddhanath Temple, Nemawar
significance: A 10th-century sandstone Shiva temple at Nemawar built under Paramara rule, with a mandapa added about a century later. Pilgrim records cut into it are dated 1196-97 and 1223-24 CE, and it has remained in worship since.

name: Mahalingapuram Ayyappan Temple
significance: An Ayyappan temple built in 1974 in the Mahalingapuram area of Nungambakkam, Chennai, laid out in Kerala style with the eighteen steps and subsidiary shrines to Shiva, Bhagavati, Ganapathi and Subrahmanya.

name: Kootayanimoodu Chamundi Temple
significance: An 18th-century Kerala-style temple at Kootayanimoodu in Vellanad panchayat, Thiruvananthapuram district, dedicated to the goddess Chamundeswari, a fierce form of Durga.
story: The goddess is said to have been brought forth by Durga to kill the demons Chanda and Munda, and was blessed to be worshipped ever after as Chamunda.

name: Maa Markama Temple
significance: The only shrine in Odisha to the sister goddesses Markama and Karkama, at Bissam Cuttack in Rayagada district; the goddess served as tutelary deity of the Thatraja rulers, and the buffalo sacrifice once held here was discontinued in 1955.
story: Local accounts hold that Markama helped the king of Bissam Cuttack win a war by mesmerising the enemy's soldiers.

name: Mullakkal Temple
significance: A temple of nearly five hundred years standing in the centre of Alappuzha town, attributed to King Devanarayana of Chembakassery and built in old Kerala style with an open-roofed sanctum; its cracked idol was replaced with one of Rajarajeswari on 16 July 1962.
story: The goddess is said to have appeared to the king in a dream and travelled home with him, then halted at a jasmine garden where his umbrella could not be lifted, marking the spot she had chosen.

name: Cheruthazham Sree Kunninmathilakam Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Cheruthazham in Kannur district where the deity is worshipped in three aspects across the day - Dakshinamurti in the morning, Kiratamurti at noon and Umamaheshwara in the evening; the sanctum was raised by about six Brahmin families and the temple was restored from long neglect from the 1980s.
story: Legend holds that Hanuman, sent by Rama to install a lingam at Rameswaram, set down part of it here and so reached Rameswaram late.

name: Vazhappully Temple
significance: A family temple at Kazhimbram near Valapad in Thrissur district dedicated to Raja Rajeswari, noted as one of the few temples in Kerala where Gandharva is also worshipped.

name: Sree Sundareswara Temple
significance: Begun in 1908 and consecrated by Sree Narayana Guru in April 1916, this Shiva temple at Talap is one of two he consecrated to serve the Thiyya community of Malabar under British rule.

name: Sun Temple, Madkhera
significance: An east-facing Surya temple in Madkhera village, Tikamgarh district, raised under the Pratiharas and listed as a state protected monument; its sanctum holds a standing Surya on a lotus pedestal and its walls carry Dashavatara sculptures.

name: Karaikandeswarar Temple, Kanji
deity: Shiva (Karaikandeswarar), with Parvati as Periyanayagi Amman
significance: A Shiva temple at Kanji in Tiruvannamalai district, counted as the first of seven Karaikandeswarar temples strung along the banks of the Cheyyar river; its present masonry structure was put up by Se. Ve. Venkataraman Chettiar.

name: Maa Kaali & Bhagwan Shankar Temple
significance: A village temple to Kali and Shiva at Bisauri in Jaunpur district, Uttar Pradesh, administered by the Bisauri gram panchayat.

name: Nelliparampu Sreekrishna Swami Temple
significance: A Krishna temple at Nellipparambu in Kollam district, Kerala, locally reckoned to be some 1,800 years old and among the better known Vaishnava shrines of the district.

name: Kundrathur Nageswarar Temple
significance: A 12th-century Shiva temple at Kundrathur built by the Shaiva saint Sekkizhar and modelled on the Thirunageswaram temple at Kumbakonam; it is counted among the Navagraha temples associated with Rahu.

name: Sri Rajagopala Swamy Temple, Rajamadam
deity: Rajagopalaswamy (Krishna), with Sridevi, Bhudevi and Senkamalavalli Thayar
builtDisplay: built under Serfoji II of Thanjavur
significance: A Vishnu temple at Rajamadam in Thanjavur district built by the Thanjavur Maratha ruler Serfoji II, who also founded the village of Rajamadam around it.
story: The king, who had long prayed for an heir, is said to have been visited by the deity in a dream and granted a son, and raised the temple in thanks.

name: Kalika Mata Temple, New Dhrewad
significance: A Maitraka-period temple of the sandhara type, with an interior ambulatory, standing near New Dhrewad village in Devbhoomi Dwarka district; it is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India as Monument of National Importance N-GJ-122.

name: Thiruporur Kandaswamy Temple
significance: A Murugan temple on the Old Mahabalipuram Road about 28 km south of Chennai, traced to a Pallava-era foundation and largely rebuilt and enlarged in the 17th and 18th centuries under the saint Chidambara Swamigal. It is among the better known Murugan shrines of the Chengalpattu coast.
story: Legend holds that the god's image lay buried beneath a palm tree after a deluge drowned the site, until the sage Chidambara Adigal unearthed it.

name: Rajagopalaswamy Temple, Kumbakonam
deity: Vishnu as Rajagopalaswamy, with consort Sengamalavalli
significance: A Vishnu temple in the north of Big Street in the temple town of Kumbakonam, where the god is worshipped in his Rajagopalaswamy form alongside his consort Sengamalavalli.

name: Shiva Temple, Kera
significance: A ruined medieval Shiva temple about 22 km south of Bhuj, dated to the later 10th century (with a wider 9th–11th century range proposed) and ascribed to the ruler Ra Lakha Phulani during Chaulukya rule. It is one of the oldest surviving stone temples in Kutch.

name: Kaleshwari Group of Monuments
deity: Shiva, with shrines to Kaleshwari Mata, Mahishasuramardini, Nataraja, Ganesha and Vishnu
dynasty: Undetermined; restored by Mala Rana of Lunavada (1549)
style: Anarta school of the Maha-Gurjara style, with Dravidian influences
significance: A cluster of temples, stepwells and a kund near Lunavada built between the 10th and 16th centuries, with a 10th-century Shiva temple at its core and later structures added through the 15th and 16th centuries. Parts were restored in 1549 by Mala Rana of Lunavada and reconstructed again after the 18th century.
story: Local legend attributes one of the stepwells to a daughter-in-law who dug her own after her mother-in-law refused her water from hers.

name: Sri Parashakthi Kshetra
significance: A temple of the goddess Vaishnavi at Madyar in Kotekar, about 20 km from Mangalore in coastal Dakshina Kannada. Note: the article's infobox coordinate (13.2705, 75.3414) places it far inland and contradicts its own text; the Wikidata point matching the article's stated location near Mangalore is used here.

name: Kunnandarkoil Cave Temple
significance: A rock-cut Shiva temple in Pudukkottai district believed to date to the 8th century under the Muttaraiyar kings, who were lieutenants of the Pallava ruler Nandivarman II, and later expanded under the Vijayanagara Empire. It is read as a specimen of late Pallava art and of early Chola work.

name: Thripaya Trimurti Temple
deity: Trimurti — Shiva at the centre, Vishnu to the right, Brahma to the left
significance: A Kerala-style temple near Irinjalakuda in Thrissur district that is unusual in enshrining all three of the Trimurti together, with Shiva at the centre flanked by Vishnu and Brahma.
story: The temple's legend tells of a learned Namboodiri whose sacred conch broke at Koodalmanikyam, after which the combined power of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva appeared at this spot to bless him.

name: Sivasailam Temple
significance: A Dravidian-style Shiva temple in the hill village of Sivasailam, about three miles from Alwarkurichi in Tenkasi district, where the god is worshipped as Sivasailanathar with the goddess Paramakalyani. Its stone inscriptions record gifts by King Ravivarman and local zamindars.
story: Legend says a landlord's cows stopped yielding milk and instead gathered on a hill and flooded a rock with it, whereupon a shivalingam appeared there.

name: Nilakkal Sree Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple completed in 1960 at Nilakkal in the forested Pathanamthitta hills, on the pilgrim route towards Sabarimala.
story: Devotees hold that Shiva here blesses his son Ayyappa in his fight against evil spirits, casting his own anger upon them.

name: Renukeshwar Mahadev Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at the industrial town of Renukoot in Sonbhadra district, built by the Birla Group and completed in 1972 as a copy of the Khajuraho temples. Its name comes from the nearby Rihand river, also called the Renu.

name: Achaleshwar Mahadev Temple
place: Achalgarh, Abu Road tehsil, Sirohi district
significance: A Shiva temple just outside Achalgarh Fort in the Mount Abu hills, believed to have been built in the 9th century by the Paramara dynasty and renovated in 1979 by the crown prince of the former Sirohi state.
story: Local legend tells that the temple's Nandi statue drove off Muslim invaders by loosing swarms of bumblebees at them.

name: Shinde Chhatri
significance: A memorial hall at Wanawadi marking the cremation site of the Maratha commander Mahadji Shinde, raised around the Shiva temple he built there in 1794. The samadhi outside the sanctum was added in 1910 by the Scindia rulers of Gwalior.

name: Kodandarama Temple, Buchireddipalem
significance: A Rama temple in Buchireddipalem town of SPSR Nellore district, begun in 1765 by the landholder Dodla Rami Reddy and finished nineteen years later. Subsidiary shrines house Lakshmi, Lakshmi Narasimha, Andal and Hanuman.
story: Rama is said to have appeared to Dodla Rami Reddy in a dream and told him to raise the temple at Buchireddipalem.

name: Valinath Mahadev Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Tarabh in Mehsana district whose present Maru-Gurjara structure was begun in 2011 and completed in 2024 on a monastic seat several centuries old. It is a principal centre of faith for the Rabari community, with subsidiary shrines to Dattatreya and Hinglaj.

name: Kothandaramaswami Temple, Nandambakkam
significance: A Vijayanagara-period Rama temple in the Chennai suburb of Nandambakkam, where the original shrines honoured Rama with Lakshmana and Sita. Later additions brought in Srinivasa, the Alwars and Hanuman.
story: The site is traditionally linked to the sage Bhrigu.

name: Adhyatma Niketan
significance: An ashram on Koteshwar Road in Gwalior, named in April 1960 during a visit by Swami Vishnu Tirth and established the following year by Sant Yogi Man Singh. Shiva and Krishna are the deities worshipped there.

name: Valmiki Ashram
significance: A pagoda-style shrine inside Chitwan National Park in Nepal, revered as the hermitage of the sage Valmiki and worshipped with images of Rama, Sita and Valmiki.
story: Tradition holds that Valmiki composed the Ramayana here, and that Sita stayed at the hermitage during her pregnancy and gave birth to Lava and Kusha.

name: Shringi Rishi Ashram, Singiya
significance: An ashram site in Singiya village of Madhubani district, Mithila, whose Shringeshwar Mahadev temple enshrines a Shivalinga and was built in the regional Tirhut style around the turn of the 19th century.
story: The Ramayana sage Shringi is said to have lived out his last years at this spot, which took its name from him.

name: Vishwamitra Ashram, Bisaul
significance: An ashram site at Bisaul village in Harlakhi block, Madhubani district, held to be the Mithila residence of the Vedic sage Vishwamitra and dedicated to the Gayatri Mantra he is credited with.
story: Vishwamitra is said to have halted here overnight with the young Rama and Lakshmana on their way into Mithila, where the brothers first saw Sita in a nearby royal garden.

name: Yajnavalkya Ashram
significance: An ashram at Jagban village in Madhubani district, Mithila, traditionally dated to the 8th-7th centuries BCE and associated with the Vedic sage Yajnavalkya, to whom the Shukla Yajurveda, the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad and the Yajnavalkya Smriti are ascribed. The site's temple is the Shree Yogeshwar Yajnavalkya Mandir.
story: Yajnavalkya is said to have won back the lost Yajurveda by penance to the Sun god, who appeared as a mass of light and imparted the knowledge with Saraswati's help.

name: Kapila Ashram
significance: An ashram at Kakraul in Madhubani district, Mithila, remembered as the seat of the Vedic sage Kapila and the Samkhya teaching, where a Shivalinga attributed to him is worshipped.
story: Kapila, born to Kardama and Devahuti, is said to have installed the Shivalinga at Kakraul, and King Siradhwaja Janaka of Mithila to have come there to learn Samkhya from him.

name: Sri Ramana Ashram
significance: An Advaita Vedanta ashram at the foot of Arunachala hill, which grew from December 1922 around the samadhi shrine of Ramana Maharshi's mother and became the seat of his teaching. The guru's own body is enshrined in a samadhi hall on the campus, beside a temple built between 1939 and 1949 by the sthapati Vaidyanatha.

name: Sri Aurobindo Ashram
deity: Samadhi of Sri Aurobindo and the Mother
significance: A spiritual community founded on 24 November 1926 by Sri Aurobindo and Mirra Alfassa (the Mother) in the former French quarter of Puducherry, formed around his Integral Yoga. Its central shrine is a white-marble samadhi in which both their bodies are laid to rest.

name: Kanakagiri Jain Tirth
significance: A Digambara Jain pilgrimage centre near Maleyuru whose rock-cut and structural shrines begin with a Parshvanatha temple raised under the Western Gangas. Inscriptions across Ganga, Hoysala, Vijayanagara and Wadiyar patronage mark it as a long-lived monastic and institutional seat of Karnataka Jainism.
story: Local tradition holds that Mahavira himself came here and held a samavasarana assembly, and that a Mysore queen was freed of kalasarpadosha through worship at the site.

name: Varahanatha Temple
deity: Varaha (Shveta Varaha, boar avatar of Vishnu)
significance: An ASI-protected temple on the island formed by the Vaitarani at Jajpur, enshrining the white Varaha form of Vishnu; the Madala Panji credits its building to Prataparudra Deva and it was later renovated under the Maratha ruler Raghoji I Bhonsle. Its deula and subsidiary shrines are a substantial example of medieval Kalinga temple building.
story: Legend says that when the Vedas were stolen during Brahma's ashvamedha sacrifice here, Vishnu rose from the sacrificial fire as the boar Varaha to recover them.

name: Jatileswar Temple
significance: An early Shiva shrine in the Jalpaiguri plains dated to the Gupta period and attributed to a feudatory of the Gupta kingdom. It is protected as an archaeological site and a West Bengal State Protected Monument, making it one of north Bengal's oldest surviving temple remains.

name: Vayalil Thrikkovil Mahavishnu Temple
significance: A Vishnu shrine in Kollam district historically owned by the Pisharikkal Mana of Kodungallur and now run by a local temple forum. It remains an active worship centre known for its fortnightly Lakshmi Narayana pooja and the Ashtami Rohini festival.

name: Arang Jain Temples
significance: A group of Jain temples at Arang, of which the late 11th-century Bhand Dewal is the principal survivor, built under the Haihaya rulers of the region. The sculpted tirthankara images and brick and stone detailing record Arang's standing as a joint Jain and Hindu religious centre in medieval Chhattisgarh.

name: Varadaraja Perumal Temple, Poonamallee
significance: A Vishnu temple in the Chennai suburb of Poonamallee, reckoned about a thousand years old and linked with the Vaishnava acharya Thirukatchi Nambi. Its Chola-period tank of over an acre long watered the surrounding paddy fields and supplied the town with domestic water.

name: Raidongia Doul
significance: An Ahom-period doul begun in 1742 under Swargadeo Pramatta Singha and completed in the late 1750s, originally a Devi temple and now dedicated to Shiva; it was granted to the Raidongia king on his marriage to the king's sister Yamini. The Assam archaeology department lists it as a State Protected Monument for its Ahom sculptural work depicting Hindu deities and avatars.

name: Veetrirundha Perumal Temple
builtDisplay: rebuilt in stone c. 850 (Pallava); brick original c. 400
significance: One of only two surviving pre-Pallava temple sites in Tamil Nadu, begun as a brick shrine and rebuilt in stone around 850 CE under Nandivarman II. Later renovations by Rajaraja Chola and by Krishnadevaraya in 1520 make it a compact record of successive South Indian building phases.
story: The name, meaning the seated lord, is explained by the tradition that Rama sat here in grief and was comforted by Bhumi Devi and Nila Devi fanning him with a palm leaf.

name: Gingee Venkataramana Temple
significance: The largest temple at the fort town of Gingee, raised around 1540-1550 by Muthyala Nayaka in full Vijayanagara idiom. Its ornamental pillars were dismantled by the French garrison in 1761 and further sculpture was carried off in 1860, so the ruin also documents the colonial dispersal of South Indian temple fabric.

name: Beeramgunta Poleramma Temple
significance: A village shrine in Nellore district dedicated to Poleramma, a pre-Vedic guardian goddess widely worshipped as a local form of Shakti across Andhra Pradesh. First put up by a British-era village officer roughly two centuries ago, it was later rebuilt with funds raised by the villagers themselves and remains a working centre of folk-deity worship and annual festivals.

name: Radha Gobind Temple
significance: A square laterite ek-ratna temple raised in 1729 by the Mallabhum king Krishna Singha Dev, its walls and cornice covered in bas-relief panels cut from individual blocks. It is a Monument of National Importance under the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Lalji Temple
significance: Built in 1658 by the Mallabhum king Bir Singha Dev, this single-towered stone temple measures about 12.3 m on each side and keeps a covered ambulatory behind three ornamented arched entrances. It is ASI-protected and part of the Bishnupur group on UNESCO's tentative list since 1998.

name: Trilok Teerth Dham
style: Modern, with Sultanate and Mughal elements
significance: A Digambara Jain temple begun under Acharya Sanmati Sagar and completed in 2015, laid out in the shape of the Jain emblem and rising 217 feet above ground with a 108-foot manastambha. Its levels model the three lokas of Jain cosmology and it houses a 31-foot image of Rishabhanatha alongside a meditation centre and dharamshala.

name: Madan Mohan Temple, Bishnupur
significance: Founded in 1694 by King Durjan Singha Dev of Mallabhum, this eka-ratna temple is faced with terracotta plaques showing Krishna-lila and the Dashavatara. It is now an ASI Monument of National Importance and no longer holds active worship.
story: Local tradition holds that during a Maratha raid the deity Madan Mohan himself fired the Dalmadal cannon, driving Bhaskar Rao's army back from Bishnupur.

name: Lakshmi Narasimha Temple, Dharmapuri
significance: A Narasimha shrine on the Godavari at Dharmapuri, raised under the Chalukyas and later enlarged by the Kakatiyas, where the deity is worshipped in seated, wrathful Ugra and peaceful Saumya forms. Subsidiary shrines include Venugopala with Rukmini and Satyabhama, and an image of Yama at the entrance.

name: Karmanghat Hanuman Temple
significance: One of Hyderabad's oldest surviving temples, dated to about 1198 CE and attributed to the Kakatiya king Prola II, where Hanuman is worshipped in a seated meditative form. The complex also holds shrines to Rama, Shiva, Saraswati, Durga, Krishna and Jagannath.
story: The king is said to have found a stone image of Hanuman while out hunting, and to have built the temple after the god appeared in his dream that night and asked for one.
