name: Sitaram Bagh Temple
significance: Built in 1825 by the merchant Seth Puranmal Ganeriwala with revenue support from the fourth Nizam, this walled 25-acre Rama temple blends Mughal, Rajput and Qutb Shahi forms. Its 20-foot perimeter wall is recorded as having sheltered local people from the Razakars in the late 1940s, and INTACH lists it as a heritage building.

name: Sai Baba Temple, Dilsukhnagar
significance: Completed in 1980 and widely visited since the 1990s, this Shirdi Sai Baba shrine in Dilsukhnagar keeps Marathi prayer rituals morning and evening and draws its largest crowds on Thursdays. It was damaged in a 2002 attack and was a target during the 2013 Hyderabad blasts.

name: Gokulchand Temple
significance: Raised in 1643 by the Malla king Raghunath Singha, this laterite pancharatna temple stands 64 feet high on a 45-foot square base and is the largest stone temple in Bankura district. Its stucco decoration shows avatars of Vishnu and raslila scenes; the ASI took charge of the derelict monument in 1996.

name: Kuruvathi Basaveshwara Temple
significance: A 14th-century temple on the bank of the Tungabhadra in Hoovina Hadagali taluk, built under Vijayanagara patronage and combining Vijayanagara and Western Chalukya architectural forms. Its principal festival is Maha Shivaratri.

name: Kalachand Temple
significance: Founded in 1656 by Raghunath Singha Dev of Mallabhum, this south-facing laterite shrine is the earliest surviving eka-ratna temple at Bishnupur, about 11 m square with a corridor and three arched openings on each side. Low-relief carving covers it with Krishna-lila episodes, Puranic deities, ascetics and dancers.

name: Madan Gopal Temple
significance: Commissioned in 1665 by Churamoni Devi, queen of the Mallabhum king Bir Singha II, it is the only pancha-ratna temple at Bishnupur built in laterite. Five sikharas — an octagonal central tower with four square corner towers — sit on a curved roof above a sparsely decorated 11.3 m square plan; it is an ASI Monument of National Importance.

name: Kottankulangara Devi Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Chavara in Kollam district best known for Chamayavilakku, an annual festival in which men from across Kerala dress in women's attire and carry traditional lamps in procession to the shrine.
story: Cowherds are said to have struck a coconut against a stone near the Bhoothakulam pond and seen blood drip from it; an astrologer told them to build a temple, and because the herders had made their first offerings in women's clothing the custom endured.

name: Rajagopala Perumal Temple
significance: One of three Vishnu temples at Manimangalam near Tambaram, carrying inscriptions from 1056 CE in which Rajendra Chola I names it Kamakoti-Vinnagar and Thiruvaykulam. The settlement itself is recorded far earlier as the site of a battle between the Chalukya ruler Pulakesin II and the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I.

name: Nookambika Temple
significance: The principal goddess temple of Anakapalle, renovated in 1611 by Kakarlapudi Appalaraju Payakarao after the Golconda Nawab appointed him to govern the area. Its largest gathering falls on Kottha Amavasya, the day before Ugadi.
story: The shrine is said to have been founded for the family goddess Kakatambika, who came to be known as Nookambika, one of the nine forms of Shakti.

name: Kalarivathukkal Temple
style: Kerala, Rurujith Vidhanam with four sanctums
significance: A Bhadrakali shrine near the Valapattanam river associated with the Kolathiri rulers of Chirakkal and now a Category A temple of the Malabar Devaswom Board. The goddess is revered as the mother of Kalarippayattu, the martial art from which the temple takes its name.
story: Tradition says Annapoornashwari sailed from Kashi to Chirakkal with Kalarivatukkalamma and Madayikkavilamma to see the Krishna temple, and never went back.

name: Mahasu Devta Temple, Hanol
deity: Shiva, worshipped locally as Mahasu Devta
style: Kath Kuni timber-and-stone with Nagara shikhara
significance: The principal shrine of the Mahasu Devta cult of the Jaunsar-Bawar hills, standing on the Tons river at Hanol. Its sanctum is dated to the 9th-10th century and the temple is listed in the Archaeological Survey of India's inventory of ancient temples.
story: Local tradition holds that four brother deities came from Kashmir and that Shiva slew the demon Kirmira here to protect his devotees, the site being built by Vishwakarma at Yudhishthira's request.

name: Subrahmanya Temple, Perambur
significance: A Murugan shrine in Perambur village about 14 km from Mayiladuthurai, where the six-faced principal image is the object of worship. The temple is noted locally for the snakes that live within its precincts.

name: Koranganatha Temple
significance: A small medieval Chola temple to Vishnu at Srinivasanallur on the Kaveri, counted by the historian Harle among the four earliest surviving temples of the Chola empire. It is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India and carries an inscription recording a tax-free garden endowed for a perpetual lamp.

name: Madangopal Jiu Temple
deity: Radha and Madangopala, a form of Krishna
significance: A seventeenth-century Krishna temple in the Howrah countryside, described as one of the largest ath-chala temples in West Bengal for its distinctive eight-sloped roof.

name: Thrikkovil Sree Padmanabha Swami Kshetram
significance: A Vishnu temple at Vallicode in Pathanamthitta district administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board, regarded as second of its kind after the Padmanabhaswamy temple at Thiruvananthapuram. Its ten-day annual festival includes the Rupmani Swayamvaram.

name: Huligina Maradi Temple
significance: A hill shrine to Srinivasa in Gundlupet taluk of Chamarajanagar district, also known as Huligadri, Vyagrachala and Dakshina Seshadri.
story: The Varaha Purana is said to call the hill Dakshina Sheshadri, where Srinivasa was worshipped by Rama in the Treta Yuga and by the Pandavas in the Dvapara Yuga, and where he blessed the sage Mandavya after a long penance.

name: Thirunadhikkara Cave Temple
style: Rock-cut cave temple with early Kerala-style murals
significance: A rock-cut Shiva temple in Kanyakumari district whose sanctum and hall were excavated in the late 8th or 9th century, attributed by the Archaeological Survey of India to the Ay king Vikramaditya Varaguna and by other scholars to the Pandyas. Its murals are among the earliest examples of the Kerala painting tradition, and four Vatteluttu inscriptions record donations for lamps, musicians and a festival.

name: Kuttikattu Sree Bhadra Kali Devi Temple
significance: One of the several Bhadrakali temples around Cherthala in Alappuzha district, lying about a kilometre west of the Arthungal bypass. Its observances include the Kunguma Khalasam and serpent worship.

name: Ramapuram Sree Rama Temple
deity: Rama, in a four-armed (Chathurbahu) east-facing form
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; structure held to be about a thousand years old
style: Kerala, with a circular copper-roofed sreekovil
significance: A Vaishnava temple in Ramapuram village counted among the 108 Abhimana Kshetrams and the principal shrine of the Nalambalam circuit of four temples to Rama and his brothers. It is administered by the Ramapuram Devaswom trust of three Nambudiri families.
story: Rama is said to have meditated here during his exile, with Lakshmana, Bharata and Shatrughna meditating at the three neighbouring sites that became their own shrines.

name: Lakshmana Temple, Khajuraho
deity: Vishnu in his three-headed Vaikuntha form
style: Nagara, sandhara plan of the panchayatana type
significance: The oldest and most complete of the western group of temples at Khajuraho, built by the Chandela king Yashovarman around 930-950 for a Vaikuntha Vishnu image. Part of the Khajuraho Group of Monuments inscribed by UNESCO in 1986, it carries the ten avatars of Vishnu on its sanctum doorway and a rare niche portrait of the sculptor with his pupils.

name: Manakkattu Bhadra Temple
significance: An early nineteenth-century Bhadrakali shrine near Ponkunnam, run by a committee of the Vellala Mahasabha, known for its daily Guruthi pooja and the Panthirukulam guruthi held once every twelve years. It is a well-used stop for Sabarimala pilgrims, who are given free meals there.
story: The temple is said to have been founded on the instruction of the head of the Manakkattu Mana, who prescribed a Bhadrakali shrine to appease a yakshi released by a saint whose spirit was spreading disease.

name: Kulashekharanatha Mahalingam Temple, Pathai
deity: Shiva as Kulashekharanatha Mahalingam, with the goddess Sugandha Kuntalambika
significance: A Shiva temple on the Pachaiyar river at Pathai in Tirunelveli district whose naming and iconography reflect Chera, Chola and Pandya influence. Now largely dilapidated, its processional images were moved to the Nellaiappar Temple at Tirunelveli for safekeeping after an attempted theft, and a devotees' forum works for its revival.
story: The lingam is said to have been found when a cow fell at the spot, and Rama is held to have worshipped here on his way to Lanka in search of Sita.

name: Attahas Shaktipeeth
deity: Sati as the goddess Phullara, with Kalabhairava as Vishvesh
significance: A Shakta pitha near Katwa in Purba Bardhaman district, counted among the fifty-one seats of the goddess and drawing large numbers of pilgrims, especially in December.
story: The lips of Sati are said to have fallen here as Shiva carried her body across the earth, and the name Attahas, meaning loud laughter, is taken from that episode.

name: Garjiya Devi Temple
deity: Garjiya Devi, held to be a form of Parvati
significance: A Devi shrine on a rock rising about sixty feet out of the Kosi river on the edge of Corbett National Park, north of Ramnagar. It holds a ninth-century black granite Lakshmi-Narayana image and draws thousands of pilgrims at Kartik Purnima.

name: Ekteswar Temple
significance: A laterite Shiva temple about 45 feet high on the bank of the Dwarakeswar river some 10 km from Bankura town, raised by the Malla king Raghunath Singha Dev in the 17th century. It is said to have been built as a token of unity after a boundary dispute between the kingdoms of Mallabhum and Samantabhum.
story: Local tradition holds that Shiva himself meditated at the spot to settle the boundary quarrel between the two kingdoms.

name: Kalugasalamoorthy Temple
builtDisplay: 18th c. halls on an early Pandya rock-cut core
significance: A hill temple at Kalugumalai whose core is early Pandya rock-cut work, with its images installed and pillared halls added in the 18th century. It was long controlled by the Ettaiyapuram zamindar and is now run by the Tamil Nadu HR&CE board; its 1895 Panguni Uthiram procession was the flashpoint of a deadly caste riot.
story: The sage Kalugumahamunivar, identified with Sampati the brother of Jatayu, is said to have helped Murugan against the demons Surapadman and Tarukasuran and to have won liberation here, giving the hill its name.

name: Thirupparankundram Rock-cut Cave Temple
significance: A rock-cut Shaiva shrine on the south face of Skandamalai near Madurai, its earliest excavation dated to the 8th-century early Pandya period and enlarged under Maravarman Sundara Pandya in the 13th century. An inscription there records tax-free land granted for its upkeep, and the cave is a protected national monument carrying reliefs of the Shaiva saints Appar, Sambandar and Siruthondar.

name: Billeswar Devalaya
significance: A Shiva temple at Belsor in Assam's Nalbari district, held to be about five centuries old. Maha Shivaratri and Durga Puja are its principal festivals, the latter still marked by the temple's long-standing buffalo sacrifice.

name: Varadharaja Perumal Temple, Puducherry
significance: A Vishnu temple in Puducherry town believed to have been founded by the Cholas in the 11th century and enlarged by the Pandyas in the 12th, later rebuilt in the colonial period. It sheltered the images of the Vedapurishvarar temple when that shrine was destroyed in 1748, and its Vasantha mandapa was funded jointly by the town's Hindu, Muslim and Christian residents.

name: Alamchandi Temple
significance: A Shakta shrine near the Atharanala bridge in Puri, dated on structural grounds to the later 16th century, with a natamandapa added in the 20th. It is counted among the Ashtashaktis that guard the sacred precinct of Srikshetra, and the logs cut for the Nabakalebara rite are first set down before it.

name: Bathu Temples
significance: A group of stone temples near Dhameta in Kangra district, dated by historical accounts to the 8th century, of which nine of the original eleven survive. They were submerged by the Maharana Pratap Sagar reservoir when the Pong dam filled in the early 1970s and emerge only between March and June as the water drops.
story: Local folklore credits the Pandavas with building them during their exile, and with abandoning a staircase meant to link the site to the Masrur rock temples in a single night — forty steps of it are still there.

name: Jagannath Temple, Rayagada
significance: A Jagannath temple on the southern edge of Rayagada town, known locally as Sradhha Shrikhetra. The older shrine was replaced by the present Kalinga-style structure, inaugurated on 20 June 2007 in the presence of the Gajapati Raja of Puri.

name: Bhimeshvara Temple, Nilagunda
significance: A soapstone Shiva temple at Nilagunda with four sanctums, dated by the Archaeological Survey of India to the last quarter of the 11th century, though the historian Adam Hardy places it in the 12th. Its non-mainstream Later Chalukya idiom carries Hoysala touches, and it is protected as a monument of national importance.

name: Malleswar Temple
significance: A square deul-form Shiva temple at Bishnupur, 6.9 metres to a side and 10.7 metres tall, founded in 1622 by the Mallabhum king Bir Singha. Its original curved rekha tower was later replaced by an octagonal one, and the temple is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Jagatnagar Kalibari
significance: A Kali temple at Jagatnagar near Singur in Hooghly district, about 34 km from Kolkata, where the goddess is worshipped as Anandamayi Kali Ma.

name: Parshvanath Jain Temples, Varanasi
significance: A cluster of three Jain shrines at Bhelupur in Varanasi — a Digambara temple, a Shvetambara temple and the Parshvanatha–Padmavati temple. The Digambara shrine's worshipped black stone image of Parshvanatha, about 75 cm high, belongs to a group of sculptures found here dating from the 9th to 11th centuries CE.
story: Jains identify Bhelupur as the place of three of Parshvanatha's kalyanakas — his conception, birth and renunciation — in the city his father King Ashvasena is said to have ruled.

name: Vandevi Temple
significance: A temple to the forest goddess Vandevi about 6 km from Renukoot in Sonbhadra district, completed in 1953 around an image unearthed during the building of the Rihand dam. Navaratri and the month of Sawan draw its largest gatherings.

name: Buddhanath Temple
significance: A 12th-century Shiva temple at Garedi Panchana in Balipatna block, some 22 km from Bhubaneswar, attributed to king Chodaganga Dev and laid out on Tantric principles. It was renovated recently with 14th Finance Commission funds.
story: It is believed locally that a snakebite victim brought into the temple precinct will not die.

name: Jain Temple, Alappuzha
style: Jain, in Rajasthan stone and white marble
significance: The Jain temple on Gujarati Street in Alappuzha serves the community descended from forty-two Jain families brought from Kutch to help build up the port town under Dewan Raja Kesavadas. Its two shrines were restored in February 1994, and it holds an image of the 23rd Tirthankara unearthed in Kuttanad, evidence of Jainism's older presence in Kerala.

name: Dimapur Jain Temple
significance: A Digambara Jain temple on Jain Temple Road in Dimapur, built in 1947 by four members of the Sethi and Chabra families who had moved down from Kohima in 1944 to escape the Japanese advance. A rear section was added in 1989 and consecrated with a Panch Kalyanak ceremony.

name: Narasimha Jharni
significance: A cave temple at Bidar reached by wading some 300 metres along a water-filled tunnel cut under the Manichoola hills, where Narasimha is worshipped alongside a Shiva linga. It is counted among the 108 Abhimana Kshetrams of the Vaishnava tradition.
story: The demon Jharasura, slain by Narasimha, is said to have turned into water that has flowed from the god's feet through the tunnel ever since.

name: Jagannatha Perumal Temple, Tirumazhisai
significance: A Vishnu temple at Tirumazhisai near Chennai, one of the 108 Abhimana Kshetrams and revered as the birthplace of the Alvar Thirumalisai. Its oldest inscription dates from the reign of Kulothunga Chola III, and later grants record patronage by Kopperunjinga and by the Vijayanagara rulers Harihara Raya II and Virupaksha Raya II.
story: The Saptarishis are said to have asked to see the middle Jagannatha, and Vishnu appeared here between Vada Jagannatha at Puri and Keezha Jagannatha at Thirupullani.

name: Chaturmukha Basadi, Karkala
deity: The Tirthankaras Aranatha, Mallinatha and Munisuvrata
significance: A four-sided Jain basadi built in 1586 by Immadi Bhairarasa Vodeya on Chikkabetta hill at Karkala, near the Gommateshwara monolith. Its square granite hall opens through pillared porticoes on all four sides under a roof of massive slabs, and a contemporary inscription describes the building by its four symmetrical faces and records the village grants endowed for its worship.

name: Yoga Madhava Temple, Settikere
significance: A soapstone Vishnu temple at Settikere in Tumkur district, built in 1261 CE by an officer of the Hoysala empire under king Narasimha III. It follows a three-shrine plan on a raised jagati platform, with the central vimana laid out on a semi-stellate ground.

name: Jagannath Temple, Chennai
significance: A modern shrine at Kannathur off the East Coast Road south of Chennai, built in Kalinga style for the divine trinity of Jagannath, Baladeva and Subhadra. It was consecrated on 26 January 2001 and serves the city's Odia community.

name: Ardhagiri
significance: A hill shrine to Hanuman at Aragonda in Chittoor district, Andhra Pradesh, whose name means 'half mountain'. It is known for a perennial spring on the hill that pilgrims regard as medicinal.
story: Legend holds that when Hanuman was carrying the Dronagiri mountain of healing herbs, Bharata shot him down with an arrow and half the mountain fell here, giving the place its name.

name: Ghaghar Burhi Temple
deity: Kali, worshipped as Ghaghar Buri Chandi Mata
significance: A shrine of the goddess Kali on the bank of the Damodar near Asansol in Paschim Bardhaman district, West Bengal. It is one of the most visited local pilgrimage spots of the Asansol industrial belt.
story: Local tradition tells of a wedding party trapped by a flooded rivulet who prayed to the goddess and crossed safely, but the king forgot his vow of a sacrifice and the party was cursed to remain beneath the water.

name: Chakra Narasimha Temple
significance: A Vaishnava shrine near the seashore at Chakratirtha in Puri, Odisha, where forms of Narasimha are worshipped alongside a large granite wheel venerated as the Sudarshana Chakra. It is counted among the tirthas of the Puri pilgrimage circuit and also serves as a shrine to Varuna.
story: The site is said to mark the spot where the sacred wood for the first images of Jagannath, Balabhadra, Subhadra and Sudarshana came ashore after floating in the sea for Indradyumna.

name: Olakkannesvara Temple
significance: A stone temple to Shiva perched on the rock above the Mahishasuramardini cave at Mahabalipuram, raised under the Pallava king Rajasimha in the early 8th century. Its walls carry panels of Shiva as Kalantaka, Dakshinamurti, Nataraja and in the Ravananugraha episode.

name: Krishna Mandapam
significance: A rock-cut relief panel at Mahabalipuram carved in the mid-7th century under the Pallavas, showing Krishna raising Govardhana amid scenes of cowherd village life. A pillared mandapa was built in front of it in the 16th century under the Vijayanagara empire.
story: The relief depicts Krishna lifting the Govardhana hill on one finger to shelter the cowherds from the deluge sent by Indra.

name: Ganesha Temple, Idagunji
significance: A much-visited Ganesha shrine at Idagunji in Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka, near Honnavara, traced in the article to the 4th–5th century CE. The two-armed standing image is unusual and draws large numbers of pilgrims each year.
story: It is said that the sage Valakhilya, obstructed in a sacrifice on the Sharavathi bank, was advised by Narada to worship Ganesha, who agreed to remain at Kunjavana, the grove that became Idagunji.

name: Sani Monastery
significance: A Drukpa Kagyu monastery in the Zanskar valley of Ladakh, a few kilometres from Padum, whose foundation is traditionally carried back to the Kushan emperor Kanishka. It is unusual among Zanskar gompas in standing on flat ground rather than a crag, and encloses the ancient Kanika stupa.
story: Padmasambhava is said to have spent five years in a small chapel at the site, and the monastery is also linked in tradition to the yogi Naropa and to the epic king Gesar.

name: Devipuram
deity: Sahasrakshi, a form of Lalita Tripurasundari, with Kameshwara
significance: A Shakta temple complex in Anakapalli district, Andhra Pradesh, founded by the nuclear physicist N. Prahalada Sastry, whose Sahasrakshi Meru shrine is built as a three-dimensional Sri Meru Yantra. Construction ran from 1985 to consecration in 1994.
story: Its founder described a meditative vision of himself lying on the peetam while four figures performed a homa with flames rising from his body, after which a panchaloha Sri Chakra Maha Meru was found at the site.

name: Jagannath Temple, Hyderabad
significance: A temple on Road 12, Banjara Hills, built in 2009 by Hyderabad's Odia community and run by the Kalinga Cultural Trust. Its design follows the Jagannath temple at Puri, with a shikhara of about seventy feet.

name: Banashankari Temple, Amargol
significance: An early 13th-century stone temple at Amargol between Hubli and Dharwad, notable for pairing a nagara shrine of stepped-diamond plan with a dravida one. It stands beside the Shankarlinga temple and is a protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Ananthagiri Temple
significance: A hill temple to Vishnu in the Ananthagiri forest of Vikarabad district, Telangana, dated by the article to roughly four centuries ago and endowed by the Nizams, with the seventh Nizam Mir Osman Ali Khan funding work there. The hills around it are the source of the Musi river.
story: Tradition says the deity appeared to a Nizam in a dream asking that a temple be raised, and earlier that the sage Markandeya installed the image here and had the Ganga brought for his bathing.

name: Mounagiri Hanuman Temple
significance: A modern hilltop Hanuman shrine near Hampapuram in Anantapur district, developed by the Mounagiri Global Trust under Eswaraiah Swamy and consecrated in November 2010. Around a thousand artisans and five hundred volunteers worked on it, the main Hanuman image alone costing some 90 lakh rupees.

name: Baba Ranadhir Temple
deity: Baba Ranadhir, a saint venerated as a healer
significance: A shrine at Bhuna in Haryana's Fatehabad district raised in homage to Baba Ranadhir, an early saint remembered for healing the afflicted. Thursday is its principal day of visitation.
story: Devotees hold that a sprinkle of water from the shrine's tank cures every kind of skin affliction.

name: Alarnatha Temple
deity: Vishnu as Alarnath Dev, with a shrine to Mahalakshmi
significance: A Vaishnava temple at Brahmagiri, some 23 km from Puri, counted among the 108 Abhimana Kshetras. It is associated with Ramanujacharya's journey through Odisha and preserves a stone slab linked to Chaitanya Mahaprabhu's sankirtana.
story: Devotees say Jagannath directed Chaitanya Mahaprabhu here during Anavasara, the fortnight when the Puri image is withdrawn from view and the lord is believed to appear instead as Alarnath.

name: ISKCON Temple, Patna
significance: An ISKCON temple on Buddha Marg in Patna whose foundation stone was laid in 2007 and which opened in phases, the first in May 2022 and the remainder in 2023, at a cost of roughly 100 crore rupees. Subsidiary shrines hold Gaura-Nitai and Rama, Sita, Lakshmana and Hanuman.

name: Boyakonda Gangamma Temple
significance: A hill shrine above Diguvapalli in Chowdepalli mandal, Annamayya district, built and long maintained by the Boya and Pala Ekari communities of the surrounding forest. It passed to the Andhra Pradesh Endowments Department in 1990.
story: The goddess is said to have come down from the hillock to shield the forest communities from a Nawab's soldiers, destroying his army and hanging the heads of the slain on the branches of a banyan.

name: Dhirdham Temple
style: Nepali, modelled on the Pashupatinath Temple at Kathmandu
significance: A Shiva temple at Darjeeling built in 1939 by Rai Saheb Purna Bahadur Pradhan of Nepal. Beg Raj Shakya designed it as a smaller echo of the Pashupatinath Temple in Kathmandu.

name: Kolaramma Temple
deity: Kolaramma, with a second shrine to Chelamma the scorpion goddess
significance: A goddess temple at Kolar raised about a thousand years ago by the Talakad Gangas and enlarged under the Cholas, whose inscriptions and granite reliefs, including one of Rajendra Chola I in battle, survive on its walls. The Mysore maharajas were later patrons.
story: Worshippers hold that praying at the Chelamma shrine keeps a person safe from scorpion stings.

name: Kamaldah Jain Temple
significance: A Shvetambara Jain temple built at Patna in 1729 to commemorate the acharya Sthulabhadra, with a second shrine dedicated to Sudarshana and an inscription of 1792. It is a fixture of Bihar's Jain pilgrimage circuit.
story: The temple is believed to stand on the ground where Sthulabhadra, successor of Bhadrabahu, spent his last days.

name: Gurdwara Nada Sahib
deity: Guru Granth Sahib; commemorates Guru Gobind Singh's halt here
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; marks a halt of 1688
significance: A gurdwara in Panchkula district marking the spot where Guru Gobind Singh halted while travelling from Paonta Sahib to Anandpur Sahib after the Battle of Bhangani in 1688, his first battle, fought at nineteen. The site lay forgotten until a villager, Bhai Motha Singh, raised a platform on it; management passed to the PEPSU Dharmarth Board in 1948 and to the SGPC after 1956.

name: Shantinath Shiva Temple
significance: An 1828 nine-pinnacled nava-ratna Shiva temple in the Mitrasenpur quarter of Chandrakona, roughly nineteen and a half feet square and protected as a state monument. Its terracotta panels carry Ramayana battle scenes, Krishna lila, Bhishma on his bed of arrows, the Dashavatara and rows of musicians.

name: Katta Maisamma Temple
deity: Katta Maisamma, a manifestation of Shakti
significance: A goddess shrine raised beside a tank bund by the Golconda Patel family when the bund was built, its name taken from katta, the bund itself. The Nizams offered here in the month of Ashadha for the safety of the kingdom, and the sixth Nizam, Mir Mahbub Ali Khan, made an offering on the banks of the Musi during the flood of 1908.
story: The 1908 flood is said to have subsided the moment the Nizam completed his offering to the goddess.

name: Kodlamane Vishnumurthy Temple
place: Kodlamane, Honnavar taluk, Uttara Kannada district
significance: A Vishnu temple at Kodlamane in Honnavar taluk of Uttara Kannada district, about a kilometre from Idagunji and 23 km from Honnavar town. A natural stream called Vishnu Tirtha runs beside it.
story: The shrine is said to have been found several centuries ago deep inside dense hill forest.

name: Lakshmeshwara Jain Temples
deity: Neminatha at the Shankha Basadi and Anantanatha at the Anantanatha Basadi
dynasty: Badami Chalukya; Western Ganga; Kalyani Chalukya
style: Badami Chalukya, with rekhanagara and phamsana shikharas
significance: A group of Jain basadis at Lakshmeshwara in Gadag district, known in antiquity as Puligere or Hugligere, of which the Shankha Basadi dates from the 7th century and the Anantanatha Basadi from about the 12th. Inscriptions of the 7th and 8th centuries record grants to them, and Kunkuma Mahadevi, sister of Vijayaditya, built a large Jain temple here in the reign of Kirtivarman II.

name: Gurdwara Dukh Nivaran Sahib
deity: Guru Granth Sahib; commemorates the visit of Guru Tegh Bahadur
significance: A Patiala gurdwara on the ground of the old village of Lehal, where Guru Tegh Bahadur stayed beneath a banyan tree on 24 January 1672. Raja Amar Singh laid out a memorial garden on the spot, Maharaja Bhupinder Singh had a proposed railway line moved so the tree would survive, and Maharaja Yadavindra Singh built the present shrine and sarovar between 1930 and 1942.
story: The villagers of Lehal are said to have begged the Guru to come because a mysterious sickness was killing them, and devotees still hold the water of the sarovar to be healing.

name: Umamaheshwaram Temple
significance: A Shiva temple set in the Nallamala forest about 4 km from Rangapur village near Achampet, some 100 km from Hyderabad. It is regarded as the northern gateway to Srisailam, one of the twelve jyotirlingas.

name: Bhu Varaha Swamy Temple
deity: Varaha as Bhu Varaha Swamy, with Ambujavalli Thayar
significance: A Vishnu temple at Srimushnam dedicated to the boar avatar Varaha, whose earliest endowments date to the medieval Cholas. Its present form owes most to the Thanjavur Nayak ruler Achuthappa Nayak, with the rajagopura added under the Vijayanagara Empire.
story: Varaha is said to have taken boar form here to lift the earth goddess Bhudevi away from the asura Hiranyaksha, and the temple tank is held to have formed where his sweat fell.

name: Markandeshwar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple standing on the bank of the Markandeshwar tank north of the Jagannath temple at Puri. Both shrine and tank are dated to the 12th century and the tank counts among the sacred water bodies of the Puri pilgrimage.
story: The sage Markandeya is said to have meditated on Shiva here, and to have seen an infant afloat on a banyan leaf upon the waters, a vision Vishnu explained to him.

name: Ambika Jain Temple, Girnar
builtDisplay: present shrine 15th c.; earliest temple 8th c.
significance: A hilltop shrine to the yakshi Ambika on Girnar, its earliest temple traced to the middle of the 8th century and the standing building to the 15th, after patronage by Vastupala and Tejapala and a rebuilding funded by the merchant Samal Sah in 1468. It draws Hindu as well as Jain pilgrims.
story: Newly married couples visit to tie their garments together and make offerings, in the belief that the goddess will grant them a long and happy marriage.

name: Karikkakom Devi Temple
deity: Chamundi Devi, worshipped as Maha, Raktha and Bala Chamundi
significance: A Chamundi temple on the western edge of Thiruvananthapuram, reckoned more than six centuries old, where the goddess is served in three distinct forms in separate sanctums.
story: Under the Travancore Maharajas the accused were brought before the sanctum of Raktha Chamundeswari to swear their innocence, in the belief that the goddess protects the truthful and punishes the liar.

name: Gurdwara Baba Atal
deity: Guru Granth Sahib, at the shrine of Baba Atal Rai
significance: A nine-storey octagonal tower some 40 metres high, raised over the samadhi of Baba Atal Rai, son of Guru Hargobind, just south of the Golden Temple. Its lower storeys were directed by Jodh Singh Ramgarhia and the rest funded by sardars and public donation, with the gilt dome given by Desa Singh Majithia.
story: Atal Rai is said to have restored his snake-bitten friend Mohan to life, and when his father rebuked the display of a miracle he withdrew and gave up his own life in 1628.

name: Gurdwara Mehdiana Sahib
deity: Guru Gobind Singh, commemorated at his resting place
significance: A gurdwara at Mehdiana marking where Guru Gobind Singh and his followers rested after the battle of Chamkaur in 1705 and where he set about composing the Zafarnamah. Begun under Jathedar Jora Singh Lakha around 1970, the complex has since grown to some 25 acres.
story: Sikhs hold that the place carries Guru Gobind Singh's blessing, and that prayers made on a visit here do not go unanswered.

name: Sathyagirisvarar Temple, Thirumayam
deity: Shiva as Sathyagirisvarar, with the goddess Venuvanesvari
significance: A rock-cut Shiva temple carved into the hill of Thirumayam Fort and attributed to the Pallavas. It stands beside a Vishnu temple, the pair long cited as an emblem of sectarian accord.

name: Gurudwara Guru Nanak Dham
deity: Guru Nanak, commemorated at the site of his visit
significance: A gurdwara on the island of Rameswaram built to mark the visit of Guru Nanak, the first Sikh Guru, to the town in about 1511.

name: Parthasarathy Temple, Parthivapuram
deity: Vishnu as Parthasarathy, named Vishnu-bhattarakar in the inscriptions
significance: A Vishnu temple founded in 869 CE by the Ay king Karunandadakkan, its three-storeyed vimana fronted by a Garuda namaskara mandapa. Its copper plates record the endowment of an attached Vedic school for 95 students, making it a key document of early south Indian temple learning.

name: Raghunatha Temple, Alangiri
significance: A nine-pinnacled nabaratna temple of 1810 raised by the Das family within the walled courtyard of their residence at Alangiri near Egra. Standing about forty feet high with triple-arched verandahs on three sides, it is among the largest temples of the Midnapore country.

name: Chowdeshwari Temple, Dasarighatta
deity: Chowdeshwari Devi, as Sri Ramalinga Chowdeswari Ammanavaru
significance: A goddess temple at Dasarighatta about ten kilometres from Tiptur, drawing pilgrims for its Tuesday worship and for Navaratri.

name: Narasimha Temple, Puri
deity: Narasimha, in his Shanta and Ugra forms
significance: A west-facing Narasimha temple about sixty feet high standing between the Gundicha temple and the Indradyumna tank at Puri, laid out on Vaishnava Agama principles and housing both the calm and the wrathful images of the deity.
story: The Skanda Purana tells that king Indradyumna had a Narasimha image carved in black stone and worshipped it here while preparing his Ashwamedha sacrifice, whence the deity is called Yajna Narasimha.

name: Mata Kuan Rani Temple
significance: A slate-roofed shrine built over a deep well on the bank of the Beas at Mandi, honouring the princess Mandarava. It is venerated by Tibetan Buddhists and Hindus alike, linking the town to the Padmasambhava tradition centred on nearby Rewalsar.
story: Legend says the king condemned Mandarava and Padmasambhava to a seven-day fire, and when the smoke cleared a lake had formed with a lotus at its centre, convincing the king of the master's power.

name: Gurudwara Buddha Johad
place: Dabla, Raisinghnagar tehsil, Sri Ganganagar district
deity: Guru Granth Sahib; the gurdwara commemorates Bhai Sukha Singh and Bhai Mehtab Singh
significance: A Sikh shrine in the Rajasthan desert marking the spot to which Sukha Singh and Mehtab Singh carried the head of Massa Ranghar, the Mughal official who had desecrated the Golden Temple in 1740. It is one of the principal historical gurdwaras of the Sri Ganganagar district.

name: Parshuram Temple, Chiplun
place: Parshuram village, Chiplun taluka, Ratnagiri district
deity: Parashurama, the sixth avatar of Vishnu
significance: Also called Shree Kshetra Parshuram, this Konkan hill temple was raised in 1700 on the initiative of Swami Paramhans Brahmendra, with funding from the Siddi commander Rasul Yakut Khan. It is the principal shrine of Parashurama in the region his myth claims he created.
story: Tradition holds that Parashurama shot an arrow into the Arabian Sea to push it back and reclaim the Konkan, then chose the Mahendragiri peak here as his permanent home.

name: Jurahareswarar Temple
significance: A small Pallava-period Shiva shrine in Kanchipuram, attributed to Narasimhavarman II, though some scholars place it instead in the reign of the Chola king Kulottunga III. Its name means 'remover of fever', and the deity is invoked against sickness.
story: The legend holds that Shiva opened his third eye and the fire that issued from it struck the devas with fever, and that they were cured by praying to him and bathing in the waters of this place.

name: Konetirayala Swamy Temple
significance: A Venkateswara temple in the village of Keelapatla near Palamaner, where the deity carries the local name Konetirayudu. It draws pilgrims travelling the Chittoor district route towards Tirumala.
story: Local tradition says Venkateswara set his foot at Keelapatla first, before going on to Tirumala.

name: Sri Peddamma Thalli Temple
deity: Peddamma Thalli, a form of the Divine Mother
significance: A village-goddess shrine in the middle of Jubilee Hills, Hyderabad, dedicated to Peddamma Thalli as a form of the Mother goddess. It is one of the busiest neighbourhood temples in the city, with a large annual Bonalu observance.

name: Arjunesvara Siva Temple
deity: Shiva as Arjunesvara (the article's infobox lists Vishnu)
significance: One of the many small medieval shrines of Bhubaneswar's old town, built of grey sandstone laid as dry masonry in the Kalinga manner. It is dated to the 12th–13th century and survives as part of the city's dense temple landscape.

name: Chakreshvari Siva Temple
deity: Shiva, as a lingam set in a circular yonipitha
significance: A modest rekha-order shrine on Hatiasuni lane in Bhubaneswar's Rajarani Colony, holding a Shiva lingam in a circular yonipitha. It is dated to the 10th–11th century and belongs to the temple cluster around the Rajarani complex.

name: Brahma Temple, Bindusagar
significance: A late-Kalingan shrine on the Bindusagar tank in old Bhubaneswar, unusual in India for having Brahma as its presiding deity. It was built under the Gajapati rulers and is tied ritually to the Lingaraja temple nearby.
story: It is said that Brahma came to Lingaraja's coronation and promised to return every year in the month of Chaitra to serve as the charioteer of Lingaraja's car.

name: Aryankuzhi Devi Temple
deity: Aryankuzhi Bhagavathi, a swayambhu panchaloha image of Parvati
significance: A Bhagavathi shrine in southern Kerala whose presiding image is held to be swayambhu, self-manifested rather than installed. It serves as a local Devi centre in the Thiruvananthapuram district.
story: The temple's origin story tells of a child who fell on a rock that then bled; astrologers read a divine presence in the sign, and worship at the spot grew into the temple.

name: Banapuriswarar Temple
deity: Shiva as Banapuriswarar, with the goddess Somakamalambal
significance: A Shiva temple in Kumbakonam whose name and myth tie it to the story of the town's origin as the place where the pot of amrita came to rest. Shiva is worshipped here as Banapuriswarar alongside the goddess Somakamalambal.
story: The legend holds that this was the spot from which Shiva took aim with his bow and arrow at the floating pot of amrita.

name: Bata Mahadeva Temple
deity: Shiva, as a lingam in a circular yoni pitha
significance: A small pidha-deula shrine standing in the middle of a road in old Bhubaneswar, also known as Mukteswara Shiva. Its pancharatha plan places it in the late Kalingan sequence of the 15th–16th century.
story: It is said that Mahadeva rested at this spot when he visited Ekamra Nagari, and because the shrine sits in the middle of the road he is called Bata Mahadeva, the lord of the way.

name: Kasba Ganapati Temple
significance: The shrine of Pune's gramadevata, traditionally traced to Jijabai Bhosale's arrival in the city around 1630. It ranks as the first of the Manacha Ganpati and was central to Bal Gangadhar Tilak's 1893 reshaping of the Ganesh festival into a public celebration.
story: The image is said to have been self-manifested and no bigger than a grain of rice at first, growing to its present size under successive coats of red sandalwood paste.

name: Kartikesvara Siva Temple
significance: A small thirteenth-century Shiva shrine standing about a hundred metres from the eastern gateway of the Lingaraja temple in Bhubaneswar's old town. It survives as a modest example of late Kalingan temple building, though vegetation and water seepage have left it in poor repair.

name: Parvati Temple, Khajuraho
significance: A small Chandela-era shrine dedicated to Parvati in the western group at Khajuraho, with a heavily restored sanctum. It forms part of the Khajuraho Group of Monuments inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Chitragupta Temple, Kanchipuram
significance: One of very few Indian temples where Chitragupta, the record-keeper who assists Yama, is the presiding deity; the masonry structure dates to the ninth century under the Medieval Cholas. It is a notable Kanchipuram landmark and holds particular importance for the Kayastha community.
story: The temple's legends explain Chitragupta's origin variously, including an account in which Shiva drew his image into being and another in which the divine cow Kamadhenu bore him as a child of Indra.

name: Kunjal Mata Temple
significance: A goddess shrine at Deh in Nagaur district set on some thirty-eight bighas of land beside the Nagaur–Ladnun road. Kunjal Mata is venerated as the kuldevi of Pareek Brahmin families of several gotras.

name: Mahavinayak Temple
deity: Mahavinayak — Shiva, Vishnu, Durga, Surya and Ganesha worshipped as one
significance: A hilltop shrine at Chandikhole whose single sanctum holds five deities — Shiva, Vishnu, Durga, Surya and Ganesha — worshipped together as one. Among the oldest Ganesha sites in Odisha, it draws pilgrims from across the state.
story: The temple is said to mark the spot where Rati's devotion won Kamadeva's release from Shiva's curse, five divine hands reaching out together for her offering to reveal the five gods present as one.

name: Lokanatha Siva Temple
significance: An eleventh-century Shiva temple in Bhubaneswar often read as a miniature prototype of the Lingaraja, and so as a trial run for that far larger project. Buried up to its bandhana and known locally as the Amuha deula, or doorless temple, it was excavated by Debala Mitra in 1972.

name: Mandodari Temple, Betki
significance: The shrine of Mandodari, a water goddess worshipped as the gramadevata of Betki village near Marcel in Goa and distinct from the Ramayana figure of the same name. Its present institution marked its centenary in 2013, though the shrine itself is held to be considerably older.
story: Villagers recount miracles worked by the water goddess and the sacrifice the village made on her account.

name: Narasimha Temple, Bhubaneswar
significance: A late-medieval shrine in Bhubaneswar enshrining a four-armed seated Narasimha, dated on architectural grounds to the fourteenth or fifteenth century. It stands within a precinct shared with other Hindu temples and is kept in good repair by the local community.

name: Nilkantheswar Shiva Temple
significance: A tenth-century Shiva temple on the western embankment of the Bindusagar tank in Bhubaneswar, locally attributed to the Kesari or Somavamshi rulers. Its niches carry parsva devata images of Ganesha, Kartikeya and Parvati, and it remains in worship at Sankranti and Shivaratri.

name: Mandhradevi Kalubai Temple
significance: A hilltop shrine about 20 km from Wai, standing at roughly 4,650 feet and held to be over four centuries old though no firm construction date is recorded. Its ten-day Kalubai Jatra each January draws more than 300,000 pilgrims, and the site became widely known after a fatal stampede there in 2005.
story: Local tradition holds that the goddess defeated demons at this hill, an event still marked by the sacrificial offerings of the annual jatra, and devotees credit the grove around the shrine with miraculous properties.

name: Mahakala-Mahakali Temple
deity: Shiva as Mahakala, with Mahakali (two lingams)
significance: An eleventh-century shrine just beyond the eastern compound wall of the Lingaraja temple, its two lingams set in yonipithas about four metres below present ground level. The superstructure is gone, leaving the sanctum itself as the surviving fabric.
story: Local tradition holds the two lingams to be the parents of Lord Lingaraja.

name: Pabaneswara Temple
significance: A grey sandstone rekha deula of the tenth century, formerly known as the Daitesvara Shiva temple, enshrining a lingam in a circular yonipitha. Heavily renovated and now hemmed in by houses and a market on three sides, little else of its history is recorded.

name: Mahamaya Dham
significance: A Shakta shrine at Bogribari in Kokrajhar district, once the tutelary deity of the zamindars of Parvatjowar and carrying a four-century-old tradition of animal sacrifice. It is regarded as Lower Assam's foremost pilgrimage site after Kamakhya.
story: The adjoining Mahamaya Snaanghat is said to be the spot where the goddess used to bathe.

name: Kumaran Kundram
significance: A hilltop Murugan shrine at Chromepet in Chennai, reached by a climb of about eighty steps and consecrated in 1979 after a proposal by the Kanchi seer Chandrashekarendra Saraswati in 1956. Modelled on Swamimalai, it draws thousands each month for circumambulation and hosts an annual Soorasamharam.
story: Devotees recount that Murugan's vel was found on the hillside as it was being cleared, which spurred the community to press on with building the temple.

name: Mallikarjuna Temple, Canacona
significance: One of Goa's oldest surviving temples, raised in the mid-sixteenth century at Sristhal in Canacona by forebears of the local Kshatriya Samaj and refurbished in 1778. Its halls, rich in wood and silver carving, house some sixty deities, and it is known for the Rajbag beach jatra and the Shisharani ritual.
story: The shrine's name is explained both by Shiva's reunion with Parvati at this spot after their separation and by his killing of the demon Malla in defence of Arjuna.

name: Erumely Sree Dharmasastha Temple
significance: A Travancore Devaswom Board shrine that serves as the main gathering point for Sabarimala pilgrims on the forest route, where the Erumely Pettathullal procession is performed each pilgrimage season.

name: Agnipureeswarar Temple, Thirupugalur
deity: Shiva as Agnipureeswarar, consort Karundar Kuzhali
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam sung in the Tevaram, its masonry attributed to the 10th-century Cholas and carrying inscriptions from the reign of Uttama Chola recording tax-free grants for festivals and upkeep.
story: Agni, the fire god, is said to have worshipped Shiva at this spot, which is why the presiding deity is called Agnipureeswarar.

name: Nepali Mandir
significance: A carved wooden pagoda temple at Lalita Ghat begun by the exiled Nepali king Rana Bahadur Shah and completed by his son Girvan Yuddha Bikram Shah around 1843; modelled on Kathmandu's Pashupatinath and still owned by the Government of Nepal.

name: Shanmughanathar Temple, Kunnakudi
significance: A hill temple to Murugan whose 8th-century Pandya rock-cut caves preserve what are held to be the earliest sculpted dvarapalas in South Indian temple art; it is administered by the Kunnakudi Thiruvannamalai Mutt founded in the 16th century.
story: The sage Agastya is believed to have worshipped Murugan at this hill.

name: Sreevaraham Lakshmi Varaha Temple
deity: Lakshmi Varaha (Varaha with Lakshmi seated on his lap)
significance: One of only three Varaha temples in Kerala and a rare shrine showing Varaha together with Lakshmi; run by the Travancore Devaswom Board, it has a round copper-roofed sanctum and a 2.5-acre tank described as the largest temple pond in the state.

name: Vettuvan Koil
significance: An unfinished monolithic shrine cut downward into the top of a hillock under the early Pandya ruler Netunjadaiyan, the only known Pandya-era temple carved in three dimensions in situ; it is a protected monument of the Tamil Nadu archaeology department.

name: Khudneshwar Asthan Morwa
significance: A Shiva shrine in Morwa built in 1858 by the Narhan Estate; it draws crowds through the year and especially at Mahashivratri and in the month of Shravan.
story: A Muslim woman named Khudni is said to have found the lingam at the spot where her cow began yielding milk of its own accord, and the shrine carries her name.

name: Mahishasuramardini Mandapa
significance: A Pallava rock-cut cave shrine of Narasimhavarman Mahamalla's reign at Mamallapuram, part of the UNESCO-listed Group of Monuments; its three relief panels show Durga defeating the buffalo demon, the reclining Vishnu, and Somaskanda.

name: Sri Sunama Jakini Matha
deity: Sunama Jakini Mata and Malkuma Jakini Mata
significance: A modern shrine of the Suryavamshi Kshatriya Are-Katika community whose foundation was laid in February 2002 and whose consecration followed in February 2003; its annual celebrations draw an estimated 15,000-20,000 pilgrims.
story: Sunama Jakini is remembered as a devout woman buried alive on the order of her intoxicated husband around 1803 and venerated as a goddess thereafter.

name: Trichambaram Temple
deity: Krishna (in raudra form after the slaying of Kamsa)
builtDisplay: 15th–16th c. carvings and murals; attested 11th c.
significance: A Krishna temple at Taliparamba in north Kerala whose sanctum preserves carvings and murals of the 15th and 16th centuries, with the shrine already named in an 11th-century Sanskrit text. Its tank shrine to Durga is counted among the 108 ancient Durga temples of Kerala.

name: Valiyasala Mahadeva Temple
significance: One of the old Trimurti temples of Thiruvananthapuram, standing on the site historically associated with Kanthaloor Sala, a celebrated centre of learning in early Kerala.
story: Local tradition holds that temples to Brahma, Venkata Perumal and Mahadeva arose at the spots where queens of the Chera, Chola and Pandya kings performed sati after their husbands died in the Kanthaloor country.

name: Vaigalnathar Temple
builtDisplay: Early Chola (attributed to Kochengannan); century unrecorded
significance: A Shiva temple in the Kaveri delta held to be one of the three principal shrines raised by the early Chola king Kochengannan, and praised in the Tamil Saiva canon.

name: Sukutesvara Temple
significance: A living Shiva temple in the old town of Bhubaneswar behind the Lingaraja market, built of dry laterite masonry in the Kalinga pidha deul form and dated by its navagraha panel and structure to the 16th century.
story: Local tradition attributes the shrine to the heyday of the Kesari rulers.

name: Hridayaleeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Thirunindravur west of Chennai, credited to Pallava builders of the 6th century and built in the Dravidian manner.

name: Vrindavan Chandrodaya Mandir
significance: An ISKCON temple under construction at Vrindavan whose foundation stone was laid in 2014 and which, at a planned 210 m and 75 floors, is intended to be the tallest religious monument in the world.

name: Vasudevapuram Temple, Tavanur
deity: Krishna (youthful form holding butter in both hands)
significance: A Krishna temple on the southern bank of the Bharathapuzha at Tavanur, one of a group of old shrines there that includes a Shiva and a Brahma temple and faces Thirunavaya across the river.
story: The child Krishna is said to have appeared to the saint Vilwamangalam Swamiyar here, and the image of the youthful Krishna was installed after the saint left his body.

name: Lalita Gauri Mandir
significance: A Shakta shrine near Kashi Vishwanath built in the first years of the 19th century by the exiled Nepali king Rana Bahadur Shah; the Ganga ghat beside it takes its name from the temple.

name: Kambatta Viswanathar Temple
significance: One of the twelve Shiva temples of Kumbakonam associated with the twelve-yearly Mahamaham festival; its name records a Chola-period mint that struck gold and silver coins on the spot.

name: Someshwara Temple, Marathahalli
significance: A Shiva temple at Marathahalli in eastern Bengaluru, recorded as having been completed in 1508. The Wikipedia entry is a short stub and carries maintenance notices about sourcing.

name: Shri Tilbhandeshwar Mahadev Mandir
significance: One of the older and better-known Shiva temples of Varanasi, believed to have been built in the 18th century in the Bhelupur quarter. Its lingam stands about three and a half feet high with a base roughly three feet across.
story: The lingam is said to have emerged of its own accord 2,500 years ago and to grow each year by the width of a sesame seed, from which the temple takes its name.

name: Sundaresvarar Temple, Kundayur
significance: One of the Vaippu Sthalams praised in the hymns of the Nayanar Sundarar, near Thirukkuvalai in Nagapattinam district. The temple has no gopuram but opens to both east and west, keeps two atti trees, and holds an annual Nel Atti Vizha during Masi Maham.
story: Sundarar is said to have asked the god at Tirukkuvalai to send on the paddy he had been given, and the deity had it delivered by his attendants.

name: Gopnath Mahadev Temple
significance: A shore temple to Shiva on the Gulf of Khambhat coast at Gopnath, described as nearly seven hundred years old and flying two flags for its Mahadev and Vishnu shrines. A fort of the ruler of Gohilwad also stands at the site.
story: The devotional poet Narsinh Mehta is said to have had his decisive spiritual experience at this Shiva temple some five centuries ago.

name: Mariyamma Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Urwa in Mangaluru raised roughly eight centuries ago by the Mogaveera fishing community, whose members offer gold ornaments shaped as mackerel, sardine, prawn and pomfret in thanksgiving. Fishermen have long prayed here during crises at sea, and the Mari Puja festival falls in early March.
story: A member of the Mogaveera community is said to have been possessed by the goddess and told by her to build a temple for her at Urwa.

name: Kote Anjaneya Temple
significance: A Hanuman temple at Tumakuru whose image was consecrated more than five centuries ago by Vyasaraja, rajaguru of the Vijayanagara empire and teacher of Kanakadasa and Purandaradasa, as one of 732 Hanuman images he installed across India. A 75-foot statue of the god was unveiled at its entrance in May 2005.

name: Swamithope Pathi
significance: The foremost of the five pathis of the Ayyavazhi tradition, in Kanyakumari district. Its inner Palliyarai keeps objects held to have been used by Ayya Vaikundar, including a rattan cane and wooden sandals, and the Ayya Vaikunda Avataram festival draws followers from across the country.
story: Followers hold that Vaikundar performed austerities at this spot for six years and was afterwards interred within the temple.

name: Agastheesvarar Temple, Kuzhaiyur
significance: A Shiva temple at Kuzhaiyur counted among the Vaippu Sthalams sung by the Nayanar Appar. It has no gopuram, only a walled entrance and a single prakaram, and holds further shrines to Subramanya, Kasi Visvanatha and Varadharaja Perumal; its last kumbhabhishekham was in July 2009.
story: When Shiva's wedding on Kailash tilted the earth's balance, he sent the sage Agastya south to restore it, and the sage is said to have worshipped here on that journey, giving the place its name.

name: Talikotta Mahadeva Temple
significance: One of the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala and one of the four thali temples named in the 108-temple hymn, where the god is worshipped in his fierce aspect. It was a principal shrine of the Thekkumkur kingdom, which Marthanda Varma annexed to Travancore after the Changanassery war of 1750.
story: Folklore credits the sage Parashurama with installing the Shiva image here.

name: Rajah Annamalaipuram Ayyappan Koil
significance: An Ayyappa temple on Santhome High Road in Chennai, founded in 1981 and consecrated in 1982 by the industrialist M. A. M. Ramaswamy Chettiar of the Chettinad group on land given by Rajah Sir Muthiah Chettiar, and built as a close copy of the Sabarimala shrine after his 1973 pilgrimage there. Its panchaloha image of Ayyappa, made by the sculptor Bhattanachariar, was installed on 25 January 1982.

name: Kulathupuzha Sastha Temple
significance: One of the five major Sastha temples of Kerala, where the deity is worshipped as a child and known as the Kulathupuzha Balakan; it is administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board. Devotees seeking relief from skin ailments make the Meenoottu offering of feeding the fish in its pond, which shelters the endangered Tor khudree and Hypselobarbus thomassi.
story: Sastha is said to have allowed a mermaid-like being drawn to him to live on in the temple pond in the form of a fish.

name: Karivellur Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple near Payyanur in Kannur district, counted among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala. It was formerly held by the Chirakkal Kovilakam.

name: Cheruvathur Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple about a kilometre from Kunnamkulam, reckoned among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala. Its east-facing sanctum is circular and roofed in copper.
story: Tradition holds that the sage Parasurama installed the image, as at the other temples of the 108 Shiva group.

name: Masilamaninathar Temple, Tharangambadi
significance: Built in 1306 by the Pandya king Maravarman Kulasekara Pandiyan I, this is one of the few surviving shore temples in India, standing 300 m north of the Danish Fort Dansborg. Its design mixes Tamil and Chinese elements, said to have been intended to draw Chinese merchants, and it is one of the Vaippu Sthalams sung by the Nayanars Appar and Sundarar.

name: Maa Pratyangira Kalika Alayam
significance: A temple at Moranapalli near Hosur devoted chiefly to Pratyangira, alongside Sharabha, Narasimha and Mariamman, and said to carry the largest image of the goddess, set on its gopuram. Worshippers offer garlands and light ghee lamps below the deity, and the temple draws heavy crowds through the week.

name: Sasthamangalam Mahadevar Temple
deity: Shiva as Uma Maheshwara, with Parvati
significance: A Shiva temple in the Sasthamangalam ward of Thiruvananthapuram, dated by surviving records to more than seven centuries ago. The kings of Travancore worshipped here regularly, and it is now run by the Travancore Devaswom Board.
story: A woman sharpening her knife on a rock is said to have made it bleed, revealing a Shiva lingam, and the temple was raised on that spot.

name: Thanthondreeswarar Temple, Woraiyur
significance: A Shiva temple attributed to the Pandya ruler Varaguna Pandiyan II in the 9th century, with inscriptions of 885 CE from the Chola period and a further record of a donation by a feudatory's queen in 911 CE under Parantaka I. It has a single prakaram and a two-tiered vimana but no gopuram, six daily services, and a bangle festival in the month of Thai as its chief celebration.
story: Shiva is said to have appeared here of his own accord as a lingam to grant the Chola queen Kanthimathi a safe delivery.

name: Chowalloor Siva Temple
significance: One of the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala and one of five Shiva shrines ringing Guruvayur. Its sanctum carries a copper roof with a golden finial, and a Subrahmanya shrine was added in renovations in 2001.
story: Folklore holds that the sage Parashurama installed the Shiva image here.

name: Aneswaram Siva Temple
significance: A west-facing Shiva temple at Chemmappilly, about three kilometres from the Thriprayar temple, once owned by a Namboothiri illam and now under the Cochin Devaswom Board. The annual Vavu bali offering to ancestors is performed here.
story: The Thriprayar Thevar is said never to have passed Aneswaram silently on his village circuit, because this deity had once lent him paddy and coconut.

name: Umiya Mata Temple, Unjha
significance: The principal temple of Umiya, clan deity of the Kadava Patidars, at Unjha in Mehsana district; it marked its silver jubilee in November 2009 with Chief Minister Narendra Modi in attendance. The shrine is a fixture for politicians seeking Kadava Patidar support, and the community has founded related Umiya Mata temples abroad, including one at Macon, Georgia in 2013.

name: Bodyguard Muniswaran Temple
significance: A folk-deity shrine of 1919 about 1.5 km from Chennai Central station, set up by labourers who had come from North Arcot district. Thousands visit daily, many of them holding that Muneeswarar guards them against accidents.
story: The labourers are said to have placed the idol under a neem tree beside the British military barracks; the commander who objected met with an accident the same day and thereafter allowed the installation.

name: Ghanteshwar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the bank of the Ratnakar river in Hooghly district, rebuilt in 1943 by the local zamindar Bipin Bihari Sinha after flood damage, with subsidiary shrines to Durga, Kaal Bhairav, Surya, Kali, Shashti, Sitala, Dharmaraj, Radha Krishna, Annapurna and Shani, and a Sufi pir's shrine. Its calendar keeps the Bengal folk festivals of Neel Puja, Gajan, Shivratri, Bhimekadashi and Ratha Yatra.
story: Local belief holds that the same Shiva lingam has been worshipped on this spot for more than five hundred years.

name: Kameeswarar Temple, Villianur
deity: Shiva as Kameeswarar, with Parvati as Kokilambigai
significance: A two-acre Shaiva complex at Villianur whose origins lie in the 12th century, with additions by the later Cholas and the Vijayanagara empire and a present masonry structure of the 16th century; Raja Narayana Sambuvarayar, who ruled 1339 to 1363, was a major donor. Concentric granite walls enclose its shrines, and the Aadi-month Brahmotsavam is the chief festival.

name: Mankameshwar Temple, Agra
significance: Reckoned among the oldest temples in Agra, this Shiva shrine near Agra Fort railway station is reached by descending a flight of steps to a sunken sanctum holding a silver-clad lingam. Smaller shrines behind it are given to Ganga, Saraswati, Hanuman, Krishna and Rama among others.
story: Tradition holds that Shiva himself established the lingam here in the Dvapara Yuga, at the time Krishna was born in Mathura.

name: Bhand Deva Temple
significance: A 10th-century Shaiva temple of the tantric tradition inside the Ramgarh meteor crater in Baran district, built by Raja Malaya Verma of the Nag dynasty of Malwa and renovated in 1162 by Raja Trisna Verma of the Med dynasty. Its sculpture has earned it the name Little Khajuraho, and it is protected by the state archaeology department; over 750 steps climb Ramgarh hill to cave shrines of Kisnai and Annapurna built by Jhala Jalim Singh, where a Kartik Purnima fair is held.

name: Bhagavan Kovil, Kosavalasu
significance: A Vaishnava temple near Dharapuram in Tiruppur district completed in the 19th century and credited to Aadhi Gounder. It is best known for its Ugadi festival on the Telugu new year in March or April, which draws hundreds of thousands of visitors.

name: Kanthaswamy Temple, Cheyyur
deity: Murugan as Kanthaswamy, with Valli and Deivasena
significance: A 10th-century Chola foundation at Cheyyur with rectangular granite walls and a flat rajagopuram on the north, now under the Tamil Nadu HR and CE board. Its sanctum holds a five-foot granite Vel, and rare carvings of the twenty-seven Bhutaganas ring the shrine.
story: Murugan is said to have installed a Shiva image here to cleanse himself of the sin of killing the demon Sooran, and the village is said to take its name from his son Sei, who worshipped him at this spot.

name: Mritangeshvara Shiva Temple, Nandchand
significance: The chief standing landmark of an archaeological site at Nandchand in Panna district that preserves remains of the Kalachuri kingdom. Sculpture recovered around the temple and across the site is now held in the Sagar University Museum.

name: Kailasanathar Temple, Karaikal
builtDisplay: Pallava rebuilding, 8th c.; repaired under French rule
significance: The largest temple complex in Karaikal town, rebuilt by the Pallavas in the 8th century and again during French rule, with four ornate doorways facing the cardinal directions. Besides the consort Soundarambal it carries shrines to Nataraja, Dakshinamurthy, Vinayaka, Muruga and many saints, and keeps the Mangani, Theppotsavam and Rathotsavam festivals.
story: Local belief holds the shrine to be more than two thousand years old.

name: Karkuvel Ayyanar Temple
deity: Karkuvel Ayyanar, with consorts Poornam and Porkamalam
significance: A guardian-deity temple about 14 km from Thiruchendur, set in a tract of red sand dunes often called the only desert in South India and ringed by cashew and palm. Its Kallar Vettu festival across late Karthigai and early Margazhi involves coconut-breaking and holy water carried from the Thamirabarani, and the last consecration was held on 1 September 2022.
story: The deity is said to have emerged from a tree called Karkuva, and devotees gather the sand where the festival coconut water falls, believing it brings prosperity and guards against theft.

name: Kalki Mandir, Jaipur
significance: An 18th-century temple built by Jai Singh II opposite the palace gate in Jaipur's old city, dedicated to Kalki, the tenth and final avatar of Vishnu foretold in Hindu tradition, alongside Lakshmi. A white marble horse stands in its courtyard.

name: Nariampara Puthiyakavu Devikshethram
significance: A Devi shrine in the high range about 3 km from Kattappana on the Kuttikkanam road, rebuilt in 1989 by the Kalloorath family under K. K. Thankapan in place of an earlier 20th-century shrine, and historically linked to the Moothedathu Devi Temple at Vaikom. Its festival is the Kumbha Bharani Mahotsavam in February and March.

name: Arjuneswarar Temple, Kadathur
deity: Shiva as Arjuneswarar, with Gomathi Amman
significance: An east-facing Chola-period Shiva temple on the bank of the Amaravathi in Tiruppur district, run by the Tamil Nadu HR and CE department with the Arjuneswarar Trust. Twice a year sunlight reflected off the river falls on the lingam, a cremation ground lies before the sanctum as at Kashi, and a marble Dakshinamurthy brought from Kashi is enshrined here.
story: The temple takes its name from the belief that Arjuna worshipped this lingam in the time of the Mahabharata, and the lingam is said to carry the root impressions of an ancient Arjuna tree.

name: Gomateshwar Mahadev Temple, Kerakat
significance: Dated to the era of Harshavardhana in the 7th century, this is the largest and most ornate temple of the medieval group at Kerakat and is counted among the better-preserved medieval temples in India. Its lingam was buried by raiders and later recovered, and villagers rebuilt the temple in 1990; the name means the great god of the Gomti, on whose bank it stands.

name: Varadharajaperumal Temple, Thirubuvanai
significance: A Chola temple at Thirubuvanai in Puducherry raised by Parantaka I and carrying later inscriptions of Rajaraja Chola and Rajadhiraja I; those records show it also functioned as a teaching centre for the Vedas and other scriptures, and the building survived the French invasion of the region.

name: Thukkachi Abatsahayesvar Temple
builtDisplay: 11th c. (Rajendra Chola I); enlarged under Vikrama Chola
significance: A Chola temple on the Arasalar river at Thukkachi, east of Kumbakonam, built under Rajendra Chola I and enlarged by Vikrama Chola; its vimana resembles that of the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram, and a restoration carried out between 2015 and 2023 drew UNESCO recognition.
story: Vikrama Chola, afflicted with vitiligo, is said to have been told by the deity in a dream while camped near Thukkachi to worship here for forty-eight days, after which he was cured.

name: Puttur Shree Mahalingeshwara Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the town of Puttur, Dakshina Kannada district, built in Kerala style and credited to a Banga ruler; the article dates it to the 12th century while its own infobox gives the 8th.

name: Trivikrama Temple, Ter
builtDisplay: 2nd-3rd c. CE apsidal shrine; mandapa added from 6th c.
significance: An apsidal shrine at Ter in Dharashiv district regarded as the oldest standing structure in Maharashtra, built in Satavahana times to an early Buddhist caityagriha design and given a flat-roofed mandapa from about the 6th century when it passed into Hindu worship. Henry Cousens read the original building as Buddhist, a view M. S. Mate disputed in 1957.

name: Balasubramaniyaswamy Temple, Vennaimalai
significance: A hill temple to Murugan at Vennaimalai in Karur district, Tamil Nadu, run by the state Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments department and among the district's best-known visitor sites.
story: When Brahma grew proud of his role as creator, Shiva is said to have sent him to do penance at Vanjimalai, and the divine cow Kamadhenu took over creation, raising a hill of butter - vennai in Tamil - and filling the sacred tank with her milk.

name: Sun Temple, Sesai
significance: A west-facing temple to the sun god Surya in the village of Sesai, Shivpuri district, Madhya Pradesh, raised on a jagati platform.

name: Kumara Swamy Devasthana, Bengaluru
significance: A hilltop shrine to Kartikeya at Hanumanthanagar in Bengaluru, on the rise known as Mount Joy; its original panchaloha image is now kept on separate display while a later granite idol receives worship, and the shrine is likened to the Swaminatha Swamy temple in Thanjavur.

name: Prabhadevi Temple
significance: A goddess temple in Mumbai built in 1715 with funds raised by the Pathare Prabhu community to house a 12th-century image of Shakambari Devi, held to have been the family deity of the Seuna Yadava king Bimba of Devagiri; the idol was taken to Karnataka, attacked during Mughal times and finally brought to Mahim Creek before installation here.
story: Local folklore says the goddess appeared in a dream to Shyam Nayak, a devotee of the Pathare Prabhu community, who then built her a temple.

name: Thiruvullakkavu Sree Dharma Sastha Temple
deity: Dharma Sastha (Ayyappan), standing with a bow
significance: A Sastha temple at Cherpu in Thrissur district, long resorted to for Vidyarambham, the rite at which small children are initiated into letters and learning.

name: Aadi Himani Chamunda
builtDisplay: at least as old as the adjacent palace ruins of c. 1660
significance: A high mountain shrine of Chamunda Devi above Kangra in Himachal Pradesh, reckoned at least as old as the palace ruins of about 1660 beside it. Long derelict, it was restored from 1992 largely through two decades of work by the retired officer P. D. Saini, destroyed by fire in 2014 and rebuilt.
story: The goddess is said to have killed the demons Chanda and Munda by hurling great boulders down on them from the mountain top, and to take her name from them.

name: Maa Barunei Temple
deity: Barunei, a manifestation of Shakti (with Karunei)
significance: A hill shrine on Barunei Hill in Khordha district, Odisha, whose sanctum holds images of the twin goddesses Barunei and Karunei; the stream called Swarna Ganga runs from the hills beside it.

name: Maa Jhanjiri Mangala Temple
significance: A temple of the goddess Mangala, the presiding deity of Cuttack, raised by villagers and counted among the oldest in the city; a theft from it in 2015 led to the arrest of a gang.
story: A priest living in the forest is said to have seen the goddess Mangala in a dream, who asked him to build a small temple for her.

name: Ponmeri Shiva Temple
significance: A large Mahadeva temple near Vatakara in Kozhikode district commissioned by the Kadathanad kings in the 11th century, unusual for carrying a sub-shrine to Brahma, a deity seldom given one.
story: A quarrel between the ruler and his architect is said to have left the building forever unfinished, and gave Malayalam the proverb 'as incomplete as the work at Ponmeri'.

name: Ekalavya Temple
significance: A temple at Khandsa village in Gurugram, built in 1721 by a well-off villager, described as the only Hindu temple anywhere dedicated to Ekalavya of the Mahabharata.
story: Ekalavya, self-taught and found to outshine Arjuna, cut off his right thumb when Dronacharya asked for it as gurudakshina, and the temple stands where the thumb is said to have been buried.

name: Jasmalnathji Mahadev Temple, Asoda
significance: A 12th-century panchayatana Shiva temple at Asoda in Mehsana district, raised during the reign of the Chaulukya king Jayasimha Siddharaja and now a Monument of National Importance maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Chennamangalam Temple
significance: An Ayyappa temple at Chorode in Kozhikode district that also houses Shiva, Ganesha, Vishnu and Annapurneshwari; described as one of Kerala's oldest and known as a second Sabarimala, it drew large numbers when a fire kept pilgrims from Sabarimala itself.

name: Sri Gangamma Devi Temple
significance: A temple to the local goddess Gangamma in the Malleswara layout of north-western Bengaluru, given a permanent building in 2004; the annual Gangamma Jathre has been held in the locality since 1928.

name: Soundararajaperumal Temple, Thadikombu
significance: A 16th-century temple at Thadikombu in Dindigul district credited to the Vijayanagara ruler Achyuta Deva Raya, with work begun under his predecessor Aliya Rama Raya and the outer halls added in 1629 under Thirumalai Nayak; it carries rare sculpture and inscriptions from several reigns.
story: A sage cursed to live as a frog and tormented by a demon is said to have worshipped Vishnu here, who killed the demon and freed him.

name: Dudhadhari Temple
significance: A math and temple at Mathpara in Raipur founded in the 16th century by Swami Balabhadradas, who was called Dudh Ahari because he lived on milk alone and so gave the place its name. The Bhonsle Maratha ruler of Nagpur, Raghuji, later issued a charter conferring the title Rajeshri on each head of the math.

name: Aryankavu Sastha Temple
style: Dravidian, blending Kerala and Tamil traditions
significance: One of the five principal Sastha temples of Kerala, at Aryankavu in Kollam district, where the deity is worshipped as a youth seated on an elephant with Pushkala at his left and Shiva at his right; it is administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board.
story: The image is held to have been consecrated by Parashurama, and Sastha is said to have married Pushkaladevi here, an event kept each December as the Thiru Kalyanam festival.

name: Avanibhajana Pallaveshwaram Temple
significance: A Pallava cave temple cut at Seeyamangalam under Mahendravarman I in the early 7th century, among the earliest examples of rock-cut architecture in the region and holding one of the oldest surviving depictions of Nataraja; Chola and Vijayanagara additions came later.

name: Jamalapuram Temple
significance: A Venkateswara temple at Jamalapuram near Errupalem in Khammam district, described as of considerable antiquity and renovated under Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara; it is popularly called the Chinna Tirupati of Telangana.
story: The sage Jabali is said to have performed penance at a spot here called Suchi Gutta and been blessed by Venkateswara, who is worshipped as a self-manifested form.

name: Polur Temple, Kozhikode
significance: A Subrahmanya temple at Polor in Kuruvattoor panchayat, Kozhikode district, counted among the oldest in the area and connected with the Porlathiri king from whom the region takes its name; Ganapathi, Vettakkorumakan, Ayyappan and Devi are also worshipped here.

name: Mahalakshmi Temple, Dahanu
significance: A temple of the goddess Mahalakshmi in Dahanu taluka of Palghar district, recorded as built in 1306 by the Koli king Jayaba Mukne at the founding of Jawhar State. It is a major pilgrimage draw in the coastal Palghar region.
story: Local tradition says the goddess, first worshipped atop Mahalakshmi Gad hill, came down to settle at the foot of the hill for the sake of a devotee who could no longer climb it.

name: Namakkal Anjaneyar Temple
builtDisplay: image traditionally dated to the 5th c.
significance: A Hanuman temple in Namakkal town whose eighteen-foot standing image is traditionally held to have stood here since the 5th century. The shrine faces the Narasimhaswamy temple across the Namakkal rock, and the two are worshipped as a pair.
story: The temple's legend tells that Hanuman was carrying a saligrama for Lakshmi's penance when it grew into a hill at this spot, and Narasimha appeared and made it his abode.

name: Vedapureeswarar Temple, Puducherry
significance: A Dravidian-style Shiva temple in the town of Puducherry, destroyed in 1748 during the colonial conflicts on the Coromandel coast and rebuilt in 1788 by Divan Kandappa Mudaliar.

name: Kalyana Varadharaja Perumal Temple
significance: A Vishnu temple at Kaladipet in Thiruvottiyur, north Chennai, estimated at some five hundred years old, whose construction in the early 1700s was funded by Joseph Collett, the East India Company's President of Madras, at the request of his administrator Vijayaraghavachariar.
story: The temple's founding tale says Vijayaraghavachariar kept travelling to Kanchipuram even after a local temple was built because of the beauty of the processional deity there, so Collett had that deity brought to the new shrine.

name: Gude Mahalingeswara Temple
deity: Shiva as Gude Mahalingeswara, worshipped as a lingam
significance: A Shiva temple at Herenjalu in Kundapura taluk of coastal Udupi district, where the god is worshipped in lingam form as Gude Mahalingeswara.

name: Karikkode Bhagavathy Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Karikkode near Thodupuzha in Idukki district, believed to be about 460 years old, where Bhadrakali presides with subordinate shrines to Shiva and Ganesha.
story: Tradition holds that a raja of Vadakkumkoor undertook long penance and prayer to bring the Kodungallur Bhagavathy to this temple.

name: Karyat Sree Ayyappa Temple, Vanimal
significance: An Ayyappa temple at Vanimal in Kozhikode district that began in 1987 as a small bhajana madam and grew into a full temple.

name: Maa Dewri Temple
deity: Dewri Devi, a sixteen-armed village goddess
significance: A goddess shrine about 60 km from Ranchi, founded around 1300 by the Adivasi Munda king Kera of Singhbhum and held to be some seven centuries old. It is worshipped by both Hindu and Sarna tribal devotees, and its sixteen-armed image is unusual in the region.
story: The temple's founding story says King Kera, defeated in battle, worshipped at the sacred grove here and won his kingdom back by the goddess's blessing.

name: Shiva Bhagwati Temple, Akingam
significance: A goddess shrine at the head of Akingam village in Anantnag district, near the foothills. It is the only one of four shrines in Jammu and Kashmir to hold a tract of forest land as jagir entered in its own revenue records.

name: Lalguan Mahadeva Temple
significance: A small ruined granite Shiva temple at Khajuraho dated to about 900 CE, the second oldest surviving temple on the site after the Chausath Yogini temple. Its curvilinear tower has fallen and its entrance porch is gone, leaving a pyramid-roofed shell.

name: Vallakottai Subramaniyaswami Temple
