significance: A Murugan temple on the Sriperumbudur–Singaperumalkoil road in Kanchipuram district, held by hagiographical records to date from the 9th century and partly rock-cut.
story: Its name is explained by the legend that Murugan killed a demon called Vallan here, making the place Vallan Kottai, the fort of Vallan.

name: Parippu Mahadeva Temple
significance: An east-facing Shiva temple at Parippu in Aymanam panchayat, Kottayam district, whose present structure is dated to 825 CE and which is counted among the 108 Shivalayas of Kerala. It is administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board. Note: the article's coordinate (9.6197, 76.4771) is used here in place of the Wikidata point about 7 km away.
story: Tradition explains the temple's two Balikkalpuras, unique in Kerala, as the work of two rival rajas who each built their own frontage so as never to meet the other.

name: Adikesava Perumal Temple, Sriperumbudur
deity: Vishnu as Adi Kesava, with Lakshmi as Ethiraja Nadhavalli
significance: A Vishnu temple at Sriperumbudur, the birthplace of the Vaishnava teacher Ramanuja, carrying Vijayanagara inscriptions of 1556 and 1572 and combining Chola and Vijayanagara features. It is maintained by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Endowment Board.
story: The temple's legend tells how Ramanuja travelled to Delhi to recover a stolen image, which fell of its own accord into his lap.

name: Pallimanna Siva Temple
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; murals of the 17th–18th c.
significance: A Shiva temple at Kumbalangad in Thrissur district, described as a classical dravida-style temple of Kerala. Its wall murals, dated to the 17th and 18th centuries, have been protected by the Archaeological Survey of India as a monument of national importance since 1983.

name: Punnainallur Kailasanathar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Punnainallur near Thanjavur, one of the 88 shrines of the Thanjavur Palace Devasthanam administered by the Tamil Nadu HR&CE department. A Nataraja bronze stolen from it in 1971 was recovered from the Asia Society Museum in New York and returned in 2021.

name: Swayambhu Sri Abhista Gnana Ganapathi Temple
significance: A modern Ganesha temple at Mayuri Greenland in Kurnool district, built by the Jampala family and consecrated over three days in August 2013. It is run by the Jampala Abhinay Charitable Trust.

name: Naulakha Temple, Deoghar
significance: A tall temple to Radha and Krishna about 1.5 km from the Baidyanath Temple in Deoghar, completed in 1940 for Rani Charushila of the Pathuriaghata Ghosh family of Kolkata, who built it on the advice of the saint Balananda Brahmachari after losing her husband and son. Its design echoes the Ramakrishna Mission's Belur Math.

name: Patan Devi
deity: Durga, as Maa Sarvanand Kari Patneshwari
dynasty: Mughal era; attributed to Man Singh
significance: An old goddess temple in Patna City, revered as a Shakti Peetha and known in two shrines, Bari and Chhoti Patan Devi. Fragmentary remains point to a temple here between the 9th and 11th centuries, while the Chhoti Patan Devi's present form is placed in the 16th or 17th century and the Bari Patan Devi was founded by Badrinath Chaudhary in the British period.
story: The Shakti Peetha legend holds that the right thigh of Sati fell at this spot when Vishnu cut her body with his Sudarshan Chakra.

name: Valliyamkavu Devi Temple
deity: Durga, worshipped in her fierce Bhadra form
significance: A goddess temple at Paloorkavu in Kottayam district whose present structure was completed in 2001. Worship there was long held by tribal custodians under the Vanchipuzha Thamburan, and the Travancore Devaswom Board took over its rights in 1993. Note: the article's coordinate is used here in place of the Wikidata point about 5 km away.
story: Its legend says the exiled Pandavas gave a Durga image to local tribespeople, whose improper worship turned the goddess into the fierce Bhadra and made the country uninhabitable until she moved to Valliyamkavu.

name: Pazhaya Sreekanteswaram Temple
significance: The older of the two Sreekanteswaram temples of Thiruvananthapuram, at Puthenchantha, which the historian Elamkulam Kunjan Pillai held to have existed since at least 1000 CE. Its linga is traditionally said to have been installed by Parashurama.
story: The temple's legend tells of a Yadava prince cursed by the sage Athiyara Potti into a centaur-like form, who won release after ten years of servitude and devotion to Sreekanteswara.

name: Thanthondreeswarar Temple, Nedungadu
significance: A red-sandstone Shiva temple built by Chola rulers at Nedungadu in Karaikal district. Excavations in 1948 recovered 14th-century bronze sculptures from the site.
story: The village's name is said to come from the goddess Nedunthuyar Theertha Nayaki, consort of Tantondreeswara, whose name means the one who ended the people's long sorrow.

name: Ekambaranathar Temple, Tiruvekambathur
significance: A Shiva temple at Tiruvekambathur, also called Tiruvekambattu or Tiruvekambam, in Ramanathapuram district, where the god is worshipped as Ekambaranathar with the goddess Snehavalli.

name: Baneswar Shiva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple about ten kilometres from Cooch Behar town whose linga stands in an underground sanctum beneath a squarish domed structure with a curved cornice. Its foundation is contested between several traditions, variously crediting Raja Jalpeswar, the Khen ruler Nilambar, and the Koch rulers Nara Narayan and Pran Narayan, and it draws large crowds at Maha Shivaratri.
story: Tradition tells that the demon king Banasura persuaded Shiva to come down to earth, and that when Banasura halted at Baneswar the god vanished, leaving a linga on the bank of the Bangti river.

name: Mahudi Jain Temple
deity: Padmaprabha (complex also centred on Ghantakarna Mahavir)
significance: A Shvetambara Jain pilgrimage complex founded by the monk Buddhisagarsuri, its foundation stone laid in 1916 and the temple established the following year. Scholars credit it with turning the worship of the protective deity Ghantakarna Mahavir from a largely private monastic transmission into a public devotional cult that now draws well beyond the Jain community.

name: Adhirangam Ranganathaswamy Temple
significance: A five-acre Vishnu temple built up by Chola and Vijayanagara patrons, holding a reclining image some 29 feet long and counted among the 108 Abhimana Kshetrams of Vaishnavism. It is reputed to be older than Srirangam, which gives it the name Adhi Rangam, and it preserves an unusual brick grain store.
story: The temple's legend has Ranganatha rise from the water here to recover the Vedas stolen by the demon king Somukan and to counsel Brahma.

name: Kamteswari Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Gosanimari raised in 1665 by Maharaja Pran Narayan of Cooch Behar to replace an earlier shrine that had been destroyed. Standing 14 metres high on a square base with a curved cornice and circular dome, it is a state-protected monument and holds Pala-era sculpture alongside its images.

name: Bezor Doul
significance: A late-medieval brick temple with an octagonal sanctuary, built under the Ahom king Rudra Singha in memory of a Bezbarua, a court physician granted extensive land in the area for his skill in traditional medicine. Though it holds no images inside, it remains in worship and is a State Protected Monument of Assam.

name: Vijayanarayana Temple, Gundlupet
significance: A Vishnu temple in Gundlupet town going back to 10th-century Western Ganga rule, with patronage continuing into the Vijayanagara period. Its yali-pillared entrance, Garuda and Hanuman sculpture, and garbhagriha-navaranga-mandapa plan make it a working example of medieval South Indian temple craft.
story: Tradition credits the Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana with consecrating the image of Vijayanarayana here.

name: Murali Mohan Temple
significance: A Krishna temple at Bishnupur built in 1665 by Churamoni Devi, wife of the Mallabhum king Bir Singha Dev. Its single tower over a pillared covered ambulatory is a textbook example of the Bengal ek-ratna form, and the ASI holds it as a Monument of National Importance.

name: Surya Temple, Ranchi
significance: A modern sun temple near Bundu whose foundation was laid in 1991 and consecrated in 1994 by the Sanskriti Vihar trust under Sita Ram Maroo. Shaped as a great chariot with eighteen wheels and seven horses and also housing Shiva, Parvati and Ganesha, it has become a leading Chhath Puja destination with bathing and pilgrim facilities.

name: Kalyaneshwari Temple
significance: A Shakta shrine near Asansol described as some five centuries old, with the present temple built by Gurudin Prasad Pal. It is best known as a place of pilgrimage for childless women seeking a boon from the goddess.
story: Legend holds that human sacrifices were once offered at Kalyaneshwari in the distant past.

name: Patali Srikhetra
significance: A pilgrimage site at the foot of Trikut Hill in Subarnapur district, revered as the place where the Jagannath images were hidden for safekeeping and drawing together Shakta, Buddhist and Vaishnava strands of worship. The hill also carries evidence of prehistoric settlement, giving the site archaeological as well as devotional weight.
story: The Madala Panji relates that King Sovanadeva concealed the images in the caves of Trikut Hill during Raktavahu's invasion, where they stayed 144 years until King Yayati Keshari recovered them.

name: Jagannath Temple, Delhi
significance: A Jagannath temple in the Safdarjung Development Area of Hauz Khas, built by Delhi's Odia community as its main religious centre in the capital. Its annual Rath Yatra procession draws thousands and is among the largest Odia cultural observances outside Odisha.

name: Malleswara Shiva Temple
significance: A laterite Shiva temple at Chandrakona, 26 feet square and about 60 feet tall, carrying five ridged rekha turrets over a triple-arched porch and finished in decorative stucco. Built in the Bhan period and renovated by Maharaja Tejchandra in 1831, it is a notable survival of 18th-century Bengal temple architecture.

name: Rani Sati Mandir, Mahuda
significance: A temple to Rani Sati Dadi in the Mahuda area of Dhanbad district, completed on 20 February 1992. It is a prominent local shrine whose calendar centres on the annual Varshika Puja and on the celebration of its founding day.

name: Vasudev Doul
significance: A Vaishnava temple of mud brick on a pancharatha plan, raised around 1680 under the patronage of the Ahom king Sulikphaa and counted among the better examples of late-medieval Ahom building. Protected by both the Assam government and the ASI, it remains the focus of local Doul Utsav and Bohag Bihu observances.
story: Local tradition says the temple once bore a golden finial that was carried off during invasions.

name: Char Bangla Temples
significance: Four 18th-century Shiva temples at Baranagar built under the patronage of Rani Bhabani of Natore, the northern one dated 1760. Two carry rich terracotta facades of mythological and everyday scenes, one is finished in incised plaster and one is plain; shifting courses of the Ganges now run within yards of the ASI-protected group.

name: Maha Ganapathi Mahamaya Temple
significance: The kuladevata shrine of about 125 Goud Saraswat Brahmin families at Shirali, housing Ganesha as Mahaganapati together with the goddess Mahamaya. Built roughly four centuries ago and renovated in 1904, it is the final home of images carried out of Goa during successive upheavals.
story: The deities are said to have been moved from Ella in Goa to Divar Island in the 13th century, and when Portuguese rule threatened them around 1560 devotees invoked their presence into a silver elephant trunk and a mask of Mahamaya and carried them north to Shirali.

name: Ramachandi Temple
significance: A Shakta pitha on the Kushabhadra estuary about 5 km from Konark, held to be older than the Sun Temple itself. Architecturally modest, it matters as one of Odisha's well-known seats of the goddess, whom some accounts identify instead with Mayadevi, consort of Surya.
story: When the iconoclast Kalapahad came for her, the goddess is said to have met him disguised as a maidservant, asked him to wait at the door while she fetched water from the river, and escaped to the Kushabhadra, later appearing in a priest's dream to ask for a temple on its bank.

name: Lakhmi Varaha Temple
significance: A Kalinga-style deula raised in 1550 by the ruling family of Aul for Varaha, the boar incarnation of Vishnu, worshipped here with Lakshmi. After roughly five centuries of decay it was restored in the 20th century by Brajasundar Dev, the late king of Aul.
story: The king of Aul, cut off from his usual worship at the Biraja temple by floods, dreamed the deity had come to his house; walking home he heard footsteps behind him that stopped at Aul, and there he built the temple.

name: Gundicha Temple
significance: The garden house at the far end of Puri's Grand Road that is the destination of the annual Rath Yatra, occupied by Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra for nine days each year. Empty the rest of the year, it is built of light-grey sandstone in the Kalinga deula manner.
story: The temple is named for Gundicha, queen of the legendary Indradyumna who built the main Jagannath temple; pleased with her devotion, Jagannath is said to have promised to visit her house once a year.

name: Rampara Kalibari
significance: A Kali temple about 35 km from Kolkata founded more than three centuries ago by the Nandy family of Rampara and rebuilt in the early 20th century, reportedly by artisans who had worked on the Victoria Memorial. The complex holds the Kali and Panchanan sanctum, a separate Jagannath temple, an assembly hall, a pond and a ceremonial rath.

name: Dharmaraya Swamy Temple
builtDisplay: over 800 years old; predates the city (1530)
significance: Bengaluru's oldest temple, standing before the city was founded in 1530 and named in Chalukya-period inscriptions, dedicated to Draupadi and the five Pandavas by the Vahni Kula Kshatriya community. It is the seat of the Bengaluru Karaga, the spring festival in which a priest carries an ornate clay pot through the old town in Draupadi's honour.
story: The temple's ritual cycle re-enacts episodes from the Mahabharata — Draupadi's disrobing, the Pandavas' exile and the death of her sons — from which she emerges as the ideal of womanly strength.

name: Bhubaneswari Temple
significance: A charchala-roofed shrine on the Gomati about 55 km from Agartala, built in the 1660s-70s during the reign of Maharaja Govinda Manikya, who also raised the palace beside it. Its setting entered Bengali literature through the writings of Rabindranath Tagore.

name: Lakshmi Narayan Temple, Agartala
significance: A Lakshmi-Narayana temple in the grounds of the Ujjayanta Palace at Agartala, built during the reign of Maharaja Birendra Kishore Manikya of Tripura (1909-1923). Krishna Janmashtami is its principal festival.

name: Sadhimataji Temple
significance: A shrine near Kherva in Mehsana district to Sadhimata, kuldevi of the Raval Yogi community, built by a former pujari, Khodabhai Raval, and served by his descendants. Its rectangular-domed sanctum stands under a large neem tree with courtyards for the annual Dharo Atham No Melo fair on Bhadrva Sud Aatham.

name: Shantinatha Temple, Khajuraho
builtDisplay: rebuilt c. 1870 around an 11th-c. Chandella core
style: 19th-c. Jain quadrangular courtyard around Chandella-period stonework
significance: The living Digambara temple in eastern Khajuraho, whose nucleus is Chandella work of the 11th century — the pedestal of the main image is inscribed Samvat 1085 (1027-28 CE) — enclosed in a courtyard rebuilt around 1870 by Kanchhedtilal Jain of Nagaur. A 4.3 m Shantinatha stands in the central shrine, surrounded by all twenty-four tirthankaras and eighteen further shrines holding sculpture spanning ten centuries; it falls within the Khajuraho World Heritage Site.

name: Radhabinod Temple
significance: Built in 1659 by Raghunath Singha Dev of Mallabhum in the Khar Bangla quarter of Bishnupur, this is one of only two at-chala temples in the area, its eight-section roof broken by a narrow band that reads almost as char-chala. The small east-facing shrine, about 6.4 by 6.2 m and 10.7 m high, is an ASI Monument of National Importance.

name: Shri Kalika Devi Temple
significance: A Shakta temple at Sirsangi in Belagavi district, reputedly of great antiquity, whose village appears in records of 1148 and 1186 under the names Rishishringapura and Pirishingi. Ugadi, Halegodi Amavasya and Vishwakarma Mahotsava are its main festivals.
story: The sage Vrushya Shrunga is said to have performed penance here and been harassed by demons, whereupon the goddesses who drove them off settled at the spot, and the temple was raised for them.

name: Shantinath Jain Temple, Kothara
significance: A Shvetambara Murtipujaka temple consecrated in V.S. 1918 (1861 CE), paid for at some £40,000 by Shah Velji Malu, Shah Keshavji Nayak, Shivji Nensi and the Osval Vania merchants of Kothara. Modelled on an Ahmedabad temple, its 78-by-69-foot marble hall carries domed porches, sixteen pillars and twenty-two pilasters around a 90 cm white marble Shantinatha in padmasana, earning it the epithet Kalyan Tunk.

name: Wargal Saraswati Temple
significance: One of the few Saraswati temples in Telangana, built on a hillock at Wargal through the efforts of the scholar Yayavaram Chandrashekhara Sharma and maintained by the Kanchi Shankara Mutt. It runs a Veda pathashala and daily annadanam, and families bring children here for akshara abyasam, their first lesson in letters.

name: Amreshwar Dham
significance: A Shiva temple complex near Khunti, about 45 km from Ranchi, established in 1985 on a site formerly called Angrabari and renamed Amreshwar Dham by Shankaracharya Swami Swarupananda Saraswati. It also holds shrines to Ganesha, Rama, Sita and Hanuman, and fills with pilgrims through Sawan and on Maha Shivaratri.

name: Lake Kalibari
significance: Formally Sree Sree 108 Karunamoyee Kalimata Mandir, this Kali temple on Southern Avenue was founded in 1949 by Haripada Chakraborty and began as a thatched hut before being rebuilt in masonry. Run by the Karunamoyee Kalimata Trust, it has been under reconstruction since 2002 and also holds shrines to Bagala, Santoshi Maa and, from 2020, Dhumavati.
story: The founder is said to have been told by Kali in a vision to install her image, and when he pleaded that he was too poor to pay for her worship, the goddess assured him she would meet the cost herself.

name: Radha Shyam Temple
significance: Dated by its foundation plaque to 1758 and built by the Mallabhum king Chaitanya Singha, this eka-ratna temple carries a domed shikhara over a square curved roof. Terracotta plaques on the walls show Ramayana episodes, Anantasayin Vishnu and repeated Radha-Krishna figures; the ASI protects it and it sits on UNESCO's tentative list with the rest of Bishnupur.

name: Bhavaniswar Mandir
style: Lime-and-mortar dome over a circular ambulatory
significance: An 18-metre lime-and-mortar Shiva temple at Baranagar built in 1755 by Tarasundari, daughter of Rani Bhabani of Natore, with an inverted-lotus dome and a circular corridor around the sanctum. It is an ASI-listed monument, noted for the floral carving on the sanctum's outer wall.
story: Rani Bhabani is said to have meant to raise 108 temples at Baranagar so that it might rival Varanasi, and to have stopped at 107 for reasons no one has recorded.

name: Jagannath Temple, Nayagarh
style: Pancharatha Rekha Deula with Pidha Deula jagamohana
significance: Raised between 1788 and 1808 by Vinayak Singh Mandhata of Nayagarh, with the poet Yadumani's father as architect, and reconstructed in 1972 by Nilakantha Sahu. Its rekha deula sanctum is fronted by pidha-roofed assembly and dance halls, and the principal image, DadhiVanana, was brought from the temple at Tikiripada.

name: Manapullikavu Temple
significance: A Bhadrakali shrine at Palakkad, once the property of the Brahmin family of Mattappilly Bhadrakali Mana, whose four-armed black image holds soolam, kapalam, gadkam and khedam. Its Manapulli Vela, held between late February and early March with elephants, panchavadyam and fireworks, is among the best known velas of the district.
story: An asura named Neelan is said to have tormented the country until the people appealed to Parasurama, and Shiva took female form as Bhadrakali and sent her to Akamalavaram to kill him; thereafter she settled here as Manappulli Bhagavathy.

name: Tripurantaka Temple
significance: A Western Chalukya temple of about 1070 CE at Balligavi, now dilapidated, whose friezes carry erotic sculpture rare in Chalukyan work alongside deities and dikpalas and perforated window panels of interlocked nagas. Balligavi was a medieval centre of learning shared by Shaiva, Vaishnava, Jain and Buddhist communities, with over eighty inscriptions recovered from the site.

name: Majhighariani Temple
builtDisplay: current temple late 20th c.; founded 16th c.
significance: The presiding goddess temple of Rayagada, first built inside a fort on the Nagavali by King Vishwanath Dev Gajapati of the Suryavansh line in the 16th century and rebuilt in its present Kalinga form in the late 20th century. Durga Puja and the Chaitra Puja are its two great gatherings.
story: It is said that the king made Rayagada his capital, and only after finishing the goddess's temple did he go on to conquer a wide dominion.

name: Lokanatha Temple
significance: One of the five principal Shiva temples of Puri, alongside Markandeswara, Jambeswar, Banambara and Kapalamochana, whose linga stands submerged in water. Its festival image is kept inside the Jagannath temple complex, where Lokanatha is regarded as the guardian of Jagannath's treasury; Shivaratri and the Mondays of Vaishakha, Shraavana and Kartika are its main observances.
story: Rama himself is said to have installed the linga here, and the Ganges is believed to flow through its crown as a hidden stream.

name: Baidyapur Jora Deul
significance: A pair of joined brick rekha deuls at Baidyapur completed around 1550 by Subhananda Pal, with carved brick facades and an inscription over the larger doorway. They are protected as a Monument of National Importance.

name: Radhakanta Temple, Chetla
deity: Krishna as Radhakanta Jiu, with Radha and Lakshmi-Narayana
significance: A nearly hundred-foot naba-ratna temple at Chetla raised between 1796 and 1809 by Babu Ramnath Mondal of the Bawali Raj family, and said to have been an inspiration for the later Dakshineswar Kali Temple. It survives as one of the last traces of the zamindari and ghat landscape that once lined the Adi Ganga.

name: Madhava Temple, Niali
style: Kalinga, pancharatha plan with rekha deula, pidha jagamohana and flat-roofed natamandapa
significance: A thirteenth-century Vishnu temple at Madhab village near Niali, built by the Eastern Ganga king Ananga Bhima Deva III and holding a rare Madhava image. Its plan parallels the Sakhigopal and Ananta Vasudeva temples, and it preserves an old black sandstone Garuda and carvings drawn from the Krishna Lila and the Mahabharata.

name: Koulutla Chennakesava Temple
deity: Vishnu as Sri Koulutla Chennakesava Swamy
significance: A Vishnu temple in Kappatralla village of Kurnool district whose complex is credited to the Vijayanagara king Krishnadevaraya, its image said to have been reconsecrated in the 11th century. Subsidiary shrines to Mallikarjuna, Bhramaramba, Vijaya Vinayaka, Dakshinamurthy and Vishwanatha stand in the same enclosure.
story: The image is said to have been installed at the Koundinya ashrama on the advice of the sage Vasistha to redeem Janamejaya after his serpent sacrifice, and to have been rediscovered centuries later by a cowherd, Golla Koulutla, whose cow poured her milk over the anthill covering it.

name: Thanthania Kalibari
dynasty: Pre-colonial, refounded in the colonial era
significance: A Kali temple on Bidhan Sarani older than the city of Kolkata itself, founded in 1703 by the tantrik Uday Narayan Brahmachari and re-established in 1806 by the businessman Shankar Ghosh, whose descendants remain its custodians. The 1806 rebuilding added the ath-chala Pushpeswar Shiv Mandir.
story: The name Thanthania is said to come from the than-than sound of the temple bells that travellers once heard through the surrounding forest.

name: Triyuginarayan Temple
deity: Vishnu as Lakshmi Narayana, with Shiva and Parvati
significance: A Himalayan temple in Rudraprayag district holding a two-foot silver image of Vishnu with Lakshmi, its founding ascribed to Adi Shankaracharya in the 8th century. A perpetual fire burns before the shrine and four kunds in the courtyard are fed by a single stream.
story: The site is held to be where Shiva married Parvati in the Satya Yuga with Vishnu as witness, and the fire before the temple is said to be the flame that burned at that wedding.

name: Kuchadri Venkateshwara Swamy Temple
significance: An old Venkateswara temple at Kuchanpally in Medak district, declared a protected monument by the government of Andhra Pradesh in 2011.

name: Sri Varadharaja Perumal Kovil, Tirunelveli
deity: Vishnu as Varadharaja Perumal, with Mahalakshmi Thayar
builtDisplay: reported to be about 400 years old
significance: A Vishnu temple on the bank of the Thamirabarani at Tirunelveli, reported to have stood in some form for around four centuries.

name: Santram Mandir
significance: The principal temple of the Santram Maharaj sampradaya at Nadiad in Kheda district, run by the Santram Maharaj organisation and a leading pilgrimage draw in central Gujarat.

name: Ranganathaswamy Temple, Jiyaguda
significance: A roughly four-hundred-year-old Vaishnava temple on the Musi river in Hyderabad, established by the Nanganur Prathama Peetham during Qutb Shahi rule and said to be the first temple that lineage founded in the city. It follows the Vanamamalai sampradaya and was granted a three-year exemption by the Telangana Endowments Department in 2015.

name: Ranganathaswamy Temple, Shivanasamudra
deity: Vishnu as Ranganatha, here called Madhya Ranga
significance: The middle shrine of the tri-ranga group of Ranganatha temples set on natural islands in the Kaveri, standing at Shivanasamudra in Chamarajanagar district. Renovation work on the remote temple began in February 2021.
story: In Sri Vaishnava belief the three island Ranganathas mark stages of the god's life, and the Shivanasamudra deity is revered as his youthful form.

name: Jor Bangla (Keshto Ray) Temple, Bishnupur
deity: Krishna, worshipped here as Keshto Ray
style: Jor-bangla, twin do-chala roofs with a ratna turret
significance: Raised in 1655 by Raghunath Singha of the Malla kingdom, this is the largest surviving jor-bangla temple and among the best known terracotta temples of Bengal. It is a Monument of National Importance under the Archaeological Survey of India and was added to the UNESCO tentative list in 1998.

name: Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple, T. Nagar
significance: A Venkateswara temple run by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams on Venkatanarayana Road in T. Nagar, which by June 2024 had become the highest earning TTD temple after Tirumala itself. Its shrines include images of Hayagriva, Varaha, Rama, Krishna, Andal, Ranganatha, Lakshmi, Brahma and Ramanuja.

name: Ananta Shayana
significance: A colossal rock-cut image of the reclining Vishnu at Saranga in Dhenkanal district, Odisha, carved in the first quarter of the 9th century under Nandodbhava feudatories of the Bhauma-Kara kings. It is among the largest Vaishnava rock sculptures in eastern India.
story: The sculpture shows Vishnu asleep on the serpent Ananta upon the cosmic ocean, with a lotus rising from his navel on which Brahma sits creating the world.

name: Draupadi Ratha
significance: The smallest of the Pancha Rathas at Mahabalipuram, cut from a single rock around 650 CE under the Pallavas and shaped like a thatched hut. Its sanctum holds Durga as Mahishasuramardini, and it forms part of the UNESCO-listed monuments of the town.
story: The monument is popularly named for Draupadi, shared wife of the five Pandavas of the Mahabharata, although the article notes that history does not support the name.

name: Bhagyalakshmi Temple
significance: A small shrine to Lakshmi abutting the south-east minaret of the Charminar in Hyderabad's old city. The structure standing today was put up in the 1960s, and historians hold that the stone it grew around was a guard stone set to protect the monument's corner from traffic.
story: Local tradition dates the stone to the Qutb Shahi period and links the shrine's name to Bhagmati, the queen after whom the city is said to have first been named.

name: Ashtalakshmi Temple, Hyderabad
deity: Ashta Lakshmi, the eight forms of Lakshmi
significance: A temple at Ramakrishnapuram, Kothapet in Hyderabad enshrining Lakshmi in her eight aspects, from Adilakshmi to Varalakshmi. Raised under the auspices of the Kanchi Kamakoti Peetam after five years of work, it was consecrated in April 1996 and follows the plan of the Ashtalakshmi temple in Chennai.

name: Domlur Chokkanathaswamy Temple
builtDisplay: Chola; at least as old as 1200, with Vijayanagara additions
style: Chola, with Vijayanagara navaranga and pillars
significance: One of the oldest surviving temples in Bengaluru, at Domlur, whose Tamil inscriptions show it standing by 1200 CE. Later grants from Hoysala and Vijayanagara rulers, including Devaraya II, funded the navaranga and pillars added in Vijayanagara style.

name: Maa Mangala Mandir, Kakatpur
deity: Mangala, a form of the goddess Durga
significance: A Shakta shrine on the Prachi river at Kakatpur in Puri district, Odisha, whose present pidha-vimana temple was built in 1548 by the zamindar Panchanan Mitra Roychudamoni. It is closely tied to the Jagannath tradition, as the carpenters seek the goddess's guidance before the Nabakalebara rite.
story: The goddess is said to have appeared in a boatman's dream and directed him to lift her image from the Prachi, and the town's name is explained from Odia words for a crow that was detained at the spot.

name: Gangamma Temple, Dhenuvakonda
significance: A shrine of the goddess Gangamma at Dhenuvakonda near Garlapadu in Prakasam district, Andhra Pradesh. It is a focus of devotion for the Yadava community, who hold its jatara on the April full moon.

name: Shri Shri Hari Baladev Jew Bije, Baripada
style: Kalinga (rekha deula with jagamohana and nata mandira)
significance: The Jagannath temple of Baripada in Mayurbhanj district, Odisha, built in 1575 by Maharaja Baidyanath Bhanj according to its inscription. Its Rath Yatra is noted for the Subhadra chariot being pulled by women alone.
story: The king is said to have been turned away from darshan at Puri and, after penance, told in a dream to build a temple at Baripada where Jagannath himself would come down to his devotee.

name: Gaurishvara Temple, Yelandur
significance: A 16th-century Shiva temple at Yelandur in Chamarajanagar district, Karnataka, built by the local chief Singedepa Devabhupala of the Hadinadu chiefdom under Vijayanagara overlordship. Its plan is plain, with sanctum, closed hall and a granite-pillared open hall behind an unusually large mahadwara.

name: Ganesha Ratha
significance: A monolithic rock-cut shrine at Mahabalipuram carved around 650 CE in the reign of the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I. It originally held a Shiva linga; in the 1880s villagers replaced it with an image of Ganesha with the District Collector's permission, and the old linga now stands under a nearby tree.

name: Anantasaayi Vishnu Temple
significance: A rekha-deula temple at Kamali Bazar in Sambalpur, Odisha, built in the early 16th century under the Chauhan ruler Balaram Dev. It enshrines Vishnu reclining on the serpent Ananta.
story: The image of Narayana is said to have come to Sambalpur as part of the queen's dowry, after which the king raised the temple to house it.

name: Akkanna Madanna Temple
significance: A 17th-century Mahankali temple at Shah Ali Banda in Hyderabad's old city, about a kilometre from the Charminar, associated with the brothers Madanna and Akkanna who served the Golconda ruler Tana Shah as prime minister and commander-in-chief. It is one of the principal starting points of the city's Bonalu procession.
story: The brothers are remembered as worshipping here every morning before going to court, and the shrine is said to have been shut after their deaths until it was revived in the last century.

name: Dichpally Ramalayam
significance: A 14th-century temple to Rama on a hillock at Dichpally in Nizamabad district, Telangana, built of black and white stone under Kakatiya rule. Its dense figural carving has earned it the local name of an Indianised Khajuraho.

name: Shyam Ray Temple
significance: A laterite-and-brick temple at Bishnupur in Bankura district, West Bengal, founded in 1643 by the Malla king Raghunath Singha. Its five-towered pancha-ratna form and dense terracotta panels of the Krishna story make it one of the best known of the Bishnupur temples.

name: Jagannath Temple, Koraput
significance: A Jagannath temple in Koraput, Odisha, known as Shabara Shrikshetra for its tribal associations. It is open to worshippers of every caste and creed, and visitors may enter the sanctum area, unlike at Puri.

name: Andhra Shiridi
significance: A Sai Baba shrine at Balabhadrapuram in Bikkavolu mandal, East Godavari district, Andhra Pradesh, whose image was installed on 17 February 2005. Devotees keep a forty-one day Sai Deeksha that ends at the temple's annual Varshikotsavam on that date.

name: Jaladheeswara Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Ghantasala in Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh, unusual in placing Shiva and Parvati together on a single peetam. The temple's own history carries its origin back beyond the 2nd century CE.
story: The peetam is said to have been set up by the sage Agastya, and the Skanda Purana is cited as promising that darshan here equals that of the twelve jyotirlingas and eighteen shakti peethas together.

name: Chhatia Bata
significance: A Jagannath shrine at the village of Chhatia between Cuttack and Jajpur in Odisha, named for the banyan tree at the site and tied in local belief to the coming Kalki avatar. It is a well-known stop for pilgrims travelling the Cuttack-Jajpur road.
story: The seer Hadidas is said to have foretold that when the sea rises and fish play on the steps of the Puri temple, Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra will leave Puri and take up residence at Chhatia, the one land left untouched.

name: Govindarajula Gutta
deity: Rama, with a Hanuman shrine below
significance: A rocky hill in Warangal, Telangana, crowned by a temple to Rama with a Hanuman shrine at its foot. The hill is a local landmark and gives its name to the surrounding neighbourhood.

name: Ghanteswari Temple
significance: A goddess shrine on the Mahanadi at Chiplima, some thirty kilometres from Sambalpur in Odisha, hung with bells offered by devotees. It is called a lighthouse without light, because early boatmen used the sound of its bells as a warning of dangerous winds at the river bend.

name: Mrinmoyee Temple
deity: Durga in the form of Mrinmoyee
significance: The oldest temple of Bishnupur in Bankura district, West Bengal, founded in 997 CE by the Malla king Jagat Malla for Durga as Mrinmoyee, whose image is made of clay. Its Durga Puja, held with the Malla royal rites, is among the oldest continuously observed in Bengal.
story: Jagat Malla is said to have moved his capital from Pradyumnapur to Bishnupur at the goddess's own direction, and to have raised the clay shrine beside his new palace.

name: Baladevjew Temple
deity: Balarama as Baladevjew, with Jagannath and Subhadra
significance: The principal temple of Kendrapara district, Odisha, at Ichhapur or Tulasi Kshetra, where Balarama rather than Jagannath is the presiding deity. An earlier shrine was demolished in 1661 under Aurangzeb and the images hidden along the Govari river before the present temple was built in 1761 by the Kujanga ruler Gopal Sandha with the zamindar Srinivas Narendra Mahapatra.

name: Balaji Temple, Ketkawale
significance: A temple to Venkateswara at Ketkawale on the Pune-Satara road in Pune district, Maharashtra, built between 1996 and 2003 by the Venkateshwara charitable trust and the V H Group. It follows traditional south Indian temple architecture and is often described as a Tirupati of Maharashtra.

name: Balkampet Yellamma Temple
significance: A temple of the mother goddess Yellamma at Balkampet in Hyderabad, believed to date from the 15th century. Its image stands below ground level in spring water, which is why the goddess here is also called Jala Durga.

name: Gurdwara Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib, Dhubri
deity: Guru Granth Sahib; commemorates the visit of Guru Tegh Bahadur
significance: A gurdwara on the Brahmaputra bank at Dhubri, established in the 17th century after Guru Tegh Bahadur travelled here from Dhaka in late 1669 and Sikhs of his retinue stayed on to maintain it. During the Dundiya rising of the early 1790s it quartered Sikh and Punjabi barkandaze militiamen, and President Giani Zail Singh visited in 1983.
story: Sikh lore tells of a washerwoman who hurled trees and rocks at the Guru by witchcraft and, when none of it touched him, became his devotee.

name: Joranda Gadi
deity: Sunya Brahma, the formless lord, worshipped as Alekha
significance: The chief seat of Mahima Dharma, an Odishan sect that rejects image worship, standing where the villages of Joranda, Natima and Patna meet, about 24 km north of Dhenkanal. It holds the samadhi pitha of the sect's founder Mahima Goswami; the present temple was built in the early 20th century on a shrine the article traces to the early 14th, and the order's ascetics may not sleep two consecutive nights in one place.

name: Oorali Appooppan Kavu
deity: Oorali Appooppan, also called Kalleli Appooppan, lord of the mountain gods
significance: A kavu on the Achankovil river at Kalleli, roughly 19 km from Pathanamthitta town, whose rites follow the usage of the early Dravida-Naga tribes rather than the tantric procedure of ordinary Kerala temples.
story: Appooppan is honoured as lord of the 999 Mala Daivangal, the mountain gods, with Oorali Ammoomma revered as his mother.

name: Gurdwara Mata Sundri
deity: Guru Granth Sahib; a memorial to Mata Sundri, wife of Guru Gobind Singh
style: Sikh architecture, with square domed sanctums, arched copings and a traditional gateway
significance: A Delhi gurdwara on Mata Sundri Road raised in memory of Mata Sundri, who married Guru Gobind Singh in 1684 and bore his eldest son Ajit Singh in 1687. After the Guru's death in October 1708 she guided the Khalsa for forty years, issuing hukumnamas between 1717 and 1730 until her death in 1747; she lived in a newly built house on this site from 1727, and the Delhi Gurdwara Committee later put up the present shrine.

name: Chandrawati Jain Temple
significance: Jain temples at Chandrawati village on the left bank of the Ganga near its confluence with the Gomti, about 23 km from Varanasi, where the surviving architectural remains are assigned to the ninth and tenth centuries and an inscription of 1091 records grants under the Gahadavala king Chandradeva. A. C. L. Carlleyle surveyed and documented three Jain temples on the site in 1877.
story: Jain tradition places three of Chandraprabha's five kalyanakas here, and local memory credits the founding of Chandrawati to a ruler named Domana Deva.

name: Jain Temple, Kundalpur
significance: A Digambara Jain complex at Kundalpur near Nalanda, built in 2003 in yellow Jaisalmer stone with a shikhara about 51 feet high beside an older temple on the same ground, and run by the Bhagwan Mahavira Janmabhoomi Kundalpur Digambar Jain Samiti. Digambaras hold Kundalpur, an ancient Licchavi capital, to be Mahavira's birthplace, while other Jain traditions point instead to Basukund near Vaishali.
story: Four of Mahavira's eleven ganadharas, Gautama Swami among them, are believed to have been born here.

name: Pulimukham Devi Temple
significance: A Bhagavathi temple in the Thazhava neighbourhood of Kollam district, reckoned about four hundred years old and built in traditional Kerala style, with a number of subordinate shrines and a round of seasonal festivals.
story: A kavu of serpent gods and the temple's Karimbana and Ezhilam Pala trees are worshipped in the belief that gandharvas and yakshis live in them.

name: Chamatkarji Jain Temple
significance: An early medieval Digambara Jain temple in Sawai Madhopur district, known in archaeological literature as the Alanpur Jain temple and protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. Its later worship grew up around an image of Adinatha found near the site.
story: The name comes from chamatkar, miracle: the principal image is held to work wonders, and a fair is held here each Sharad Purnima.

name: Gurdwara Nanaklama
deity: Guru Nanak, commemorated at the site of his third udasi visit
significance: A gurdwara at Chungthang in north Sikkim raised in 1969 by the Assam Rifles under Subedar Major Bhullar, helped by the local MLA Tasa Tangey Lepcha, in remembrance of Guru Nanak's visit during his third udasi.

name: Sri Lakshmi Venkateswara Swamy Temple, Manyamkonda
deity: Venkateswara as Sri Lakshmi Venkateshwara Swamy
significance: A hill shrine to Venkateswara about five kilometres from Devarakadra in Mahabubnagar district, and the first temple in Telangana to be given ropeway access.

name: Guru Ka Tal
deity: Guru Tegh Bahadur, to whose memory the shrine is dedicated
significance: A gurdwara at Agra dedicated to the memory of the ninth Guru, Tegh Bahadur, built in the 1970s through the efforts of Sant Baba Sadhu Singh Mauni beside a red sandstone reservoir of 1610 raised in Jahangir's reign for water conservation. Eight of the tank's original twelve towers survive, their carving akin to Agra Fort and Fatehpur Sikri.
story: Sikh tradition holds that it was here that Guru Tegh Bahadur laid down his arms and offered himself for arrest before his martyrdom.

name: Keshabeshwar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Ramnathpur founded in 1748 by the zamindar Keshab Roychowdhury, whose architect Basudeb took twelve years over it. Its atchala roof carries a kalash and trishul, corridors run along three sides of the sanctum, and the Charak Puja fair is still held in its grounds.

name: Gurdwara Dam Dama Sahib
deity: Guru Gobind Singh, commemorated at the site of his 1707 meeting
significance: A Delhi gurdwara marking the meeting of Guru Gobind Singh with Prince Muazzam, later Emperor Bahadur Shah, in 1707. A bungalow of 1664 on the spot was rebuilt as a gurdwara by Sardar Baghel Singh in 1783 and later renovated under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, though most of the standing structure dates from after 1947.

name: Chehni Kothi
significance: A tall timber-and-stone tower at Chehni in the Banjar valley, about 350 years old and known as the Bhagwati temple for the goddess shrine it holds. It belongs to the wider Himachali tradition of village goddess cults and is celebrated for having withstood Himalayan earthquakes.
story: Local lore holds that the tower was the fortified seat of a ruler remembered as Queen Chaini, from whom the village takes its name.

name: Ladnu Jain temple
significance: A Jain temple complex at Ladnu of five Digambara and two Shvetambara shrines, its principal Shantinatha temple carrying an inscription of 1295 CE. The town has been a Jain centre since the 10th century, is the birthplace of Acharya Tulsi and hosts Jain Vishva Bharati University.

name: Annapurna Temple, Titagarh
significance: A nine-pinnacled navaratna temple opened on 12 April 1875 by Jagadamba Devi, youngest daughter of Rani Rashmoni, on the model of the Bhavatarini temple at Dakshineswar. Ramakrishna opened it to devotees; the Shiva image is silver and the Annapurna image of ashtadhatu, and the courtyard holds a natmandir, six Shiva shrines and two nahabatkhanas.

name: Muktidham
deity: Krishna, alongside replicas of the twelve Jyotirlingas
significance: A marble temple complex in the Nashik Road suburb, founded in 1971 on a donation from the industrialist J. D. Chauhan-Bytco. Rajasthani sculptors built it from Makrana marble, and it holds replicas of the twelve Jyotirlingas along with paintings by Raghubir Mulgaonkar.

name: Subai Jain temples
builtDisplay: 4th c. by the site record; others date it before 750 CE
significance: A group of six Jain temples at Subai in Koraput district, ascribed to Jain gemstone traders of the region and described by the state as a medieval Jain monastic site. A four-foot Jain image was recovered here in a 2020 excavation, and the annual Parab festival is still kept at the site.

name: Gurdwara Patalpuri Sahib
deity: Memorial to Guru Hargobind, Guru Har Rai and Guru Har Krishan
significance: A gurdwara on the left bank of the Sutlej at Kiratpur where Guru Hargobind and Guru Har Rai were cremated and the ashes of Guru Har Krishan immersed. It remains the foremost place at which Sikhs consign ashes as part of the Antam Sanskar rites.
story: It is told that a Rajput raja and his followers threw themselves into Guru Hargobind's funeral pyre.

name: Nilamadhav Temple
significance: A hill temple to Vishnu as Nilamadhava above Kantilo, near the meeting of the Mahanadi, Kuanria and Kusumi that Odias call their triveni sangam. Its structure follows that of the Jagannath temple at Puri.
story: The shrine is said to have begun when the Sabara chief Biswabasu worshipped the deity, known in his tongue as Kitung, as a blue sapphire image in a cave of the Brahmadri hills, before a wooden form took its place.

name: Kochi Jain temple
significance: A Shvetambara Murtipujak temple at Mattancherry built in 1904 by Hirubai Jivraj Dhanji in memory of her husband and run by the Cochin Swetamber Murtipujak Jain Sangh. Its white marble and sculptured pillars follow the Jain temples of Gujarat, the homeland of Kochi's Jain merchant community, and a second shrine holds Chandraprabha.

name: Gurdwara Baba Gurditta
place: Chandpur Rurki, Kiratpur Sahib, Rupnagar district
deity: Baba Gurditta, commemorated at his cremation place
significance: A gurdwara near Kiratpur marking where Baba Gurditta, son of Guru Hargobind and father of Guru Har Rai, died and was cremated on 15 March 1638. It is also kept in memory of Baba Kesra Singh.
story: Tradition holds that Gurditta reluctantly brought back to life a cow he had killed while hunting, and that rebuked by his father for working a miracle he withdrew from Kiratpur and died the same day, a neem tree at the spot springing from the twig in his hand.

name: Hanuman Temple, Kedara-Gouri
significance: A laterite shrine on the Kedara-Gouri road in Bhubaneswar's old town, housing a two-armed Hanuman. It is one of the later Kalingan-style structures in the historic temple quarter.

name: Chakrapani Temple
deity: Chakrapani (Vishnu as the Sudarshana chakra), with Vijayalakshmi Thayar
significance: One of the principal Vishnu temples of Kumbakonam, where the deity is worshipped in the form of the discus Sudarshana rather than as an anthropomorphic image. Lacking inscriptions, it is dated to the 15th century on the evidence of its granite walls, five-tiered rajagopuram and carved pillars.
story: The legend tells that the Sudarshana chakra humbled the pride of Surya, who then worshipped it until his powers were restored.

name: Byamokesvara Temple
deity: Shiva, as a lingam in a circular yonipitha
significance: Also called the Suresvara Mahadeva temple, this 10th-century shrine stands inside the Tala Bazaar market complex in old Bhubaneswar. Built of coarse grey sandstone in dry masonry, it is locally attributed to the Somavamsi (Kesari) rulers.

name: Bharati Matha Temple
significance: A monastic establishment with a Shiva shrine in Bhubaneswar, said to have been founded by Yayati Kesari, the builder of the Lingaraja temple, and to have first housed the artisans working on that project. It is dated to the 11th century and built in the Kalinga manner.

name: Baitala Deula
significance: An 8th-century shrine in Bhubaneswar built to the barrel-roofed khakara plan, a form reserved in Kalinga for goddess temples. Its tantric Chamunda sanctum and dense iconographic programme make it one of the most studied early temples of Odisha.

name: Andarkoil Swarnapureewarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Andankoil in the Valangaiman taluk of Tiruvarur district, built in the Dravidian manner. Its founding tradition connects it to a minister of the legendary king Muchukunda.
story: The story goes that the minister Kandadevar found a shivalinga after Shiva appeared to him in a dream and built a temple over it, and that King Muchukunda had him beheaded before realising his error and restoring him to life.

name: Isanesvara Siva Temple
deity: Shiva; the sanctum retains only the circular yonipitha, the lingam being lost
significance: A rekha-deula Shiva shrine in Bhubaneswar assigned on stylistic grounds to the 13th century and the Ganga period. Its lingam has disappeared, leaving the bare yonipitha in the sanctum.

name: Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, Mumbai
deity: Laxminarayan Dev with Ghanshyam Maharaj, and Radha Krishna Dev with Hari Krishna Maharaj
significance: The main Swaminarayan Sampraday temple in Mumbai, in the crowded Bhuleshwar quarter. The first temple was completed in 1868 by Ranchhoddas Pranjeevandas, and the present three-spired shikharbandh structure replaced it in 1903 under Acharya Lakshmiprasadji Maharaj.

name: Madhangeeswarar Temple
significance: A small Shiva temple in Kanchipuram, also called Matangesvara, believed to have been built by the Pallavas at the close of the 8th century. It is noted for dvarapalas carved with four arms.

name: Sivatirtha Matha, Old Town
significance: A matha of the Shankaracharya sampradaya at Rathagada Chowk in old Bhubaneswar, its precinct holding pidha-order shrines in the Kalinga manner. It has a formal role in the Lingaraja temple's festival calendar.
story: Tradition holds that Lingaraja himself comes to this matha to take the community meal during Dola Purnima.

name: Mangala Temple, Patia
deity: Mangala, a four-armed form of Durga
significance: A 19th-century pidha-deula goddess temple in Patia village on the northern edge of Bhubaneswar, enshrining a four-armed Mangala. It is the village's principal shrine.

name: Manibhadresvara Siva Temple – I
deity: Shiva, as a lingam in a circular yoni pitha
significance: One of a pair of small Kalingan Shiva shrines of this name in Bhubaneswar, dated on architectural grounds to about the 14th century. Local tradition credits the Somavamsi (Kesari) rulers, an attribution the building's own features do not support.

name: Chintamanisvara Siva Temple
deity: Shiva, as a lingam with a yonipitha
significance: A 14th-century rekha-deula Shiva temple at the end of Chintamaniswar road off the Cuttack–Puri road in Bhubaneswar. Local tradition ascribes it to the Kesari (Somavamsi) kings.

name: Akhadachandi Temple
place: Badu Sahi, Old Town, Bhubaneswar, Khordha district
significance: A 10th-century goddess shrine on the south-western embankment of the Bindusagar tank in old Bhubaneswar, built of coarse sandstone to the barrel-roofed khakhara plan. It is also known as the Anshuman temple, and the image of Mahishasuramardini faces east while the building faces south.

name: Devi Jagadambi Temple
significance: One of the western group of Khajuraho temples, built under the Chandelas around 1000–1025 CE and dedicated to the goddess Jagadambika. Three encircling bands of sculpture make it among the most richly carved shrines on the site.

name: Gosagarsevara Mandapa
significance: A pillared mandapa in the Gosagaresvara precinct of old Bhubaneswar, built in the Kalingan manner. It serves as the public viewing hall during the annual Durgastami procession.
story: It is said that Lingaraja comes to the Gosagaresvara precinct at Durgastami to wash away his sins, and is then shown to the people at this mandapa.

name: Gangesvara Siva Temple
deity: Shiva, as a lingam within a circular yonipitha
significance: A rekha-order Shiva temple in Bhubaneswar raised under Eastern Ganga rule in the 13th–14th century, the standing fabric being a later renovation. Its name links it to the Ganga river goddess.
story: The legend holds that after Parvati defeated the demons, Shiva struck his trident into the ground to raise a spring, and Ganga and Yamuna were called to consecrate it.

name: Gurdwara Jand Sahib
significance: A historic gurdwara in a village some 25 km west of Faridkot city, whose history is held to be connected with Guru Gobind Singh. An old jand tree at the site is preserved along with the shrine.

name: Gurdwara Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib, Dhamtan Sahib
significance: A gurdwara at Dhamtan Sahib in Haryana's Jind district commemorating the ninth Sikh Guru, Tegh Bahadur. It is a principal Sikh place of worship for the surrounding region.

name: Gurdwara Gyan Godri Sahib
significance: A gurdwara at Har Ki Pauri in Haridwar marking a site associated with Guru Nanak's visit, built between 1866 and 1935. It was demolished in 1979 when the administration acquired the land to widen the ghat, and the site remains contested ground for the Sikh community.
story: Tradition holds that Guru Nanak, visiting Haridwar around 1504, threw water westward while Brahmins offered it to the east, telling them he was watering his fields at Kartarpur.

name: Sarvatresvara Siva Temple
place: Mahavir Lane, off Lewis Road, Bhubaneswar
significance: A Shiva temple on the road from Lewis Road toward Sisupalgarh in Bhubaneswar, dated on architectural grounds to the tenth century. It doubles as a neighbourhood gathering place for rituals, weddings and community events.
story: Local tradition credits the temple's founding to the Chedi king Kharavela, who ruled Kalinga in the first century BCE.

name: Gurdwara Guru Singh Sabha, Kedli Kalan
significance: One of the oldest gurdwaras in eastern India, completed in the eighteenth century at Kedli Kalan in Jharkhand and holding a hand-written copy of the Guru Granth Sahib some two centuries old. The congregation grew from Agrahari Sikh families who settled here from eastern Uttar Pradesh for the timber trade.
story: The site is remembered as a stop on Guru Nanak's first udasi through Bihar, where he taught the local people, and as a place later visited by Guru Tegh Bahadur travelling between Varanasi, Gaya and Patna.

name: Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha, Greater Kailash
significance: A gurdwara founded on public land by the local community in the early 1960s in Greater Kailash I, New Delhi. Alongside worship it runs the Mata Gujri Medical Centre, combining religious and welfare functions for the neighbourhood.

name: Guru Ram Rai Darbar Sahib
builtDisplay: 1699–1706 (founded mid-17th c. by Baba Ram Rai)
significance: The seat of the Ramraiya order in Dehradun, founded by Baba Ram Rai, eldest son of Guru Har Rai, on lands and funds granted by Aurangzeb; the central complex was finished in 1699 and structural work by 1706. Its minarets, domes and Mughal-style gardens and wall paintings, some over three hundred years old, are being restored by the Archaeological Survey of India.
story: The city's name is traced to the dera Baba Ram Rai pitched in the doon valley after his banishment, itself said to follow his rendering of a verse before Aurangzeb in altered words to avoid giving offence.

name: Gurdwara Guru Nanak Punjabi Sabha, Chakala
significance: A gurdwara at Chakala in Andheri East, Mumbai, built in 1956–57 and founded by Shamsher Singh Jolly to serve the local Punjabi community. The trust also runs a charitable medical dispensary and the Guru Nanak Mission High School.

name: Chirakkal Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Puliyanam near Angamaly in Ernakulam district, counted among the 108 Shiva shrines and built in the Kerala idiom. Maha Shivaratri is its principal annual observance.

name: Rameshvara Temple, Koodli
significance: A twelfth-century Hoysala shrine at Koodli in Shivamogga district, built in an early and deliberately unornamented Vesara manner. It is protected as a Monument of National Importance, and the surrounding village — a substantial town into the fourteenth century — holds the ruins of more than eight temples and mathas.

name: Pundareekapuram Temple
deity: Vishnu, seated on Garuda with Bhudevi
significance: A Vishnu temple at Midayikunnam in Kottayam district whose sanctum shows the deity astride Garuda with Bhudevi, set within a tiled, saddle-roofed chuttambalam. It is valued chiefly for its murals, among the notable surviving examples of Kerala temple painting.

name: Patit Pavan Mandir
significance: A temple at Ratnagiri built between 1929 and 1931, conceived by V. D. Savarkar and funded and constructed by the philanthropist Bhagoji Baloji Keer with the Ratnagiri Hindu Sabha. It was founded as a temple open to all Hindus regardless of caste, and its attribution became the subject of a textbook controversy in 2025.

name: Govindaraja Perumal Temple, Chidambaram
builtDisplay: 12th–13th c.; deity reinstated by Krishnappa Nayak (1564–72)
significance: A Divya Desam to Vishnu that shares its precinct with the Nataraja temple at Chidambaram — one of only two of the 108 Divya Desams housed inside a Shiva temple complex. Largely of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries with later additions, the shrine was reinstated by Krishnappa Nayak in the 1560s and is sung in the Naalayira Divya Prabandham.
story: The site is linked to the contest in which Shiva and Parvati sought to settle which of them was the better dancer, Shiva prevailing at Tillai with the urdhvatandava pose.

name: Kumarakottam Temple
builtDisplay: rebuilt 1915; chakra vimana of the Chola period
significance: A Murugan temple standing between the Kamakshi Amman and Ekambareswarar temples at Kanchipuram, rebuilt in 1915 and retaining a Chola-period circular chakra vimana. It is one of the city's twenty-one major temples; Arunagirinathar sang its icon, and the priest Kacchiyappar is said to have composed the Kandha Puranam here.
story: The Kandha Puranam relates that Murugan imprisoned Brahma for failing to explain the syllable Om, then did penance before a linga once Shiva ordered the creator's release.

name: Mukkolakkal Bhagawathi Temple
significance: A Shakta shrine at Sreevaraham in Thiruvananthapuram whose swayambhu image is the object of a wide following in southern Kerala. Navaratri and the Ooruttu Mahotsavam in March–April are its principal festivals.
story: The shrine is said to have begun when a child at play struck a rock that then bled, and diviners pronounced the stone divine.

name: Chausath Yogini Temple, Khajuraho
deity: Devi (central cell probably Durga) with sixty-four yoginis
significance: The oldest surviving temple at Khajuraho, an open-air yogini shrine of about 885 CE with sixty-four small cells around a larger one. Uniquely rectangular among yogini temples, it attests to tantric goddess worship in the Chandela capital and forms part of the UNESCO-listed Khajuraho group.

name: Ramaswamy Temple, Kumbakonam
builtDisplay: begun under Achuthappa Nayak, completed under Raghunatha Nayak (1600–34)
significance: A Rama temple at Kumbakonam begun under the Thanjavur Nayaks in the later sixteenth century and completed by Raghunatha Nayak, with later Maratha additions. Its mandapa pillars carry a pictorial Ramayana counted among the fullest renderings of the epic in Indian sculpture, and it is one of five Kumbakonam temples tied to the twelve-yearly Mahamaham festival.
story: The temple's images are said to have been recovered from a temple tank in the nearby village of Darasuram.

name: Poovattoor Bhagavathy Temple
significance: A goddess temple in Poovattoor village in Kerala's Kollam district, built in the traditional Kerala manner. It stands at about fifty metres above sea level and serves as the village's principal shrine.

name: Narayani Temple
significance: An early Odishan shrine to Durga as Narayani, dated in the sources to the seventh century and built in the Kalinga manner. The goddess is invoked here as a giver of wealth and abundance.

name: Purvesvara Siva Temple
significance: A living Shiva temple at Kancha Sahi in Bhubaneswar's old town, with vimana and jagamohana built in the mature phase of Odishan temple architecture. Its name marks it as the eastern member of a directional set around the Lingaraja, and it is looked after by a local development association.

name: Sankarananda Matha
significance: An Advaita monastery in Bhubaneswar affiliated to the Puri establishment, whose compound holds three pidha-order shrines raised over the burial places of its mahantas. The buildings are badly decayed, with vegetation growth and partial collapse.

name: Shenbagavalli Amman Temple, Payanam
significance: A goddess temple at Payanam near Marthandam in Kanyakumari district, its sanctum carried on seventeen pillars and its image shown holding a trident and a child. Its annual festival falls in late February or early March and includes a procession through the surrounding villages.

name: Subarnesvara Siva Temple
significance: A 10th-century rekha deul in Bhubaneswar named for the goldsmith settlements that historically surrounded it, its decoration matching other temples of the period; seepage from the adjacent canal is now weakening its foundation.

name: Madneswar Siva Temple
significance: A ruined Shiva shrine in Bhubaneswar whose superstructure has collapsed, leaving only the pabhaga of the base standing; it is catalogued among the city's lesser-known monuments.

name: Svapnesvara Siva Temple
significance: A 16-metre light-grey sandstone deul in Bhubaneswar laid in dry masonry and rebuilt from pista to kalasa by Orissa State Archaeology under the Tenth and Eleventh Finance Commission awards; its small sanctum is now empty and standing drain water threatens the foundation.

name: Kukutesvara Siva Temple
significance: A roughly thousand-year-old Somavamshi shrine built of fine-grained ochreous sandstone in dry masonry; unlike many of its neighbours it remains a living temple, with two priests performing Sankranti and abhisheka rites.

name: Ladu Baba Temple
significance: A 26-metre pancharatha temple in Bhubaneswar formerly known as the Kainchi temple, originally a Shiva shrine; the structure is now dilapidated, with water damage and plant growth pushing at the masonry.
story: Local tradition holds that the deity was carried away from Ravana's Lanka to Ekamra Kshetra when Svarna Lanka was destroyed before the war with Rama.

name: Mahishamardini Temple
significance: A laterite rekha deula with chlorite doorjambs near Balasore, dated to Somavamshi rule and renovated in the 19th century; broken sculptures from the site are in the care of the Archaeological Survey of India and the shrine is busiest at Navaratri and Dussehra.

name: Suka Temple
deity: Shiva (original dedication indicated by the wall sculpture)
significance: An abandoned rekha deul in Bhubaneswar that now stands about 1.8 m below ground level, taken as an example of the mature phase of Odishan temple building; it was repaired by Orissa State Archaeology under the Tenth and Eleventh Finance Commission awards.

name: Vishvanatha Temple, Khajuraho
significance: A Chandela temple commissioned by King Dhanga in the UNESCO-listed Khajuraho group, laid out as a panchayatana with four subsidiary shrines of which two survive; the emerald linga named in its dedicatory inscription is lost and a stone linga stands in its place.

name: Malamakkavu Ayyappa Temple
significance: Counted among the 108 Ayyappan shrines of Kerala and owned by the Padinjarepat Nambiar zamindar family, this Palakkad temple keeps its annual Thalapoli on the last Saturday of Dhanu and is known for the rare Chengazhinir flower in its pond.
story: A Cherumi couple is said to have struck a rock in the forest that bled, after which the deity was formally installed and the temple founded.

name: Swarnadhisvara Siva Temple
significance: A late-Ganga Shiva temple in Bhubaneswar, no longer in worship, repaired by Orissa State Archaeology under the Tenth and Eleventh Finance Commission awards; vegetation, seepage and encroachment continue to threaten it.

name: Ettampadai Temple
significance: A Murugan shrine in Triplicane founded in 1845 on land given by a woman named Pachayammal and regarded by its devotees as an eighth padaiveedu of the god; the Bhajaneshwara music group formed in 1978 raised funds for its rebuilding.
story: Its kavadi procession recalls the demon Hidumba, credited in legend with carrying the two hills of Palani.

name: Kunnathoor Padi
significance: A Muthappan shrine at about 3,000 feet on Udumbumala in the Sahyadris where the rites are held in a natural forest clearing with no permanent buildings; long tied to the Mannanar house, its management passed to the Karakkatidam Nayanar family after the British took the dynasty's lands following the killing of its last ruler in 1902.
story: Muthappan is said to have asked for nothing more than fallen leaves, a spring, a mountain, a round stone, forest and palm trees for his worship.

name: Ekambeswarar Temple, Kumbakonam
significance: A Shiva temple in Kumbakonam counted among the twelve shrines linked to the Mahamaham festival held once every twelve years; its most recent consecration took place in October 2015.

name: Veerateeswarar Temple, Vazhuvur
deity: Shiva as Veerateeswarar in the Gajasamhara form, with the goddess Bala Gujambigai
significance: One of the eight Atta-veerattanam shrines of Shiva, built in the 9th century under the Cholas and enlarged by the Thanjavur Nayaks; it holds an 11th-century bronze of Shiva as slayer of the elephant demon.
story: Challenged by sages who doubted his power, Shiva is said to have taken the Gajasamhara form here, killing the elephant demon and wearing its hide as a garment.

name: Krishnapuram Venkatachalapathy Temple
significance: A 16th-century Vishnu temple near Tirunelveli raised by the Madurai Nayak ruler Krishnappa Nayak and regarded as a showcase of Nayak sculpture and pillared halls; worship follows the Pancharatra agama in the Thenkalai tradition.

name: Varaha Cave Temple
deity: Vishnu as Varaha, lifting Bhudevi from the ocean
significance: A rock-cut Pallava mandapa at Mahabalipuram, carved in the later 7th century and celebrated for its panel of Varaha raising the earth goddess; it forms part of the UNESCO-listed Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram.
story: The central panel recalls how Vishnu took the form of a boar to defeat the demon Hiranyaksha and lift the earth back from the bottom of the cosmic ocean.

name: Athmanathaswamy Temple, Avudaiyarkoil
deity: Shiva as Athmanathaswamy (worshipped without an image of the lingam)
significance: The Shiva temple of Tirupperunturai on the south bank of the Vellar in Pudukkottai district, which inscriptions connect with the Saiva saint Manikkavasagar and which gives the village its name of Avudaiyarkoil.

name: Jagannath Temple, Ahmedabad
significance: The Jagannath temple at Jamalpur in Ahmedabad, best known for its annual Rath Yatra, described as the largest such chariot festival after the one at Puri.

name: Vayalur Murugan Temple
deity: Murugan (Kumarasubramaniyar Swamy); Shiva in the older shrine
significance: A Murugan temple west of Tiruchirappalli, about twelve centuries old and built in the medieval Chola period; it is associated with the 15th-century poet Arunagirinathar and with the modern expounder Kirupanandha Variyar, and is administered by the Tamil Nadu HR&CE department.
story: The temple tank, called Agni or Shakthi Theertham, is said to have been opened by Murugan himself with his lance.

name: Venugopala Swamy Temple, Hosa Kannambadi
deity: Krishna as Venugopala, playing the flute among the cows
significance: A 12th-century Hoysala temple that was drowned by the Krishna Raja Sagara reservoir in 1930 and, between 2002 and 2011, taken apart stone by stone and rebuilt on higher ground near Hosa Kannambadi.

name: Vatavaranyeswarar Temple
builtDisplay: Chola; consecrated under Kulothunga Chola III
significance: A Shiva temple at Thiruvalangadu whose present structure belongs to the Chola period, its last recorded consecration falling in the reign of Kulothunga Chola III.
story: The Saiva saint Karaikal Ammaiyar is believed to have attained liberation at this shrine.

name: Varinjam Sree Subramanya Swamy Temple
significance: A Murugan temple at Nadakkal near Chathannoor in Kollam district, built in the Kerala style and a long-standing local place of worship.
story: A fisherman named Kumaran is said to have found a golden image of Subrahmanya while fishing and to have raised the temple where it was enshrined.

name: Vengeeswarar Temple
deity: Shiva (Vengeeswarar), with the goddess Saanthanayaki Ambal
significance: A Shiva temple at Vadapalani in Chennai whose structure is reckoned more than a thousand years old, fronted by a large rajagopuram covered in stucco figures.

name: Venugopalaswami Temple, Kaliappettai
significance: A Krishna temple founded in the 17th century at Kaliappettai in Kanchipuram district, the settlement having begun as an agraharam originally called Doddacharpuram.

name: Vellayani Devi Temple
style: Dravidian (kovil form) with a bronze roof
significance: A Bhadrakali temple beside Vellayani Lake south of Thiruvananthapuram, known for the Kaliyoottu Mahotsavam held once every three years, a festival of some sixty-five to seventy days said to be the longest continuous temple festival in south India.
story: A blacksmith named Kelan Kulasekhara is said to have found a divine frog near Vellayani Lake and consecrated an image in which the goddess took her seat.

name: Velveeswarar Temple, Valasaravakkam
significance: A Shiva temple in the Valasaravakkam quarter of Chennai, traditionally held to have been built under Kulothunga Chola I, with a large temple pond within its precinct.

name: Vayilyamkunnu Bhagavathi Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Kadampazhipuram in the old Valluvanad country, about 24 km from Palakkad on the road to Cherpulassery.

name: Karunellinathar Temple
deity: Shiva as Karunellinathar (lingam), with Chokki Amman (Parvati)
significance: A rock-cut Shiva temple at Thiruthangal near Sivakasi, ascribed to the Pandyas and extended in 1233 CE by Gurukalathirayan, a minister of Sundara Pandya.
story: Thiruthangal is said to take its name from Ranganatha's halt here for a night on his way to seek the hand of Andal.

name: Shitala Mata Temple, Butapaldi
significance: A small twelfth-century shrine of the goddess Shitala in the Mehsana district village of Butapaldi, where she is worshipped under the local name Brahmani. It is protected by the state of Gujarat as monument S-GJ-286 and survives as a modest example of Maru-Gurjara temple building in north Gujarat.

name: Ved Mata Gaytri Mandir
significance: A recently built Hindu temple at Kushinagar in eastern Uttar Pradesh dedicated to Gayatri, the goddess who personifies the Vedic Gayatri mantra. It was founded by Rampravesh Kushwaha and opened on 8 December 2013.

name: Alavaimalai Subrayar Murugan Temple
significance: A hill shrine of Murugan on Alavaimalai near Alavaipatti in the Vennandur block of Namakkal district, built in the Dravidian manner and served by a climb to the summit sanctum.

name: Mahakal Temple, Darjeeling
significance: A hilltop shrine of Shiva above Darjeeling, raised in 1782 by Lama Dorjey Rinzing on the site of the Dorje-Ling monastery of 1765 from which the town takes its name. Hindu and Buddhist worship are carried on together at the same site.
story: Three Shiva lingams standing for Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva are said to have manifested themselves on the hill in 1782.

name: Radha Madhab Temple, Bishnupur
significance: A brick ek-ratna temple of Radha and Krishna founded at Bishnupur in 1737 by Churamoni, wife of the Mallabhum ruler Bir Singha Dev. Its terracotta facing carries scenes of the Krishna lila together with Dashavatara panels and floral ornament.

name: Goravanahalli Mahalakshmi Temple
significance: A much-visited shrine of the goddess Mahalakshmi in the Tumkur district village of Goravanahalli in Karnataka. Its worship was sustained through the twentieth century by the devotee Kamalamma, who came to the village in 1925 and settled there in 1952.
story: The goddess is said to have blessed a poor man named Abbayya with wealth, and later to have appeared to Thotadappa in his dreams asking him to raise a shrine for her.

name: Karinjeshwara Temple
place: Karinja, Bantwal taluk, Dakshina Kannada district
significance: A hill temple in Bantwal taluk of Dakshina Kannada, completed in 1200 CE, where Shiva is worshipped at the summit with Parvati and Ganesha in shrines on the slope below. Feeding the resident troop of monkeys is part of the daily ritual.

name: Venugopalaswamy Temple, Karvetinagaram
significance: A Vaishnavite temple at Karvetinagaram in Chittoor district where Krishna is worshipped as Venugopala, the flute player, with Rukmini and Satyabhama beside him. It was built by King Venkataperumal of the Venkataraja line.

name: Ithiyapuram Kaavu
significance: A sacred-grove shrine (kaavu) on the Kanyakumari-Thiruvananthapuram highway about 30 km from Nagercoil, where Vana Sastha and Vana Durga are the chief deities alongside Bala Ganapati, Nagaraja and Krishna. A copper plate said to have been granted by the Travancore ruler Marthanda Varma is kept there.
story: Devotees hold that Vana Durga came here from the deep forest of Pechiparai, followed by troops of serpents, to stand guard over Vana Sastha.

name: Maa Tara Chandi Temple
significance: A cave shrine of the goddess Tara Chandi set in the Kaimur hills at Sasaram in Bihar, counted among the Shakta seats of the region and drawing large crowds at Navratri.
story: The right eye of Sati's corpse is said to have fallen at this spot when Vishnu cut the body apart with his Sudarshana chakra.

name: Gupteshwar Mahadev, Udaipur
significance: A Shiva shrine set inside a cave near the top of a hill at Titardi village on the outskirts of Udaipur. Pilgrims reach it by a climb of roughly 800 metres from the road, and darshan is offered from morning to late afternoon.

name: Sree Kattayattu Bhagavathi Kshethram
deity: Devi as Moovanthikkali and Arayil Bhagavathi
significance: A Bhagavathi temple in the village of Peruvayal near Kozhikode, where the goddess is worshipped in two forms, Moovanthikkali and Arayil Bhagavathi, with Ganapathi and Ayyappa as attendant deities. Its ritual year turns on the Paattulsavam and the Thottam performances.

name: Sathya Vageeswarar Temple, Kalakkad
significance: A Shaivite temple of three precincts at the centre of Kalakkad town in Tirunelveli district, first raised by the Pandyas in the 13th century. Nayak rulers added its pillared halls and principal shrines in the 15th and 16th centuries, and Boothala Veera Udaya Marthanda Varman gave the musical pillared halls at the front.

name: Vedarajan Temple, Thirunagari
significance: A Vishnu temple at Thirunagari in Mayiladuthurai district where the deity is worshipped as Vedarajan and Lakshmi as Amruthavalli. Held to have been begun by the Cholas, it received its pillared halls and larger shrines from Vijayanagara and Thanjavur Nayak patrons in the 16th century.
story: Karthama Prajapathi is said to have done penance here for Lakshmi, who hid in the temple tank among the lotuses; he was born again as prince Sangabalan and became the poet-saint Thirumangai Alvar after being given the sacred mantra.

name: Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Penna Ahobilam
place: Penna Ahobilam, Uravakonda mandal, Anantapur district
significance: A hill temple of Lakshmi Narasimha at Penna Ahobilam in Anantapur district, built up under Vijayanagara patronage with gopurams, mandapas and subsidiary shrines around the main sanctum. The Vijayanagara king Sadashivaraya is credited with installing the large image and enlarging the complex.
story: A cow is said to have emptied her milk each day into a well on the hill, and when Narasimha appeared and claimed her the cry of wonder, Aho Balam - what power! - gave the place its name.

name: Navapashanam Temple
significance: A shore shrine at Devipattinam on the Ramanathapuram coast where nine stones set in the shallow sea are worshipped as the Navagrahas, the nine planetary deities. Worshippers reach them from the beach when the tide is low.
story: Rama is said to have installed the nine planets here with his own hands, shaping them from the clay of the shore, as part of the worship he offered before crossing to Lanka.

name: Kasi Viswanathar Temple, Sivakasi
significance: The temple from which Sivakasi takes its name, a Shiva shrine with a three-tiered gopuram in Virudhunagar district. It is held to have been built by the Pandya ruler Harikesari Parakkirama Pandian in the 16th century and was extended later by the Madurai Nayaks.
story: A Pandya king is said to have carried a lingam home from Kasi, and where the cow bearing it halted and would not move he understood Shiva's wish and set the lingam down.

name: Arulmigu Prasanna Venkatesa Perumal Temple
significance: A Vishnu temple in the village of Thirupparkadal in Ranipet district, where the god is worshipped as Prasanna Venkateshvara. The Vijayanagara emperor Krishnadevaraya is recorded as having renovated it.
story: Vishnu is said to have come to a devotee here in the guise of an old Vaishnava on an Ekadashi day, and to have revealed himself standing upon a Shiva lingam.

name: Walajapet Kasiviswanathar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the Walajapet neighbourhood of Ranipet in northern Tamil Nadu, built about three hundred years ago, where the god is worshipped as Kasiviswanathar alongside the goddess Kasivisalakshi.

name: Saumyakeshava Temple, Nagamangala
significance: A Hoysala temple of the 12th century in the Mandya district town of Nagamangala, named for its six-foot image of Keshava, a serene form of Vishnu. Laid out on a stellate plan with northern nagara elements, it drew continued patronage from later rulers including the Vijayanagara emperors.

name: Jagannath Govinda Temple, Hojai
significance: A Vaishnava temple at Gauranagar in the Hojai district of central Assam, established in 1928, where Jagannath and Govinda are worshipped together.

name: Mandagapattu Tirumurti Temple
significance: A rock-cut cave shrine at Mandagapattu in Viluppuram district, excavated for Brahma, Shiva and Vishnu and attributed to the Pallava king Mahendravarman I. It is the oldest stone shrine in Tamil Nadu to have been discovered and securely dated.

name: Mangala Devi Temple, Kagpur
significance: A ruined goddess temple in Kagpur village on State Highway 19, some 33 km from Vidisha, raised in the Paramara period between the 10th and 11th centuries. Its flat-roofed mandapa stands on twelve pillars, and the image of Mangala Devi it houses was installed in 1306.

name: Radha Raman Temple, Vrindavan
significance: One of the oldest surviving temples of Vrindavan in Mathura district, established around 1542 by Gopala Bhatta Goswami, where Krishna is worshipped as Radha Ramana. The shrine is built in the Rajasthani manner.
story: The deity is said to have emerged of its own accord from a Damodara shaligrama stone, which took on the three-fold bending form of Krishna.

name: Adithyapuram Sun Temple
