significance: Described as the only shrine in Kerala with Surya as the presiding deity, standing near Kaduthuruthy in Kottayam district. Its tantric rights are held by descendants of the Nambudiri family of Kapikkadu Marangattu Mana.
story: Legend holds that a Nambudiri who meditated on the sun god was instructed by Surya himself to consecrate the idol on this spot.

name: Kidangoor Subramanya Swami Temple
significance: One of the better-known Subramanya shrines in Kerala, on the banks of the Meenachil river. Kidangoor was among the sixty-four Nambudiri settlements lying on the frontier between the Vadakkumkur and Thekkumkur kingdoms, and the site also holds a Vishnu shrine reckoned older than the Subramanya temple.
story: Temple tradition says the Subramanya idol slipped from a sage's water pot and travelled along with the water until it came to rest at the older Vishnu shrine.

name: Sukreesvarar Temple, Kurakkuthali
significance: A Shiva temple on the north bank of the Noyyal river about 8 km from Tiruppur, counted among the Vaippu Sthalams sung by the Nayanar Sundarar. It carries inscriptions of the Cholas, Pandyas and Udayars, in which the deity is named Aludaya Pillai and Milakeesan.
story: Local legend tells of a farmer who cut off the ears of the temple's Nandi; a member of his family was struck mute, and when a replacement Nandi was installed the two figures returned of themselves to their original places.

name: Dhumnath Temple
deity: Shiva, associated with the goddess Dhumesvari
style: Bhumija, with a curvilinear Nagara shikhara
significance: A state-protected Shiva temple at Sargaon raised under the Kalachuris of Ratanpur. Its shrine sits below ground level, reached by six descending steps, and later houses have encroached on the hall and ante-chamber.

name: Sringeri Sharadamba Temple
deity: Sharadamba, a form of the goddess Saraswati
significance: The principal shrine of Sringeri, traditionally founded by Adi Shankara in the 8th century and dedicated to Sharadamba. Pindari raiders sacked it during the Third Anglo-Mysore War in 1791, after which Tipu Sultan wrote to the Sringeri Shankaracharya offering protection, money and gifts to restore it.

name: Manibhadresvara Temple – II
significance: A small rekha deula on the Rath Road running from the Mausima (Ramesvara) temple to Badheibanka Chowk in Bhubaneswar. It now stands abandoned on privately owned land and is cracked on every side.

name: Devasabha Temple
significance: A pancharatha rekha deula inside the Kharakhia Vaidyanath temple precinct in the old town of Bhubaneswar, now abandoned with an empty sanctum. Its name is explained locally as the assembly hall of all the gods and goddesses.

name: Radha Madan Mohan Temple, Vrindavan
deity: Madan Mohan (Krishna) with Radha and the gopi Lalita
significance: A red-sandstone Vaishnava temple about 20 m high, rebuilt in 1580 under the direction of Sanatana Goswami with funds from the Multan trader Kapur Ram Das. The original image was taken to Jaipur in 1670 ahead of Aurangzeb's campaign and later to Karauli under King Gopal Singh; a replica was installed in 1748 and the hilltop temple rebuilt in 1819 by Nanda Kumar Basu.
story: The deity is said to have been found at the foot of an old banyan tree by Advaita Acharya and to have been worshipped by the saint Mirabai.

name: Dolagovinda Siva Temple
deity: Shiva, as a lingam set in a circular yonipitha
significance: Also called the Vaidyanatha Shiva temple, this small Kalingan shrine stands at Rathagada Chowk in the old town of Bhubaneswar. Local tradition credits it to the Kesharis (Somavamsis), though its design does not match that dynasty's usual work; the name comes from the Dola Mandapa across the street.

name: Abhimukeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the eastern bank of the Mahamaham tank at Kumbakonam, one of the twelve Shiva temples linked to the Mahamaham festival held every twelve years. Its most recent consecration was on 26 October 2015.
story: The name is explained by a legend in which Shiva turned to face the nine river goddesses when they arrived, so granting them his darshan.

name: Kedareshwara Temple, Halebidu
style: Hoysala, soapstone trikuta on a stellate plan
significance: A three-shrine soapstone temple at Halebidu raised between 1173 and 1219 CE by the Hoysala king Veera Ballala II and his queen Ketaladevi. Though Shaiva, its sculpture draws on both Shaiva and Vaishnava themes, and it is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India as a monument of national importance.

name: Karchapeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Kanchipuram built by the Pallavas and later renovated by the Vijayanagara kings, with a rajagopuram, inner gopura and temple tank. It is counted among the Vaippu Sthalams named by the Nayanar Appar.
story: The temple's name comes from the belief that Vishnu worshipped Shiva here in his kurma (tortoise) form.

name: Chitragupta Temple, Khajuraho
significance: The one temple at Khajuraho dedicated to Surya, built about 1020–1025 CE and probably consecrated on Shivaratri, 23 February 1023. Part of the UNESCO-listed Khajuraho Group and an ASI Monument of National Importance, it holds an unusual eleven-headed Vishnu showing his supreme form with the ten incarnations.

name: Patalesvara Siva Temple – II
style: Kalingan (sandstone rekha deula in dry masonry)
significance: A sandstone rekha deula on the Talabazar road between the Kedara-Gouri and Lingaraja temples in Bhubaneswar, now partly buried and broken. Water infiltration leaves the deity submerged for most of the year.

name: Sundaresvara Siva Temple
deity: Shiva as Sundaresvara, in a north-facing circular yonipitha
significance: A rekha deula at Sundarpada in Bhubaneswar dated by its architecture to about the 13th century. Villagers raised funds to install a new Shiva lingam in April 2013 after the old one decayed, and the shrine is run by the Sri Sri Dadhivamana Sundaresvara Mahadeva Trust Board under the state Endowment Department.
story: Local tradition credits the temple to the Kesari (Somavamsi) dynasty and specifically to Yajati I, the builder of the Lingaraja temple.

name: Vaithya Lingam Temple
deity: Shiva as Sri Vaithya Lingam Swami (goddess Yogambigai)
significance: A Shiva temple at Aladipatti in Nallur, Tenkasi district, where the lingam is worshipped as Vaithya Lingam Swami alongside the goddess Yogambigai.

name: Uthralikavu Rudhira Mahakalikavu Temple
significance: A small rural shrine of the goddess Kali near Wadakkanchery in Thrissur district, best known for the Uthralikavu Pooram it hosts every February or March. The festival opens with a flag-hoisting on the second Tuesday of Kumbham and culminates seven days later, and is reckoned the second most heavily attended pooram after Thrissur Pooram.

name: Valiyakulangara Devi Temple
significance: A Bhadrakali temple at Mahadevikadu in Karthikappally, Alappuzha district, about 4 km from Haripad. Its principal festival, Aswathi in February or March, is marked by fireworks and Kettukazhcha processions of decorated temple chariots and effigies.

name: Utkanteshwar Mahadev
significance: A Shiva temple on the bank of the Vatrak river in Kapadvanj taluka, Kheda district. Ali Muhammad Khan described it in the 18th-century Persian chronicle Mirat-i-Ahmadi.

name: Uttara Swami Malai Temple
place: Sector 7, R. K. Puram, New Delhi
style: Tamil, Chola style (subsidiary shrines in Pandya style)
significance: Delhi's Malai Mandir at R. K. Puram, whose foundation stone was laid on 8 September 1965 by M. Bhakthavatsalam with Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri presiding; the main temple was consecrated on 7 June 1973. Further mahakumbhabhishekams followed in 1990, 1995 and 2001, and the Adi Sankara Hall opened on 9 November 1997.

name: Valliyoorkkavu Temple
deity: Bhadrakali, worshipped in three forms as Bhagavathy, Vana Durga and Jala Durga
significance: An old goddess shrine near Mananthavady in Wayanad district whose annual fourteen-day festival falls in March and draws large crowds from across the district.
story: The image is held to be self-manifested, and the festival closes with the rudhirakkolam, which enacts the goddess's victory over the demon king Darika.

name: Vandiyur Mariamman Temple
significance: A Mariamman temple on the banks of the Vaigai about 3 km from the Meenakshi Amman Temple, raised under the Madurai Nayaks. Its large tank, the Vandiyur Mariamman Teppakulam, is fed by underground channels from the river and hosts the float festival on Thaipusam.

name: Valiyakoikkal Temple
significance: The shrine inside the Pandalam Palace grounds that serves as the family temple of the Pandalam royal family, now administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board. The annual Thiruvabharanam procession carrying Ayyappan's ornaments to Sabarimala for Makaravilakku sets out from here.

name: Uthirakosamangai Mangaleswarar Temple
significance: A roughly 20-acre Shiva temple with a seven-tiered rajagopuram, sung by the 9th-century saint Manickavasagar in the Thiruvasakam and prominent under Pandya rule. It is known for an unusual six-foot emerald image of Nataraja and is administered by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
story: Shiva is said to have appeared in Ravana's palace as a small child, and when he was lifted a fireball rose from the temple tank, at which 999 of the thousand rishis present immolated themselves while the last survived to preserve the sacred texts.

name: Trikkur Mahadeva Temple
significance: A rock-cut Shiva temple set inside a natural cave about 30 feet long on a hillock in Trikkur, with its mukha mandapa carved from the living rock. It has been a protected monument under the Kerala Department of Archaeology since 1966 and is looked after by the Paliyam Trust and a local protection committee.
story: The large Shivalinga is believed to have been consecrated by Agni, who is said to worship Shiva here perpetually, which is why the image is never taken outside in procession during the rains.

name: Vamana Temple, Khajuraho
significance: An eastern-group Khajuraho temple raised by the Chandela rulers between about 1050 and 1075 CE, comprising a sanctum, vestibule, maha-mandapa with lateral transepts and an entrance porch. It stands roughly 200 m north-east of the Brahma Temple and forms part of the Khajuraho Group of Monuments inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Unao Balaji Sun Temple
deity: Surya (the Sun God, worshipped here as Balaji)
significance: A sun temple at Unao, about 17 km from both Datia and Jhansi, whose shrine is engraved with twenty-one triangles taken to represent the twenty-one phases of the Sun, the image standing on a brick platform faced with black plates. Its main priesthood is hereditary in the Kachhi Kushwaha Kshatriya community, and pilgrims bathe for skin ailments in the sulphurous water of the nearby Pahuj river.
story: A cow belonging to a Kushwaha Kshatriya villager is said to have poured out her milk at one spot, where a statue of the Sun God was then found; the king of Datia built the temple there and made the cowherd's community its hereditary priests.

name: Valisvara Temple, Thiruvalisvaram
significance: An early 10th-century Chola foundation on the Tamraparni in Tirunelveli district, credited to Rajaraja Chola I and rated among the finest surviving examples of Chola temple architecture. Its sculpture, including Chandesanugrahamurti and an Ardhanarishvara on the vimana, was singled out by the historian K. A. Nilakanta Sastri as unsurpassed workmanship.

name: Ucchi Pillayar Temple, Rockfort
significance: A shrine to Ganesha on the summit of the Rockfort at Tiruchirappalli, reached by steps cut into the rock, whose caves were first excavated by the Pallavas in the 7th century and whose temples were completed by the Nayaks of Madurai under the Vijayanagara Empire. The site is maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India and looks out over Trichy, Srirangam and the rivers below.
story: Ganesha is said to have taken the form of a Brahmin boy and set down the image of Ranganatha that Vibhishana was carrying to Lanka, so that it stayed at Srirangam.

name: Valayanad Devi Temple
significance: A north-facing goddess temple with four gopurams that served as the family shrine of the medieval Zamorins of Kozhikode. Worship follows the Saktheya tradition under Pidarar Brahmin priests, with hereditary rights held by five Moosad families, and the annual festival runs seven days from Karthika in Makaram.
story: The Zamorin is said to have done penance until Bhagavathy appeared and agreed to follow him to his kingdom; when he looked back on the way she halted and flung her bangle, which spun for a week before falling where the temple now stands.

name: Upper Bagh Devi Temple
deity: Bagh Devi (Byaghra Devi), a form of Shakti
significance: A hilltop Shakti shrine at Kulada in Ganjam district, about 8 km from Bhanjanagar, long associated with the Odia poet Upendra Bhanja. A second shrine was later built at the foot of the hill so that pilgrims unable to climb could worship.
story: Local tradition holds that three sisters divided the region by hurling vessels and a temple was raised wherever one fell, the third having sunk from sight, and that the goddess appeared to Upendra Bhanja in a dream telling him to build the shrines.

name: Pura Meduwe Karang
deity: Batara Meduwe Karang ("lord possessing the ground")
significance: A large north Balinese temple raised in 1890 by villagers who had resettled at Kubutambahan from the abandoned village of Bulian, addressed to the deity who owns the ground and petitioned for the fertility of unirrigated farmland. Its outer terrace carries thirty-six stone figures from the Ramayana and its walls the flowery relief carving typical of the north coast.

name: Pura Pulaki
significance: One of the sea temples set around the coast of Bali to form a protective chain, founded in 1489 by the Majapahit brahmin priest Dang Hyang Nirartha. Left abandoned for centuries, it was leased to a Chinese trader under the Dutch administration in 1920 and restored by the Indonesian government after 1950.
story: Local tradition holds that when Nirartha reached the shore the forest macaques escorted him to the spot where the temple would stand.

name: Pura Beji Sangsit
significance: A subak temple of the Sangsit rice-growing community, dedicated to the rice goddess Dewi Sri and dated to the fifteenth century, when brahmins arrived from the Majapahit kingdom. It takes its name from the beji, the pond used for purification, and is covered in the heavy foliate carving that distinguishes north Balinese work from that of the south.

name: Pura Taman Saraswati
significance: Commissioned by the prince of Ubud, Cokorda Gede Agung Sukawati, and designed by the sculptor and ritual architect I Gusti Nyoman Lempad, the temple was begun in 1951 and finished in 1952. Dedicated to Sarasvati, goddess of learning, literature and art, it is among Ubud's best-known landmarks for the lotus pond and water garden fronting its outer courtyard.

name: Pura Gede Perancak
significance: A sea temple on the Perancak estuary in Jembrana marking the place where the priest Dang Hyang Nirartha is held to have come ashore in Bali in 1546. Once sited on a hilltop and known as Tanjung Ketapang, it was moved to the marshland side and rebuilt twice as a dang kahyangan temple, anchoring the Hindu community in a largely Muslim district.
story: The name is traced to ancak, meaning split: when the village head I Gusti Ngurah challenged Nirartha, the stone seat beneath him is said to have cracked apart.

name: Pura Dalem Segara Madhu
significance: The death temple of Jagaraga in Buleleng, dedicated to Durga and Shiva and thought to have been founded in the twelfth century. Destroyed during the Dutch intervention of 1849, it was rebuilt from 1865 and is known for dense north Balinese wall carving that includes reliefs of early aeroplanes and motor cars.

name: Garuda Wisnu Kencana statue
significance: A 121-metre statue of Vishnu riding the divine bird Garuda, designed by the sculptor Nyoman Nuarta in 1990, begun in 1997 and completed in 2018 after a sixteen-year halt caused by the Asian financial crisis. It is the tallest statue in Indonesia and the tallest depiction of a Hindu deity anywhere.
story: The myth it renders has Garuda agree to carry Vishnu in exchange for the elixir with which he freed his enslaved mother.

name: Pura Penataran Agung Lempuyang
deity: Sang Hyang Widhi and the Trimurti
significance: The first and lowest of the seven temples of the Pura Lempuyang complex, standing about 603 m up the south-western flank of Mount Lempuyang in Karangasem, with Pura Lempuyang Luhur at the summit. Epigraphs record a ruler named Jayacakti being sent to build it in the late tenth century, and worship on this mountain is held to predate most Hindu temples on Bali; the temple was restored in 2001.

name: Pura Dalem Agung Padangtegal
deity: Hyang Widhi in the form of Shiva the Transformer
significance: The main temple of the three-temple group inside Ubud's Sacred Monkey Forest Sanctuary, standing in the south-western part of the grounds. Thought to have been raised around 1350, it remains a working centre of ritual life for the Padangtegal community.

name: Pura Rambut Siwi
deity: Dang Hyang Nirartha (his hair relic; sea temple)
significance: A cliff-top sea temple on the Jembrana coast of western Bali, counted among the island's most important pura segara. Its red-brick shrines carry reliefs of scenes from the Arjuna Wiwaha, and a cave below the site holds a water temple guarded by a statue of the priest Nirartha.
story: The name means roughly 'hair worship', from the legend that Nirartha left a lock of his hair here to protect the temple.

name: Pura Maospahit
deity: Ratu Ayu Mas Maospahit and Ida Bhatara Lingsir Sakti
style: Balinese, bare red brick in the Majapahit manner
significance: A Denpasar temple whose surviving main shrine, the Candi Raras Maospahit, is credited to the architect Sri Kbo Iwa in 1278. A second shrine for wayang performance was added in 1553 by the architect I Pasek under the Badung kingdom, and the bare red brickwork recalls thirteenth-century Majapahit building.

name: Pura Parahyangan Agung Jagatkarta
deity: The perfect divine nature, with deified ancestors including King Siliwangi of Pajajaran
significance: A large modern temple on the slopes of Mount Salak, begun in 1995 through the joint labour of the Hindu Nusantara community and serving as a Pura Kahyangan Jagad for devotees around Greater Jakarta. Its Padmasana, Balai Pasamuan Agung and paduraksa gates are finished, but the compound as a whole is not.
story: The site marks the belief that Prabu Siliwangi of Pakuan Pajajaran attained moksha here together with his soldiers.

name: Sri Vadapathira Kaliamman Temple
significance: One of Singapore's oldest Hindu temples, grown from a modest 1830s shrine founded by Rengasamy Mooriyar into a major Serangoon Road sanctuary of the fierce Kali form Vadapathira Kaliamman. Rebuilt in 1984 and again renovated in 2015, it was reconsecrated in December 2016 with a pair of 4.2-metre Garuda and Hanuman figures.

name: Sri Manmatha Karuneshvarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on Kallang Road begun in 1888 as a shrine by Tamil Hindu workers of the Municipal Gasworks depot, which is why it is still known locally as the Kallang Gasworks Sivan Temple. It was rebuilt in brick in 1934 with funding from the sons of A. V. Irullappa Pillay and renovated again in 1974.

name: Sri Sivan Temple
deity: Shiva as Viswanathar, with Parvati as Visalatchi
style: North Indian exterior with Tamil Shaivite interior
significance: A Tamil Shaiva Siddhanta temple that stood at Dhoby Ghaut from about 1850 until 1983, spent a decade in a transit temple on Serangoon Road, and was rebuilt at Geylang East for S$6 million on an octagonal plan consecrated in May 1993. Its towers follow North Indian design while worship inside follows Tamil Shaivite custom, an unusual pairing in Singapore.

name: Sri Darma Muneeswaran Temple
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; on site over a century
significance: A Serangoon North temple to the guardian deity Dharma Muneeswaran, a form of Shiva, which the article records as having stood on its present site for more than a century. It is known for its Navagraha sanctum, where devotees petition against Kala Sarpa Dosha, and for a Naga statue it claims is the largest in Southeast Asia.

name: Sri Siva Krishna Temple
significance: Founded in 1962 by Kunjukrishnan and moved to Marsiling in 1982, this temple joins Shiva as presiding deity with Krishna and more than twenty other murtis across a 25,000 sq ft complex. Ground was broken on the present building in 1987 and it was consecrated on 1 September 1996; its early congregation was drawn largely from taxi drivers.

name: Sri Ruthra Kaliamman Temple
significance: Begun in 1913 as a wooden shrine raised by Lakshmana Nadar and Hindu workers at the Alexandra Brickworks, rebuilt in brick in 1923, and moved in the early 1980s from Pasir Panjang Road to Depot Road, where the present temple was consecrated on 11 September 1983. Alongside Kali it houses Vinayagar, Subramaniar, Muneeswaran and the Navagrahas.

name: Sri Siva Durga Temple
significance: A Potong Pasir temple to Shiva and Durga first completed in 1906. Persistent water leakage and cramped, poorly ventilated quarters led to its demolition in 2014, and a S$2.7 million rebuild reopened in 2016 with a consecration on 4 December that year.

name: Sree Ramar Temple
significance: A Rama temple at Changi Village founded in 1946 by Ram Naidu of the British Indian Army, on a site the British Army donated at the end of the Second World War, and long patronised by Hindu workers at the nearby RAF Changi base. It grew from a shrine at the foot of a tree; granite images were installed in newly built sanctums during the 1991 rebuilding, and displaced shrines were absorbed into it in 1999.

name: Sri Senpaga Vinayagar Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple on Ceylon Road in Katong whose origins go back to the 1850s and a modest attap-roofed shelter raised under the Ceylonese Tamil pioneer Ethirnayagam Pillai. The Singapore Ceylon Tamils' Association bought the land in 1923 and remains its keeper; a concrete temple was completed in 1929 and a full rebuilding in the late 1990s added a 21-metre raja gopuram, consecrated in 2003.
story: The temple is said to have begun where a statue of Vinayagar was found beside a pond, next to the chempaka tree — senpaga in Tamil — that gave the temple its name.

name: Sri Krishnan Temple
significance: The only Tamil temple in Singapore dedicated to Krishna together with Rukmini, begun in 1870 by the wealthy merchant Hanuman Beem Singh, who set images of the deities at the foot of a banyan tree to serve a growing Hindu population in the district. The main shrine was rebuilt in 1933 on donations from Naraina Pillai and Pakirisamy Pillai, in a classical Dravidian idiom following Agama Sastra, and has been renovated repeatedly since, most recently between 2016 and 2018.

name: Sri Layan Sithi Vinayagar Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple at the junction of Keong Saik Road and Kreta Ayer Road in Chinatown, built in 1925 by the Nattukottai Chettiar community with funding from the Chettiars of Tamil Nadu. It replaced an older attap-roofed temple near Singapore General Hospital, which had served hospital employees, Outram Prison staff and soldiers of the Sepoy Lines until the government acquired that land in 1920; its five-tier gopuram tapers to represent the five senses.

name: Sri Poyatha Moorthi Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple on Jalan Tukang Emas in Malacca, built in 1781 by Thavinayagar Chitty, leader of the Chitty community, on a plot the Dutch colonial government of Malacca granted him for a Hindu temple; the Dutch freehold grant supplies its date. A further altar within the temple is dedicated to Muruga.

name: Sri Mahamariamman Temple, Penang
significance: The mother-goddess temple of George Town's Tamil quarter, begun as a shrine on land granted in 1801 and built up into a temple by 1833. It has been reconsecrated five times between 1933 and 2016, taking the honorific Arulmigu at the 1980 kumbabishekam.

name: Arulmigu Sri Rajakaliamman Glass Temple
significance: A Kaliamman temple in Johor Bahru that began in 1922 as a simple shelter and was rebuilt in 1996. Between 2008 and October 2009 its interior was sheathed in glasswork, giving it the name by which it is now known.

name: Arulmigu Maha Muthu Mariamman Thevasthanam
significance: A Perak temple founded in 1962 as a Kaliamman shrine, reordered in 1964 so that Mariamman became the principal deity, and registered under her name in 1967. A wholly new temple was begun in December 2006 and consecrated at its kumbabishekam in December 2010.
story: Devotees hold that the eagles which circled overhead during the 2010 kumbabishekam were Garuda, Vishnu's mount, marking the new temple with divine assent.

name: Jalan Baru Sri Muniswarar Temple
significance: One of the older Tamil shrines on the Penang mainland, set up in the 1870s by Indian labourers who came with the East India Company. It opened as Sri Muniandy Temple and was later renamed for Muniswarar, the village guardian deity worshipped at its main altar alongside Ganesha and Murugan.
story: The guardian is said to ride the neighbourhood after midnight on a white horse with an arivaal blade and a cigar, and a Chinese devotee who saw him enter the temple grounds so mounted paid for an altar in his honour.

name: Arulmigu Karumariamman Temple
significance: A temple to the rural South Indian mother goddess Karumariamman that descends from an estate shrine serving Paduma Estate workers at Perai and was moved when Seberang Jaya township was laid out in the 1970s. The present RM2.3 million building was started in 1996, with the works minister S. Samy Vellu laying its foundation stone on 16 February 1997.

name: Sri Sithi Vinayagar Temple
significance: A Dravidian-style Ganesha temple on Jalan Selangor in Petaling Jaya, completed in 1964 and first consecrated that November. It is run by the Petaling Jaya Hindu Association, registered in 1959, and has been rebuilt and reconsecrated three times since, most recently in 2007.

name: Sri Sundararaja Perumal Temple
significance: A Vaishnava temple in the royal town of Klang dedicated to Vishnu as Perumal, built in 1892 and wholly reconstructed in 2015 as the first granite temple in Malaysia. Its gopuram carved with images of the deities has made it a principal Perumal shrine for Malaysian Tamils, who call it the Tirupati of Southeast Asia.

name: Seafield Sri Maha Mariamman Temple
significance: A Mariamman temple in the USJ suburb of Subang Jaya, believed but never proven to have been founded in 1891. Its forced relocation from land sold by Sime Darby to the One City developer MCT Bhd produced a long dispute that erupted into rioting in 2018, making it the best-known temple land case in Malaysia.

name: Sree Maha Mariamman Devasthanam Temple, Butterworth
significance: One of the oldest Hindu foundations on mainland Penang, established at Bagan Luar in Butterworth in 1853 and given a permanent temple by Ponnusami Pillai in 1903. The present Dravidian structure, whose gopuram towers over the surrounding buildings, was raised in the 1980s and consecrated in 1988.
story: The temple is said to have begun when an image of Ambal was found by the seaside in 1853 and a small hut was put up on the spot to shelter her for worship.

name: Maravijaya Buddha
significance: A 25 m marble image of the seated Buddha at Naypyidaw, cut from stone quarried at Sagyin near Mandalay. Work began on 14 June 2020 and the statue was consecrated on 1 August 2023, the project driven by the ruling State Administration Council and funded largely by military-linked businessmen and retired officers.
story: Its name Maravijaya means to conquer Mara, the demon the Buddha overcame at the moment of his enlightenment.

name: Win Sein Taw Ya
significance: A Theravada monastic site near Mudon in Mon State holding the world's largest free-standing reclining Buddha, 180 m long and 30 m tall. Work on the image began on 29 February 1992 under the founding monk Win Sein Sayadaw, and its hollow interior carries a multi-level museum of chambers depicting scenes from the Buddha's life.

name: Shwethalyaung Buddha
significance: A 55-metre reclining Buddha west of Bago, traditionally credited to King Migadippa in 994 CE and reckoned the largest Buddha image in pre-colonial Southeast Asia. Twice abandoned to the jungle, it was rediscovered by British railway workers in 1881 and sheltered under an iron pavilion in 1906.

name: Kyauktawgyi Buddha Temple
style: Modelled on the Ananda Temple at Bagan
significance: Royal temple at the foot of Mandalay Hill housing a Buddha carved from a single block of pale green Sagyin marble, consecrated in 1865. Begun by King Mindon Min in 1853, it took until 1878 to finish after a palace rebellion and other disorder stalled the work.

name: Nanpaya Temple
style: Brick, stone and mud-mortar shrine with a square sanctum, mandapa and perforated stone windows
significance: A rare Brahmanical shrine in the overwhelmingly Buddhist landscape of Bagan, said to have served the captive Thaton king Manuha before being turned into a temple. Its four stone pillars carry celebrated reliefs of Brahma seated on lotuses.
story: Its sculpture shows Vishnu reclining on the serpent Shesha with a lotus rising from his navel to give birth to Brahma, the creation of the cosmos.

name: Shri Kali Temple, Yangon
significance: Built by Tamil migrants in 1871 when Burma was governed as a province of British India, this temple anchors the Hindu community of downtown Yangon's Little India. Its roof is densely covered with painted images and stone carvings of Hindu deities.

name: Laykyun Sekkya
significance: A standing Buddha of 116 metres (129 metres with its base) raised near Monywa on the initiative of the abbot Ven. Nãradã and completed in 2008. It briefly ranked as the tallest statue in the world and stands beside a reclining Buddha depicting the Mahaparinirvana.

name: Budha Subba Temple
deity: Budha Subba (deified spirit of Buddhi Karna Raya Khebang Limbu)
significance: A shrine at Bijayapur near Dharan venerating the spirit of Buddhi Karna Raya Khebang Limbu, the last Limbu king, who was killed in 1773; local Limbu people began worshipping his wandering soul at his tomb as an old king, and he is honoured as a protective deity.
story: Shiva and Parvati are said to have come to Vijayapur in disguise on a hunt, planted their bows in the ground and sat in penance, vanishing when they sensed the approach of Kali Yuga, while bamboo sprouted from the bows they left behind.

name: Bala Tripura Sundari Temple
deity: Durga as Bala Tripura Sundari Bhagawati
builtDisplay: est. 1057 CE; said to be 12th c.
significance: A goddess temple on the bank of the Thuli Bheri river near Tripurakot in Dolpa District, dedicated to Durga in her Bala Tripura Sundari form and traditionally dated to the 11th-12th century.
story: King Bikram Shahi is said to have uncovered an image of Bhagwati in an excavated pit, from which butterflies flew out and turned to stone, one of them marking the spot where the temple was raised.

name: Tal Barahi Temple
significance: A two-storey stone pagoda on a small island in Phewa Lake at Pokhara, dedicated to the goddess Barahi and reachable only by boat; pilgrims come chiefly in Baisakh and Kartik and during Dashain.

name: Siddha Baba Temple
significance: A Shiva shrine on the left bank of the Tinau river at Dobhan, about two kilometres from Butwal, whose precincts also hold images of Ganesh, Nag, Mansa Devi and Bishwokarma; it was registered with the Palpa district administration in 1998.
story: The site is held to be where King Bhartrihari, elder brother of Vikramaditya, performed his penance.

name: Sankata Temple
deity: Sankata (identified by Buddhists with Chanda Maharoshan)
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; founded by King Gunakama Dev
significance: A shrine at Te Bahal in central Kathmandu, credited to King Gunakama Dev, whose deity is petitioned to turn away misfortune and sickness; Hindus worship the goddess as Sankata while Buddhists identify the image with Chanda Maharoshan.
story: A Bajracharya guru named Bandhu Ratna is said to have used tantric power to confine Sankata and a Yogini inside holy pitchers, which were then enshrined in the temple built for them.

name: Palanchok Bhagawati Temple
significance: A pagoda temple on the summit of Palanchok hill in Kavrepalanchok District, some 42 km from Kathmandu, enshrining an eighteen-armed image of Bhagawati revered as a protector against danger and misfortune; it is believed to have been raised during the reign of King Manadeva in the fifth century.
story: She is held to be the elder sister of all the other Bhagawati goddesses of Nepal.

name: Venkatesh Mandir, Kathmandu
significance: A Vaishnava temple at Battisputali in Kathmandu founded in 1898, after the devotee Garudhwaj Ramanuja Dasi and her husband Govindacharya brought an image of Balaji home from the Tirumala Venkateswara temple in India.

name: Dolakha Bhimsen Temple
deity: Bhimsen (Bhindyo), worshipped as god of trade and fortune
significance: A shrine in Bhimeshwar, about 4.5 km east of Charikot in Dolakha District, where Bhimsen is worshipped as the god of trade, commerce and fortune; its founding date is unknown, but an inscription of 1611 records a renovation.
story: Porters cooking rice beside the shrine are said to have realised that a triangular black stone was Bhimsen himself when the rice touching it stayed raw, and the stone bled milk mixed with blood when struck.

name: Dakneshwori Temple
place: Pato Bazaar, Dakneshwori Municipality, Saptari District
significance: A pagoda-style goddess temple at Pato Bazaar in Dakneshwori Municipality of Saptari District, dedicated to Dakneshwori Bhagawati; the municipality takes its name from the shrine, whose present structure was reconstructed in the 1990s.

name: Balkumari Temple, Lalitpur
deity: Balkumari, one of the Ashtamatrika mother goddesses
significance: A pagoda shrine at Tyagal in Lalitpur (Patan) dedicated to Balkumari, counted among the Ashtamatrika mother goddesses; its origin is disputed, with estimates placing it anywhere between the 7th and the 17th century.
story: The original image was stolen twice, and on one occasion the aeroplane it had been loaded onto at Tribhuvan International Airport could not take off, so the idol was recovered and returned to the shrine.

name: Krishna Temple, Rawalpindi
significance: Rawalpindi's principal working Hindu temple, raised in 1897 in the Saddar quarter by two local businessmen, the brothers Kanji Mal and Ujagar Mal Ram Rachpal. Shut during the Partition violence and reopened in 1949, it now serves some 7,000 Hindus of Rawalpindi and Islamabad and has been restored with Punjab government funding since 2018.

name: Kalat Kali Temple
significance: A Kali temple in the Shahi Bazaar of Kalat, ascribed to the pre-Islamic Sewa dynasty, from which the town's older names Kalat-i-Seba and Kalat-i-Nichari derive. Its marble image of the goddess standing on Shiva is reckoned the second largest Kali statue in Asia; looted and broken in 1909-10, it was mended and reconsecrated, and a three-day festival is kept each January.

name: Umarkot Shiv Mandir
significance: A Shiva temple in Umerkot whose lingam is the focus of a three-day Maha Shivaratri fair drawing around 250,000 pilgrims from across Sindh, among the largest religious gatherings in Pakistan. The present building was put up roughly a century ago by a local Muslim, a shrine of Durga stands behind the main temple, and the site is managed by the Pakistan Hindu Panchayat.
story: Local tradition holds that the spot was discovered when a cowherd saw one of his cows pouring her milk over a lingam there.

name: Dargah Pir Ratan Nath Jee
deity: Shiva, at the seat of the Nath saint Sri Ratan Nath
significance: A Shaiva shrine in Jhanda Bazar honouring Sri Ratan Nath of the Nath sampradaya, reopened after some sixty years of closure and, with the Kalibari Mandir, one of the only Hindu temples in daily use in Peshawar. Its chief observance is Maha Shivaratri and it is looked after by the Pakistan Hindu Council; a government-posted guard was shot dead at the premises in January 2016.

name: Kargah Buddha
significance: A standing Buddha some fifty feet tall carved into a cliff in the Kargah nallah about six miles west of Gilgit, dated to the 7th century and brought to notice in 1938-39. A monastery and three stupas excavated nearby in 1931 yielded Sanskrit manuscripts, marking the valley as a centre of Buddhism from roughly the 3rd to the 11th century.
story: Local folklore holds that the figure is a man-eating giantess whom a holy man pinned to the rock face to stop her preying on the villagers.

name: Churrio Jabal Durga Mata Temple
significance: A Durga temple atop the multicoloured granite hill of Churrio near Nagarparkar in Tharparkar district, Sindh. Thousands of pilgrims come through the year and about 200,000 at Shivratri, when devotees immerse cremation ashes in its sacred water; the hill itself is being cut away by government-licensed granite quarrying with dynamite.

name: Trilokpur Mahamaya Bala Sundari Temple
deity: Bhagwati Tripur Mahamaya Bala Sundari (Durga in her child form)
significance: A marble temple about 24 km south-west of Nahan, begun in 1570 and dedicated in 1573 by the ruler of Sirmour using artisans brought from Jaipur, and later renovated by Maharaja Fateh Prakash in 1823 and Maharaja Raghubir Prakash in 1851. It is run by a temple trust headed by the Deputy Commissioner of Sirmaur and draws several million pilgrims a year.
story: A sacred stone is said to have appeared in a salt merchant's sack in 1570 after the goddess came to Ram Dass in a dream, and the temple was raised where she had shown herself.

name: Velleeswarar Temple, Mylapore
significance: A roughly two-acre south-facing Shiva temple with a five-tier vimana on South Mada Street in Mylapore, close to the Kapaleeswarar Temple. It is counted among the seven Sapta Sthana Shiva temples of Mylapore and holds shrines to Ganesha, Kamakshi, the seven mother goddesses, Durga, Kartikeya, Bhairava and the Navagrahas.
story: Shukra, blinded by a blade of darbha grass from Vamana, is said to have meditated on Shiva at this spot and recovered his sight, which is why devotees pray here for eyesight.

name: Sheetala Chaukiya Dham
significance: A goddess temple near Jaunpur that takes the name Chaukiya from the raised platform on which the deity was first installed; its founding is credited to the Ahir ruler Heerchand Yadav, while some historians attribute it to the Bhars. It is among the busiest shrines of the district and has been the subject of a state tourism modernisation project.
story: Durga is said to have taken birth as Katyayani and then as Shitala Devi, carrying the implements of healing, to undo the fevers and diseases spread by the demon Jvarasura.

name: Thamaramkulangara Sree Dharma Sastha Temple
significance: A Dharma Sastha temple built in the Kerala architectural tradition at Tripunithura, on the eastern edge of Kochi. Its founding date is not recorded, and the temple appears in the 2019 survey Pilgrimage to Temple Heritage.

name: Binsar Mahadev Temple
significance: A rock temple in the Chauthan region of Pauri Garhwal, dated to the 9th or 10th century and held to have been raised by Maharaja Prithu in memory of his father Bindu. The original structure with its rock-cut images was pulled down in October 2017 to make way for a new building; an annual fair is still held here on Vaikuntha Chaturdashi.
story: Villagers hold that the Pandavas built the temple in a single night during their exile, or else that the divine architect Vishwakarma raised it.

name: Shri Kali Devi Temple, Patiala
significance: A Kali temple opposite the Baradari Gardens in Patiala, begun in 1936 and completed in 1938 by Maharaja Bhupinder Singh, who had the six-foot images of Maa Kali and the Paawan Jyot brought from Bengal. The goddess is kept as a kul devi by many families and the shrine draws large crowds through the Navratras.

name: Somanatha Pashana Lingeswarar Temple, Timiri
significance: A modern Shiva temple in the village of Timiri in Vellore district, completed in 1985. It takes its name from its presiding lingam, Somanatha Pashana Lingeswarar.

name: Bhutanatha Group of Temples, Badami
style: Dravida and Early Chalukya; Nagara phamsana
significance: Two clusters of Shiva temples on the east bank of Agastya lake at Badami: the main Bhutanatha group of the 7th-8th centuries under the Badami Chalukyas, whose principal shrine has a gudha-mandapa on four pillars beneath a three-storeyed superstructure, and the Mallikarjuna group of the 11th-12th centuries built under the Kalyani Chalukyas. A late 9th-century inscription naming Sridharbuteswara shows the site was still in use between the two building phases, and a smaller northern shrine is thought to have been Vaishnava before it passed to Lingayat worship.

name: Buddha of Kyaikhtiyo
significance: A seated Buddha of 77.9 metres at Kyaikto, raised over a seventeen-storey pagoda whose height was fixed to echo the Buddhist year 2556. It was opened in April 2019 to coincide with the Buddha's Birthday festival and feeds pilgrims free of charge.

name: Kailashnath Mahadev Statue
significance: A 44-metre Shiva in steel, concrete, zinc and copper standing above the Araniko Highway at Sanga, funded by Kamal Jain and the Hilltake group. Built from 2003 and opened on 21 June 2011, it is described as the tallest Shiva statue in the world.

name: Bindhyabasini Temple
significance: The principal Shakta temple of Pokhara, established around the 1760s and given a royally appointed priest by King Girvan Yuddha Bikram Shah in 1815. Its hilltop compound also holds shrines to Saraswati, Shiva, Hanuman and Ganesha.
story: The goddess is held to be Yogamaya of the Vindhya hills in India, brought to Pokhara by royal order after a king's pilgrimage vision.

name: Ichangu Narayan Temple
significance: One of the four great Narayan shrines of the Kathmandu valley, ascribed to the Licchavi king Haridutta in the 5th century and rebuilt in the 18th. Its courtyard is set with images of Garuda and Mahalaxmi, and its idols have been stolen and recovered more than once.

name: Adinath Lokeshwar
significance: A hilltop shrine at Chobhar to one of the four Lokeshwars of the Kathmandu valley, revered by Buddhists and Hindus alike; built in the 15th century and rebuilt in 1640. Visitors know it for the pots, pans and other household vessels nailed across its walls as offerings.
story: The image is said to have been fished out of the river by Suval Acharya and installed on Kacchapala hill, where an annual bathing rite was founded for it.

name: Budhanilkantha Temple
style: Open-air shrine around a single black basalt image
significance: An open-air shrine north of Kathmandu whose five-metre black basalt Vishnu lies on a coiled serpent in a 13-metre recessed pool. The image is over 1,400 years old, is venerated by Buddhists as well as Hindus, and is protected under Nepal's ancient monuments act.
story: The stone is said to have been struck by a farmer's plough and unearthed by chance; King Pratap Malla's vision that a monarch who looked on it would die early has kept Nepal's kings away ever since.

name: Ambikeshwori Temple
significance: A Shakta temple on the bank of the Katuwa Khola a short way north of Ghorahi, counted among the Shaktipeethas and known locally as Maiko Than, the Mother's Place. Shivaratri, Teej, Dashain and Kalratri are its principal festivals.
story: The Swasthani Purana holds that this Shaktipeetha arose where the right ear of Sati fell to earth.

name: Arjundhara Dham
deity: Arjuna, with shrines to Shiva and Hanuman
significance: A pilgrimage complex 6 km north of Birtamode in Jhapa, built around a spring associated with the Mahabharata hero Arjuna. A gurukul for Brahmin students and a cow farm are maintained in its grounds.
story: During the Pandavas' exile Arjuna is said to have loosed an arrow into the ground here, and water burst from the spot.

name: Lava Temple, Lahore Fort
significance: A small Hindu shrine standing inside the walls of Lahore Fort, dating to the Sikh period and dedicated to Lava. It sits on Pakistani government property and is looked after by the Pakistan Hindu Council.
story: Lahore is said to take its name from Lava, son of Rama and Sita, who founded it as Lavapuri while his twin brother Kusha founded Kasur.

name: Mansehra Shiva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple about 15 km from Mansehra, rebuilt in the 1830s by the Raja of Jammu around a lingam reported to be some two thousand years old. Sealed from 1948, it became accessible again in 1998 and has been partially restored by Pakistani Hindus, who gather here for Shivaratri.

name: Valmiki Mandir, Lahore
significance: A temple to the sage Valmiki on Bhim Street in the Neela Gumbad quarter of Anarkali, held locally to be about twelve centuries old. With the Krishna Temple it is one of only two functioning Hindu temples left in Lahore; courts returned it from private occupants to public custodianship and it was restored in 2022 under the Pakistan Hindu Council and the Evacuee Trust Property Board.

name: Kalibari Mandir, Peshawar
significance: One of the few surviving Hindu temples in Peshawar, in the Cantonment, and among the very few in daily use — pilgrims come to it from across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Durga Puja is its principal festival. Renovation from 2017 added a langar hall and repaired the structure; the Pakistan Hindu Council administers it.

name: Shivala Teja Singh Temple
significance: A shivala in Sialkot raised by Sardar Teja Singh, sealed at Partition in 1947 and partly demolished by vandals in 1992. After 72 years shut it was reopened in 2019, renovated by the Pakistani government and handed to the Pakistan Hindu Council.

name: Ramapir Temple, Tando Allahyar
significance: A temple to Ramdev Pir founded in the British period, whose annual Ramapir Mela is reckoned the second-largest Hindu pilgrimage in Pakistan.
story: A local Hindu vowed to hold a Rama Pir mela if he were granted a child; when the wish was answered he carried an earthen lamp 460 km from the original shrine at Ramdevra in Rajasthan and built this temple around it.

name: Chandragup
deity: Shiva, worshipped here as Baba Chandrakup
significance: A mud volcano in Hingol National Park venerated by Hindus as an embodiment of Shiva under the name Baba Chandrakup, and a station of the four-day Hinglaj Yatra held each April alongside the nearby Hinglaj Mata Temple.
story: Pilgrims hold that the Hinglaj Mata temple may be entered only after homage has first been paid to Baba Chandrakup.

name: Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, Karachi
significance: The only surviving Swaminarayan temple in Pakistan, spread over more than 32,000 square yards on M. A. Jinnah Road in central Karachi; Gujarati merchants built a Swaminarayan shrine here in the 1890s, and the walled complex also shelters a gurdwara used by the city's Sikhs.

name: Shree Ratneshwar Mahadev Temple, Karachi
significance: A historic underground Shiva temple at Clifton in Karachi, reached by two staircases near the Jehangir Kothari Parade and descending six levels to a marble courtyard floor and a freshwater spring inside the cave. Its Shivratri observance draws some 25,000 pilgrims.

name: Samadhi of Ranjit Singh
deity: Funerary urns of Maharaja Ranjit Singh
patron: Kharak Singh; completed by Duleep Singh
style: Sikh with Hindu and Islamic elements
significance: A 19th-century Sikh shrine in Lahore holding the funerary urns of Maharaja Ranjit Singh along with the ashes of four Hindu queens who became sati and seven concubines. Begun by his son Kharak Singh in August 1839 and finished by his youngest son Duleep Singh in 1848, it was the last great state-funded building of independent Punjab before the British annexation of 1849; gilded domes and frescoes of the Sikh gurus and scenes from the Hindu epics cover it.

name: Jal Binayak Temple
significance: The foremost Ganesh shrine of the Chobhar area south of Kathmandu, first raised in Nepal Sambat 723 by the Malla king Shiva Singh; Sri Nivas Malla of Patan added its finial in 789 NS and Rajya Prakash Malla of Kathmandu rebuilt the present pagoda in 871 NS.

name: Daunne Devi Temple
significance: A wayside shrine on the Daunne pass at Dumkibas in Bardaghat, Nawalparasi District, holding both a Durga shrine and a Shivalaya; its founding is attributed to Jung Bahadur Rana, while the present building dates from 2055 BS and has been looked after by the local user committee since 2049 BS.
story: The Daunne hill was known in ancient times as Trikut Parbat and is held to have been a place of meditation for the sage Valmiki and for Mayadevi, the mother of the Buddha.

name: Balkumari Temple, Thimi
significance: A seventeenth-century pagoda at Thimi in Bhaktapur District dedicated to the goddess Balkumari and counted among the four Kumari temples of the Kathmandu Valley; a Bhairab shrine stands in the same courtyard, and the Sindoor Jatra is celebrated here at Nepali New Year.
story: A merchant of Thimi is said to have won a princess of Lubhu who would come with him only if the goddess Balkumari came too, and so the goddess moved from Lubhu to Thimi.

name: Dungeshwor Temple
place: Naule Katuwal, Dullu Municipality, Dailekh District
significance: A pagoda-style Shiva temple at Naule Katuwal in Dullu Municipality of Dailekh District, worshipped as Sidheshwor Mahadev and sharing its precinct with shrines to Kalika Bhagwati, Ganesh, Kalsaini Bhairab and Batuk Bhairab; the article records that the saint Sagar Giri organised its worship and that its ritual regalia were restored in 1960 BS.

name: Chandannath Temple
place: Khalanga Bazar, Chandannath Municipality, Jumla District
significance: The chief temple of Jumla, standing above Khalanga Bazar in Chandannath Municipality and dedicated to Dattatreya; it was raised under the Kalyal dynasty, of whose rule and of whose connection with Chandannath few written records survive.
story: Chandannath Baba is said to have carried an image of Dattatreya here from Kashmir, and a cow that gave up her milk of her own accord on the spot is said to have revealed the sacred ground on which the temple was then built.

name: Rajarshi Janak Mandir
significance: A temple at Janak Chowk in Janakpur, Dhanusha District, dedicated to Rajarshi Janak, the Vedic king of Videha after whom the city is named; it stands in the Mithila region among other shrines tied to the Ramayana.

name: Bhairabsthan Temple
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; founded by King Mukunda Sen
significance: A hilltop Bhairab temple about 9 km northwest of Tansen in Palpa District, at roughly 1,470 m, established by King Mukunda Sen of the Sena dynasty during the period when Palpa was his capital.
story: Mukunda Sen is said to have carried off an image of Bhairav from the Matsyendranath temple during his attack on Kathmandu and to have installed it here in Palpa.

name: Satyawati Temple
significance: A goddess shrine beside a hill lake at Satyawati in Palpa District, about 30 km south of Tansen and 19 km north of Butwal, revered by the Magar community as their own deity and reached on a foot trail from the Jhumsa bridge on the Siddhartha Highway.
story: On the night of the festival the goddess is said to grant the wishes of pilgrims who walk three times round the lake and call their wish aloud.

name: Gokarneshwor Mahadev Temple
place: Gokarna, northeast of Bodhnath, Kathmandu District
significance: A Shiva temple near Gokarna village, northeast of Bodhnath in the Kathmandu Valley, whose sanctum houses a lingam of considerable importance in the valley's Shaiva worship.

name: Kasthamandap
significance: A great wooden public pavilion beside Kathmandu Durbar Square, later given an inner shrine to the yogi Gorakshanath; excavation with radiocarbon and OSL dating placed its oldest fabric in the Licchavi era of the 7th century. It collapsed in the 2015 earthquake and has since been rebuilt.

name: Pumdikot Shiva Statue
significance: A 51-foot Shiva on a white stupa base, 108 feet in all, set on a ridge above Pokhara at 1,500 m and ringed by 108 Shiva lingas. Completed in late 2021, it is the second tallest Shiva statue in Nepal.

name: Dantakali Temple
significance: A hill shrine above Bijayapur in Dharan, kept as a Shakta seat and thronged at Navaratri and Dashain. Its name joins danta, tooth, to the goddess Kali.
story: The temple is held to mark the place where the teeth of the goddess Sati came to rest.

name: Chandeshwori Temple
significance: A 17th-century pagoda temple on the Punyamata river a kilometre from Banepa, carrying carved struts and a vast painted Bhairava said to be the largest wall painting in the Nepal Mandala. Its outer wall bears a mural of the goddess killing the demon Chanda.
story: The goddess is said to have destroyed the demon Chanda, whom Shiva's boon had made invulnerable to all but a woman, after he felled the tree she hid in; a lingam grew from his body and stands in a small shrine nearby.

name: Andhimul Temple
significance: A pagoda temple at Satrasay Phant in Tanahu District built in 2035 BS, its Shivalinga installed in 2054 BS. It draws pilgrims from Tanahun, Kaski, Gorkha and Lamjung and closes through the month of Shrawan and on new-moon days.
story: The name is explained by a girl who came searching for water and found a spring here, from the local words aan, thirst, and dhi, water.

name: Badimalika Temple
significance: A Shakta pitha at about 4,200 m in Bajura District, served by priests drawn from both Kalikot and Bajura and reached by pilgrims chiefly at Malika Chaturdashi and Ganga Dussehra.
story: The shrine is said to stand where the left shoulder of Sati fell on the Mallagiri mountain, and King Dipraj Chhatyal is remembered as having raised a temple to Malika Devi after a vision instructed him to.

name: Bhadrakali Temple, Kathmandu
builtDisplay: 1817; image ascribed to the Licchavi kings
significance: One of the best known Shakta pithas of Nepal, standing beside Tundikhel opposite Singha Durbar and formerly called Mudule Thumpko. The temple dates to 1817 and its black stone image is credited to the Licchavi kings; Navaratri, Dashain and Paahacharey are its great festivals.
story: A farmer is said to have left his bread at the edge of the field he was ploughing here and found it turned to gold, whence the temple's other name, Lumadhi, golden bread.

name: Karya Binayak Temple
significance: One of the four celebrated Vinayaka shrines of the Kathmandu valley, dedicated in 1661 near Bungamati under the local leader Purna Singh at the start of Shri Niwas Malla's reign. Worship began at a natural stone shaped like Ganesha, now sheathed in silver, and devotees come before starting new undertakings.

name: Bhairabi Temple, Nuwakot
dynasty: Attributed variously to Jagat Jaya Malla and the reign of Prithvi Narayan Shah
significance: Also called Gandaki Bhairavi for the river below, this pagoda stands 200 m south of the Nuwakot palace; Bahadur Shah roofed it in copper in 1793 with a plate marking Nepal's victory in the first Sino-Nepalese war, and arms from that war were kept there. Badly damaged in the 2015 earthquake, it was restored by August 2020.

name: Rana Ujeshwori Bhagwati Temple
builtDisplay: 1872 BS (c. 1815); rebuilt after the 1990 BS earthquake
significance: Raised at Tansen Durbar Square by Ujir Singh Thapa in 1872 BS to mark the Nepali army's victory in the Anglo-Nepalese war, and rebuilt by Pratap Shamsher Jung Bahadur Rana after the 1990 BS earthquake. Its Bhagwati Jatra, also called Sindoor Jatra, has been held the day after Krishna Janmashtami since 1877 BS.

name: Shashwat Dham
significance: A twelve-acre Shiva complex on the East-West Highway at Devchuli built by the CG Group and inaugurated by President Bidya Devi Bhandari on 7 March 2017. Besides the Ekambareshwor temple it holds a Vedic karmakanda gurukul, a yoga and meditation centre and a museum, and its pond is filled with water gathered from Badrinath, Kedarnath, Muktinath and Pashupatinath.

name: Maula Kalika Temple
significance: A temple of the goddess Kalika above Gaindakot town in Nawalpur District of Gandaki Province, one of the better-known Shakta shrines of central Nepal.

name: Swargadwari
significance: A hill pilgrimage centre in Pyuthan District dedicated to Narayana and Shiva, established in 1895 (Vaisakha Purnima 1952 BS) by Guru Maharaj Narayana Gautama Khatri, known as Swami Hamsananda, who spent most of his life on the ridge herding and milking thousands of cows; the site is closely bound to the veneration of the cow in Hinduism.

name: Ganeshthan Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple in ward 11 of Bharatpur in Chitwan District whose original shrine is placed in the fifteenth century and credited to Muni Makunda, king of Palpa; the present building went up in 1952 during the reign of King Mahendra, and worshippers gather chiefly on Tuesdays.

name: Kumbheshwar Temple
significance: A five-storey free-standing pagoda dedicated to Shiva, standing about 200 m north of Patan Durbar Square in Lalitpur and built around 1392 by King Jayasthiti Malla.
story: The ponds within the temple courtyard are believed to be fed by a spring rising from Gosainkunda, some 43 km north of Kathmandu.

name: Naradevi Temple
deity: Sweta Kali, called Nyata Ajima by Newars
significance: A shrine in central Kathmandu dedicated to Sweta Kali, known among Newars as Nyata Ajima, and believed to have been founded in the ninth century by Gunakamadeva, the founder of the city; its three-tiered roof includes a gilded storey carried on carved struts.
story: A king of Patan who lost his way while hunting and was chased by a wild elephant is said to have hidden in a tree at this spot, where the goddess Swetakali appeared and gave him back his life, upon which he founded the temple.

name: Bhutandevi Mandir
significance: A pagoda temple in Hetauda, Makwanpur District, dedicated to Bhutandevi, identified with Hidimbi, a wife of Bhima and the mother of Ghatotkacha.
story: Hidimba is held to be another manifestation of Durga, and the name of Hetauda itself is believed to come from the goddess.

name: Bhadrakali Temple, Pokhara
place: Kundahar, east of Pokhara, Kaski District
significance: A hilltop pagoda at Kundahar east of Pokhara in Kaski District, founded in 1817 and dedicated to Bhadrakali as goddess of power and strength; it stands at about 2,930 feet over some 135 ropanies and is reached by stairways of 292 steps from the east and 265 from the south.
story: The goddess is said to have told a priest to dig into the hill, where her image was uncovered and thereafter worshipped as Bhadrakali.

name: Kapileshwar Temple, Janakpur
significance: One of the Shiva shrines that mark the corners of Janakpur in Dhanusha District, worshipped as Kapileshwar Mahadev; raised originally in the Simrangad style, it was rebuilt after the earthquake of 1934.
story: King Janak is said to have built Shiva temples at the four corners of his capital Janakpur in the Treta Yuga, and the sage Kapil to have kept his ashram at this one, which is how it got its name.

name: Bishnupaduka
significance: A shikhara shrine at Dharan in Sunsari District built over a rock bearing two footprints venerated as those of Vishnu.
story: Local people are said to have come upon a rock marked with two clear footprints, which are believed to be Vishnu's own.

name: Manakamana Temple, Sankhuwasabha
significance: A pagoda temple of Manakamana Devi about 5 km north of Tumlingtar airport in Sankhuwasabha District, eastern Nepal, distinct from the better-known Manakamana shrine in Gorkha.
story: A farmer ploughing his field is said to have struck a stone that oozed milk and blood, which the devotee Lakhan Thapa read as the return of a seventeenth-century queen of Gorkha who had committed sati after her husband's death.

name: Sheshnarayan Temple
significance: A pagoda temple of Vishnu in his Sheshnarayan form near Pharping in the southern Kathmandu Valley, believed to have been raised in the reign of the Licchavi king Vishnugupta; it is counted among the four Narayana temples of the valley.
story: The four Narayana temples are said to stand on hilltops at the cardinal points to guard the Kathmandu Valley.

name: Kalika Bhagawati Temple
significance: A pagoda temple southeast of Baglung town on the southern bank of the Kali Gandaki in Gandaki Province, dedicated to Kalika, one of the fiercest forms of Shakti.
story: A king is said to have received the goddess's image as dowry, and when the wedding party halted overnight in a forest and no one could lift the idol the next morning, he built the temple on that spot.

name: Rajdevi Temple, Gaur
significance: A Hindu temple at Gaur in Rautahat District of Madhesh Province whose presiding deity is the goddess Rajdevi; the surrounding municipality takes its name from the shrine.

name: Kulpani Mandir
place: Badahara, Gadhawa Rural Municipality, Dang District
significance: A pagoda-style Shiva temple at Badahara in ward 1 of Gadhawa Rural Municipality, Dang District, Lumbini Province.

name: Chintang Devi Temple
significance: A goddess temple in Dhankuta District dedicated to Chintang Devi, also called Jalpadevi, and held in reverence in both Hindu and Kirati worship.
story: The shrine takes its name from Chintang, one of the seven daughters of Budhahang.

name: Bhaleshwor Mahadev Temple
significance: A pagoda temple of Shiva on the summit of Chandragiri hill on the southwestern rim of the Kathmandu Valley in Bagmati Province.
story: The shrine is said to mark the place where the forehead of Sati Devi fell as Shiva carried her lifeless body across the world after her death at her father's sacrifice.

name: Bahal Temple
significance: Three red-brick Vajrayana Buddhist sanctuaries standing about 500 m apart on the Padang Lawas plain, and the only temples of that scattered complex to have been fully restored. Archaeologists place their construction between the 11th and 13th centuries and link them to the Pannai kingdom, a trading polity inside the Srivijayan sphere.

name: Maha Vihara Maitreya
significance: A modern Mahayana complex covering 4.5 hectares in the Cemara Asri estate at Medan, built from 1991 by the Indonesian Buddhist association and inaugurated in 2008. Its three worship halls seat between 1,500 and 2,500 people each, and it is described as the largest modern Buddhist temple in Indonesia.

name: Banyunibo Temple
significance: A single-cella Buddhist candi in the valley south of the Ratu Boko plateau, unusual among surviving Central Javanese Buddhist temples for a curved roof crowned by one solitary stupa. Discovered collapsed in 1940 and reconstructed by 1978, it carries Kala-Makara ornament, Bodhisattva and Tara figures in its niches, and reliefs of Hariti and Vaisravana.

name: Jabung Temple
deity: Buddhist mortuary shrine of Bhre Gundal of Majapahit
style: Red-brick East Javanese candi, octagonal body with stupa roof
significance: A tall red-brick Majapahit sanctuary dated by a carved doorframe block to 1276 Saka, or 1354 CE. The Pararaton records it as the mortuary temple of the royal Bhre Gundal, and the Nagarakretagama names it Bajrajinaparamitapura, visited by King Hayam Wuruk on his tour of East Java in 1359.

name: Jawi Temple
style: East Javanese candi with cube-and-stupa pinnacle
significance: A slender 24.5 m temple raised as the mortuary shrine of Kertanegara, the last king of Singhasari, and built to express the Shiva-Buddha synthesis he professed: a Shaivite cella holding a yoni, with Durga, Ganesha, Nandi and Brahma images, set beneath a pinnacle combining a cube with a Buddhist stupa.
story: When lightning struck the monument in 1331 the image of the Buddha Akshobhya is said to have vanished from it, a disappearance read as a manifestation of shunyata, emptiness.

name: Merak Temple
significance: A Shaivite temple in Klaten with a main shrine and three ancillary perwara chapels, assigned to the Mataram kingdom of the 9th or 10th century on the evidence of its yoni and its Ganesha and Durga Mahishasuramardini images. Reconstruction of the 1,480 sq m compound was completed in 2011, and its stairway carries unusual makara-naga chimeras.

name: Bubrah Temple
deity: Buddha (guardian shrine of the southern direction in the Manjusrigrha mandala)
style: Buddhist candi within a mandala plan
significance: A 9th-century Buddhist candi between Sewu and Prambanan that served as the southern direction-guardian shrine of the great Manjusrigrha mandala centred on Sewu. Its Javanese name means broken or disorderly, earned by centuries in ruins; a reconstruction costing 11 billion rupiah ran from 2011 and was inaugurated in December 2017.

name: Sojiwan Temple
significance: A Mahayana Buddhist temple south of Prambanan, dated by the Rukam inscription to between 842 and 850 and understood as a dedication to Queen Pramodhawardhani, whose name the site carries. Its main shrine rises 27 m and its base is carved with bas-reliefs illustrating Pancatantra and Jataka fables; reconstruction, delayed by the 2006 earthquake, finished in December 2011.

name: Gunung Wukir Temple (Canggal)
significance: The earliest structure attributed to the ancient Mataram kingdom, a Shaivite compound of one main shrine and three perwara with a Nandi and a yoni pedestal. The Canggal inscription found here in 1879 records King Sanjaya ordering a lingam raised in 654 Saka, 732 CE, which fixes both the temple and the kingdom's beginning.

name: Kimpulan Temple
significance: A small, plainly decorated Shaivite shrine near Yogyakarta holding a lingam-yoni with Ganesha and Nandi images, its chambers probably once roofed in wood in the manner of Balinese meru. It came to light by accident on 11 December 2009 during excavation for a university library, buried some five metres deep under Merapi ash like Sambisari, Morangan and Kedulan.

name: Puneshwar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple that stood on the bank of the Mutha river and from which the city of Pune takes its name; it was pulled down in the late 13th century and a dargah rose over the site, where temple artefacts resurfaced after a river wall collapsed in 2006.

name: Punjai Siva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the Kaveri delta village of Punjai, about 6 km from Semponnarkoil, whose best-known possession is a bronze Nataraja cast around 1000 CE in the time of Rajendra Chola.

name: Pisharikavu Temple
significance: A Bhadrakali shrine built in the traditional Kerala manner at Kollam near Koyilandy, counted among the thirteen principal Shakteya temples of Kerala.

name: Perunna Subrahmanya Swami Temple
significance: A Kartikeya temple at Perunna in Changanassery, notable as the first temple in Kerala opened to Hindus of every caste, ahead of the state's own proclamation; Gandhi worshipped here during his first visit to Kerala.
story: The deity is said to stand in a furious mood immediately after slaying the asura Tarakasura, his vel pointing downward.

name: Prasanna Venkatachalapathi Temple, Thuraiyur
significance: A hilltop Vishnu temple on Perumalmalai about 3 km from Thuraiyur; it is traditionally held to have been founded by descendants of the early Chola king Karikala, who are themselves venerated at the shrine.

name: Pisharnath Mahadev Mandir
significance: The oldest temple in the hill station of Matheran, standing on the bank of Charlotte Lake, where Pisharnath is worshipped as the village deity in a swayambhu lingam of unusual L shape.

name: Punnainallur Mariamman Temple
significance: A Mariamman temple some 5 km east of Thanjavur whose small original shrine was raised in the reign of Tulaja and greatly enlarged by Serfoji II, who added the mahamandapa, narthana mandapa, gopura and second inner prakara; the Thanjavur court endowed it richly and connected it to the palace by an underground passage.
story: Legend holds that the sage Sadashiva Brahmendra formed the goddess's image from an anthill, and that the king founded the shrine after Mariamman appeared to him in a dream among the punnai trees that name the village.

name: Lakhesvara Siva Temple
significance: A 13th-century Shiva shrine on a saptaratha rekha-deula plan behind the Lingaraja market in Bhubaneswar's old town, a short distance northeast of the Lingaraja temple, enshrining a lingam set in a circular yonipitha; local tradition ascribes it to the Ganga rulers.

name: Sree Perunthatta Siva Temple
significance: A Kerala-style Shiva temple at Guruvayur with a double-storeyed tile-roofed sanctum; it lay under the Zamorin of Calicut and was wrecked during Tipu Sultan's 18th-century campaign, and excavation at the site has recovered two cannons from the defence mounted by the Zamorin's forces.
story: Folklore holds that the sage Parashurama installed the Shiva idol here in the Treta Yuga.

name: Maa Baulasuni Temple
significance: A Shakta shrine in the village of Nilok, about 27 km from Bhadrak town, where the goddess is venerated as a stone bearing a painted red face. The present temple dates from 1969 and its yagya mandap from 2000; the Makar Mela at Makar Sankranti is its principal gathering.
story: A Brahmin visitor is said to have seen children playing with a round stone under a tamarind tree, and after he and a villager both dreamt that Baulasuni dwelt there in the stone, the village began worshipping her as its protector.

name: Nandeeswarar Temple
deity: Shiva as Nandeeswarar, worshipped in the form of Nandi; goddess Aavudai Nayagi
builtDisplay: c. 11th c. (described as about 950 years old)
significance: A Shiva temple at Adambakkam in Chennai, near St Thomas Mount station, unusual in that the presiding form is Nandi standing before the sage Bringi rather than a linga. The article gives its age as roughly 950 years; a local attribution to a Chola patron is unverified.
story: Shiva is said to have appeared here to the sage Bringi in the form of Nandi, and the adjoining hill, once called Bringi Malai, came to be known as Parangi Malai.

name: Joy Dol (Keshavnarayan Vishnu Dol)
significance: A brick-and-stone Vishnu temple raised in 1698 by the Ahom king Rudra Singha on the bank of the Joysagar tank in memory of his mother Joymoti. Its walls carry carvings of celestial figures and of everyday Ahom life, and it stands with the Sivadol, Devi Ghar and Ghanashyam House as part of the Joysagar group.

name: Draupati Amman Temples, Kumbakonam
significance: A set of neighbourhood shrines to Draupati Amman spread across Kumbakonam, on the streets flanking the Chakrapani and Sarangapani temples and near the bus stand. Several also hold shrines to Vinayaka, Kali and Mariamman and sculpted heads of Aravan; their recorded consecrations fall between 2001 and 2016.

name: Parvati Temple, Bhubaneswar
significance: A small grey-sandstone shrine to Parvati in the old town of Bhubaneswar, near the Lingaraja temple, built in dry masonry and dated by its materials to the 14th century. Its pidha deul with a porch carries Dravidian decorative elements alongside the local Kalinga idiom.

name: Sree Narayanapuram Thrikkayil Temple
deity: Vishnu, in the four-armed form of Krishna
significance: One of the older temples of Perissery in Alappuzha district, where Vishnu is worshipped as a four-armed Krishna bearing conch, discus, mace and lotus and adorned with tulsi garlands. Its main observance is the twelve-lamp festival.

name: Prasanna Venkateswara Temple, Appalayagunta
significance: A Venkateswara temple near Tirupati completed in 1232 under Venkata Perumalaraju Brahmadeva of Karvetinagaram, where the deity's right hand is held in abhaya rather than the pose usual at Venkateswara shrines. It has been administered by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams since 1988.

name: Dibbesvara Temple
significance: An early-medieval Shiva temple at Saripalli in Vizianagaram district, protected by the Archaeological Survey of India as a monument of national importance. Its square sanctum and tiered curvilinear shikhara follow the Kalinga rekha deul type, evidence of building contact between coastal Andhra and Odisha.

name: Bhimashankar Jyotirlinga (Dakinyam), Bhimpur
significance: A Shiva shrine at Bhimpur village on the Mahendratanaya river in the western Mahendragiri hills of Rayagada district, which came to notice when the site was excavated in 1974. The linga stands within a quadrangular Shakti and carries a sculpted sacred thread.
story: Citing the Linga Purana, local tradition holds this to be the jyotirlinga of the Dakini country, one of the twelve.

name: Chemmanthatta Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Chemmanthatta in Thrissur district counted among the 108 Shiva shrines of Kerala, with a gopuram rising about 33 m. The Archaeological Survey of India and the Kerala Ooralma Devaswom share responsibility for it.
story: Local tradition credits the sage Parashurama with installing the temple's idol.

name: Karppillikkavu Sree Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Manjapra in Ernakulam district where the deity is worshipped in his hunter form, Kirathamoorthy or Vettakkaran, and which is reckoned among the 108 major Shiva shrines. Its main festival runs eight days in the Malayalam month of Makaram.
story: The shrine is said to have first held an image of Devi, and Kartavirya Arjuna, finding her presence absent when he came for darshan, is held to have consecrated Shiva in her place.

name: Veerabhadreswarar Temple, Kumbakonam
deity: Shiva as Agora Veerabhadra, with the goddess Bhadrakali
significance: A west-facing Shiva temple in Kumbakonam whose presiding form is the fierce Agora Veerabhadra, paired with Bhadrakali. The Tamil poet Ottakoothar is said to have composed his Thakka Yaga Barani here.

name: Adikesava Perumal Temple, Mylapore
deity: Adi Kesava Perumal (Vishnu), with Mayuravalli Thayar
significance: A Vishnu temple of about 1.5 acres in Mylapore, Chennai, counted among the 108 Abhimana Kshetrams of the Vaishnava tradition and revered as the birthplace of the Alvar poet-saint Peyalvar. It is administered by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments board, and its very old temple tank was desilted for the first time in 2016.
story: Lakshmi is said to have come to the hermitage of sage Bhrigu after the churning of the ocean of milk and to have been accepted as his daughter Bhargavi, whom the presiding deity then married; the saint Peyalvar is held to have been found in the temple's Manikairavam well.

name: Chokkeeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Kanchipuram raised by the Cholas in the 9th century CE and also known as the Kousikeswarar temple. It is one of the protected monuments of Tamil Nadu under the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Aazhimala Shiva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on a cliff beside the Arabian Sea near Vizhinjam in southern Kerala, built in a style close to that of Tamil Nadu with a sculpted gopuram. It is known above all for an 18-metre Gangadhareshwara figure carved by the local artist P. S. Devadathan between 2014 and 2020, the tallest Shiva sculpture in Kerala.

name: Sitaleshwar Temple
significance: A 7th-century Shiva shrine in the Chandrabhaga temple group at Jhalrapatan, to which a pillared hall was added in the 10th century; its columns were praised by James Fergusson, who surveyed the ruins in the 19th century. The original shikhara has collapsed and the rebuilt sanctum now carries a flat roof with a small dome; it is a Monument of National Importance (N-RJ-71).

name: Boro Maa Kali Temple, Naihati
significance: A Kali shrine at Naihati begun in 1923 by Bhavesh Chakraborty, a jute-mill worker and social worker, famous for the twenty-two-foot image raised each year at Kali Puja and dressed in some twelve kilograms of gold and two hundred of silver. A permanent temple with a stone image was inaugurated in 2023, and the immersion procession draws crowds large enough to need over a thousand police.
story: Chakraborty is said to have been told by Kali in a dream to shape her as a giant twenty-two-foot image like those he had seen at Nabadwip.

name: Tholung Monastery
deity: Nyingma lineage; relics of Lama Lhatsun Chenpo
significance: A remote Nyingma monastery at about 8,000 feet in Upper Dzongu, inside the buffer zone of Khangchendzonga National Park, first raised under Chogyal Phuntsog Namgyal II and built in its present form in 1789 by Pema Dechhen Gyatso, with the standing structure reconstructed in 1980. It safeguards manuscripts and relics carried here during the Gorkha invasions, shown to the public only once every three years at the Kamsil ceremony in April.
story: The site is held to have been revealed as sacred ground in 1760 by the fourth Lhatsun, Kunzang Jigmed Gyatso.

name: Arunachalesvarar Temple, Ammapettai
significance: A Shiva temple at Ammapettai in Papanasam taluk, about 21 km east of Thanjavur, laid out with a prakara, mahamandapa and kosta niches holding several subsidiary shrines. Its most recent consecration, the Kumbhabhishekam, was performed on 15 September 2005.

name: Shikari Devi Temple
deity: Durga as Shikari Devi (goddess of the hunt)
significance: A roofless stone shrine to Durga on Shikari peak, at 3,332 m the highest point in Mandi district and the centre of the Shikari Devi Sanctuary above the Janjheli and Karsog valleys. Long resorted to by local hunters seeking a good chase, it draws its largest crowds at Navratri.
story: The Pandavas, exiled and hunting here, are said to have chased a deer that vanished into the forest, understood the animal to have been the goddess guiding them, and founded the shrine where they then meditated.

name: Karuvalarcheri Agastheeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the Thanjavur delta whose lingam is worshipped as Agastheeswarar, with the goddess Akilandesvari enshrined alongside. It draws childless couples who come to seek the blessing of children.
story: The goddess here is held to be self-manifested and is invoked as Karu Valarkkum Nayaki, the one who nurtures the growth of the unborn child.

name: Basuki Nath Mahadev Mandir
significance: A Shiva temple near the Indo-Nepal border in Madhubani district, founded by a local Maithil Brahmin family and reckoned to be more than a century and a half old. It is a regional pilgrimage point, busiest during Sawan jalabhisheka and Mahashivratri.

name: Jagannath Temple, Angul (Saila Srikhetra)
significance: Known as Saila Srikhetra, this Angul shrine houses the Jagannath triad and reproduces the ritual calendar of the great temple at Puri. Its Ratha Yatra and Snana Yatra make it a focal pilgrimage site for the surrounding district.

name: Pennadam Meikandar Temple
significance: An unusual shrine dedicated not to a god but to Meykandar, the Shaiva Siddhanta philosopher, and managed by the Thiruvaduthurai Adheenam. It was renovated and reconsecrated in June 2014.
story: The spot at Achuthakalappalarmedu in Pennadam is held to be the place where Meykandar was born.

name: Bhimambika Temple, Itagi
significance: A temple and mutt at Itagi in north Karnataka honouring Bhimambika Devi, also called Bheemavva, remembered as a Shiva Sharane. The seat has passed down one family line and is now in its eighth generation of custodians.
