name: Uthanda Velayudhaswamy Temple, Uthiyur
deity: Murugan as Uthanda Velayudhaswamy, with Valli and Deivanai
significance: A ninth-century Murugan temple set on the Uthiyur hills in Tiruppur district, sung of as Uthimalai in Arunagirinathar's Thiruppugazh. It is a customary halt for pilgrims walking to Palani.

name: Shri Kamaksha Temple, Jaidevi
deity: Goddess Kamaksha (Kamakhya), with Mahunag Ji and Bala Tika Ji
significance: The shrine of Kamaksha at Jaidevi in Mandi district is the tutelary deity of the Suket royal house and a Himachali form of the goddess Kamakhya. It anchors the regional festival calendar, above all the Suket fair.
story: The goddess is said to have been carried from the old Suket capital at Pangana to the new palace when King Shyam Sen moved his seat, and the temple was raised for her at Jaidevi.

name: Shanaleshwara Swayambhu Temple
significance: A Shiva shrine near Rajpura built around a lingam held to be self-manifested, with a structure commissioned by the Maharaja of Patiala and a sadhu presence recorded from the fifteenth century. Hundreds of thousands of devotees converge on it at Maha Shivaratri.
story: A cowherd is said to have found the lingam after his cow kept letting down her milk at one spot; when the buried stone was struck it bled, and a sage nearby recognised it as divine.

name: Theeyathur Sahasralakshmeeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Theeyathur in Pudukkottai district whose presiding lingam is called Sahasralakshmeeswarar, with Periyanayaki as goddess and a large complement of subsidiary shrines.
story: Vishnu is said to have worshipped Shiva here with a thousand lotuses and, finding himself one short, offered his own eye; Shiva later gave darshan to Mahalakshmi when she made the same thousand-flower offering.

name: Nellukkadai Mariamman Temple
significance: A Mariamman shrine in Nagapattinam town with a rajagopura and prakara, run by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department. Besides the four-armed goddess it houses shrines to Vinayaka, Subramanya, Kathavaraya Swamy, Periyachchi, Ayyanar and Ellaiyamman.

name: Achankovil Sastha Temple
deity: Shasta (Achankovil Arasan), with consorts Purna and Pushkala
significance: A forest shrine on the Achankovil river where Shasta is worshipped in his householder form flanked by Purna and Pushkala, unlike the celibate Ayyappan of Sabarimala. It is best known as a healing shrine for snakebite: sandalwood paste and holy water from the idol's right palm are given as medicine, and the sanctum is opened at night for victims.
story: The image is said to have been consecrated by Parashurama.

name: Sree Krishna Swami Temple, Thodupuzha
significance: The principal Krishna temple of Thodupuzha town, standing on the bank of the Thodupuzhayar. The article records that a raja of Keezhmalanadu built the shrine and consecrated the image; tantric rights belong to the Aramallur Kavanattu Mana.
story: A Brahmin pilgrim resting here is said to have received a vision of Krishna, bathed in the river and worshipped him on the Chothi day of Meenam, the day still kept as the temple's origin.

name: Santhoor Subramanya Temple
significance: A coastal Karnataka shrine where Kartikeya is worshipped as Subramanya, lord of serpents. Its main draw is the Shashti Mahotsav, alongside Kiru Shashti and Nagara Panchami, which brings thousands of pilgrims to the village.

name: Siddheshwar Temple, Solapur
significance: Solapur's central temple, built in an island setting within a lake by the yogi Siddharameshwar, a 12th-century Shiva devotee revered as a god in the Lingayat faith, who took samadhi here in 1167 CE and installed sixty-eight lingams in the courtyard. A marble samadhi marks the spot, and the temple and lake have been managed by the Shri Siddheshwar Devsthan Panch Committee since 1899.
story: Solapur is said to have begun prospering from the moment Siddheshwar was born.

name: Nava Toran Temple
significance: An 11th-century Varaha temple at Khor named for the decorative arches, ten of them set in two rows, that frame it. Its carving includes leaf-shaped borders and makara heads.
story: A tunnel is said to run from beneath the temple to Chittor Fort, used by Maharana Pratap to come and worship here.

name: Karat Shiva Temple
builtDisplay: c. 1,000 years old; rebuilt after 18th-c. destruction
significance: A hill-country Shiva temple near Mananthavady reckoned about a thousand years old, destroyed in the 18th century during Tipu Sultan's campaigns. It was rebuilt through an effort led by Krishnan Nambeesan with help from residents of several faiths, and the reconsecration is marked each year on 10-11 May.

name: Narapura Venkateswara Temple, Jammalamadugu
significance: An old Venkateswara shrine at Jammalamadugu in the Rayalaseema country, whose administration was handed to the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams on 23 October 2008.
story: The temple takes its name from Narapuraiah, a devotee said to have built it in the form he believed the god wished.

name: Shri Raghunath Ji Temple
significance: A roughly 650-year-old Rama and Sita temple beside the Jalsen reservoir at Hindaun City, credited in the article to Tulsidas. Diwali, Rama Navami and Dussehra are its principal festivals.

name: Abhaya Varadeeswarar Temple
deity: Shiva as Abhaya Varadeeswarar, with Parvati as Kadal Partha Nayaki
significance: A coastal Shiva temple near Point Calimere whose original complex is attributed to the Cholas, with the standing masonry structure raised by later ruling powers. It is maintained by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
story: Devas beaten in war by the asuras are said to have worshipped Shiva here on the thirteenth lunar day under the star Adhira, and because he sheltered them he is called Abhaya Varadha, the giver of refuge.

name: Kiruthivakesvarar Temple, Sulamangalam
deity: Shiva as Kiruthivakesvarar (lingam), with the goddess Alankaravalli
significance: A Shiva temple on the Thanjavur-Kumbakonam road whose lingam is called Kiruthivakesvarar and whose goddess is Alankaravalli. It is counted among the shrines associated with the Nayanar saint Appar.
story: Shiva is said to have taken this name after killing the asura Kayasuran who was tormenting the people, and Parvati is held to have performed penance at the site.

name: Brahmapureeswarar Temple, Thiruppattur
deity: Shiva as Brahmapureeswarar (swayambhu lingam), with Brahma Sampath Gowri
significance: A Shiva temple at Thiruppattur in Tiruchirappalli district, unusual for its association with Brahma, who is said to have installed twelve lingams here. It is administered by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
story: Brahma, punished by Shiva with the loss of his fifth head for his pride, is said to have come here in penance, worshipped beneath a magizha tree, and had his curse lifted and his powers of creation restored.

name: Roda Group of Temples
deity: Shiva, Vishnu, Surya, Ganesha and the Navagraha across seven shrines
style: Maha-Gurjara (Anarta school), latina and phansana spires
significance: A group of seven small stone shrines about 18 km from Himmatnagar, raised over perhaps two centuries during the tripartite struggle between the Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas. Scholars treat them as the ancestor of the later Solanki or Maru-Gurjara manner, and an idol inscription at the site is dated Samvat 1104 (1048 CE).

name: Thiru Nayathode Siva Narayana Temple
significance: A twin-deity temple near Cochin International Airport where Shiva and Mahavishnu are worshipped together, its founding attributed to Cheraman Perumal Nayanar. It is a protected monument under the Kerala Department of Archaeology.

name: Dharmapureesvarar Temple, Vadakandam
significance: A small Shiva shrine about 7 km from Tiruvarur, counted among the Vaippu Sthalams praised in the hymns of the Saiva saint Appar. It has no gateway tower, its lingam sanctum instead sitting inside a plain walled prakara with a nandi mandapa and subsidiary shrines.

name: Bharali Namghar
significance: A Vaishnavite namghar (village prayer house) near Hatbor in Kaliabor, first founded on the initiative of Bapuram Deo of Balisatra and rebuilt on its present site after the Burmese army burnt the original during the invasions of 1817-1826. Its bamboo-and-thatch fabric has since been replaced with concrete pillars and a tin roof.
story: Villagers hold that wishes made at the namghar, which is associated with the guardian spirit Burha Dangoria, are granted.

name: Nandinadesvarar Temple, Poikainallur
significance: A Shiva temple in North Poikainallur, the half of the twin settlement that carries the Vaippu Sthalam status conferred by Appar's hymns. Maha Shivaratri is its principal festival.

name: Alanduraiappar Temple, Nallatthukkudi
deity: Shiva (Alanduraiappar), with the goddesses Kuyiladu Nayaki and Kuyilanda Nayaki
significance: A Shiva temple 2 km from Mayiladuthurai on the Nedumaruthur road, without a gopuram and entered through a single gateway into its prakaram of subsidiary shrines. Its most recent kumbhabhishekham was performed on 8 June 1970.
story: The lingam here is said to have been worshipped by Surya, and the temple's Surya Pushkarani tank is believed to cure long-standing illness.

name: Rudrakodisvarar Temple, Sempankudi
significance: A Shiva temple counted among the Vaippu Sthalams sung by Appar, enclosed by a compound wall with a prakara of minor shrines and sculpted kosta niches. Worship is offered once a day.
story: The site is identified as the place where the body of the asura who stole the amrita fell after being severed, giving rise to Rahu and Ketu.

name: Divyagnanesvarar Temple, Koviladi
significance: A Shiva temple at Koviladi, known as Sadaimudi in Appar's day and later as Tirupper Nagar, and listed among the Vaippu Sthalams. Its inscriptions record Chola-period administrative divisions and refer to Kochengat Cholan's capture of a Chera king at the site.

name: Iravathesvarar Temple, Nemam
deity: Shiva (Iravathesvarar), with the goddess Alangara Nayaki
significance: A Shiva temple 3 km from Thirukattupalli with an east-facing three-tier gopura, counted among the Vaippu Sthalams praised by Appar.
story: Tradition holds the site bore different names in successive ages - Parijatha Vanam, Beemesvaram and Indira Vanam - before becoming Iravathesvaram.

name: Chidambaresvarar Temple, Kotlambakkam
significance: A Shiva temple near Panruti founded in the 9th century, whose sanctum was rebuilt in granite in 1267 by the Kadava chief Kopperunchinga of Senthamangalam. Further inscriptions of the 15th and 16th centuries record later additions, and its niches carry Brahma, Dakshinamurthy, Surya and Bhairava.
story: Shiva is said to have appeared here as an old man to the saint Sundarar, who was resting at a nearby monastery, and blessed him by placing his foot on the saint's head.

name: Samayapuram Pojeeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Samayapuram administered by the far better known Samayapuram Mariamman Temple nearby. It has two vimanas but no rajagopura, with the east-facing lingam sanctum and a south-facing goddess shrine, a tank called Agni Tirttam and a vilva as its sacred tree.

name: Rama Lakshamana Temples, Baradia
significance: A pair of small unicellular shrines five kilometres south-east of Dwarka, raised on high moulded plinths and each comprising cella, antarala, sabhamandapa and porch. Built under Bhima II, they are reckoned the oldest surviving Vaishnava temples in Gujarat and are protected by the Archaeological Survey of India as a Monument of National Importance.

name: Chaturbhuj Temple, Gwalior
significance: A monolithic shrine roughly twelve feet square cut into the rock face of Gwalior Fort in 875 CE by Alla, grandson of Nagabhata II, with reliefs of four-armed Vishnu and Varaha and subsidiary dedications to Shiva and the nine Durgas. Its dedicatory inscription carries the earliest known use of a circular symbol for zero, making the temple a landmark in the history of mathematics.

name: Munsar Lake and Shrines
significance: A large medieval reservoir at Viramgam ringed by small stone shrines, credited to Minaldevi, mother of the Chaulukya king Jayasimha Siddharaja, and dated to 1090. Among the shrines are pedestals thought to have held a Krishna image and basins associated with Shiva worship.

name: Kodandarama Temple, Gollala Mamidada
significance: Begun in 1889 by the local zamindar brothers Dwarampudi Subbi Reddy and Rami Reddy and rebuilt in stone by 1939, with tall gopurams added through the 1950s. Its scale and pilgrim draw have earned it the nickname Chinna Bhadradri, the little Bhadrachalam.

name: Sri Santhana Venugopala Swamy Temple, Thettu
significance: A Krishna shrine in Kurabalakota mandal whose early fabric is linked to Chola and Ganga patronage, and which the Hoysala king Veera Ballala endowed with land in 1298. It is sought out by couples praying for children, the deity being invoked as Santana Venugopala.
story: Krishna is said to have appeared in a Ganga ruler's dream; his chariot wheel stuck fast at the spot, and digging there revealed the image that was installed at Sage Koundinya's ashram.

name: Basudev Devalaya
significance: A Vaishnava temple in Nalbari district raised under the Ahom king Sutanphaa in the first half of the eighteenth century. It remains an active local centre of Basudev worship in lower Assam.
story: A fisherman's net is said to have stayed snagged in the Jaymangal Beel for seven days until a villager, Gada Kahar, dreamed that Basudev wished to be freed from it; when the king could not lift the stones from the spot, he built the temple over them.

name: Vazhukaruteeswarar Temple
significance: A small Shiva temple on Gandhi Road in Kanchipuram whose lingam is described as showing sixteen shades. Devotees resort to it when entangled in litigation, praying for cases to be cleared.
story: The devas and asuras are said to have set up the lingam here while arguing over the meaning of sat and asat, and Shiva appeared to settle the doubt, whence the name Vazhukaruteeswarar.

name: Rathasena Mata Temple
significance: A hilltop goddess shrine in the Maruwas area of Udaipur, reached by a walking path up the slope, housing a stone image of Rathasan Mata. It is a local devotional site rather than a monumental temple.

name: Rajacholeesvarar Temple, Thirumalairayanpattinam
deity: Rajacholeesvarar (Shiva, as a lingam); goddess Abirami
significance: A Shiva temple in Thirumalairayanpattinam, the settlement founded as the seat of Saluva Thirumalairayan, a fifteenth-century Vijayanagara representative in the Karaikal region. Its prakara carries sculptures of the sixty-three Nayanmars.

name: Kali Bari, Shimla
deity: Shyamala, a form of the goddess Kali
significance: Established in the early nineteenth century by Bengali surveyors who came to Shimla as the British built their summer capital, and administered by a trust formed in 1902. The goddess Shyamala worshipped here is one suggested source of the city's own name.

name: Nandeesvarar Temple, Nandivanam
deity: Nandeesvarar (Shiva, as a lingam); goddess Soundaranayaki
significance: A Shiva temple at Nandivaram near Guduvancheri, with the lingam of Nandeesvarar in the sanctum and a separate shrine for the goddess Soundaranayaki. It serves as the principal temple of the town.
story: A herdboy is said to have noticed that one cow gave its milk each day at a particular spot and came home dry; when the spot was dug, a lingam was found rising from the ground.

name: Kali Temple, Visakhapatnam
significance: Built in 1984 on the Ramakrishna Beach road, this Kali temple copies the nine-spired navaratna form of the Dakshineswar temple in Kolkata. It is a landmark of the Visakhapatnam seafront and draws crowds at Vijayadashami.

name: Gandhari Amman Kovil
significance: A goddess temple at Mele Thampanoor in the Kerala capital, close to Thiruvananthapuram Central station, with subsidiary shrines to Ganesha, Muruga, the naga deities, Bhairava and the navagrahas. Its main festival is Chithra Pournami in May.

name: Someswara Swamy Temple, Appikonda
significance: An eleventh-century Shiva temple on the coast near Visakhapatnam, attributed to the Chola king Kulottunga I and known locally as the Chola monument. It is a protected site under the Archaeological Survey of India and draws very large crowds at Maha Shivaratri.

name: Talesavara Siva Temple – II
significance: A small Kalinga-style Shiva shrine of the twelfth to thirteenth century standing in the Bharati Matha precinct at Badhaibanka chowk in old Bhubaneswar, with the lingam set in a circular sanctum. The matha maintains it and repaired cyclone damage to the structure.

name: Tara Devi Temple
deity: Tara Devi, one of the ten Mahavidyas
significance: A timber-and-stone kath kuni temple on a ridge some seven kilometres from Shimla, built by the Sen rulers around 1766 and credited to King Bhupendra Sen. It is one of the best known Mahavidya shrines in the Himachal hills.
story: Bhupendra Sen is said to have been asked in a vision by the goddess Tara to enshrine her, and a later king, Balbir Sen, was told in a similar vision to place the temple on the Tarav hilltop where it stands.

name: Gangeshwar Mahadev Temple
significance: A shore shrine near Fudam village on Diu where five Shiva lingas of different sizes are carved among rocks at the tide line, submerged at high tide and exposed at low. The name is read as Ganga plus Ishwar, for Shiva who received the descending Ganga in his hair.
story: The five lingas are said to have been carved and worshipped by the Pandavas while they were living in disguise during their exile.

name: Rajarajeswaramudaiya Mahadevar Temple
deity: Rajarajeswaramudaiya Mahadevar (Shiva), also called Theerthapaleeswarar; consort Kamakshi Amman
significance: A tenth-century Shiva temple at Sivapuram built under Rajaraja Chola and extended by his son Rajendra Chola I, now cared for by the Tamil Nadu Department of Archaeology. Its walls carry a dense body of Chola inscriptions, including a grant of 180 goats by Rajendra I to keep two perpetual lamps burning.

name: Shyama Mai Temple
significance: Built in 1933 by Maharaja Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga on the cremation site of his father Maharaja Rameshwar Singh, this Kali temple is among the most visited shrines in Mithila.
story: The dark form worshipped here is explained by the Ramayana episode in which the goddess turned black with fury after Rama slew Sahastraanan, and grew calm and abashed only when her foot came to rest on Shiva's chest.

name: Atishaya Kshetra Lunwa Jain Temple
significance: A Digambara Jain pilgrimage centre (atishaya kshetra) at Lunwa village in Rajasthan, whose Khandelwal Digambar Jain Mandir enshrines an image of Adinatha and whose adjoining Nasiya Ji shrine is dedicated to Neminatha. The temple's ancient images have long drawn Digambara pilgrims to the site.
story: An image of Chandraprabha is said to have been unearthed by a farmer digging a well, then placed on a bullock cart that ran some 45 km before halting of its own accord at the Adinatha temple at Lunwa.

name: Simhanagadde Jain Temple
significance: A Digambara Jain atishaya kshetra in Chikkamagaluru district whose principal shrine is dedicated to the yakshi Jwalamalini, shown seated in sukhasana with eight arms. The site is associated with the Yapaniya branch of the Mula Sangha, and a fourteenth-century inscription survives on an image in its Shantinatha basadi.
story: Tradition holds that the ascetic Chikka Samantabhadra brought the Jwalamalini image from another Jain centre and installed it at Simhanagadde.

name: Shree Pavapuri Tirth Dham
significance: A modern Svetambara Jain tirtha near Sirohi, begun in 1998 and completed in 2001 through the patronage of the K. P. Sanghvi family. Alongside the Parshvanatha temple the complex runs a large animal welfare centre, in keeping with the Jain principle of ahimsa.

name: Brahma Jinalaya, Lakkundi
significance: The largest of Lakkundi's Jain temples, raised in 1007 CE by Attimabbe, wife of the general Nagadeva, and the earliest dated example of the Western Chalukya idiom in the village. Its sanctum lintel carries Mahavira, though the temple is now worshipped as a shrine of Neminatha.

name: Odegal Basadi
significance: A fourteenth-century three-celled Jain basadi on Vindhyagiri hill at Shravanabelagola, housing dark schist images of Rishabhanatha, Neminatha and Shantinatha. Its name comes from the stone buttresses propping its walls, and it is a protected monument.

name: Badut Temple
significance: Reckoned the oldest temple in East Java, a Shaivite shrine whose garbhagriha holds a lingam and yoni and whose outer niche carries Durga Mahishasuramardini. The Dinoyo inscription places it in 682 Saka, 760 CE, under King Gajayana of Kanjuruhan, and it keeps the older Central Javanese temple form despite its East Javanese setting.

name: Gebang Temple
deity: Ganesha (with a yoni in the inner chamber)
significance: A compact 8th-century Hindu shrine on a 5.25 m square base, holding a yoni in its cella and a Ganesha seated on a spouted yoni on its west side, with niches for Nandiswara. Buried under Merapi lahar deposits, it was found in 1936 and rebuilt by Van Romondt between 1937 and 1939; its roof figures peering from window frames echo the Bima temple at Dieng.

name: Sari Temple
significance: A two-storey Buddhist building beside Candi Kalasan, raised under the same Kalasan inscription of 778 that ordered a sanctuary for the bodhisattva Tara and a vihara for monks; scholars read Sari as that monastic dwelling. Its walls carry 36 Buddhist figures in tribhanga pose along with Tara, bodhisattva and kinnara reliefs, once coated in the protective vajralepa plaster.

name: Pura Penataran Sasih
significance: The former state temple of the Pejeng kingdom, dated by a chronogram at its entrance to 1266 and holding a tall stone seat for Ganesha in the main courtyard along with Hindu sculpture of the 10th to 12th centuries. It is best known as the home of the Moon of Pejeng, a colossal early bronze kettledrum kept in the temple.

name: Rimbi Temple
deity: Parvati (as the deified Queen Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi)
style: Andesite East Javanese candi on a brick foundation
significance: A Shaivite Majapahit temple in the Jombang hills raised in memory of Queen Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi, whose portrait statue took the form of Parvati. About 12 m of the andesite structure survives on a three-tiered base, carrying 51 reliefs on themes of water and purification; it was noted by Alfred Russel Wallace and listed as a Cultural Property of Indonesia in 2020.

name: Ijo Temple
deity: Shiva (linga and yoni), with three perwara for the Trimurti
significance: The highest-set of the temples around Prambanan, standing at about 410 m on a hill some 4 km from Ratu Boko. Its main shrine holds a large linga and yoni wreathed by a naga, read as the union of Shiva and Parvati, while three smaller perwara facing east honour the Trimurti of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva.

name: Kedulan Temple
significance: A Shaivite compound of one east-facing main shrine and three ancillary temples, with a lingga-yoni in the cella and images of Durga Mahishasuramardini, Nandiswara, Mahakala, Ganesha and Agastya; associated inscriptions date it to about 869. Sand miners struck it by accident on 24 November 1993 some six metres below the modern surface, where Merapi lava flows had buried it, and restoration has run in stages since 2017.

name: Ngawen Temple
deity: The five Dhyani Buddhas (a Ratnasambhava image survives in the north shrine)
significance: A row of five andesite Buddhist shrines near Muntilan, thought from the detail of their carving to be slightly older than Borobudur and understood as a dedication to the five Dhyani Buddhas; the north temple keeps a headless meditating Ratnasambhava in varamudra. Rampant lion figures at the corners and ratna pinnacles more usual on Hindu temples mark the group out.

name: Surawana Temple
deity: Memorial shrine of Wijayarajasa, Prince of Wengker
significance: A modest west-facing Majapahit temple built in 1390 and dedicated in 1400, at the shraddha rite for Wijayarajasa, Prince of Wengker and an uncle by marriage of King Rajasanagara. Only the reconstructed base stands intact, but it carries dense reliefs of the Arjunawiwaha, Sri Tanjung and Babuksha tales together with naga, makara and gana figures.

name: Lumbung Temple
significance: A 9th-century Buddhist group a few hundred metres north of Prambanan, laid out like Sewu with one main shrine ringed by sixteen stupa-crowned perwara. Its original name is lost; the nearby Kelurak inscription naming a compound dedicated to the bodhisattva Manjusri is generally taken to refer to Sewu rather than to this temple.

name: Tep Pranam
significance: A Buddhist terrace inside Angkor Thom whose colossal seated Buddha is assembled from sandstone blocks and reached by a 75-metre laterite causeway from the east. The wooden hall that once sheltered the image has vanished, leaving the cruciform foundation and the boundary markers of its terrace.

name: Wat Langka
deity: Buddha (bronze Buddha images enshrined in the stupa, facing the four directions)
significance: One of the older Theravada monasteries of Phnom Penh, founded in 1442 by Ponhea Yat as a refuge, a repository for the Tripitaka and a meeting place for Khmer and Sri Lankan monks. It escaped destruction under the Khmer Rouge because the regime used the compound as a storage warehouse.
story: Its name commemorates the gathering of Khmer and Sri Lankan monks, tied to the account of Buddhaghosa copying the scriptures brought from Sri Lanka.

name: Thottuva Dhanwanthari Temple
deity: Dhanwanthari (Adi Dhanwanthari), the physician form of Vishnu
significance: Described as the only temple in Kerala with Dhanwanthari as its principal deity, its east-facing image standing close to six feet and holding the vessel of amrita. The shrine belongs to the Koramboor Mana family and is run by the Sree Dhanwanthari Moorthi Seva Trust.
story: A Namboodiri Brahmin cursed by Shankaracharya for withholding hospitality is said to have been consoled at this spot by the voice of Dhanwanthari, and the place where he set down his umbrella is still called Kudappadom.

name: Tiruvaneshwar Temple
deity: Shiva as Tiruvaneshwar (Gajaranyeswarar / Karivananathar), consort Kamakshi Ambal
significance: A Shiva temple at Ranganathapuram in the Thiruvaiyaru taluk of Thanjavur district, where the deity carries the elephant-forest names Gajaranyeswarar and Karivananathar. The Kanchi Kamakoti pontiff Chandrashekharendra Saraswati is recorded to have stayed a week here in meditation.

name: Thrikkavu Temple
deity: Durga Bhagavathy, worshipped in the three forms of Parvati, Lakshmi and Saraswati
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; restored after Tipu Sultan's raid
significance: A Durga temple at Ponnani whose idol was destroyed when Tipu Sultan's forces turned the shrine into an ammunition depot; the Zamorin afterwards had it restored.
story: It is counted among the 108 Durga shrines said to have been consecrated by Parashurama, and its name is traced to the old forest tract called Thrikkani Kaadu.

name: Talesvara Siva Temple
place: Kedar Gouri road, Old Town, Bhubaneswar
deity: Shiva (lingam set in a circular yonipitha)
significance: A small rekha deul on the Kedar Gouri road in old Bhubaneswar, a short walk from the Parasuramesvara temple, believed to have been founded in the 8th century. It stood ruined until the Odisha state archaeology department repaired it, and it remains in private hands.

name: Tirthesvara Siva Temple
deity: Shiva (lingam set in a circular yonipitha)
significance: A west-facing Shiva shrine on the Talabazar road that runs from Bindusagar towards the Lingaraja temple in old Bhubaneswar. Its architectural detail matches Ganga-period work, on which basis it is dated to about the 14th century, and it is still served by local priests.

name: Thottipal Bhagavati Temple
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; renovated in the late 19th c.
significance: A Bhagavathy temple in Thrissur district that was wrecked during Tipu Sultan's campaigns and rebuilt in the late 1800s. It takes part in both the Arattupuzha Pooram and the Peruvanam Pooram.
story: It is counted among the 108 Devi shrines said to have been installed by Parashurama, and the goddess is held to be the sister of Urathammathiruvadi and of the Chathakudam Sastha.

name: Tirusoolanathar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Tirusulam on the south-western edge of Chennai, credited to the medieval Chola king Kulothunga I and later renovated, with inscriptions of the Chola and Pandya periods. A Tripurasundari image damaged during an invasion is kept beside the presiding deity.
story: Tradition speaks of a hidden passage beneath the temple leading to the nearby Pancha Pandava hills where the king had his palace, along which treasure is said to have been concealed.

name: Thrippara Shiva Kshetram
builtDisplay: said to be about 800 years old
significance: A Shiva temple at Vallicode in Pathanamthitta district reckoned to be some eight centuries old, unusual among the shrines nearby in that its sanctum stands in the open directly above the temple ghats.

name: Varasiddhi Vinayaka Temple
deity: Ganesha as Valampuri Varasiddhi Vinayakar, with his consort Siddhi
significance: A Ganesha temple near the beach at Besant Nagar in Chennai whose image was first worshipped on a site opposite the present one inside the CPWD quarters; the enlarged temple had its first kumbhabhishekam in April 1979. An auditorium and a goshala were added later, and music programmes mark Vinayaka Chaturthi.

name: Velleeswarar Temple, Mangadu
deity: Shiva as Velleeswarar (also called Sukreswara and Bhargaveswarar)
significance: One of the three principal temples of Mangadu on the western edge of Chennai, about two kilometres from the Kamakshi Amman temple, counted in the Navagraha circuit around the city as the shrine of Sukra and administered by the Tamil Nadu HR&CE department.
story: Sukra, the planet Venus, is said to have worshipped Shiva here, which is why the deity is called Velleeswarar or Bhargaveswarar; the same tradition places Kamakshi's penance at Mangadu before her marriage to Shiva at Kanchipuram.

name: Puttingal Temple
significance: A Bhadrakali temple at Paravur in Kollam district whose Meena Bharani festival is known for its competitive fireworks. On 10 April 2016 an unauthorised display set off the stored fireworks, killing 114 people and injuring more than 350.
story: The temple is said to have been founded where the goddess made her presence felt on an ant hill, puttu in Malayalam, which gives the shrine its name.

name: Pattupurakkavu Bhagavathi Temple
significance: A Bhadrakali temple a kilometre north of Pandalam junction on the Thiruvananthapuram–Angamaly MC Road, with subsidiary shrines to Ganapathi and Shiva. It hosted the first Devi Bhagavatha Sathram held in Kerala, from 28 April to 7 May 2010.

name: Poruvazhy Peruviruthy Malanada Temple
deity: Mala Appooppan, the sankalpa murti of Duryodhana
significance: A hill shrine in Kollam district, rare in being dedicated to Duryodhana of the Mahabharata and in having neither an idol nor a sanctum, worship instead being offered through sankalpam. It is run by a committee drawn from seven territorial divisions.
story: Duryodhana, searching for the exiled Pandavas, is said to have been given toddy on this hill by an elderly Kurava woman, and, moved by the place and its people, to have worshipped Shiva there and endowed the shrine with farmland.

name: Punkunnam Seetha Ramaswamy Temple
deity: Rama with Sita, sharing a single pedestal; shrines to Lakshmana and Hanuman
significance: A Rama temple in the Pushpagiri agraharam at Punkunnam in Thrissur, built in 1899 by T. R. Ramachandra Iyer, a justice of the Cochin court, as his personal shrine. Rama and Sita share one pedestal, older Shiva and Ayyappan shrines stand in the same compound, and a 55-foot Hanuman statue was unveiled in April 2023.

name: Prasanna Venkatesa Perumal Temple, Saidapet
deity: Vishnu as Prasanna Venkata Narasimha, with Sridevi and Bhudevi
significance: A Vishnu temple at Saidapet in Chennai where the east-facing Prasanna Venkata Narasimha stands with Sridevi and Bhudevi. The article dates it to the 12th century and attributes its building to the Balija Chetty community under Vijayanagara rule; the Ramanuja Vijaya Vilasam hall, now the Ramanuja Koodam, was added in 1901.

name: Podhu Aavudayar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Parakkalakkottai near Pattukkottai in Thanjavur district, unusual in its hours: it opens only at midnight on Mondays and closes three or four hours later, with additional access on the morning of Thai Pongal.
story: Two sages, Vankobar and Mahakobar, are said to have argued over whether celibacy or married life was the higher path and, unable to settle it, asked Shiva to judge; he appeared to them at Parakkalakkottai and gave his verdict.

name: Venkatachalapathy Temple, Thiruvananthapuram
significance: A Vishnu temple a minute's walk from the southern gate of the Padmanabhaswamy temple in Thiruvananthapuram, built in 1898, its idol consecrated by the fortieth Azhagiya Singar of the Ahobila Matha; the sanctum follows Tamil rather than Kerala practice, without the elaborate carving or a gopuram.
story: The image is said to have been found in a pond near the house of Ranga Iyengar of Veeravanallur about a century before the temple was raised, and his family's eldest son has served as chief priest for three generations.

name: Shri Guru Kottureshwara Temple
significance: A Veerashaiva pilgrimage centre in the town of Kotturu, which takes its name from the saint Guru Kottureshwara; the complex is made up of four mathas, among them the Murkal Matha, where the saint is said to have first appeared, and the Darbar Matha, where he heard people's troubles.
story: Local tradition holds that Nandi came down from Kailasa in the form of the saint to protect the Veerashaiva faith, that those who harassed him were struck blind, and that he brought a dead buffalo back to life with a touch of his hand.

name: Kanichukulangara Devi Temple
significance: A Bhagavathi temple about 7.5 km from Cherthala in Alappuzha district, known for its Thiruvonam festival in the Malayalam month of Kumbham, with chikkara, pongala, thooka chadu and fireworks.

name: Sri Pralayakala Veerabadrar Temple
significance: A temple in the Gavipuram Guddadahalli neighbourhood of Bengaluru dedicated to Pralayakala Veerabadra.

name: Bagheswari Temple, Bongaigaon
significance: A goddess temple in the southern part of Bongaigaon city, described as one of the oldest of the fifty-one Shakti Pithas and a major Hindu pilgrimage stop in western Assam; its precinct preserves a medieval rock-cut Ganesha and architectural members of a stone temple datable to the 10th-11th century.

name: Siddheshwari Kali Mandir
significance: A Shakta temple in north-eastern Kalna near the Bhagirathi-Hooghly, built in 1740 by Chitrasen Roy, a zamindar of Burdwan, and regarded as a fine example of jor-bangla architecture; five 18th-century Shiva temples stand in the same compound and the image of the goddess, about five feet tall, is carved from neem wood.

name: Parasuramesvara Temple, Gudimallam
builtDisplay: later Chola-Vijayanagara structure; linga c. 2nd-1st c. BCE
significance: The temple at Gudimallam, about 24 km south-east of Tirupati, enshrines a linga that scholars count among the earliest surviving and unmistakable images of Shiva, dated variously from the 3rd-1st century BCE to the early centuries CE; the apsidal stone sanctuary around it is usually assigned to the later Chola and Vijayanagara periods, and the shrine, still in worship, has been protected by the Archaeological Survey of India since 1954.

name: Keleswaram Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Keleswaram in Thiruvananthapuram district, administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board, whose lingam faces west - an orientation the article notes as rare; Maha Shivaratri and Thiruvathira are its principal festivals.

name: Varahaperumal Temple, Kumbakonam
significance: A Vishnu temple in Kumbakonam where the god is worshipped in his boar incarnation alongside Bhoomidevi; it is one of the five Vishnu temples tied to the Mahamaham festival held there once every twelve years.
story: The temple recalls how a demon carried the earth down into the netherworld, and Vishnu took the form of a boar, fought him and raised the earth back up at the gods' plea.

name: Shri Dev Rameshwar Temple
place: Rameshwar Wadi, Devgad taluka, Sindhudurg district
significance: A 16th-century Shiva temple in Devgad taluka approached by a rock-cut passage some 250 yards long and fifty feet deep; the Angre admirals of the Maratha navy enlarged it through the 18th century and a sabha mandap was added in 1780, while its four-armed image seated on a bull is of solid silver said to weigh about a hundred kilograms and a bell taken from a captured Portuguese ship in 1791 hangs at the eastern gate.

name: Sri Krishnapuram Temple
deity: Krishna, with Shiva and the goddess worshipped in paired form
builtDisplay: Krishna deified 1078 ME; Shiva shrine 1124 ME
significance: A Krishna temple at Thalappalam near Erattupetta in Kottayam district, where Radha-Krishna and Parvati-Parameswara are venerated as paired deities. Long held by the Kochupurakkal Nair family, it later passed to the NSS Karayogam of Thalappalam.
story: Villagers tell of farmers whose iron tools struck something buried in the fields, revealing a divine presence, and the shrine was raised there in a season of famine and epidemic.

name: Bhagavadh Vinayaga Temple, Kumbakonam
significance: A Ganesha temple in Kumbakonam whose 1692 inscription records grants made under the Thanjavur Maratha rulers at the time of a renovation. It also holds a Navagraha Vinayaga, and at Vinayaka Chaturthi the deity is decorated with currency notes.
story: The site is said to have revealed itself when the ashes of the sage Bhagavar Maharishi's mother turned into flowers as they were immersed in the Kaveri here.

name: Chandikan Devi Temple (Chandikan Dham)
significance: A Kali shrine at Sandwa village, some 24 km from Pratapgarh town, around which a trading fair gathers every Tuesday. Its largest fair falls on Budhwa Mangal, and the Chandika Mahotsava is kept on the eighth and ninth days of Chaitra and Ashwin Navratri.

name: Puthoorppilly Sree Krishnaswamy Temple
significance: A Krishna temple at Manjapra in Ernakulam district, listed as a protected monument by the Kerala state archaeology department. Sreekrishna Jayanthi is its principal festival.

name: Shaktheeswaram Temple
significance: A Shakta temple at Aymanam near Kottayam whose presiding deity is Adi Parashakti, worshipped through Sri Chakra puja and tantric upasana. It is reached from Kottayam city by the Kudayampadi–Parippu road.

name: Chauharjan Devi Temple
significance: A shrine of the mother goddess Barahi, known locally as Chauharjan Devi, standing on the bank of the Sai river at Chauharjan Parasrampur in Pratapgarh district.

name: Koncheswar Mahadev Temple
significance: A brick Shiva temple at Konch in Gaya district, dated to about the 14th century, with a heavy curvilinear nagara sikhara over seven-faced outer walls. Cunningham and Beglar recorded it for the Archaeological Survey in 1872–73, when the tower still carried a cylindrical pinnacle; a Dashavatara panel and images of Vishnu, Hara-Gauri, Ganesha and Surya stand in the premises.

name: Akkanna Madanna Caves
style: Rock-cut, with early Nagara-rekha shikhara carving
significance: Rock-cut Shiva cave temples at Vijayawada excavated by the Eastern Chalukyas around the middle of the 7th century, the upper cave holding three shrines to different forms of Shiva and the lower caves showing experimental carving of a nagara-rekha superstructure. They are protected monuments of national importance, and take their present name from Akkanna and Madanna, ministers of Golconda a thousand years later.

name: Kapileshwar Temple, Madhubani
deity: Shiva (Kapileshwar linga), with Parvati and Hanuman
significance: One of the better-known Shiva temples of Madhubani district, set in a walled compound with subsidiary shrines and old sculptures. A large tank was dug beside it with help from the Darbhanga Raj to supply water for ritual, and in Shrawan pilgrims come from across Bihar for the jalabhishek of the linga.
story: The linga is said to have been installed here by the sage Kapila, from whom the temple takes its name.

name: Wangath Temple Complex, Naranag
builtDisplay: 8th c. (Lalitaditya Muktapida, Karkota); origin traced to c. 220 BCE
style: Kashmiri grey granite, with pyramidal roofs and domed ceilings
significance: A ruined group of Shaiva temples in grey granite beside the spring at Naranag in Ganderbal district, expanded in the 8th century under the Karkota ruler Lalitaditya Muktapida. Now centrally protected by the Archaeological Survey of India, the site is the starting point of the annual Gangbal yatra to Gangabal lake.
story: Kalhana's Rajatarangini credits King Jaluka, son of Ashoka, with raising the Bhuteshvara and Jyestarudra shrines here around 220 BCE.

name: Padiyanoor Devi Temple
deity: Chamundi Devi, a fierce form of Kali
significance: An old goddess temple at Poovachal, about 30 km from Thiruvananthapuram, where Chamundi is the cardinal deity and subsidiary shrines hold Yakshiyamma, Ganapati, Yogeshwara, Nagar and Brahmarakshas. Its three-day Makam Thozhal in Meenam is the year's main observance.

name: Dada Darbar, Khandwa
deity: Dadaji Dhuniwale — the samadhi of Shri 1008 Keshwanand ji Maharaj
significance: A shrine in Khandwa built over the samadhi of the Avadhoot saint Keshwanand ji Maharaj, known as Bade Dadaji or Dadaji Dhuniwale, who came here from Barwaha and took mahasamadhi on 3 December 1930. Twenty-seven further dhams of the same lineage exist in India and abroad.

name: Ootukulangara Bhagavathy Temple, Peruvemba
deity: Ootukulangara Bhagavathy, with Ganapathy and Ayyappan
significance: A Bhagavathy temple at Peruvemba in Palakkad district whose sanctum is left roofless, the idol standing under an asoka tree that is said never to have grown. Its main festival, Patham Padiyam, closes 41 days of lamp-lighting in the month of Vrischikam.
story: A farm worker is said to have turned up a metal image while ploughing a paddy field; an astrologer called in by the landlord judged it a self-manifested form of Bhagavathy, and the temple was raised on the spot.

name: Kalyana Venkateswara Temple, Srinivasamangapuram
significance: A Venkateswara temple at Srinivasamangapuram near Tirupati, listed by the Archaeological Survey of India as a monument of national importance and administered by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams since 1981. Newly married couples come here for blessings.
story: Venkateswara is said to have spent the first six months after his marriage to Padmavathi at this place.

name: Kapalikulangara Sree Mahavishnu Temple
significance: A Mahavishnu temple at Taliparamba in Kannur district, built in the traditional Kerala manner and standing close to the Sree Rajarajeshwara temple.

name: Sri Ananda Lingeshwara Temple
builtDisplay: rebuilt 2000–2012; origin traced to the 13th c. Chola era
style: Modern Indian; the earlier Chola structure was demolished
significance: A Shiva temple on Ananda Giri hill near Hebbal in Bengaluru, traced in origin to the Chola period of the 13th century but rebuilt in successive renovations in 2000, 2009 and 2012. Maha Shivratri draws thousands to the hill.
story: Devotees first propitiate Kaala Bairaveshwara as guardian of the place, and a tunnel is said to have run from the hill to Nandi Hills for kings escaping attack.

name: Neendoor Subrahmanya Swami Temple
style: Traditional Kerala (laterite, terracotta tile and teak)
significance: A Murugan temple at Neendoor in Kottayam district, built of laterite and teak with carved woodwork throughout and a monolithic stone lamp, where the deity is worshipped in his fierce form as commander of the divine armies after the killing of Tharakasuran. It is said to be the only Subrahmanya temple performing the Ottanarangamala Samarppanam.
story: The Pandavas and the sage Vyasa are said to have worshipped at this temple.

name: Ashtabhuji Temple, Adbhar
deity: Ashtabhuji Devi, the eight-armed goddess identified with Saraswati and Durga
significance: A stone temple at Adbhar village in Janjgir-Champa district housing an eight-armed image of the goddess, built in the nagara manner during the Gupta period and since restored under the Archaeological Survey of India. Navratri is its chief festival.

name: Muthumariamman Temple, Tiruvappur
significance: A Mariamman temple at Tiruvappur in Thirukokarnam, about 5 km from Pudukkottai, where the goddess is enshrined seated behind a front mandapa, flagstaff and bali peetam. Its prakara also holds shrines to Meenakshi of Madurai and Kamatchi of Kanchipuram, and the Fridays of Aadi draw the largest crowds.

name: Karuvathoor Sreeramaswami Temple
significance: A Rama temple in Velur panchayat, Thrissur district, with a rectangular shrine under a domed and tiled roof and sculpture entirely in the Kerala idiom. Consecrated by the Azhvancheri Thamprakkal and long held by Azhvancheri Mana and later Avanaparambu Mana of Kiralur, it now runs under the Cochin Devaswom Board through the Nelluvai Mullakkal Devaswom.

name: Rankini Temple, Jadugora
place: Rohinibera, Potka block, East Singhbhum district
deity: Rankini, worshipped as a form of Kali
significance: A goddess shrine near Jadugora whose object of worship is a stone taken to be Rankini herself; the present building was put up between 1947 and 1950 after Dinbandhu Singh began the worship, and a family trust has run it since 1954. Originally a Bhumij tribal cult, it saw human sacrifice until the British stopped the practice around 1865.
story: The goddess is said to have taken the form of a girl fleeing a shepherd who hid in a washerman's bundle of clothes at Kapadgadi Ghat, whereupon the pile of cloth turned to stone.

name: Lingdum Monastery
deity: Zurmang Kagyu lineage, seat of Zurmang Gharwang Rinpoche
significance: A modern monastery near Ranka, about an hour from Gangtok, completed in 1999 and also known as Ranka Lingdum or the Pal Zurmang Kagyud Monastery. It belongs to the Zurmang Kagyu tradition of Tibetan Buddhism and is led by Zurmang Gharwang Rinpoche.

name: Mahamaya Temple, Raipur
significance: The goddess temple of Raipur's old quarter, ascribed to Raja Mordhwaj and rebuilt in Nagara style under the Marathas in the 17th–18th centuries, with a second shrine to Samaleswari. It is counted among the thirty-six Shakti pithas of Chhattisgarh and is run by the Shree Rajrajeshwari Maa Mahamaya Devi Mandir Raipur Trust.
story: King Mordhwaj is said to have found the image in the Karun river as a rock ringed by three giant serpents, and the goddess revealed herself to him as his family deity and asked that a temple be raised for her.

name: Kamna Devi Temple
deity: Kamna Devi, a form of Ambika
significance: A goddess temple on Prospect Hill above Boileauganj, one of Shimla's seven hills, at 2,176 m among deodar, pine, oak and rhododendron, with views across southern Shimla to the Tara Devi temple. It is credited to the Rana of Junga in the 18th century, though the exact date of its founding is unknown, and pilgrims come chiefly with family and marriage concerns.

name: Engan Brahmapurisvarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple, also called Brahmeesvaram, in the village of Engan about 13 km from Tiruvarur. Its walled prakara holds several subsidiary shrines, including a prominent Murugan sannidhi reached from the southern entrance.

name: Pathala Ponniamman Temple
significance: An Amman temple in Kilpauk, Chennai, traced to the time of Chennappa Nayak and now administered by the Tamil Nadu HR&CE department. It serves as the kuladeivam of roughly a lakh families across the city and its outskirts.
story: The image of the goddess is said to have come to light about thirty feet underground when a well was being dug at Purasawalkam, which is why she is called Pathala, of the netherworld.

name: Venugopalaswamy Temple, Ganapathy
significance: A Vaishnava temple in the Ganapathy quarter of Coimbatore, credited to a Mysore ruler of Yadava descent about a thousand years ago and renovated in 1764. It is now run by the Tamil Nadu HR&CE department, and the surrounding neighbourhood takes its name from the old Kottai Ganapathy shrine that stood before it.

name: Ramalingeswara Temple, Nandikandi
significance: An eleventh-century Shiva temple raised under the Kalyani Chalukyas, notable for its Bhumija shikhara over a star-shaped sanctum. It survives as a rare Deccan example of that form, though reported to be in poor repair.

name: Sankara Narayanasamy Temple, Sankarankovil
deity: Sankara Linga Swamy (Shiva) with Gomathi Amman, and Sankaranarayana, the joined form of Shiva and Vishnu
significance: The great temple that gives Sankarankovil its name, attributed to the Pandya king Ukkira Pandiyan in the tenth century and unusual in enshrining Shiva and Vishnu in a single joined form. Its Chithirai car festival and the Aadi Thabasu observance draw large crowds each year.

name: Kanak Bhawan
significance: One of Ayodhya's principal shrines, housing images of Rama and Sita in a palace-like building rebuilt in 1891 by Maharani Vrishabhan Kunwari and Maharaj Mahendra Pratap Singh. Its form deliberately echoes the palaces of Rajasthan and Bundelkhand.
story: Tradition holds that Kaikeyi gave this golden mansion to Rama and Sita as their private residence immediately after their marriage.

name: Hanuman Dandi Temple
significance: A shrine on the island of Beyt Dwarka that is rare in showing Hanuman together with his son Makaradhwaja, an unusual pairing given Hanuman's celibacy. Pilgrims to Dwarka commonly include it in their circuit.
story: Makaradhwaja is said to have been born of a drop of Hanuman's sweat swallowed by a fish, and father and son met in battle during the Ramayana.

name: Manokamna Mandir
significance: A Shiva temple in the Mithila country of north Bihar, roughly thirteen miles from Janakpur, whose name marks it as the place where wishes are granted. Its main gathering is the annual Sravani Mela.
story: Sita is said to have worshipped Girija Devi for twelve years and then to have been directed to this spot, where prayers are fulfilled.

name: Ratneshwar Mahadev Temple
significance: Varanasi's celebrated leaning temple, standing at the foot of Manikarnika Ghat with a tilt of about nine degrees and its sanctum flooded for much of the year. Revenue records date it to 1825-30, though its patron is disputed between a servant of Raja Man Singh, the Amethi royal house, Baija Bai of Gwalior and Ratna Bai, a servant of Ahilya Bai of Indore.
story: One account holds that Ahilya Bai cursed the temple to lean because her servant Ratna Bai had named it after herself.

name: Shri Viswa Vinayaka Mandir, Rhenock
significance: A four-storeyed Ganesha temple 108 feet tall on a 2.56-acre site in eastern Sikkim, housing fifty-one forms of the god. Its foundation was laid on 20 April 2008 and it was inaugurated on 3 October 2016, built with materials from Thailand and craftsmen from Nepal and West Bengal.

name: Shree Brahma Baidarkala Garadi Kshetra
significance: A garadi shrine on the Mangalore-Bangalore highway about 4 km from central Mangalore, sacred to the Tuluva community. It venerates the twin heroes Koti and Chennayya, placed by the article in the period c. 1556-1591 CE.

name: Aryadurga Devi Temple, Devihasol
significance: A goddess temple in Devihasol village of Rajapur taluka, about 18 km from Rajapur and 380 km from Mumbai, and a regional centre of Devi worship in the Konkan. The article gives no coordinates, so the Wikidata point is used.
story: The shrine is said to stand where the goddess appeared for a moment before an aged devotee named Palsule Desai and vanished, leaving her footprints inside the mandir; she is also remembered for destroying the demon Vratsaru.

name: Sundernath Temple
significance: A major historic Shiva temple of the Mithila region, standing close to the India-Nepal border in Araria district. It draws worshippers from northern Bihar and southern Nepal, especially at Maha Shivaratri and on Purnima days.

name: Uttara Guruvayurappan Temple
significance: Delhi's Guruvayurappan temple, founded on 17 May 1983 by the Arsha Dharma Parishad and completed on the same date in 1989, modelled on the Kerala shrine of the same deity. Built in Kerala style with gopurams to east and west and a two-chambered sanctum, it is a focus of the city's Malayali and Tamil communities.

name: Tulja Bhavani Temple, Peddamunigal
significance: A Tulja Bhavani temple built in the mid-1950s by Kethavath Chandru Naik with local support, standing above the Krishna river near Nagarjuna Sagar Dam on the edge of the Nallamala forest.
story: The goddess is said to have come to the aid of Anubuti, a sage's wife whose penance on the Mandakini was being disturbed by the demon Kukur, and to have taken the name Tulja Bhavani after destroying him.

name: Alampur Papanasi Temples
deity: Shiva (as the dancing Natesha), with shrines to Devi and Vishnu
significance: A cluster of twenty-three Nagara-plan shrines at Alampur raised between the 9th and 11th centuries under the Rashtrakutas and later Chalukyas. With the neighbouring Navabrahma temples they formed the Brahmeshvara tirtha, a Kalamukha and Pashupata Shaiva centre of wide regional influence until the Delhi Sultanate raids of the 14th-15th centuries; the Archaeological Survey of India shifted the group to higher ground after 1980 to save it from the Srisailam reservoir.

name: Macchapurisvarar Temple, Koyildevarayanpettai
deity: Shiva (Macchapurisvarar), with the goddess Sugantha Kunthalambigai
significance: A Shiva temple 3 km from Papanasam credited to Aditya Chola I and counted among the Vaippu Sthalams sung by Sambandar. Its prakaram holds an unusual Subramania shrine in which the god stands with Valli and Devasena while holding the conch and discus.

name: Dakshinakokarnesvarar Temple, Pulivalam
significance: A Shiva temple about 3 km from Pulivalam on the Tiruvarur-Thiruthuraipoondi road, listed among the Vaippu Sthalams praised by Appar. Two further temples of the same name stand in Tiruchirappalli district.

name: Kodiyalur Agastheeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple near Peralam notable for its solar and planetary shrines: Surya stands with his consorts Sayadevi and Ushadevi, with Yama on the south and Shani on the north, and the prakara adds Muruga, Vinayaka, Chandikesvara, the Navagraha, Bhairava and Lakshmi.
story: The site is held to be the birthplace of the planetary deities Shani and Yama, both sons of Surya.

name: Shiva Temple, Bavka
significance: A panchayatana Shiva complex near Dahod built during the reign of the last Chaulukya king Bhima II, with a central shrine ringed by four subsidiary ones. Its dense erotic carving has earned it the nickname 'the Khajuraho of Gujarat'; it is an ASI Monument of National Importance and was restored in 2009.
story: Local tradition credits the temple to a devadasi who is said to have raised it in a single night.

name: Agastheeswaram Agastheeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple 5 km from Kanyakumari that gives its name to the surrounding taluk, counted among the Vaippu Sthalams sung by Appar and associated with the sage Agastya and his wife Lopamudra.

name: Vishamangalesvarar Temple, Thudaiyur
significance: A Shiva temple about 10 km from Tiruchirappalli on the Lalgudi road, counted among the Vaippu Sthalams sung by Appar. It is unusual in placing Vishnu with his consorts in the niche that a Shiva temple normally gives to Chandra and Surya, and its inner prakara holds shrines to Vinayaka, Subramania and Saraswati.
story: The name recalls the churning of the ocean of milk, when Shiva is said to have held back the poison that rose from it and so saved the world.

name: Aayiram Kaliamman Temple
significance: A coastal Kaliamman temple at T.R. Pattinam whose image is made entirely of wood and kept in wooden caskets. Its name comes from the thousand-item puja performed once every five years in the Tamil month of Vaikasi, which draws pilgrims from across Tamil Nadu and Puducherry.
story: A Senguntha Mudaliar devotee is said to have dreamt of a casket on the shore, and found there the next morning a silver box holding the goddess with a palm-leaf instructing that she be worshipped daily with a thousand offerings.

name: Varahaswamy Temple, Tirumala
significance: A shrine on the Tirumala hill held to be older than the Venkateswara temple beside it and renovated by Pedda Tirumalacharya in 1535. Pilgrims are enjoined to take darshan of Varaha before Venkateswara, without which the Tirumala pilgrimage is not counted complete; it is administered by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams.
story: Having lifted the earth clear of the demon Hiranyaksha, Varaha is said to have settled on this hill, and at the opening of the Kali age to have granted land here to Venkateswara at his request.

name: Galteshwar Temple
significance: A 12th-century Shiva temple near Dakor, unusual for its period in following the central Indian bhumija form of Malwa rather than Paramara models while carrying Gujarati Chaulukya ornament. Its square sanctum opens into an octagonal pillared hall; the shikhara and mandapa fell in 1908 and the Archaeological Survey of India completed their restoration in September 2021.
story: The site is linked in tradition to the sage Galava, whose name it carries, and to the mythical king Chandrahas.

name: Sri Ranganayaka Swamy Temple
significance: Built in Saka 1685 (about 1763) by Baheri Gopala Rao of the Wanaparthy Samsthanam as a deliberate copy of the Ranganatha temple at Srirangam, which earned it the name Uttara Srirangapuram, the Srirangam of the north. A tank called Ranga Samudram was dug alongside it, and mukha mandapas were added later by Sankaramba, wife of a succeeding ruler.

name: Sankat Mochan Temple, Shimla
significance: A Hanuman temple at 1,975 m on the Chandigarh-Shimla highway, begun by Neem Karoli Baba in 1950, laid out in 1962 under Lieutenant Governor Bajrang Bahadur Singh and inaugurated on 21 June 1966. It also houses Rama, Sita and Lakshmana, Shiva and Ganesha, with a shrine to Neem Karoli Baba added in 1998, and serves bhandara meals on its busiest days.

name: Kodumbu Subramanya Swamy Temple
deity: Murugan (Subramanya Swami) standing with Valli and Deivanai
significance: A Murugan temple in the Soka Nasini valley about 10 km south-east of Palakkad, built in Dravidian form by Sengunthar Kaikola Mudaliyar weavers who had migrated from Kanchipuram during the Vijayanagara period to escape heavy taxation.
story: The weavers are said to have heard a voice calling 'I am coming' as they returned from Avinashi, and to have found in the bushes a shining stone which they installed as their community deity Subramanya.

name: Rishabesvarar Temple, Sengam
significance: A Shiva temple at Sengam counted among the Vaippu Sthalams sung by Appar. The settlement appears as Sengama in the Sangam poem Malaipatukatam and was later known as both Sengam and Kannai.

name: Kukadeshwar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the bank of the Kukadi river about 15 km west of Junnar and some 3 km from Chavand fort, known for its carved sculpture. Its roof is now in a dilapidated state.

name: Avanangattilkalari Vishnumaya Temple
deity: Vishnumaya (Chathan), shown in fierce form riding a buffalo
builtDisplay: over 500 years old; rebuilt under Sakthan Thampuran
significance: Regarded as the head shrine of the Vishnumaya (Chathan) temples of Kerala, more than five centuries old and reconstructed with the financial backing of Sakthan Thampuran. It keeps Shakteya usages now rare in Kerala, including the niyogam oracle pronounced by a possessed velichappadu, and holds the ten-day Vellattumaholsavam in Kumbham.
story: Vishnumaya is said to have been born one of four hundred brothers, ten of whom swallowed the brahmastra in battle and helped Shiva's bhutas destroy the rakshasa.

name: Pokkunny Siva Temple
significance: One of the 108 celebrated Shiva temples of Kerala, built by the ruler of Kollengode, formerly Venganad, and long held by the Kollengode palace as a favoured shrine. It stands within a pond called Perumkulam and keeps Maha Shivaratri as its chief festival.
story: Parashurama is said to have set the lingam within the pool so that the water would temper the god's fierceness and calm him.

name: Chandramouleesvarar Temple, Thazhamangai
significance: One of the seven Saptamangai or Chakkarapalli shrines linked to the Saptamatrikas. Unusually for Thanjavur district its sanctum is built of brick rather than granite, and its Chandikesvara image is dated to the 10th century.
story: Chandra, cursed by Daksha for favouring one daughter above the rest, is said to have come to Thazhamangai and been freed of the curse by worshipping here.

name: Shiva Temple, Narayanapur
significance: An 11th-century trikutachala temple about 4 km from Basavakalyan, its sanctum opening onto two pillared mandapas, with salabhanjika figures on the outer walls and floral ceilings within. The abundance of Vishnu and Lakshmi imagery suggests it may first have been a Vaishnava foundation; a concrete roof has recently been added against water damage, and the deity is taken in procession round the village each August.

name: Burhi Gosani Devalaya, Jorhat
deity: Burhi Gosani, the primordial goddess identified with Durga
significance: A Shakta temple founded in 1794 by the Ahom king Gaurinath Singha after he moved his capital from Rangpur to Jorhat. Its image had earlier been brought from the Jaintia hills by Rudra Singha, and Durga Puja remains the temple's principal observance.

name: Thiruvettisvarar Temple, Thiruvettisvaranpettai
significance: A Shiva temple on Triplicane High Road in Chennai, also called Thirupattinam and counted among the Vaippu Sthalams sung by Appar. Hymns of Pamban Swamigal and Ramalinga Swamigal are inscribed here, and stucco panels depict the six abodes of Murugan.

name: Begunbari Kali Temple
deity: Sashan Kali, mistress of the cremation ground
significance: A temple of Sashan Kali near Khirai in Panskura, traced to the reign of Raja Rajnarayan Roy in the third quarter of the 18th century. After the original shrine was destroyed it was rebuilt as a replica of the Dakshineswar Kali temple, and its Jyoisho Utsob in June draws thousands to a large attendant fair.
story: Two wrestler brothers of a poor Bagdi family, Hinu and Dinu Dung, are said to have survived cholera after vowing worship to Kali here, and, too poor to pay for it, to have turned to robbery to keep the vow.

name: Bhavatarini Shmashanpith Kali Temple
significance: A Kali temple raised in 1994 on a plot that had served the village of Balidangri as a Hindu cremation ground. Night worship kept up there for decades by local residents was eventually formalised into a permanent shrine to Bhavatarini, a form of Kali.

name: Iswara Temple, Jalasangvi
significance: An eleventh-century Shiva temple attributed to the reign of Vikramaditya VI, with a dance hall on eight pillars, a Nandi chamber and a linga sanctum. Its salabhanjika bracket figures are regarded as a source for the later Hoysala bracket-figure tradition.

name: Sree Vasudevapuram Mahavishnu Temple
significance: A Vishnu temple near Aluva whose idol shows the god embracing Mahalakshmi, so that worship here is addressed jointly to Vishnu and to Lakshmi in her eight forms. After a long decline under its early Brahmin custodians the temple's standing was restored through the intervention of Vilwamangalam Swamikal, and the Tambula Samarpanam offering remains its central rite.
story: Mahalakshmi is said to have promised to appear here in eight forms over the eight days beginning at Akshaya Tritiya, granting a different boon in each.

name: Virundeeswarar Temple
significance: One of the older Shiva temples of the Coimbatore region, credited to Chola kings and reckoned over 1,300 years old, with a self-manifested linga and a second linga in the sanctum. It is administered by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
story: Sundaramurthy Nayanar is said to have been fed here by an old couple who then revealed themselves as Shiva and Parvati; because the god offered virundhu, a feast, he is called Virundeeswarar.

name: Kanadikavu Shree Vishnumaya Kuttichathan Swamy Temple
significance: Described as the oldest temple in Kerala dedicated to Vishnumaya Kuttichathan, some 20 km from Thrissur, where 390 Kuttichathans are venerated as attendant deities alongside shrines to Bhadrakali, Bhuvaneswari, Nagaraja and Brahmarakshas.
story: A sage remembered as Koonamuthappan is said to have won mantras from the Goddess through severe penance, meditated in the Himalayas, and returned to Peringottukara to install Chathan Swamy for the good of humankind.

name: Kankaleshwar Temple
significance: A star-plan Shiva temple at Beed, its domed roof carried on twenty-four pillars and its niches filled with carved gods and goddesses. No inscription records its date; after the region passed to a Muslim kingdom a parapet was added on the roof for prayers there while Hindu worship continued below, and it was then known as the Khanqah Deval.

name: Idangazhi Nayanar Temple, Kodumbalur
significance: A Shiva temple at Kodumbalur commemorating Idangazhi Nayanar, the local king counted among the Saiva saints, who built temples and endowed worship in the town. Aippasi Karthigai is among the festivals kept here.
story: A devotee who had spent everything on worship stole paddy from the royal store; on hearing why, Idangazhi freed him and threw the granary open to all who needed grain for offerings to Shiva.

name: Chengalamma Parameshwari Temple
builtDisplay: 10th c. (Chola shrine); worship from the 4th–5th c.
significance: A goddess temple on the bank of the Kalangi river at the southern edge of Sullurpeta, whose worship is traced to the fourth and fifth centuries and whose first built shrine, a small hut, is credited to the Cholas around the tenth century. The image is revered as Trikale Chengali, its left side read as Parvati, its right as Saraswati and its centre as Mahalakshmi.

name: Agastheesvarar Temple, Purisai
significance: A Shiva temple at Purisai whose presiding deity is Agastheesvarar and whose goddess is Akilandesvari. It is counted among the Vaippu Sthalams, shrines named in passing in the hymns of the Nayanar Sundarar.

name: Tarkeshwar Nath Temple
builtDisplay: c. 1727, with the founding of Jaipur
significance: One of the best known of the old Shiva temples that earned Jaipur the name Chhoti Kashi, dated to about 1727 and believed to have been laid out by the city's planner Vidyadhar Bhattacharya. Its priesthood was entrusted to Vyas family priests brought from Amer, and Mahashivaratri and the Mondays of Shravan draw the largest crowds.
story: After a fight between a lion and a goat on the spot, a voice is said to have risen from the ground; digging there uncovered the self-manifested Shivalinga now worshipped in the temple.

name: Trinetreshwar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Tarnetar attributed to the Pratihara ruler Mihira Bhoja in the eighth century. It is best known today for the Trinetreshwar Mahadev Mela, the annual fair held around it.

name: Devunigutta Temple
significance: A sixth-century Shiva temple on a forested plateau some 60 km east of Warangal, its carving dominated by Ardhanarishvara and close in feeling to Gupta-period sculpture. Recorded by the Archaeological Survey of India in 2012 but left abandoned, it drew wide attention only when photographs of it spread online in 2017.

name: Rudrakodisvarar Temple, Tirukalukundram
significance: A Shiva temple at Tirukalukundram whose presiding deity is Rudrakodisvarar and whose goddess is Tiripurasundari, the main shrine facing east and hers facing south. It is counted among the Vaippu Sthalams named in the hymns of the Nayanar Appar.

name: Nameswara Temple, Pillalamarri
dynasty: Recherla Reddi, feudatories of the Kakatiyas
significance: A Saiva temple on the bank of the Musi built about 1202 by Namireddi of the Recherla Reddi family, vassals of the Kakatiyas, and named for him. It is one of four closely carved stone and granite temples of the Kakatiya era at Pillalamarri, its pillars finely worked but heavily defaced.

name: Erakeswara Temple, Pillalamarri
dynasty: Recherla Reddi, feudatories of the Kakatiyas
significance: A Saiva temple at Pillalamarri commissioned in the early thirteenth century by Erakasani, wife of the Recherla chief Beti Reddi, and named lord of Eraka after her. Its workmanship is close to that of the Ramappa temple and Kota Gullu; vandalised during the raids of Alauddin Khilji, it was re-established by 1357 under a chief serving Kapaya Nayaka of the Musunuri line.

name: Tungareshwar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the Tungareshwar plateau above Vasai, more than 2,000 feet up, with a shrine to the goddess Khodiyar Mata beside it and a linga ringed by a brass serpent. Mahashivaratri and the Mondays of Shravan bring the largest gatherings and a communal feast.
story: Parashurama is said to have killed a demon named Tunga at this spot, and the temple to have been raised in his honour.

name: Pazhavangadi Ganapathy Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple at East Fort, close to the Padmanabhaswamy temple, whose seated image was kept by the Nair Brigade at Padmanabhapuram and installed here when the brigade moved to Thiruvananthapuram. It passed to the Indian Army after the state forces were integrated, and holds thirty-two further sculptures of Ganesha.

name: Mudhai Devi Temple
deity: Mudhai Devi (with an Uma-Maheshwara image in the sanctum)
significance: A partly ruined twelfth-century goddess temple in the Khandesh village of Waghali, built on a stellate plan with twenty-four pillars carrying sanctum, ardhamandapa, mandapa and portico. The Archaeological Survey of India declared it a monument of national importance in 1914.

name: Mahadev Temple, Deobaloda
significance: A thirteenth-century Kalachuri Shiva temple at Deobaloda, protected by the Archaeological Survey of India, whose shikhara is now missing. Local tradition that it went up in only six months earned it the nickname the six-month temple, and a stepped tank beside it is held to be linked to Arang by a tunnel.
story: The sculptor is said to have worked so absorbed that he laboured naked; when his sister came with his food both leapt into the ponds in shame, and he is said to have taken the tunnel from the tank to Arang, where he turned to stone.

name: Dronacharya Temple, Gurugram
significance: A temple to Dronacharya, the teacher of the Pandavas and Kauravas after whom Gurugram is named, founded in 1872 by Singha Bharat, a devotee of Drona's wife Shitala Devi. It grew from a single room to two and is looked after today by five families.

name: Sri Aastik Swami Mandir, Raebareli
significance: A temple on the bank of the Sai river at Lalupur, about 10 km from Raebareli town, counted among the principal places of worship in India for Aastik Swami, revered as the lord of snakes. Nagpanchami is its main festival.
story: In the Mahabharata account retold here, Astika halted Janamejaya's snake sacrifice and saved the serpents, who in return blessed him so that those who worship him are protected from venomous creatures.

name: Nilkanth Temple, Mandu
significance: A Shiva temple at Mandu raised over an older shrine between April 1574 and April 1575 by Shah Badgah, Akbar's governor of Mandu, and commissioned by the emperor for his Hindu consort Mariam-uz-Zamani. Built to serve as both palace and temple, it is now used purely as a temple and draws pilgrims from across India.
story: The name Neelkanth, the blue-throated one, is traced to Shiva swallowing the Halahala poison churned from the ocean, which stained his throat blue.

name: Gadarmal Devi Temple
significance: A sandstone yogini temple at Badoh with a rectangular shrine under a tall massive shikhara, forty-two niches for goddess images and seven subsidiary shrines around it; eighteen of the broken goddess figures that once sat in its grooves survive. It is compared with the Teli ka Mandir at Gwalior and now holds both Hindu and Jain images.
story: Locals hold that the temple was raised by shepherds, gadariya, which is how it came by the name Gadarmal.

name: Keezhtali Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Kodungallur counted among the 108 Shiva temples of the Chera country and one of its four thali temples, which held a place in the administration of ancient Kerala. It is among the few Hindu temples recorded as destroyed during Tipu Sultan's campaign.
story: Folklore holds that the sage Parashurama himself installed the Shiva image here.

name: Na-Pukhuri Shiva Dol
significance: A 26 m Shiva temple on the south bank of the Rudrasagar tank, some 8 km from Sivasagar, built in 1773 in the reign of Lakshmi Singha under the supervision of Madan Darika Hajarika and consecrated under Gaurinath Singha. It is the last temple of the Ahom period and marks the end of that kingdom's temple building.

name: Jwala Ji Temple, Khrew
significance: A twentieth-century shrine at Khrew commissioned by Raja Daya Krishna Kaul to Jwala Ji, the family goddess of many Kashmiri Hindu households. Kalhana's Rajatarangini names the village as Khaduvi and describes its springs; the annual Jwalamukhi fair here is kept by Hindus and Muslims alike.
story: The goddess is said to have shown herself first as a radiant flame, and to have settled here for good after stopping the gods on their way to seize Kubera's treasure.

name: Sanchareswar Mahadev Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the village of Umarda in Udaipur district, worshipped as Sanchareswar Mahadev. The published account of it is slight and records neither a date nor a patron.

name: Altharakkal Sree Muthappan Madapura
significance: A madapura, or shrine, to Muthappan in Pullur village about 6 km from Kanhangad in northern Kerala, built in the kavu idiom of the region. Local tradition treats Muthappan as a manifestation of Shiva.

name: Laxminrusingha Temple
significance: A Kalinga-style Narasimha temple in Purbakachha village in the Salipur area of Cuttack district. Its principal observances are Nrusingha Chaturdashi and Dola Purnima.

name: Harimukteesvarar Temple, Ariyamangai
deity: Harimukteesvarar (Shiva, as a metre-high lingam); goddess Gnanambikai Amman
significance: A modest Shiva temple with a small vimana and no gopura, standing about ten kilometres from Chakkarapalli on the Thanjavur–Kumbakonam road. It is one of the seven Saptamangai shrines of the Matrikas, and holds five saptamatrika figures of the ninth century and a Dakshinamurthy of the thirteenth.
story: Vishnu is said to have worshipped the lingam here, and from Hari, a name of Vishnu, the deity is called Harimukteesvarar.

name: Tribeniswar Temple
significance: A Kalinga-style Shiva temple at Chasakhanda in the Mahanga block, about thirty-three kilometres north-east of Cuttack city off National Highway 5. Mahashivratri and Kartik Purnima are its principal festivals.

name: Siddheshwar Temple, Toka
deity: Shiva (large lingam, with Parvati on the rear wall)
significance: A twelfth- to thirteenth-century Seuna (Yadava) temple complex of three shrines, to Shiva, Vishnu and the Devi, with later additions from the Peshwa period. Its walls carry a dense programme of carvings drawn from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas.

name: Shrimant Bhausaheb Rangari Ganapati Temple
significance: The Ganesha installed here in 1892 by Bhausaheb Lakshman Jawle, known as Shrimant Bhausaheb Rangari, was the focus of India's first sarvajanik or public Ganesh celebration. The wood-and-bran idol shows Ganesha slaying a demon, an image the freedom-fighter founder intended as the victory of good over evil.

name: Gurdwara Guptsar Sahib
deity: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru
significance: A gurdwara at Chhattiana marking the visit of Guru Gobind Singh to the village after the Battle of Muktsar in 1705. The shrine of the recluse Ibrahim, whom the Guru is said to have named Ajmer Singh, stands to its north-west.

name: Gurdwara Karamsar Rara Sahib
deity: Named for Sant Karam Singh; the village was sanctified by Guru Hargobind, the sixth Sikh Guru
significance: Founded in 1936 after Sant Isher Singh and Sant Kishen Singh settled at Rara at the request of Sardar Gian Singh Rarewala, on land bought and partly donated by neighbouring villagers. It takes its name from Sant Karam Singh of Hoti Mardan.
story: The village is said to have become Rara Sahib, rather than plain Rara, after the sixth Guru, Hargobind Sahib, visited it.

name: Gurdwara Manji Sahib, Alamgir
deity: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru
significance: A historic gurdwara near the village of Alamgir in Ludhiana district, marking a place where Guru Gobind Singh stayed briefly.

name: Gurdwara Naulakha Sahib
deity: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru, and Mata Gujri
significance: Established in 1830 in Naulakha village, roughly thirteen kilometres from Sirhind, to commemorate a visit by Guru Tegh Bahadur and Mata Gujri.
story: Lakhi Shah Wanjara, having lost an ox, is said to have vowed an offering to Guru Tegh Bahadur; when the animal returned he gave nine takas, which the Guru declared equal to nine lakh, and told the villagers to call the place Naulakha.

name: Vedadri Narasimha Temple
significance: A hill temple on the Krishna river housing five forms of Narasimha, counted among the Pancha Narasimha Kshetras. It was patronised under the Kakatiya empire and renovated in the nineteenth century by Raja Vasireddy Muktiswara Prasad Nayudu.
story: The demon Somakasura is said to have stolen the Vedas and hidden them in the ocean, whereupon Vishnu took the form of Narasimha to recover them and turned them into the hill of Vedadri beside the Krishna.

name: Shanti Stupa, Leh
deity: Relics of the Buddha, enshrined at the base by the 14th Dalai Lama
significance: A white peace pagoda above Chanspa in Leh, begun in 1983 under the Japanese monk Bhikshu Gyomyo Nakamura and finished in 1991, with relics of the Buddha installed at its base by the 14th Dalai Lama, who inaugurated the foundation in 1985. Built by the Ladakh Shanti Stupa Committee with Japanese and Indian support and the backing of Kushok Bakula Rinpoche, it departs deliberately from traditional Ladakhi form.

name: Deopani Durga Mandir
significance: A trust-run Durga temple at Bokajan in Karbi Anglong, built around an image dug up together with other archaeological material on the Deopani Tea Estate by its owner, the Rajput planter Surendra Nath Roy. Durga Puja is its main annual observance.

name: Mankeshwar Temple, Zodage
dynasty: Yadava or Shilahara, under Chalukya suzerainty
significance: A thirteenth-century basalt Shiva temple at Zodage in Nashik district, thought to have been raised by the Yadavas or the Shilaharas under Chalukya overlordship, with carvings of Chamunda, Bhairava and Vishnu. Mahashivratri is its chief festival and a fair is held on the thirteenth day of Magha.

name: Shri Kedar Temple
