significance: A Shiva temple on Madanachala hill at Hajo, completed in 1753 under the Ahom king Rajeswara Singha; it is one of the principal shrines of the Hajo pilgrimage cluster in lower Assam.
story: The linga in the central chamber is revered as swayambhu, said to have arisen of itself rather than being carved.

name: Pathrol Kali Temple
significance: A Kali shrine near Madhupur in the Santhal Pargana, attributed to Raja Digvijay Singh some six or seven centuries ago; it draws large crowds at Kali Puja and during the Durga festival.

name: Buddha Samyak Darshan Museum and Memorial Stupa
significance: A modern memorial stupa and museum at Vaishali built to enshrine the relics of the Buddha that had been given to the Licchavi rulers of the city, approved in 2013 and completed for inauguration in July 2025. It was assembled from more than 42,000 Rajasthani sandstone blocks without modern reinforcement.
story: Tradition holds that after the Buddha's mahaparinirvana his remains were divided into eight shares among eight kings, each of whom raised a stupa over his portion.

name: Nidhivan
significance: A dense sacred grove of tulsi and other trees in the heart of Vrindavan, containing the Rang Mahal, the Bansichori Radharani shrine and the Raslila Sthali, and associated with the saint-musician Swami Haridas.
story: Devotees believe Radha and Krishna still dance the rasa-lila in the grove at night, so it is barricaded shut after dark.

name: Khema Baba Temple
significance: A folk shrine at Baytu in the Barmer desert dedicated to Khema Baba, a social reformer of Baytu Bhopji who came to be venerated as a deity across western Rajasthan and Gujarat.

name: Ahmedabad Kali Bari
significance: A Kali temple in west Ahmedabad built in 2014 by the Bengal Cultural Association of Ahmedabad; it serves the city's Bengali community and also houses shrines to Shiva, Rama, Sita, Hanuman and Krishna.

name: Arulmigu Munthi Vinayagar Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple in the Puliakulam quarter of Coimbatore, opened in its present form in 1982, known for a monolithic granite Vinayagar image about 19 feet high and weighing some 190 tonnes.

name: Changdeva Temple
significance: A stone temple at the Tapi-Purna confluence dedicated to the yogi Changdeva Maharaj, built in dove-tailed black rock in the Hemadpanthi manner; ASI excavations from 2008 uncovered foundations of earlier stone temples and images of Ganesha, Vishnu and Hanuman.
story: Local legend holds that the temple was raised in the course of a single night that lasted six months.

name: Mamal Temple (Mamaleshwar)
builtDisplay: c. 400 CE, rebuilt in the medieval period
significance: One of the oldest surviving Shiva temples in Kashmir, dated to about 400 CE and rebuilt in medieval times; the Rajatarangini records King Jayasimha crowning it with a golden kalasa.
story: The name is glossed as 'Mam Mal', 'do not go', from the tale that Parvati set Ganesha to guard the spot and Shiva, refused entry, struck off his head and replaced it with an elephant's.

name: Jagannath Temple, Dibrugarh
significance: An 85-foot Jagannath temple in Dibrugarh completed in 2014 at the initiative of Janaki Ballabh Patnaik, then Governor of Assam, and run by the Sri Sri Jagannath Cultural Trust; its plan follows an earlier form of the Puri temple and its grounds hold seven subsidiary shrines.

name: Agatheeswarar Temple, Karur
significance: A Shiva temple at the river confluence near Karur, over a thousand years old and credited to Rajendra Chola I (r. 1014-1044).
story: The sage Agastya is said to have consecrated a lingam of sand here before Vaali could install a lingam brought from Kashi, so Vaali founded the Valeeswarar temple on the opposite bank instead.

name: Maha Mrityunjay Temple
significance: A Shiva temple near Puranigudam in Nagaon district begun in 2003 by Acharya Bhrigu Giri Maharaj and finished in February 2021; the 126-foot structure is itself shaped as a shivalinga and is claimed to be the largest of its kind.
story: The site is held to be where the guru Shukracharya recited the Mahamrityunjaya mantra.

name: Haleshwar Sthan
significance: A Shiva shrine north-west of Sitamarhi town in the Mithila region, documented as older than the 17th century and one of the busier pilgrimage sites of northern Bihar, especially during Shravan.
story: The temple is said to have been founded by King Videha while he performed the putra-yeshti sacrifice, and named Haleshwarnath after him.

name: Chaukhandi Stupa
significance: A terraced brick stupa at Sarnath marking the place where the Buddha is said to have met his first disciples on the way from Bodh Gaya; an octagonal tower was later raised on it by Govardhan, son of Raja Todar Mal, to mark a visit by the Mughal emperor Humayun.

name: Kshemkari Mata Temple
significance: A goddess temple at the old town of Bhinmal in Jalore district dedicated to Kshemkari Devi, locally called Khimaj Mata.

name: Badhangarhi Temple
significance: A hilltop Kali temple in the Pindar valley of Garhwal, founded by a Katyuri king and altered in 1670 and again in the colonial period, when Commissioner G. W. Traill built a shrine for a relocated Nanda Devi image.
story: Local tradition says Traill was struck with snow-blindness by the offended goddess and recovered only after building her a temple.

name: Baba Mukteshwar Dham
significance: A Shiva temple at Deohar in Madhubani district, believed to be roughly two hundred years old and built in the Tirhut idiom of Mithila; excavation at the site brought up a shivalinga and images of Ganesha and Parvati that were installed for worship.

name: Shri Chamunda Devi Mandir
significance: A Shakta temple on the Baner river in Kangra district, roughly four centuries old, which houses an image brought down from the far older hill shrine of Aadi Himani Chamunda.
story: A king and his priest are said to have prayed for the goddess's leave to move her image to an accessible spot, and she revealed its location to the priest in a dream.

name: Ahichchhatra Jain Temples
significance: A Jain tirtha on the ancient mound of Ahichchhatra in Bareilly district, held to be the place where Parshvanatha, the twenty-third Tirthankara, attained kevala jnana. Both Digambara and Svetambara establishments stand here; the Digambara temple was rebuilt in 1975 and further shrines added in 2002 and 2007, on a site whose antiquities run back to the Indo-Scythian, Kushan and Gupta periods.
story: While Parshvanatha meditated, a demon is said to have flooded him to the neck, whereupon the serpent king Dharanendra spread a thousand-hooded canopy above him and the goddess Padmavati coiled about his body to hold him clear of the water.

name: Chavundaraya Basadi
significance: A Jain temple on Chandragiri hill at Shravanabelagola, raised in 982 CE by the Ganga minister Chavundaraya during the reign of Marasimha II and completed by his son Jinadeva. Its sanctum holds an image of Neminatha, and the temple is also called Sruta-tirtha because the acharya Nemichandra is said to have composed the Gommatsara here.

name: Aharji Jain Tirth
significance: A Digambara Jain tirtha near Baldeogarh in Tikamgarh district, known for an eighteen-foot standing (khadgasana) colossus of Shantinatha. The main temple was built in 1180 CE by two brothers, Jahad and Udaichandra, under the Chandela ruler Paramardi, within a phase of Jain building at the site running from the tenth to the thirteenth century.

name: Andeshwar Parshwanath Jain Temple
significance: A Digambara Jain atishaya kshetra in Kushalgarh tehsil of Banswara district, some 40 km from Banswara town. The fourteenth-century temple's chief image is a mulnayak of Parshvanatha thought to be older still, of the twelfth or thirteenth century.
story: The Parshvanatha image is said to have come to light when local tribespeople turned it up while working their fields.

name: Tirumalai Jain Complex
builtDisplay: 9th–10th c. (Chola); later shrines to the 17th c.
significance: A Jain hill complex near Polur with three caves, two temples and a 16-foot sculpture of the Tirthankara Neminatha, in use from at least the ninth century. The Kunthavai Jinalaya was endowed by the Chola princess Kundavai in the tenth century, and inscriptions of Rajendra Chola I survive here; Mahavira and Parshvanatha shrines were added in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
story: Tradition holds that eight thousand Jain monks who came south with Bhadrabahu performed penance on this hill and attained nirvana here.

name: Bijolia Parshvanath Temple
significance: A Digambara Jain pilgrimage centre at Bijolia, also called Tapodaya Tirth Kshetra, dedicated to Parshvanatha. Five temples were built here in 1160 CE by the merchant Lala during the reign of the Chahamana king Somesvara, laid out in a panchayatana arrangement beside a stepped reservoir.

name: Tijara Jain Temple
significance: A Digambara Jain atishaya kshetra at Tijara in Rajasthan, established in 1956 around a 15-inch white marble mulnayak of Chandraprabha, the eighth Tirthankara, whose inscription records its installation in V.S. 1554 (1497 CE). The temple is decorated with carvings, paintings and glasswork and stands about 110 km from Delhi.

name: Parsvanath Jain Temple-II, Khandagiri
significance: A twentieth-century Digambara Jain temple in the Khandagiri precinct at Bhubaneswar, built in the Kalinga idiom. Its sanctum enshrines a standing image of Parshvanatha crowned with a serpent hood.

name: Nakoda Parshvanath Tirth (Nakodaji)
significance: One of the principal Svetambara Jain tirthas of western Rajasthan, standing between the villages of Vikrampura and Nakoda in Barmer district. The present temple dates to the eleventh century and was renovated by Acharya Kirtisuri in 1449; its 24-inch black stone image of Parshvanatha is worshipped alongside the guardian Nakoda Bhairava, and the temple is managed by the Tapa Gaccha of the Murtipujaka Svetambaras.
story: The buried image is said to have eluded searchers until Bhairava appeared in a dream and pointed out the exact spot where it lay.

name: Bhagawan Chandraprabha Jain Temple, Kumbakonam
significance: A Jain temple in the temple town of Kumbakonam, established in 1903 with its consecration (panchakalyanaka) celebrated in 1905. Its presiding image is Chandraprabha, the eighth Tirthankara.

name: Shri Atma Vallabh Jain Smarak
significance: A Svetambara Jain memorial complex on the GT Karnal Road north of Delhi, raised between 1979 and 1989 by followers of Acharya Vijay Vallabh Suri in his memory. The main shrine enshrines Vasupujya, the twelfth Tirthankara, and the buildings follow traditional Jain temple architecture.

name: Neminatha Jain Temple, Malkheda
significance: A ninth-century Jain temple of Neminatha at Malkheda on the Kagina river, the settlement that as Manyakheta was the imperial capital of the Rashtrakutas under Amoghavarsha I and later of the Western Chalukyas. Its pillars and walls span the ninth to eleventh centuries, and a Jain Bhattaraka math continues at the site.

name: Mirpur Jain Temple
significance: A Svetambara Jain temple at Mirpur in Sirohi district, dedicated to the twenty-third Tirthankara Parshvanatha under the name Bhidbhanjan Parshvanath. Built in the ninth century under Solanki rule, it is noted for its marble domes, pillars and carved borders.
story: The main image shows the serpent king Dharanendra raising a five-hooded canopy over Parshvanatha to shield him from the storm loosed by his adversary Kamatha.

name: Dehra Temple
significance: A tenth-century Jain temple at Bhond near Ferozepur Jhirka in Haryana's Nuh district, dedicated to the Tirthankara Ajitanatha and carrying an inscription of 1451. Its fabric mixes Hindu temple forms with the Lodi idiom of the Delhi Sultanate; a Shiva lingam once kept here was later moved to the Jain temple at Ferozepur Jhirka.

name: Jahaj Mandir
significance: A Svetambara Jain temple at Mandwala in Jalore district, built between 1993 and 1999 in the shape of a ship some 55 feet high and faced in Makrana marble. Shantinatha is its mulnayak, at the centre of the shrine.
story: Devotees recount that at the cremation of Acharya Jin Kantisagar Suri on 3 December 1985 the master's right hand rose from the pyre and swayed, taken as a last blessing to the thousands watching.

name: Vahelna Jain Temple
significance: A twentieth-century Digambara Jain atishaya kshetra at Vahelna village in Muzaffarnagar district, formally titled Shri 1008 Parshvnath Digamber Jain Atishaya Kshetra. Its principal image is Parshvanatha seated in padmasana.

name: Vijayamangalam Jain Temple
significance: One of the oldest surviving Jain temples in the Kongu country, founded in 678 CE by the Velir king Konguvelir at Vijayamangalam in Erode district. Also called the Chandraprabha Tirthankarar temple, it is dedicated to Chandraprabha, the eighth Tirthankara.
story: Local tradition recalls a Tamil assembly convened here when Konguvelir composed the epic Perunkathai, his maidservant helping him answer the scholars' questions — an episode later commemorated by images installed at the temple.

name: Sarvodaya Jain Temple, Amarkantak
significance: A large Jain temple under construction at Amarkantak in Madhya Pradesh since 2006. Its mulnayak is a 24-tonne ashtadhatu image of Rishabhanatha set on a lotus-shaped ashtadhatu pedestal weighing 28 tonnes.

name: Lachhuar Jain Temple
significance: A Svetambara Jain temple at Lachhuar in Jamui district, built in 1857 under the patronage of Raja Dhanpat Singh Bahadur. It is dedicated to Mahavira and for a time sheltered an ancient image of the Tirthankara.

name: Mangi-Tungi
builtDisplay: images from 595 CE; 1343 inscription; 108-ft colossus consecrated 2016
significance: A twin-pinnacled Digambara Jain pilgrimage hill in Nashik district, honeycombed with rock-cut caves and shrines holding Tirthankara images in padmasana and kayotsarga. Images installed in 595 CE survive here and an inscription of 1343 is recorded in the Adinatha cave; a 108-foot statue was consecrated in 2016 at the inspiration of the nun Gyanmati Mataji.
story: Jain tradition holds that Rama, Hanuman, Sugriva and ninety-nine crore ascetics attained moksha from these hills.

name: Shantinatha Basadi, Jinanathapura
significance: A Hoysala-period Jain temple at Jinanathapura, just north of Shravanabelagola, dedicated to the sixteenth Tirthankara Shantinatha. Raised around 1117 during Vishnuvardhana's reign and attributed to Recana, a general and minister of Ballala II, it is admired for the dense lathe-turned pillars and wall sculpture typical of Hoysala work.

name: Ghantai Temple, Khajuraho
significance: A ruined Digambara Jain temple in the eastern group at Khajuraho, built around 995 CE under the Chandela king Dhanga and dedicated to Rishabhanatha. Only its pillared hall survives, and it takes its name from the chain-and-bell motif carved on those pillars.

name: Rinchenpong Monastery
significance: The third-oldest monastery in Sikkim, founded in 1730 by the Ngadakpa Lama above the twin villages of Rinchenpong and Kaluk at over 1,700 m, and begun with some ninety-eight lamas. It is a training centre for monks and keeps a rare image of the primordial Adi-Buddha in the Yab-Yum posture, in whose sanctum photography is now barred; the nearby Poison Pokhri lake is remembered as a symbol of resistance to foreign invasion.

name: Kapilnath Temple
significance: A 17th-century Shiva temple near Navratangarh in Gumla district, built in 1643 CE by the Nagvanshi king Ram Shah, successor of Durjan Shah, after the dynasty moved its capital from Khukhragarh. Unusually the Shiva linga stands outside rather than inside the shrine, and the temple draws its largest crowds at Shivratri.
story: Ram Shah is said to have seen his cow's milk dripping into the mouth of a cobra and then to have beheld Shiva himself, and on his guru's advice resolved to build the temple.

name: Tsuklakhang Palace
significance: The royal chapel of the Chogyals of Sikkim at Gangtok, established in 1898, whose altars carry images of the Buddha, bodhisattvas and tantric deities and whose halls hold a large collection of Buddhist scripture. It served as the setting for royal coronations, marriages and victory ceremonies, and hosts the Pang Lhabsol festival in mid-September in honour of Mount Khangchendzonga.

name: Maa Khadgeshwari Kali Mandir
deity: Kali, with Shiva in the same premises
significance: A Kali temple in the town of Araria whose image was first housed in a thatched hut in 1884; work on the present building began in 1987 and finished in 2011, funded by donations and public subscription. At 152 feet it is claimed to be the tallest Kali temple in the world, and it has been managed since the early 1970s by Sarojanand Dixit, a former footballer known as Nanu Baba.

name: Phensang Monastery
significance: A monastery of the Nyingma order about 9 km north of Gangtok, established in 1721 in the time of Jigme Pawo. Its principal festival falls on the 28th and 29th days of the tenth Tibetan month.

name: Ghanteshwar Temple, Mumbai
significance: A Hanuman temple in Khar West, Mumbai, founded in 1960 by a local man, Sakharam Rahate, and busiest on Tuesdays and Saturdays and at Hanuman Jayanti. Its name comes from the great number of bells hung about it.
story: Devotees hold that a wish granted here must be repaid with a bell, which is why the temple has accumulated so many.

name: Ulagalandha Perumal Temple, Singanallur
deity: Ulagalandha Perumal (Vishnu), with Sridevi and Bhoodevi
significance: A Vishnu temple in the Singanallur quarter of Coimbatore whose north-facing presiding image is cast in panchaloha. It was renovated in 2000 and its seven-tiered tower consecrated at a Kumbhabhishekam in 2005.
story: The temple's own account holds that the Chola king Karikalan founded it while passing through Singanallur on a campaign, for the welfare of the people.

name: Bermiok Monastery
deity: Amitābha and the thousand-armed Avalokiteśvara (Karma Kagyu)
significance: A Karma Kagyu monastery above Singtam in southern Sikkim, founded in 1873 and rebuilt in 1954 after earthquake damage. Its manilhakang holds images of Amitabha and the thousand-armed Avalokiteshvara, and its prayer-wheel building, also of 1954, was rebuilt in 1987.

name: Shri Raghunath Mandir, Kullu
significance: Founded in 1660 by Raja Jagat Singh of Kullu, this temple's Raghunath is treated as the presiding deity of the whole Kullu valley. Some three hundred village gods are carried in to attend him at the Kullu Dussehra, which draws hundreds of thousands of visitors.
story: Jagat Singh is said to have fallen ill with leprosy after an astrologer he wrongly accused died, and to have been cured only when images of Rama, Sita and Hanuman were fetched from Ayodhya and installed here.

name: Modheshwari Mata Temple, Modhera
deity: Modheshwari Mata, a form of Shakti
significance: Built under Bhima I of the Solanki dynasty in 1026–27, this goddess temple stands close to the celebrated Sun Temple at Modhera. Modheshwari Mata is the clan deity of the Modh community, and the shrine fills at Chaitra Navaratri.
story: The goddess Parvati is said to have appeared here as Modheshwari with eighteen arms to destroy the demon Karnat, who was ravaging the village.

name: Prasanna Venkatachalapathy Temple, Tallakulam
deity: Vishnu as Prasanna Venkatachalapathy, facing south
significance: A Vaishnava temple in the Tallakulam quarter of Madurai, credited to the Nayak ruler Thirumalai Nayak and administered within the Kallalagar temple establishment. Its Venkatachalapathy is unusual in facing south.
story: The king is said to have come upon an angry image of Hanuman while hunting for a broken bell, and then to have received a vision of Venkatachalapathy that prompted him to raise the temple.

name: Shri Laxmi Narsimha Temple, Nira Narsingpur
place: Nira Narsingpur, Indapur taluka, Pune district
significance: A Narasimha temple at the meeting of the Bhima and Nira rivers, its present black-stone structure dating from 1787 and its river ghats from 1527. Vaisakha Navaratri, ending in Narasimha Jayanti, is its principal festival.
story: The original image of Narasimha is said to have been swapped for a copy for safekeeping in the time of Aurangzeb.

name: Bisaldeo Temple
significance: A 12th-century Shiva temple beside the Bisalpur dam on the Banas, commissioned by the Chahamana king Vigraharaja IV, called Bisal Deo, after whom the place is named. It has a sanctum, vestibule and domed square mandapa with pancharatha projections and carved pillars, and is an ASI Monument of National Importance.

name: Kadakkad Sree Bhadrakali Temple
significance: A Bhadrakali temple north of Kadakkad on the Pathanamthitta MC Road near Pandalam, whose compound also holds shrines to Brahmarakshas, Yakshi and the Nagas.

name: Vardayini Mata Temple
significance: The goddess temple of Rupal village near Gandhinagar, known across Gujarat for its Palli festival on the ninth night of Navratri, when a rath of khijada wood carrying fire at five points is drawn to twenty-seven halts through the village and devotees pour ghee over it.
story: Villagers hold that the Palli was begun by the Pandavas in the age of the Mahabharata.

name: Pattupurackal Bhagavathy Temple
significance: A Bhadrakali temple at Njeezhoor in Kottayam district traced by the article to the 10th century, with Yakshi and Bhagavathy as attendant deities. It is managed by NSS Karayogam No. 336.

name: Shree Shyam Mandir, Guwahati
significance: Guwahati's temple to Khatushyamji, begun in late 2009 by the head priest Gopal Sharma with support from the city's Shyam devotees and consecrated over a seven-day ceremony ending 14 April 2016. Its subsidiary shrines take in Ganesha, Hanuman, Shiva, Lakshmi, Rani Sati and Santoshi Mata.

name: Ashokdham Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Balgudar whose worship the article traces to Narayan Pal in the 8th century and whose temple is credited to King Indradyumna in the 12th. A giant lingam was unearthed at the site on 7 April 1977 by two boys, Ashok and Gajanand, at play; the Shankaracharya of Puri inaugurated the rebuilding on 11 February 1993 and the present complex was begun on 15 November 2002.

name: Parhul Devi Temple
significance: A Durga temple on the right bank of the Rind river at Lamahra, 3 km off the Rura-Shivli road, with twin domes to north and south of identical shape and size and three goddesses carved on a single stone. Navratri is its chief festival. The article's coordinates differ from the Wikidata point and have been used here.

name: Pala Ganesh Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple about a kilometre from Udaipur's Surajpole, reckoned some five hundred years old. Its central shrine allows a circumambulatory path, and pilgrims enter by the Riddhi Pole and leave by the Siddhi Pole.

name: Puliyannoor Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in Mutholy panchayat about 3 km from Pala, founded according to the article by Chonar Chettiar of the Chathamplackal family and now held by the Namboothiri families of the Puliyannoor Oorayma Temple Devaswom. Ganapathi, Yogeeswara, Sastha, the Nagas, Krishna, Devi and Yakshiyamma are worshipped alongside.

name: Varakkal Devi Temple
significance: A seaside Durga temple at Westhill in Kozhikode, near Bhat Road beach and about 6 km from the city's railway station. It is administered by the Zamorin of Calicut and keeps Navaratri as its principal festival.

name: Pindara Group of Temples
place: Pindara, Kalyanpur taluka, Devbhoomi Dwarka district
style: Neo-Dravidic Maitraka, Nagara and early Maha-Gurjara
significance: A cluster of Shiva shrines near the sea about eleven miles east of Dwarka, built between the 7th and 10th centuries under Saindhava rule, with the phamsana-roofed temples placed in the middle of the 8th century. They mix the neo-Dravidic Maitraka manner with Nagara and early Maha-Gurjara forms.
story: Local people connect the monuments with the sage Durvasa and call the site Durvasa Rishi Ashram.

name: Trilokinath Temple, Mandi
significance: A stone Shiva temple in Mandi town commissioned around 1520 by Sultan Devi, queen of Raja Ajber Sen; its shikhara carries chaitya-arch dormers in relief and its walls bear images of Narada, Sharda and other deities.

name: Khodaldham
significance: A large temple to the goddess Khodiyar at Kagvad in Saurashtra, begun in 2012 and inaugurated in January 2017 by the Shree Khodaldham Trust of the Leuva Patel community; the complex covers about 158 bigha and cost some 250 crore rupees.

name: Radha Damodar Temple, Junagadh
deity: Radha and Damodar (Krishna in four-armed form)
significance: An ancient pink-sandstone Krishna temple beside Damodar Kund on the road to Girnar, recorded as renovated in 462 CE under the Gupta emperor Skandagupta; it also holds shrines to Balarama with Revati and to Ganesha.
story: The temple's founding is credited to Vajranabha, the great-grandson of Krishna, and bathing in the adjoining Damodar Kund is held to bring salvation.

name: Bhadreshwar Jain Temple
significance: A Jain tirtha in Kutch traditionally dated to 516 BCE and rebuilt nine times, with a major 13th-century renovation by the merchant Jagadusha and patronage recorded from Samprati Maurya and Vanaraja Chavda; the shrines were reconstructed after the 2001 Gujarat earthquake on a plan echoing the Dilwara temples.
story: The Parshvanatha image is said to have been installed here by Shri Kapil Kevali Muni in the 5th century BCE.

name: Panchasara Parshvanath Temple
significance: The principal Jain temple of Patan, founded in the 8th century by Vanaraja Chavda when he established the city and rebuilt in white marble in the 16th-17th century after being destroyed; it also enshrines Vasupujya and images of the Jain teachers Kakkasuri, Devachandrasuri and Yashodevsuri.
story: The main Parshvanatha image is said to have been carried to Patan from Vanaraja's ancestral village of Panchasar.

name: Naya Mandir
significance: A Digambara Jain temple in the Dharampura lane of Chandni Chowk, built in 1807 by Raja Harsukh Rai, a treasurer under the Mughals; the gold and silver used at its consecration festivities were plundered in a raid and returned only on the emperor's order.

name: Jainimedu Jain Temple
significance: One of the few surviving Jain temples in Kerala, raised in the 15th century by a family of diamond merchants from Karnataka and renovated in 2013; the Malayalam poet Kumaran Asan wrote Veenapoovu at a Jain house beside it.

name: Nareli Jain Temple
significance: A large marble Digambara complex on the outskirts of Ajmer, begun in 1994 at the initiative of Ashok Patni of RK Marbles, mixing traditional and contemporary forms; twenty-four small jinalayas for the twenty-four Tirthankaras stand on the hillside above it.

name: Guru Basadi
significance: A Jain basadi at Moodabidri dated to 714 CE: a rectangular building of three mandapas on carved pillars leading to the sanctum, with a manastambha erected before it in 1615.
story: A Jain sage is said to have seen a cow and a tiger drinking together in the forest here, and digging at the spot uncovered the Parshvanatha image around which the temple was built.

name: Chitharal Jain Monuments
builtDisplay: 9th c.; rock beds from c. 1st c. BCE
significance: A hilltop rock-cut Digambara Jain temple in Kanyakumari district with Tirthankara reliefs on its outer face, standing beside a Hindu Bhagavati shrine. The Archaeological Survey of India dates the ascetics' rock beds here between the first century BCE and the sixth century CE, while the temple work belongs to the ninth century and an inscription records the twenty-eighth regnal year of Vikramaditya Varaguna; the site is read as evidence of overlap rather than conflict between the two traditions.

name: Jina Kanchi Jain Math, Melsithamur
significance: The seat of the Digambara Jain pontiff of the Tamil country, about 10 km east of Gingee, with two temples — one of Parshvanatha and one of Mallinatha, the latter holding rock-cut images carved in the ninth century. The math was built with the permission of Venkatappa Nayak of Gingee and modified in 1860 by the Jain official Sri Baliah.

name: Naugaza Digambar Jain Temple
significance: A ruined tenth-century Digambara Jain temple in the Rajgarh area of Alwar district, dated by inscription to V.S. 979 under the Gurjara-Pratihara ruler Mahipala I of Kannauj. Of the temple only a colossal 17.5-foot standing image of the Tirthankara Shantinatha survives intact.

name: Bhandara Basadi
significance: Also called the Chaturvimsati Tirthankara Basadi, this temple in Shravanabelagola town was built in 1159 CE by Hulla Raja, treasurer and chief minister of the Hoysala king Narasimha I, and is dedicated to all twenty-four Tirthankaras.

name: Jain Temples, Abhapur
significance: A group of twelve fifteenth-century Svetambara Jain temples in sandstone at Abhapur, inside the Polo Forest of Sabarkantha district, noted for their carved ceilings and pierced jali screens. The principal image is Parshvanatha attended by the goddess Padmavati, with shrines also of Rishabhanatha and Neminatha.

name: Songadh Jain Temple
significance: A Digambara Jain temple complex at Songadh in Bhavnagar district, established in 1930 around the teaching of Kanji Swami, whose Svadhyaya Mandir of 1937 was its first building. Its white marble shrines, one of them dedicated to Simandhara, carry carved scriptural texts and murals.

name: Poondi Arugar Temple
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; built by the Cholas
significance: A Jain temple near Irumbedu, about three kilometres from Arani in Tiruvannamalai district, built by the Cholas. Its presiding image is known as Ponnezhilnathar.

name: Candi Kethek
deity: Vishnu (a tortoise image read as his Kurma form)
style: Terraced megalithic pyramid of seven levels
significance: A west-facing Hindu sanctuary of seven stone terraces on the slope of Mount Lawu, north-east of Ceto. Excavation in 2005 turned up a tortoise image understood as Vishnu in his Kurma form churning the ocean, and the top terrace still carries a small stana crowned in gold and wrapped in Balinese poleng cloth.

name: Cangkuang Temple
style: Early Central Javanese Hindu candi form
significance: A small andesite Shaivite temple on an island in Situ Cangkuang lake, 8.5 m tall on a 4.5 m square base, sheltering a 62 cm stone Shiva. Its plain three-stepped roof with pseudo-lingam pinnacles resembles the earliest Central Javanese Hindu temples, and experts put it around the early 8th century, roughly contemporary with the Dieng group.

name: Ratu Boko
style: Fortified plateau settlement with candi architecture
significance: A walled complex of gates, terraces, pools and shrines on a plateau about 3 km south of Prambanan, identified with the Abhayagiri Vihara, the monastery on the hill free from danger. Occupied through the 8th and 9th centuries, it mixes Buddhist remains such as an Avalokitesvara shrine, Dhyani Buddhas and an Akshobhya effigy with Hindu ones including a lingam and yoni, Durga, Ganesha and Garuda.
story: Javanese folklore makes the plateau the palace of King Boko, whose daughter Loro Jonggrang set Prince Bandung Bondowoso to raise a thousand temples in a night, then had the village women pound rice so the cocks would crow early, for which the prince turned her to stone.

name: Wat Ounalom
deity: A relic hair from the whorl between the Buddha's eyebrows
significance: The spiritual and administrative centre of Cambodian Theravada Buddhism and long the seat of the Mahanikaya order, a 44-building compound founded in 1443 under King Ponhea Yat over an earlier Angkorian stone sanctuary. Its name recalls the unnalom, the hair from between the Buddha's brows enshrined in its central stupa; the monastery was restored after the Khmer Rouge years.

name: Wat Damnak
significance: A Theravada teaching monastery in Siem Reap whose name records its origin as a damnak, a royal residence of King Sisowath, completed in 1927 and later given over to the sangha. Its shutters and doors are carved with Reamker scenes, its 1950s stupas copy Banteay Srei, and since 1999 it has also housed the Center for Khmer Studies.

name: Chandratiya Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the bank of the Buddha Pond near the Indravati river at Barsur, dated by a Barsur inscription of Shaka Samvat 983 (1068 CE). It was raised by Mahamandaleshwara Chandraditya, a chief of the Telugu Choda house serving under the ruler Dharavarsha, who also excavated the tank and bought a village from Rajadhiraja to endow the building work; its sanctum stands on a platform with a square pillared mandapa in front.

name: Swami Bodhayan Mandir
deity: Bhagwan Bodhayan, the Vedic sage of the Baudhayana Sutras
significance: A temple in Bangaon village of the Mithila region honouring the Vedic sage Bodhayan, author of the Baudhayana Sutras; its foundation was laid in 1956 by Devraha Baba with the Sanskrit scholar Sarvabhaum Vasudevacharya and the building finished in 1958 on twenty-five acres given by the villagers. A tank named Baudhayan Sarovar was dug beside it and an image of Vasudevacharya stands outside the shrine.
story: The site is held to be the birthplace of Bodhayan, and the old banyan tree in its grounds is remembered as the seat of his penance.

name: Bagalamukhi Temple, Bankhandi
deity: Bagalamukhi (Peetambhara), one of the ten Mahavidyas
significance: One of the three principal shrines in India to the tantric goddess Bagalamukhi, at Bankhandi in Kangra district, where the image sits on a golden throne among jewelled pillars. Worship here is sought for power over adversaries and the temple fills at Navratri.
story: Rama, guided by Hanuman, is said to have worshipped Bagalamukhi at this spot before his war with Ravana and to have been granted the Brahmastra; a fire pit in the temple is pointed out as the place of his rite.

name: Avanoor Sreekanteswaram Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Avanur in Thrissur district, built in the architecture of Kerala and counted among the 108 Shiva temples of the state.
story: It is held to be one of the 108 Shiva shrines installed across Kerala by the sage Parasurama.

name: Chelamattom Shree Krishna Swami Temple
significance: A temple to Krishna and Narasimha on the bank of the Periyar at Chelamattom near Kalady, known as the Dakshina Kasi and noted for its stone carving and bronze lamp pillars. It is one of the riverside sites where the bali tharpanam rite for the ancestors is performed, especially at Karkidaka Vavu.

name: Mama Bhanja Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Barsur in Dantewada district, now maintained as a protected monument by the Archaeological Survey of India.
story: Its name, meaning uncle and nephew, comes from the tale that the pair given the task of building it finished the work in a single day.

name: Kotulpur Sridhar Temple
deity: Vishnu worshipped as Sridhar, in the form of a shaligram
significance: A five-pinnacled terracotta temple of 1833 at Shiromanipur in Kotulpur, built by the Bhadra family, traders in salt, thread and mustard who had bought zamindari rights after Sadananda Bhadra settled here in the late 17th century. Ramakrishna, staying at nearby Kamarpukur from March to October 1880, came to the Bhadra house during that time.

name: Adikesava Perumal Temple, Paramandur
deity: Vishnu as Adikesava Perumal, flanked by Sridevi and Bhudevi
significance: A Vishnu temple at Paramandur in Pudukkottai district where the deity stands between Sridevi and Bhudevi. It is known locally for the ceremonial opening of the sorga vasal, the gate of heaven, in the Tamil month of Purattasi.

name: Gopal Mandir, Ujjain
significance: The second largest temple in Ujjain, built in the nineteenth century by Bayaji Bai Shinde, wife of the Maratha ruler Daulatrao Scindia, around a silver-clad marble image of Krishna. At Harihar Parva the Mahakaleshwar procession is brought here so that Shiva and Krishna may meet, and Janmashtami is its great festival.

name: Shali Mata Temple
deity: The goddess as Bhimakali and Shailaputri
significance: A goddess temple on the summit of Shali Tibba at about 2,862 m, some 36 km from Shimla and reached by a seven-kilometre walk through deodar and pine. The present timber-and-stone Kath Kuni building was renovated in the early twentieth century by Raja Rana Bhupinder Singh of Bushahr, and Navratri is its chief occasion.
story: Local tradition says the goddess appeared in a dream and asked to be moved to the highest peak nearby so that her blessing would reach the whole region.

name: Vedanarayana Perumal Temple, Thirunarayanapuram
deity: Vishnu as Vedanarayana, with Lakshmi as Vedanayaki
significance: A Vishnu temple in Tiruchirappalli district where the deity is enshrined in a reclining posture with Vedanayaki, built up under the medieval Cholas and later the Vijayanagara kings. Its chariot festival falls in the Tamil month of Chittirai.
story: An Araiyar of Thiru Naraiyur is said to have given his own life and those of his children to shield the deity from a fire in the temple, and Narayana granted the family liberation.

name: Bhairavesvarar Temple, Cholapuram
significance: A Chola-period Shiva temple at Cholapuram, on the Kumbakonam-Chennai road, whose presiding deity is Bhairavesvarar and whose goddess is Bhairavesvari. Only the base of its front mandapa survives, and it is known for housing sixty-four Bhairavas.
story: The place, once called Bhairavapuram, is held to be where Bhairava first appeared as a form of Shiva, and where all sixty-four Bhairavas manifested.

name: Jambukesvarar Temple, Nallichery
significance: A Shiva temple in Nallicheri village, about 13 km from Thanjavur on the Kumbakonam road, where the goddess is Akilandesvari. It is one of the seven shrines of the Saptamatrikas that make up the Saptasthanam of Chakkarappalli, and for three evenings in February or March the sun's rays fall on the linga.
story: Nandi is said to have worshipped Shiva at this place, and a sculpture in the temple shows him doing so.

name: Thinthirineesvarar Temple, Tindivanam
significance: A Shiva temple at Tindivanam whose linga is worshipped as Thinthirineesvarar and whose goddess is Maragathavalli or Marathambal; it also goes by the names Thindeechuram, Thinthiruni and Pulithinthirunvanam. It is counted among the Vaippu Sthalams named in the hymns of the Nayanar Appar.
story: The temple's vimana is said to have been raised by Vyasa, and the deity to have been worshipped by Valmiki and Vyasa among others.

name: Mitheshwarnath Shiva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Chunabhatti in Darbhanga district established in March 1949 by Mitthu Mistri Thakur and named after him. Since his death in October 1982 it has been kept up by his sons and their descendants, and it fills at Mahashivaratri, through Shravan, at Naga Panchami and at Kartik Purnima.
story: A wandering sage who came to Mitthu Thakur's house for food is said to have vanished after eating, having told him to build a Shiva temple at the spot where he had long been pouring water on a black stone.

name: Hare Krishna Golden Temple
significance: The first golden temple built in Telangana, completed at Banjara Hills in 2018 and inaugurated by Vice-President Venkaiah Naidu, with a five-tiered gilded gopuram, a 50-foot golden flagstaff and a main hall of some 4,600 square feet. It holds four shrines: to Lakshmi Narasimha, to Radha-Govinda, to Shiva as Panchajanyeshwara and to Hanuman as Japa Anjaneya.
story: Devotees hold the Lakshmi Narasimha worshipped here to be swayambhu, self-manifested several centuries ago, making it one of the oldest shrines in Hyderabad.

name: Bhooteshwarnath Temple
significance: A Shiva shrine around a natural rock linga near Marouda in Gariaband district, described as the second largest natural Shivlinga in the world after Siddheshwarnath at Ziro. Devotees hold that it keeps growing and officials measure it each year; pilgrims come at Mahashivaratri and on the Mondays of Sawan, carrying Mahanadi water in the kanwar yatra.
story: Centuries ago a zamindar named Shobha Singh is said to have heard a bull screaming and a lion roaring from the spot; when villagers found no animals there they took the sound to come from the stone and worshipped it as a Shivlinga.

name: Virateshwar Temple, Sohagpur
significance: A 70-foot Shiva temple at Sohagpur built by the Kalachuri ruler Yuvarajadeva II as a gift to the acharya of the Golaki Matha, and among the best known buildings of the Kalachuri period. It is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India, and the Banganga fair has been held in its courtyard since 1895.

name: Samadhishvara Temple, Chittorgarh
builtDisplay: 11th c.; restored in the 13th and 15th c.
significance: A Shiva temple inside Chittor Fort dated by inscription to the eleventh century and tentatively, though not securely, credited to the Paramara king Bhoja. Its image shows Shiva three-faced and six-armed as the lord of samadhi, and restorations in the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries left the building carrying several sculptural styles at once; inscriptions there record visits and gifts by nobles.

name: Madhabananda Temple
significance: A temple in Paga-Gopinathpur village near Salipur dedicated to Jagannath and to the holy man Madhabananda, resorted to locally for the healing of cattle. Dola Jatra, Dadhi Khela Jatra, Rama Navami and Janmashtami are among the festivals kept here.

name: Thoniyakavu Bhadrakali Temple
significance: A four-armed Bhadrakali shrine at Puthenpeedika, first built beside the Thiruvanikavu temple and moved to its present site at Thoniyakavu after a devaprasnam. It takes part in the Arattupuzha Pooram, and in October 2020 its administration passed from the Nair families that had held it to the Cochin Devaswom Board.
story: The goddess here is held to be the sister deity of Thiruvanikavu, and to have pointed out the new site at Thoniyakavu herself.

name: Parshvanatha Temple, Khajuraho
deity: Parshvanatha (probably built as an Adinatha shrine)
significance: The largest of the Jain temples in the eastern group at Khajuraho, raised between about 950 and 970 by a prominent Jain family in the reign of the Chandela king Dhanga and carrying an inscription of 954; its oblong plan runs from entrance porch through mandapa and vestibule to the sanctum, where a Parshvanatha image was installed in 1860.

name: Parashanatha Temple, Arrah
significance: A Jain temple at Masarh near Arrah, built in 1819 at the expense of Babu Shankar Lal of Arrah; an inscription in it some six centuries old records the old name of the place as Mahasara.

name: Anantnath Swami Temple
significance: A Jain temple at Puliyarmala outside Kalpetta, the best known Jain shrine of Wayanad, dedicated to the fourteenth Tirthankara Anantanatha.

name: Sanghiji
significance: A Digambara Jain temple at Sanganer near Jaipur dedicated to Rishabhanatha, whose last building phase an inscription of V.S. 1011 places in the 10th century; it is among the older Jain shrines of the Jaipur region.
story: It is told that when thirty-nine Jain images were recovered from the temple after Muni Sudhasagar's visit in 1999, yakshas in the form of snakes were found guarding the hoard.

name: Jirawala Tirth
significance: A Shvetambara tirtha in the Sirohi hills whose Parshvanatha image, installed by Acharya Deva Gupta Suri in 894, is counted among the 108 most venerated Parshvanatha idols; the present structure dates to 1134 and was restored by 2017 after damage in the 2001 earthquake.
story: A Brahmin boy's cow is said to have emptied her milk each day beside a cave, and a Jain merchant who dreamed of a Parshvanatha image at that spot dug there and found it.

name: Wat Botum
deity: Buddha (relics from Sri Lanka enshrined in the main stupa)
significance: One of the oldest and most important pagodas in Phnom Penh, founded as Wat Khpob Ta Yang by King Ponhea Yat in 1442 and renamed Wat Botum Vatey Reachvararam, the temple fenced with lotus, when King Norodom rebuilt and enlarged it in 1865. Its 33 m quadrangular main stupa, flanked by four 6 m corner stupas, holds Buddha relics presented from Sri Lanka in 1887.

name: Wat Saravan
significance: A Theravada monastery in Daun Penh district, north-west of the Royal Palace and south-west of Wat Ounalom, formally called Wat Saravan Techo. It keeps more than 3,400 manuscripts, a collection described as the largest library in Cambodia.

name: Dhandai Devi Temple, Mhasdi
deity: Dhandai Devi, worshipped as Adi Shakti, Mahalakshmi and Mahishasuramardini
significance: A Shakti temple in the Khandesh country of Maharashtra whose goddess is the kuladaivat of a number of Marathi communities. Clans that had come from Rajasthan raised the stone temple in the sixteenth century, and Navaratri brings the largest crowds.

name: Jnanakshi Rajarajeshwari Temple
deity: Rajarajeshwari, a form of Tripura Sundari
significance: Built in 1978, this Bengaluru temple gives its name to the surrounding Rajarajeshwari Nagar and is reckoned in the Tantra Chudamani as the 'ear' among the Shakti Peethas of India. Navaratri, Makara Sankranti and Deepavali are its principal festivals.
story: The site is said to be where the sage Atri and his devoted wife Anusuya lived and attained siddhi by propitiating Rajarajeshwari.

name: Sri Vetrimalai Murugan Temple
significance: The chief Hindu pilgrimage centre of the Andamans, begun in 1926 for the Tamil staff of the British administration on Ross Island and completed there by 1932, then shifted to Port Blair after independence. A Murugan shrine was added as the temple grew, and it is now the focus of the islands' Hindu festivals.

name: Padmakshi Temple
deity: The goddess Padmakshi (Lakshmi), also called Padmavathi
significance: One of the oldest temples of Hanamkonda, standing on a rock whose earliest Shaivite cave shrine is older than the fifth century; a Jain shrine was cut here in 1117 and a Brahmanical shrine took its place after about 1156, leaving Jain sculpture in place around the present temple. Thousands of women gather at it each year for Bathukamma.

name: Nithyakalyana Perumal Temple, Karaikal
significance: A Vishnu temple in the port town of Karaikal, standing beside the Karaikal Ammaiyar temple across the Chandra Theertham tank. It is counted among the three best-known temples of the town and keeps a full round of Vaishnava festivals.

name: Devasathan
deity: Shiva and Vishnu (with shrines to Ganesha and Brahma)
significance: The principal Brahmin temple of Thailand, founded in Bangkok in 1784 by King Rama I, housing separate shrines for Shiva, Vishnu and Ganesha. It remains the seat of the royal court Brahmins who conduct state Hindu rites.

name: Shree Shree Siddheswari Kalimandir
significance: An old Kali temple in central Dhaka, dated to 1441 and attributed to a founder named Chand Rai, whose central image of the goddess is its chief object of worship. The Siddheshwari neighbourhood of the city takes its name from the shrine.

name: Laxmi Narayan Mandir, Dhaka
significance: A roughly three-century-old two-storeyed temple on Nawabpur Road in old Dhaka dedicated to Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth. It has no dome, carries carved scenes from Hindu mythology and holds marble images brought from Jaipur; it is now run as a private temple with a residence inside its compound.

name: Lalmai Chandi Temple
significance: Also called Chandimura Mandir, this Kali temple crowns the Lalmai hill in Comilla District and is traced to a 7th-century foundation by Rani Probhaboti. It was restored in the 17th century and again in 1972-73, and a Shiva temple stands beside it.

name: Bishyanath Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in Mymensingh district, Bangladesh, noted for its unusual pagoda-like form among the region's Hindu shrines.

name: Boro Kali Bari Temple
builtDisplay: c. 18th c. (reign of Nawab Alivardi Khan)
significance: A Shakta temple in Mymensingh city said to be about three centuries old, founded by Tantric practitioners during the reign of Nawab Alivardi Khan. Its black stone image of Kali was replaced by a new one during a renovation completed in 2026.
story: Temple lore says a fisherman drew a black stone image of Kali from the Brahmaputra in his net and cried out 'Joy Kali!', giving the goddess her name; Tantrics then consecrated the image beneath an old banyan tree.

name: Kal Bhairab Temple, Brahmanbaria
significance: A Shaiva pilgrimage temple at Medda in Brahmanbaria, built about two centuries ago by the sculptor Durgacharan Acharjee on land given by Noor Muhammad, a landlord of Sarail. Its 28-foot image of Kal Bhairab is claimed to be the largest of its kind, and images of Kali and Parvati stand alongside.
story: The sculptor Durgacharan Acharjee is said to have been moved by a dream to shape the great earthen image of Kal Bhairab.

name: Joy Kali Temple
significance: A Kali temple in old Dhaka, reckoned about four centuries old, founded by the Dewans Tulsi Narayan Ghosh and Nabh Narayan Ghosh under the saint Bancharam. It has terracotta-clad walls and columns, a shikhara over the sanctum with mandapa and antarala, and a domed Shiva shrine in the compound.

name: Sugandha Shakta Pitha
significance: One of the Shakta pithas, standing at Shikarpur village about ten miles north of Barisal in Bangladesh, where the goddess is worshipped as Sunanda or Ugratara. Shiva-Chaturdashi is its principal annual festival.
story: The site is held to be where the nose of Sati fell when Vishnu's discus dismembered her body as the grieving Shiva carried it.

name: Muktagachha Shiva Temple
deity: Shiva (as Anandamoyi Shiva), with a paired Kali shrine
significance: Twin Shiva and Kali temples raised in 1820 by Rani Bimola Devi of the Muktagachha zamindar family, named for her mother Anandamoyee. Cited as fine examples of mirrored temple pairs in Bengal, they are a listed heritage site now in fragile condition.

name: Kaliya Jue Temple
significance: A Krishna temple standing just west of the Dinajpur Rajbari palace complex in northern Bangladesh.

name: Swami Bagh Temple
significance: A Vaishnava temple established in Dhaka in 1902, with subsidiary Shiva and Kali shrines, now run by ISKCON. Its annual Jagannath Rath Yatra procession travels through the city to the Dhakeshwari National Temple.

name: Pathirakali Amman Temple
builtDisplay: pre-11th c.; enlarged under Rajendra Chola I
significance: A Bhadrakali temple in Trincomalee whose foundation date is unknown but which is named in inscriptions from the 11th century and earlier, and was greatly enlarged by the Chola king Rajendra I. It draws pilgrims jointly with the nearby Koneswaram temple during the Ther Thiruvillah chariot festival.

name: Ariyalai Siddhivinayakar Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple at Ariyalai, about five kilometres from Jaffna town, rehabilitated around 1918 by Advocate Arulampalam. It has drawn notable visitors including Yogar Swami and Kunrakudi Adigal.

name: Thambiluvil Kannaki Amman Temple
builtDisplay: traditionally 2nd c. CE; royal patronage from the 14th c.
style: Non-Agamic, with four halls (karuvarai, mun, nadu and maha mandapam)
significance: A temple to Kannaki, the heroine of the Tamil epic Silappatikaram, in Ampara District in eastern Sri Lanka, traditionally traced to the arrival of the Pattini cult under Gajabahu I. Kandyan and Kotte kings patronised it from the 14th century onward, and an inscription of Vijayabahu VII of Kotte (1507-1521) was found in its grounds.
story: A golden pigeon is said to have revealed the goddess's image at Urakkai, a paddy field west of the village.

name: Choleeswaram Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Peraru near Kantalai in eastern Sri Lanka, raised in honour of the emperor Rajaraja Chola I when the island was under Chola rule. Its remains are read as Dravidian work of the Chola period.

name: Thirukkovil Chitravelayudhar Temple
builtDisplay: Chola era (993-1070); later rebuilt in stone
significance: A Murugan temple on Sri Lanka's eastern coast whose founding is placed in the period of Chola rule over the island, with a later reconstruction in stone attributed to Manuneya Gajabahu. The sanctum is identified as Pandya work.
story: An elderly devadasi named Thangammai, dismissed from temple service, is said to have reappeared the next morning as an eight-year-old girl ready to perform the rituals.

name: Shri Laxmi Narayan Mandir
significance: A seafront Hindu temple beneath Karachi's Native Jetty Bridge, dedicated to Lakshmi and Vishnu and reported to be around two centuries old. It also houses images of Hanuman and Sai Baba of Shirdi.

name: Chauchala Chhota Govinda Mandir
significance: A small four-roofed (chauchala) brick temple at Puthia in Rajshahi Division, dedicated to Govinda. Its walls carry terracotta plaques showing the ten avatars of Vishnu alongside Ramayana and Radha-Krishna scenes.

name: Sri Muthumariamman Temple, Matale
deity: Muthumariamman (Mariamman, goddess of rain and fertility)
significance: The main Hindu temple of the Sri Lankan hill town of Matale, raised on paddy land gifted in 1852 and completed in 1874 under Nattukottai Chettiar patronage. Its 108-foot rajagopuram, finished in 2007 and carrying over a thousand sculpted figures, is one of the tallest temple towers on the island.

name: Shiva Mandir, Johi
significance: A mid-19th-century Shiva temple in the Sindhi town of Johi, known locally as the Qubi for its unusual pair of domes and its mix of iron, cement and cheeroli construction. The idols once fixed to its outer walls were destroyed after Partition, and only their traces survive.

name: Kokkadicholai Thaanthonreeswarar Temple
significance: A Shaiva temple southwest of Batticaloa, ascribed to Ulaga Naachi of the Chola realm and counted among the oldest and most important Shiva kovils in Sri Lanka. Its lingam is reported to be a naturally formed one, a rarity on the island.
story: Local tradition holds that the temple's stone bull came to life, grazed on the grass and drove Portuguese soldiers away from the shrine.

name: Magderu Temple, Dhrasanvel
significance: An 8th-century saptayatana temple near Dwarka, its large central shrine ringed by six smaller ones, now a Monument of National Importance in the ASI's Vadodara Circle. Scholars link the name element Maga to the Aboti Maga Brahmins, Surya worshippers who migrated from Iran to western India, and read the site as an original sun temple.

name: Raghunath Temple, Srinagar
significance: A Dogra-period Rama temple in Srinagar, begun in 1835 under Maharaja Gulab Singh and completed in 1860 under Maharaja Ranbir Singh. Attacked and left abandoned after the exodus of Kashmiri Hindus, it is now undergoing restoration.

name: Prasat Ta Krabey
significance: A small laterite Khmer sanctuary on the Dangrek escarpment, raised under Suryavarman I and Udayadityavarman II and left unfinished, enclosing a linga called Svayambhuva. It stands on the contested Cambodia-Thailand frontier and its carvings include Yama riding his buffalo mount.

name: Wat Kamphaeng Laeng
significance: A walled Khmer complex of four laterite towers and a cruciform shrine built in the reign of Jayavarman VII, the westernmost surviving Khmer sanctuary in Thailand. An image of Uma recovered here in 1956 marks its Hindu foundation; the site later became a Buddhist wat.

name: Gopinath Temple, Pabna
significance: A Vaishnava brick temple in Pabna town built by Brajmohan Krori, a tahsildar under the Nawabs of Murshidabad, in the jor-bangla form of two joined do-chala roofs. Its terracotta panels illustrate Ramayana and Mahabharata scenes; the image was moved to a nearby Kali temple in 1910 and worship has ceased.

name: Shadani Darbar
significance: A Hindu shrine in Mirpur Mathelo taluka founded in 1786 by Sant Shadaram Sahib, reported to be the largest Hindu temple in Sindh. Its liturgy combines agni puja with recitation of the Bhagavad Gita and the Guru Granth Sahib, and the saint's birth anniversary draws an annual gathering.

name: Saraswati Gyan Mandir
significance: A temple to Saraswati on the University of Chittagong campus, financed by Adul Kanti Chowdhury and Anita Chowdhury through their foundation; its foundation stone was laid in 2019 and it opened in 2026. It gives the university a permanent shrine for the Saraswati Puja long observed there, and is described as the only one of its kind in Bangladesh.

name: Phra That Narai Cheng Weng
place: That Na Weng, Mueang Sakon Nakhon
significance: A sandstone Khmer prang on a laterite base outside Sakon Nakhon town, carved with a lintel showing Krishna slaying a lion in Baphuon-period style. It is the principal Khmer Hindu monument surviving in the province.
story: Local tradition holds that the sanctuary was raised entirely by women, in a building contest against the men who put up Phra That Phu Pek.

name: Prasat Huai Thap Than
significance: A Khmer sanctuary of the Baphuon period whose three towers on a shared platform stood for the Trimurti, registered as a national monument in 1935. Rebuilt under Lan Xang influence in the 18th-19th centuries, it passed into Buddhist use and its name changed from Prasat Ban Prasat to That Chedi and then to its present form.

name: Mahilara Sarkar Math
significance: A brick math at Mahilara in Gournadi raised by the local notable Sarkar Rup Ram Das Gupta under Nawab Alivardi Khan, built for Shiva and painted inside with Radha-Krishna imagery. Its tiered octagonal spire, with cornice mouldings that borrow from European church design, now leans noticeably and is the only tilted temple of its kind in Bangladesh.

name: Prasat Kao Noi
style: Khmer, late Sambor Prei Kuk to early Prei Kmeng
significance: Three east-facing brick towers on a shared base near Aranyaprathet, put up in the 7th century under Isanavarman I or Bhavavarman II and reckoned the oldest Khmer monument of consequence in Thailand. Lingas and pedestals found here had been broken into fragments, evidence that the shrine was deliberately desecrated.

name: Sindurmati Tirthadham
deity: Durga, Krishna, Vishnu, Rama and Kali
significance: A pilgrimage site around a large tank on the Kurigram-Lalmonirhat boundary, founded by the zamindar Raj Narayan Chakraborty and carrying shrines to Durga, Krishna, Vishnu, Rama and Kali. The complex was restored under a government programme in 1975.
story: A childless zamindar is said to have dug the tank in hope of offspring and named his two daughters Sindur and Moti after they were born; during a Navami puja held at the centre of the tank the water rose and drowned them, and after he dreamed that they had become immortal the water took their names.

name: Bhairabkunda Shiva Mandir
significance: A Shiva shrine in southern Bhutan near the Assam border, first built in timber after the 1950 Assam-Tibet earthquake and replaced by the present structure between 2002 and 2005. Its design deliberately blends Hindu temple forms with traditional Bhutanese architecture, and it draws pilgrims from across the frontier.
story: It is counted among the Shakta pithas where a part of Sati fell; Indra is said to have meditated here on his celestial elephant, Bhairab Nath to have found a self-formed Shiva lingam at the spot, and a cave beneath the temple to mark where Shiva himself meditated.

name: Prasat Phanom Wan
significance: A Khmer sanctuary outside Khorat, founded in the 11th century for Maheshwara and rebuilt in sandstone in the 13th-14th centuries, with a main prang of three arched gateways joined to a surrounding cloister. It later passed into Buddhist use and was listed as an ancient monument by the Fine Arts Department in 1936.

name: Kalka Cave Temple
significance: A cave shrine to Kali at Aror near Sukkur, known as the Asthan of Kalka Devi and one of the few active Hindu pilgrimage places in upper Sindh. Devotees gather there on the evening of the first Monday of each month.
story: Kalka Devi is said to have manifested at this spot while travelling to the Hinglaj Mata temple, and the shrine's caretaker holds that two tunnels in the cave run all the way to Hinglaj.

name: Burmese Buddhist Temple
significance: Singapore's Theravada temple in the Burmese tradition, begun in 1875 by U Thar Hnin and rehoused on Tai Gin Road in 1991; it is described as the only Burmese temple outside Myanmar built in the traditional Burmese manner, with teak carving throughout. Its 3-metre image, carved in 1918 from Sagyin marble and shipped 2,500 km to Singapore in 1921, is the largest pure white marble Buddha outside Myanmar.

name: Manuha Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (three seated images and a reclining parinirvana image)
significance: A two-storey rectangular shrine at Myinkaba in Bagan, finished in 1067 by Manuha, the captive Mon king of Thaton. Its four colossal images - three seated Buddhas and one entering final nibbana - are wedged so tightly into their chambers that the cramped setting is read as an expression of the king's captivity.
story: The Glass Palace Chronicle relates that Manuha, in remorse, raised the great images and prayed that wherever he might be reborn in samsara he would never again be conquered by another.

name: Ramkot Banashram
deity: Gautama Buddha (chest-bone relic; image in abhaya mudra)
significance: A hilltop monastery near Ramu, held to be one of the stupas raised in Ashoka's reign and named from words meaning chest bone, for the relic of the Buddha it is said to enshrine. Lost for centuries, it was rediscovered after a stone inscription came to light and was restored in 1919 by the Sri Lankan monk Jagat Jyoti Mahasthavir.
story: Tradition holds that the Buddha came here with Ananda and foretold that a pagoda would one day stand on the spot to hold a relic from his chest.

name: Taung Mingyi Pagoda
significance: One of the four great pagodas of Amarapura, built in 1786 by the minister Thaung Mingyi and sheltering a standing Buddha image nearly 14.3 metres high. Wrecked by the earthquake of 1838, it was rebuilt on the order of King Pagan Min from 1850 and finished under Mindon in 1853; the 2025 Myanmar earthquake damaged it again.

name: Kothduwa Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (Bodhi tree grown from the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi)
significance: An island temple in the Madu Ganga estuary reached only by boat, built in the 1860s by the businessman Samson Rajapakse around a Bodhi tree raised from the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi. It is remembered as a resting place of the Buddha's tooth relic in the fourth century.
story: Princess Hemamali and Prince Danthakumara are said to have carried the tooth relic from India disguised as brahmins, the relic hidden in the princess's hair, and to have concealed it at Kothduwa before handing it to King Sirimeghavanna.

name: Xá Lợi Pagoda
significance: A pagoda in District 3 of Ho Chi Minh City raised between 1956 and 1958 to enshrine a relic of Gautama Buddha, with its bell tower opened in 1961. Its sanctuary carries fourteen painted scenes running from the Buddha's birth as Prince Siddhartha to his attainment of nirvana.

name: Thầy Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha with eighteen arhats, alongside Zen master Từ Đạo Hạnh and Emperor Lý Nhân Tông
significance: A Buddhist temple complex west of Hanoi in Quốc Oai, established in the 11th century under Emperor Lý Nhân Tông and refurbished repeatedly since. Its halls venerate the Buddha together with the Zen master Từ Đạo Hạnh, around whose cult the site grew.
story: Từ Đạo Hạnh is said to have burned his finger to summon rain and healed villagers by blessing them, and to have been reborn three times - once as a Buddha, then as the son of King Lý Nhân Tông, then as the monk who saved King Thần Tông.

name: Bagaya Monastery
significance: A Theravada monastery at the old capital of Inwa, dedicated to Shin Dhammabhinanda and first built in 1593, later endowed during King Hsinbyushin's reign by the town officer of Magwe. Destroyed by fire in 1821, it was rebuilt in 1992.

name: Ngahtatgyi Buddha Temple
significance: A Theravada temple in Yangon's Bahan Township whose five-tiered pagoda shelters a seated Buddha image 6.2 m high, donated by Prince Minyedeippa and completed in 1558. A further Buddha statue was erected at the temple in 1900.

name: Girihandu Seya
significance: A hilltop stupa at Thiriyai believed to hold hair relics of the Buddha, enlarged in the 8th century and enclosed by a vatadage of concentric stone pillars like those at Thuparama and Lankarama. An inscription links it to King Silamegha, and it was later repaired under Vijayabahu I.
story: The Pujavaliya tells that the merchants Tapassu and Bhalluka, carrying the Buddha's hair relics, set the casket down on this rock and found it could no longer be lifted, so they raised a stupa over it.

name: Kyauktawgyi Buddha Temple, Yangon
deity: Loka Chantha Abhaya Labha Muni (Gautama Buddha image)
significance: A Theravada temple in Insein Township, Yangon, built around the Loka Chantha Abhaya Labha Muni, a 37-foot marble Buddha image brought to the site in August 2000 and consecrated in February 2002. Its construction was led by Senior General Than Shwe.

name: Wat Phra Singh
significance: A leading royal temple of Chiang Mai, founded in 1345 by Phayu, fifth king of Lan Na, and named for the Phra Buddha Sihing image brought there in 1400. Its Viharn Lai Kham was built between 1815 and 1821, and it was granted royal temple status in 1935.

name: Trấn Quốc Pagoda
deity: Mother Goddesses Mẫu Thượng Ngàn, Mẫu Thoải and Mẫu Thượng Thiên
significance: A Buddhist pagoda in Tây Hồ District, Hanoi, first founded under Emperor Lý Nam Đế between 544 and 548, moved to its present site in 1615 and heavily repaired in 1815. Beside its Buddhist halls it holds shrines to the three Mother Goddesses of Vietnamese tradition, and a Bodhi sapling from Bodh Gaya was planted there in 1959.

name: Abeyadana Temple
significance: A brick temple at Bagan built around 1090 during the reign of King Kyanzittha, its main image a brick Gautama Buddha. A later inscription credits its construction to Kyanzittha's queen Abeyadana, and its murals mix Tantric and Brahmanic figures with Buddhist ones.
story: Local legend holds that the temple stands on the spot where Kyanzittha's queen Abeyadana waited for him.

name: Kong Meng San Phor Kark See Monastery
significance: A Mahayana Buddhist monastery in Bishan, Singapore, founded in 1920-21 by the Venerable Zhuan Dao on land given by the businessman Tay Woo Seng and later supported by the Aw brothers. Its grounds hold a large bronze Buddha, an outdoor Guanyin statue and a Bodhi sapling descended from the tree at Anuradhapura.

name: Man Buddha Temple
significance: A Theravada Buddhist temple at Sale in Myanmar's Magway Region that enshrines the Shinbin Maha Laba Man Buddha, a hollow gold-lacquered figure of about 20 feet said to be the largest lacquer Buddha image in the country. The image itself is dated to around 1300.
story: The image is said to have floated downriver from Monywa to Sale during the great floods of 1888.

name: Bút Tháp Temple
significance: A Buddhist temple beside the Đuống River dyke in Bắc Ninh province, founded in the 13th century but whose surviving architecture, sculpture and decoration all belong to the 17th century, when the Zen master Chuyet Chuyet made it famous. Its ten buildings run for about 100 metres and hold a celebrated thousand-armed, thousand-eyed Quan Âm alongside the Buddha triad, Manjushri and Samantabhadra.

name: Quán Sứ Pagoda
deity: The Buddha (front hall); Master Minh Không (rear hall)
significance: A 15th-century Buddhist pagoda on Quan Su Street in central Hanoi, raised on the grounds of a Lê-dynasty guest house built for envoys from Champa and Laos, who as Buddhists wanted a place of worship on the premises. Renovated in 1822, it now serves as the headquarters of the Buddhist Sangha of Vietnam.

name: Changangkha Lhakhang
significance: One of Thimphu's oldest temples, set on a ridge above the city and founded in the 13th or 14th century by Nyima, a son of Phajo Drugom Zhigpo who brought the Drukpa Kagyu teachings to Bhutan. Its bronze Avalokiteshvara is the main image, and the protector Genyen Domtsangpa is invoked as the birth deity of children born at the national referral hospital below.
story: Some hold that the bronze Avalokiteshvara arose of itself rather than being carved, while others credit a Newar master craftsman working at the time the temple was built.

name: Kwan Im Thong Hood Cho Temple
deity: Guanyin (Kuan Yim), worshipped here in her Cundi form
significance: A Chinese Buddhist temple on Waterloo Street in Singapore's Rochor district, begun in 1884 after the firm Chen Liang Cheng gave the land, and rebuilt in 1895 and again in 1980. Its image of Cundi, a form of Guanyin, draws crowds of worshippers seeking good fortune.

name: Payathonzu Temple
significance: A late 13th-century brick temple at Minnanthu, southeast of Bagan, whose Burmese name means Temple of Three Buddhas: three shrines joined by narrow passages, left unfinished by its builders. Its interior murals are noted for Mahayana and Tantric elements unusual in Bagan.

name: Shwesandaw Pagoda
significance: The tallest pagoda at Bagan, raised in 1057 by King Anawrahta to enshrine hair relics of the Buddha brought from Thaton. Five receding terraces, once faced with terracotta Jataka plaques, carry a cylindrical stupa whose jewelled hti was thrown down by the earthquake of 1975.

name: Buduruvagala
deity: Standing Buddha, flanked by Avalokiteshvara, Tara, Maitreya and Vajrapani
significance: A group of seven colossal figures carved into a rock face near Wellawaya in southern Sri Lanka, dated by most authorities to the 9th or 10th century. The central standing Buddha is the island's tallest, and the flanking bodhisattvas mark the site as a rare surviving Mahayana monument in a Theravada country.
story: A hollow carved into the same rock is said to weep a mustard-scented oil that no one has been able to trace to a source.

name: Seruwila Mangala Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Forehead relic (Lalata Dhatu) and hair relics of Gautama Buddha
significance: An Early Anuradhapura-period stupa in Trincomalee District built by King Kavantissa, and the only site known to enshrine the Buddha's forehead bone relic along with hair relics. It counts as the ninth of the Solosmasthana, the sixteen holiest Buddhist pilgrimage places in Sri Lanka, and its four carved guardstones are unmatched at any other Sri Lankan stupa.
story: The Dhatuvamsa relates that the Buddha came to this spot with five hundred arahants on his third visit to the island, and that Kavantissa enshrined the forehead relic here in fulfilment of an old prophecy.

name: Somawathiya Chaitya
deity: Right canine tooth relic of Gautama Buddha
significance: A stupa on the Mahaweli floodplain in Polonnaruwa District, built in the reign of King Kavan Tissa by Prince Giri Abhaya to enshrine the Buddha's right canine tooth relic, which he received from Arahat Mahinda. It takes its name from the prince's wife, Princess Somawathi, sister of the king, and the couple handed the completed shrine to the monks.

name: Ayeik Ma Htwet Pagoda
significance: A brick stupa in Aungmyethazan Township, Mandalay, which a stone inscription credits to King Kyansittha of the Pagan kingdom in 1064; relics of the Buddha are enshrined in a chamber within it.
story: The pagoda is said to cast no shadow in sunlight, answering Kyansittha's vow that its shadow should never fall again in any of his future births.

name: Mahabodhi Temple, Bagan
significance: A Theravada temple at Bagan raised in the early 13th century under King Htilominlo as a copy of the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya; over 450 Buddha images fill the niches of its tall pyramidal tower, which was repaired after the 1975 Bagan earthquake.

name: Wat Phra That Phanom
style: Lao stupa form with Dvaravati, Khmer and Cham elements
significance: The chief Buddhist stupa of northeastern Thailand, standing near the Mekong in That Phanom district and enshrining what tradition holds to be the Buddha's breast bone; archaeology dates the earliest structure on the site to the 7th or 8th century, and the pagoda has been restored in modern times with royal Thai patronage.
story: The That Phanom Chronicle says the Buddha asked Mahakasyapa to carry his breast-bone relic to Phu Kamphra after his death, and that the disciple with five hundred arhats raised the stupa over it there.

name: Sakya Man Aung Pagoda
significance: A Buddhist temple about a kilometre northeast of the royal palace at Mrauk U, commissioned in 1629 by King Thiri Thudhamma Raza; its stupa is laid out on an eight-petalled lotus plan and turns from an octagonal form to a bell above nine rising tiers.

name: Giác Lâm Pagoda
significance: A Buddhist pagoda in the Tân Bình district of Ho Chi Minh City, founded in 1744 by Lý Thụy Long during the rule of the Nguyễn lord Nguyễn Phúc Khoát. Amitabha dominates its main altar, with Shakyamuni and four bodhisattvas set before him, and a bodhi tree brought from Sri Lanka in 1953 grows in its garden.

name: Hội Khánh Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (with Ksitigarbha and other bodhisattvas)
significance: A Buddhist temple at Thủ Dầu Một in Bình Dương province, built in 1741, destroyed in 1861 during the French colonial conflict and rebuilt soon after by Thích Chánh Đắc. Between 1923 and 1926 anti-colonial activists, among them Ho Chi Minh's father Nguyễn Sinh Sắc, met within its walls.

name: Pu Tuo Si Temple
significance: A Chinese Buddhist temple in Kota Kinabalu, Sabah, completed in 1980. Its Daxiong Baodian main hall holds a large Buddha image flanked by Guanyin on the left and Dashizhi on the right.

name: Maha Wizaya Pagoda
deity: Buddha (enshrined relics given by the King of Nepal)
significance: A stupa in Dagon Township, Yangon, built in 1980 to commemorate the First Congregation for the purification of the Buddha Sasana, out of which came the State Sangha Maha Nayaka Committee. It enshrines relics contributed by the King of Nepal, and Ne Win consecrated its crowning umbrella.

name: Vĩnh Nghiêm Pagoda
significance: A large pagoda in District 3 of Ho Chi Minh City, begun in 1964 by the monks Thích Tâm Giác and Thích Thanh Kiểm and named for an 11th-century predecessor in Bắc Giang province. It was the first in Vietnam to render traditional Vietnamese temple architecture in concrete, and its seven-storey, 40 m tower was built with help from the Japan–Vietnam Friendship Association.

name: Uruwala Valagamba Raja Maha Vihara
significance: An ancient Buddhist temple at Uruwala in the Gampaha District, formally protected by the Sri Lankan government as an archaeological site. Its old sacred fig tree stands within a rampart, and the temple is held to have belonged with neighbouring shrines to a single monastic complex of the early Anuradhapura period.

name: Sri Pushparama Vihara, Ratmalana
significance: A Buddhist temple at Ratmalana in the Colombo District, built between 1795 and 1800 by Balapitiye Dheerananda Thera. The Sri Lankan government declared it a protected archaeological monument on 23 February 2007.

name: Delgamuwa Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (Sacred Tooth Relic, formerly hidden here)
significance: A Buddhist temple at Kuruwita in the Ratnapura District, remembered as the refuge of the Buddha's Tooth Relic during Portuguese rule: King Mayadunne of Sitawaka had the relic brought here about 1549, and it lay concealed inside a kurakkan grinding stone on the premises until Wimaladharmasuriya I recovered it in 1592 and carried it to Kandy.

name: Sri Pushparama Vihara, Balapitiya
style: preaching hall in colonial church manner
significance: A Buddhist temple at Balapitiya in the Galle District, headquarters of the Mulaghandi sect of the Amarapura Nikaya and a protected archaeological monument since 6 June 2008. The doors and windows of its dhamma preaching hall follow colonial church design, with two wooden stairs rising to a balcony that runs round the inner hall.

name: Asgiriya Raja Maha Vihara, Gampaha
deity: Gautama Buddha (Samadhi image; stone Buddha footprint)
significance: A cave temple at Gampaha in the Western Province whose foundation is traced to the reign of King Valagamba (89–77 BCE), with a 5th-century inscription found on its grounds. It keeps a Samadhi Buddha statue and flanking abhaya-mudra images carved in Kandyan-period manner, together with a stone bearing a footprint of the Buddha; the provincial ruler Sakalakala Wallabha patronised it under Parakramabahu VI.
story: The place is said to have taken the name Asgiri from a horse lost there by Prince Uttiya, brother of King Kelani Tissa.

name: Yatawatte Purana Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (stupa and tempita image house)
originNote: history traced to the reign of Parakramabahu VI (15th c.)
style: Tempita vihara (image house on granite pillars)
significance: A Buddhist temple about a kilometre from Gampaha town whose history is believed to reach back to the reign of Parakramabahu VI. Its tempita image house — of the type raised on granite pillars that was popular in Sri Lanka between the 17th and 19th centuries — is dated to 21 March 1861, and a stupa stands beside it.

name: Gonagolla Vihara
builtDisplay: 3rd c. BCE stupa; frescoes 3rd c. CE
significance: An ancient Buddhist site at Gonagolla in the Ampara District where a stupa and two ponds are dated to the third century BCE, surrounded by drip-ledged caves, a vatadage, stone stairways and carved pillars. Its third-century CE frescoes have earned it the local name Punchi Seegiriya, 'little Sigiriya', and rock inscriptions of the 3rd to 5th centuries record gifts by monks and by the wives of district governors.

name: Koskandawala Raja Maha Vihara
significance: An old Buddhist cave temple at Koskandawala in the Gampaha District, with a stupa and an image house. It is counted among neighbouring cave temples said to have formed a single monastic complex in the early Anuradhapura period.

name: Nagadeepa Purana Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (gem-studded throne; stone Buddha footprint)
builtDisplay: rebuilt under Devanampiya Tissa and Dutugemunu
significance: A Buddhist temple on the island of Nainativu off the Jaffna coast, revered as the place the Buddha visited to reconcile two Naga kings. It was rebuilt under Devanampiya Tissa and again under Dutugemunu, and keeps a stone bearing the Buddha's footprint along with a gem-studded throne given by Ratnapura businessmen in 2011.
story: The Buddha is said to have come here five years after his enlightenment to settle the quarrel of the Naga kings Chulodara and Mahodara over a gem-studded throne, converting them by his miracles.

name: Sri Dharmendrarama Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (Sri Pathul Gala footprint slabs)
significance: An archaeological Buddhist temple at Mayadunna in Gonagolla village, Ampara District, protected as an archaeological site since 10 October 2014. Its remains include a stupa, Buddha-footprint slabs, fragments of moonstones, building bases, pillars and a rock inscription — footprint slabs being among the objects used to represent the Buddha before statues of him were made.

name: Mahiyangana Raja Maha Vihara
dynasty: Anuradhapura to Kandyan kings; modern rebuild
significance: One of the principal Buddhist pilgrimage sites of Sri Lanka, whose stupa is held to enshrine hair relics of the Buddha and was successively enlarged by rulers from Devanampiya Tissa and Dutthagamani through Vijayabahu I to Kirti Sri Rajasinha. The present casing over the older stupa was built between 1953 and 1980.
