story: The Buddha is said to have come here in the ninth month after his enlightenment, subduing the yakshas who then inhabited the island and giving Saman a handful of his hair, which Saman enshrined in the first small stupa.

name: Seema Malaka
deity: Gautama Buddha (with subsidiary shrines to Guanyin, Kataragama deviyo, Upulvan and Ganesha)
significance: A meditation and ordination hall of the Gangaramaya temple, set on timber-decked platforms in Colombo's Beira Lake. The original late-19th-century pavilion was replaced in 1976 by a design from the architect Geoffrey Bawa, funded by S. H. Musaji and his wife in memory of their son, drawing on the forest-monastery layouts of Anuradhapura and Ritigala.

name: Warana Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (cave image house of Buddha statues)
significance: A terraced cave monastery on three levels whose foundation is attributed to King Devanampiya Tissa, holding Buddha images, wall paintings and a stupa on its middle terrace. Later kings including Valagamba, Nissanka Malla, Parakramabahu VI and Kirti Sri Rajasinha are recorded as renovating it.

name: Thuparamaya
significance: Regarded as the first stupa raised in Sri Lanka after the island's conversion to Buddhism, built by King Devanampiya Tissa at the request of the missionary Mahinda to enshrine the Buddha's right collar-bone. The dome standing today is the product of an 1842 rebuilding, ringed by the stone pillars of its former vatadage.

name: Sunandarama Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (image houses and a sacred Bodhi tree)
builtDisplay: Bodhi planted c. 1750; temple developed from 1970
significance: A Buddhist temple in the Galle District grown up around a Bodhi tree planted about 1750, with image houses holding Buddha statues including a marble figure presented from Burma. Its systematic development as a monastery began in 1970.
story: Its Bodhi tree is held to be one of the eight branches taken from the sacred Sri Maha Bodhi at Anuradhapura.

name: Kasagala Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (two ancient stupas and a Sri Maha Bodhi sapling)
significance: An ancient monastery in the Hambantota District whose origin is traced to the planting of one of the saplings of the sacred Sri Maha Bodhi, with construction generally credited to the reign of Kavan Tissa and later patronage from Dappula I, Vijayabahu I and Kirti Sri Rajasinha. Its two stupas are attributed to Devanampiya Tissa and Saddha Tissa, and its murals show southern Kandyan work with European decorative influence.
story: Local folklore derives the name from monks spreading their saffron robes to dry on the rock, which made the outcrop appear yellow from a distance.

name: Maligatenna Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (image house, stupa and Bodhi tree, with an old devalaya)
significance: A rock and cave temple in the Gampaha District with an image house, stupa, Bodhi tree and an old devalaya; an engraved stone door frame on the site has been assigned to about the 8th century. Its later history reaches into the Kotte kingdom under Don Juan Dharmapala and the Portuguese period.
story: Folklore holds that King Valagamba sheltered here during invasions and that the Buddha's tooth relic was hidden at the site for a time before being moved on.

name: Ovagiriya
deity: Gautama Buddha (granite image in the image house)
significance: An archaeological monastery site of about three hectares in the Ampara District, dated to the fifth century or earlier and formally identified by the Department of Archaeology in 1956. Its image house holds a 3.5 m granite Buddha, restored in 2008, and its stupa stands on an unusual octagonal platform rather than the customary circular or square one.

name: Samanabedda cave temple
significance: A cave temple near Uhana on the Ampara–Mahaoya road, traditionally attributed to King Saddha Tissa and now a protected archaeological monument. It retains a Buddha image in its image house and the remains of a ruined stupa.

name: Panasawanarama Purana Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (stupa, Bodhi tree and image house)
significance: An old Buddhist temple in the Gampaha District of Sri Lanka, recognised as an archaeological site, whose surviving elements are a stupa, a Bodhi tree and an image house.

name: Ancient Kadurugoda Viharaya
deity: Gautama Buddha (relic stupas; Buddha and Bodhisattva images)
builtDisplay: Anuradhapura period; dated pillar of Dappula IV (923–935)
style: Coral-stone stupas with fixed umbrella pinnacles
significance: A field of small grey coral-stone stupas at Kantharodai in the Jaffna peninsula, the most striking Buddhist archaeological site in northern Sri Lanka. Its history reaches back to the Anuradhapura era, a stone pillar there dates to the reign of Dappula IV, Polonnaruwa-period coins have been recovered, and finds include fragments of Buddha and Bodhisattva statues and Buddha footprint slabs.
story: The little stupas are said to hold the remains of sixty arhat monks who died together at the site, by poisoned mushroom curry or by famine, while fleeing persecution.

name: Naigala Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (Bodhi tree sapling, seven stupas and an image house)
significance: A monastery in the Hambantota District laid out on the Pabbata Vihara plan with panchayatana features and seven stupas, its founding credited to the kings Gotabhaya and Mahananga. Rock inscriptions at the site have been dated to the third to fifth centuries, and its Bodhi tree is counted a sapling of the Sri Maha Bodhi planted by an arahant.
story: King Mahananga is said to have been led by a great snake to a pool of water during a drought, and the place took the name Naigala, the rock the snake showed.

name: Gori Temple
significance: A Shvetambara Jain temple of marble in the Nagarparkar area of Sindh, dedicated to Parshvanatha and holding twenty-four small cells for the twenty-four Tirthankaras. Its design is compared to the Jain temples of Mount Abu, and it survives as one of the most important Jain monuments left in Pakistan.
story: Local tradition credits the temple to a Jain devotee named Gorichom, from whom its name is said to derive.

name: Akkana Basadi
significance: A Hoysala-period Jain basadi at Shravanabelagola, built in 1181 during the reign of Veera Ballala II by Achiyakka (Achala Devi), wife of the minister Chandramouli. It is among the best preserved of the town's smaller basadis and is dedicated to Parshvanatha.

name: Bajramath Temple, Gyaraspur
significance: A ninth-century temple at Gyaraspur with three sanctums in a row, now enshrining Jain Tirthankara images and protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. Its carving is a well-known example of post-Gupta workmanship under Pratihara patronage.

name: Kere Basadi
significance: A Jain basadi standing on an island in the middle of a lake at Varanga, reached by boat, with four entrances facing the images of Parshvanatha, Neminatha, Shantinatha and Anantanatha. Inscriptions record land grants from the Vijayanagara ruler Deva Raya II in 1424 and later donors in the sixteenth century.
story: Devotees hold that a flower falling from the right side of the image is a sign of the Tirthankara's blessing.

name: Shantinath Jain Teerth
significance: A modern Digambara Jain pilgrimage temple near Indapur, opened in 2011 and built to a South Indian design. Its principal image is a 27-foot granite figure of Munisuvrata weighing about thirty tons, carved over two years from stone quarried near Bengaluru; the gilded facade has earned it the local name of the Golden Temple.

name: Shantinatha Temple, Ramtek
significance: A Digambara Jain temple at Ramtek dated to the eleventh or twelfth century and built of yellow sandstone in the northern Indian manner. Further shrines were added to the complex in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries by an official of the Bhonsle court at Nagpur, and it has since hosted several chaturmas retreats of Acharya Vidyasagar.

name: Jain Temples, Pavagadh
significance: A group of Jain temples on Pavagadh Hill, mostly of the thirteenth century and associated with Vastupala, minister of the Vaghela rulers. Originally Shvetambara foundations, they later passed to the Digambara community, and the hill's Jain associations are traced back in tradition to an image installed by King Samprati.
story: The Achalgacch order is said to have begun here when the demi-goddess Mahakali appeared before Acharya Aryarakshitsuri as he climbed the hill to undertake sallekhana and asked him not to proceed.

name: Neminath Jain Temple, Girnar
significance: The principal and largest of the Jain temples on Girnar hill, dedicated to Neminatha, whose oldest surviving portion was raised about 1129 CE by Sajjana, the Chaulukya governor of Saurashtra. It anchors one of the most important Jain pilgrimage hills in western India.
story: A layman named Ratnasar is said to have bathed an ancient clay image until it dissolved, and after a fast of twenty-one days to have received a stone image of Neminatha from the demi-goddess Ambika, consecrated in Vikram Samvat 980.

name: Digambara Jain Temple, Khandagiri
style: Kalinga, pidha deul with vimana and jagamohana
significance: The living Digambara Jain temple on the summit of Khandagiri hill above the ancient Jain caves at Bhubaneswar, its present structure built in the first quarter of the nineteenth century in Kalinga style. The main shrine holds Parshvanatha along with images of Mahavira and other Tirthankaras.
story: Local legend attributes the temple to the Kalinga king Kharavela of the first century BCE, an attribution its architecture does not support.

name: Sarnath Jain Tirth
significance: A Jain temple at Sarnath built in 1824, revered by both Digambaras and Shvetambaras, holding a large image of Shreyansanatha together with his footprint impressions. It marks the site associated with four of that Tirthankara's five kalyanakas.
story: Singhpuri beside Sarnath is held to be the ancient Simhapuri where Shreyansanatha was conceived, born, renounced the world and attained omniscience.

name: Jambudweep
deity: Jain Tirthankaras, in a complex modelling the Jambudvipa cosmos
significance: A Digambara Jain pilgrimage complex at Hastinapur founded in 1972 by the nun Gyanmati, laid out as a 250-foot circular model of Jambudvipa as described in Jain cosmology, with a 101-foot Mount Sumeru of pink marble at its centre. The model was completed in 1985 and the site is now a major teaching centre for Jain cosmography.
story: Gyanmati is said to have seen the structure of the universe in a vision while meditating in 1965, which she later matched against the cosmographical scriptures and reproduced here.

name: Bade Baba Temple
deity: Rishabhanatha (Adinatha), the first Tirthankara, known here as Bade Baba
significance: The chief Digambara Jain temple of Kundalpur, housing a post-Gupta image of Rishabhanatha venerated as Bade Baba. An eighth-century temple stood here first and was rebuilt in Vikram Samvat 1757 by Bhattaraka Surendrakirti with the help of the Bundela ruler Chhatrasal; the present larger temple was begun in 1997 under Acharya Vidyasagar and received the image in January 2006.

name: Kanishka Stupa
style: Cruciform stupa with tiered wooden superstructure
significance: The ruined mound at Shaji-ki-Dheri outside Peshawar's old walled city is the base of the colossal relic stupa raised by the Kushan emperor Kanishka; excavation there recovered a rock-crystal reliquary holding fragments of bone identified as relics of the Buddha. Chinese pilgrims described it as one of the tallest buildings of the ancient world, and the site was re-identified in 2011 though it remains unpreserved.
story: Buddhist texts record a prophecy that Kanishka would build a great stupa bearing his name on the spot where a small boy had piled up a stupa of mud, and that celestial beings helped to raise it.

name: Phra Pathommachedi
significance: Thailand's tallest stupa, rising over 120 metres at Nakhon Pathom, encases a far older Dvaravati-period monument and enshrines relics of the Buddha. King Mongkut ordered the present bell-shaped casing built from 1853, completed under his successor in 1870; the ashes of King Vajiravudh and members of his family are also interred here.
story: Local legend tells of Phraya Gong and Phraya Phan, a prince who unknowingly killed his own father and afterwards raised the great stupa in expiation.

name: National Memorial Chorten
deity: Nyingma tantric deities; memorial to Jigme Dorji Wangchuck
significance: A 108-foot whitewashed chorten in central Thimphu raised in 1974 by Queen Ashi Phuntsho Choden Wangchuck in memory of her son, the third king Jigme Dorji Wangchuck. Unusually for a chorten it holds no bodily remains, only the king's photograph, while its three interior levels are filled with paintings and sculptures of wrathful Nyingma deities; it is one of Thimphu's busiest daily places of worship.

name: Sandamuni Pagoda
deity: Gautama Buddha (iron image); memorial to Prince Kanaung Mintha
significance: Built in 1874 southwest of Mandalay Hill on the site of King Mindon's provisional palace, this Theravada pagoda commemorates his brother Prince Kanaung Mintha and three other princes killed in the Myingun rebellion of 1866, whose graves lie within. Its shrine houses a huge iron Buddha image cast by King Bodawpaya in 1802 and brought here from Amarapura.

name: Mohra Muradu
significance: A Buddhist monastery and stupa complex in a quiet valley near Taxila, set far enough from the city of Sirsukh for monks to meditate yet close enough for the daily alms round. Excavated by John Marshall in 1914-15, it preserves a main stupa on a high plinth and a two-storey monastery of 27 cells around a courtyard pool, and forms part of the Taxila World Heritage Site inscribed in 1980.

name: Thul Mir Rukan
significance: A ruined baked-brick stupa about 60 feet high standing in the Sindh plain near Kazi Ahmed and Daulatpur, the surviving core of a Buddhist religious centre. Finds from the site connect it to the veneration of Gautama Buddha, though its portable artefacts have long since been removed.

name: Phra That Kham Kaen
significance: A 19-metre gilded chedi at Ban Kham northeast of Khon Kaen that enshrines a relic of the Buddha and gives the province its name. No record of its founding survives, but scholars place it in the 17th century, when the region belonged to the Lao kingdom of Lan Xang or its successors, and date it alongside Phra That Si Song Rak in Loei.
story: Monks carrying relics of the Buddha are said to have camped by a dead tamarind stump here, and on their return journey found it sprouting fresh growth; reading this as a sign, they built the shrine on the spot with the help of local villagers.

name: Norbugang Chorten
deity: Memorial chorten of the first Chogyal’s coronation
significance: Raised at Yuksom in 1642 by Lhatsun Namkha Jigme and two fellow lamas at the moment they crowned Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal of Sikkim, this Nyingma chorten stands in Norbugang Park beside the stone coronation throne. It marks the founding of the Sikkimese monarchy and remains the focus of the site, about 42 km from Pelling.
story: The chorten is said to enclose water and earth gathered from every part of Sikkim, and a nearby stone bears what tradition holds to be the footprint of one of the lamas who performed the coronation.

name: Kunala Stupa
significance: A ruined stupa and monastery on a hill about 200 metres south of Sirkap at Taxila, named for Kunala, the son of Ashoka. Tradition credits its building to emperor Samprati in honour of his father, and Xuanzang recorded that pilgrims suffering from diseases of the eye came here in hope of a cure.
story: Kunala is said to have been blinded through the jealousy of a queen, and afterwards reunited with his father and treated by a physician at Taxila.

name: Ramagrama Stupa
significance: The only one of the eight original relic stupas raised over the divided cremation remains of the Buddha that has never been opened, built at Ramagrama by the Koliya princes and enlarged between the Mauryan and Gupta periods. The seven-metre mound still lies largely buried and unexcavated, and was placed on UNESCO’s World Heritage tentative list in 1996.
story: When Ashoka came to redistribute the relics of the Buddha, a naga guardian of the stupa is said to have stopped him, leaving Ramagrama alone undisturbed.

name: Phra That Si Song Rak
deity: Commemorative that of the Lan Xang–Ayutthaya friendship pact
significance: A 20-metre stupa at Dan Sai in Loei, raised around 1560 jointly by King Setthathirath of Lan Xang and King Maha Chakkraphat of Ayutthaya to seal a mutual-defence pact; its name means the stupa in honour of two loves. A stone inscription pledging that neither kingdom would violate the other’s territory once stood here, and the monument appears on the seal of Loei province.

name: Chorten Kora
deity: Memorial chorten of Lam Jangchub Gyeltshen
significance: A large whitewashed stupa beside the Kholong Chhu in eastern Bhutan, begun in 1740 by Lama Ngawang Lodrö in memory of Lam Jangchub Gyeltshen and to pacify a malignant spirit at the site; it took twelve years to complete and was modelled on the great stupa of Boudhanath in Nepal. Two circumambulation festivals, Dakpa Kora and Drukpa Kora, draw pilgrims from Trashiyangtse and from Tawang across the border.
story: A Dakini princess from Arunachal Pradesh is said to have had herself entombed alive inside the stupa as the Yeshe Semba, to meditate there for the benefit of all beings.

name: Gobindram Darbar, Manjhand
style: Brick Hindu temple with arched entrances, carved brickwork and frescoes
significance: A Shiva temple, known locally simply as the Shiva Temple, in the Indus-side town of Manjhand, founded by Gobindram and built of burnt brick bound with gypsum cheeroli paste. Until Partition it drew annual fairs of Hindu pilgrims from across Sindh, with a dharamshala alongside and performances by the Sindhi devotional singer Bhagat Kanwar Ram.

name: Shri Krishna Mandir, Islamabad
builtDisplay: land allotted 2016; ground broken 2020, construction pending
significance: The first Hindu temple granted permission to be built in Islamabad, on land allotted to the Pakistan Hindu Panchayat in 2016, with a groundbreaking in June 2020 and a government grant approved days afterwards. Construction had still not started as of 2025; the site was attacked and vandalised four times and its boundary wall pulled down in 2020.

name: Sri Sri Bura Shivdham
significance: A Shiva temple, also called Shivbari, standing north of the Central Shaheed Minar in Dhaka and founded during Jahangir's reign; a severe storm wrecked it in 1912 and Raja Bijay Chand Mahtab of Burdwan had it rebuilt. Its caretaker and several resident ascetics were killed by the Pakistani army in the 1971 liberation war, and the surrounding locality of Shibbari takes its name from the temple.

name: Swarved Mahamandir
deity: Swarveda — 3,137 verses of the Vihangam Yoga scripture enshrined on its walls
style: Makrana marble and pink sandstone under a 125-petal lotus dome
significance: A seven-storey meditation temple at Varanasi, inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in December 2023 at a cost of around Rs 100 crore. Covering some 300,000 square feet and seating about 20,000 people, it carries 3,137 verses of the Swarveda across its walls.

name: Prasat Sa Kamphaeng Yai
place: Ban Sa Kamphaeng Yai, Uthumphon Phisai district
deity: Shiva (the sanctuary later passed to Mahayana Buddhist use)
significance: An 11th-century Khmer sanctuary in Sisaket province, raised under Udayadityavarman II as a Shiva temple and later converted to Mahayana Buddhist use. Restoration by Thailand's Fine Arts Department recovered a 126 cm Baphuon-style bronze guardian, rated among the finest Khmer bronzes found and now in the National Museum in Bangkok.

name: Sri Lankaramaya Buddhist Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (brass image presented by Jawaharlal Nehru)
significance: A Theravada temple begun in 1920 by the Singapore Sinhala Buddhist Association; Sir Franklin Gimson laid the foundation stone of the present building in 1949 and it opened in 1952. It holds a brass Buddha given by Jawaharlal Nehru and a Bodhi tree descended, by way of the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, from the tree at Bodh Gaya.

name: Aluvihare Rock Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (reclining, standing and seated images)
significance: A cave monastery north of Matale, traced to the reign of Devanampiyatissa, whose caves carry painted walls and ceilings, Buddha images and early inscriptions. It is remembered above all as the place where the Pali Canon was first committed to writing under King Walagamba in the 1st century BCE; the site was declared a protected monument in 1974.

name: Tu Dam Temple
significance: A Hue monastery founded in the late 17th century by the Lam Te Zen master Thich Minh Hoang and granted the title Sac Tu An Ton Tu by the Nguyen lord Nguyen Phuc Chu in 1703; Emperor Thieu Tri renamed it Tu Dam in 1841. A bodhi offshoot from Bodh Gaya was planted in its forecourt in 1939.

name: Tamote Shinpin Shwegugyi Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (three encased images and a reclining Buddha)
builtDisplay: 11th c. core, encased in a stupa in the 14th c.
style: Cave temple within an encasing stupa
significance: A temple near Kyaukse begun as a single-storey hall under Anawrahta, given a second storey by Narapatisithu, then wholly enclosed in a stupa by Uzana I of Pinya in the 14th century, so that a pagoda hides a pagoda which in turn hides a two-storey temple. Its upper terrace carries stone-carved Jataka reliefs, and it was gazetted as an ancient heritage site in 2015.

name: On Lang Assembly Hall (Quan Am Temple)
significance: A Hokkien assembly hall and temple in Cho Lon, raised by Fujianese immigrants in the late 19th century and centred on Quan Am, the bodhisattva of mercy. Pure Land worship of Amitabha sits alongside altars to the sea goddess Mazu and the Jade Emperor, and its statuary includes tableaux from Journey to the West.

name: Ta Cu Pagoda
significance: A hill pagoda in Ham Thuan Nam district whose reclining Buddha, built between 1963 and 1966, measures 49 metres long and 11 metres high. It is the longest reclining Buddha image in Vietnam.

name: Quoc An Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (main hall commemorating the birth of Prince Siddhartha)
significance: Founded as Vinh An Temple between 1682 and 1685 by Thich Nguyen Thieu, a Chinese emigre monk who became the 33rd patriarch of the Lam Te Zen school, and renamed by the Nguyen lord Nguyen Phuc Tran in 1689. Repeatedly rebuilt under the Nguyen emperors through the 19th century, it is the source of the lineage most Buddhists in central and southern Vietnam trace their ordination to.

name: Andaw-thein Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (tooth relic brought from Sri Lanka)
builtDisplay: ordination hall 1515-21; enlarged into a temple 1607
significance: A stone shrine beside Shite-thaung at Mrauk-U, raised as an ordination hall by King Thazata between 1515 and 1521 and rebuilt as a temple by King Raza II in 1607 to enshrine a tooth relic he had brought from Ceylon. Its octagonal core is ringed by two concentric passageways and crowned by a bell-shaped stupa with eight smaller stupas at the corners.

name: Doi Son Pagoda
significance: A hilltop pagoda in Ha Nam built early in the 12th century by order of Emperor Ly Nhan Tong, once crowned by the tower called Sung Thien Dien Linh and still holding a stele of 1121 that documents Ly-period life and government. Ming forces wrecked it in the 15th century; it was rebuilt in 1591 and restored again in the mid-19th century.

name: Keo Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha and the monk Nguyen Minh Khong
significance: A large Ly-dynasty pagoda in Vu Thu district begun in 1061, which Emperor Ly Than Tong dedicated in the 1130s to the monk Nguyen Minh Khong alongside the Buddha. It remains one of the best-preserved historic temple complexes of the Red River delta.
story: The emperor is said to have founded the temple in gratitude after Nguyen Minh Khong miraculously cured him of leprosy.

name: Wat Bowon Sathan Sutthawat
deity: Gautama Buddha (standing bronze image in the attitude of bestowing pardon)
builtDisplay: founded under Rama III; completed mid-19th c.
significance: A royal temple inside the former Front Palace precinct in Phra Nakhon, Bangkok, begun by Prince Maha Sakdiphonlasep in the reign of Rama III and finished under King Pinklao and King Mongkut. Its gilded standing Buddha sits beneath a spired busabok throne, and the hall served as a royal funeral hall in 1900.

name: Dhammikarama Burmese Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (standing Buddha image), with a shrine to Arahant Upagutta
significance: The oldest Burmese Buddhist temple in Penang, founded on 1 August 1803 as the Nandy Moloh Temple by U. Nandamala on land bought by Nyonya Betong. Its stupa was consecrated in 1805 and enclosed by an outer stupa in 1838, and a golden pagoda bell tower was added in 2011.
story: Arahant Upagutta, whose wooden shrine stands in the grounds, is held to have the power to turn away evil spirits, obstacles and dangers.

name: Linh Sơn Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (bronze image seated on a lotus), with Avalokiteshvara
significance: A Buddhist temple in Đà Lạt built between 1938 and 1940 by public subscription, with the largest gifts from the lay Buddhists Võ Đình Dung and Nguyễn Văn Tiến. Its main hall holds a bronze Buddha seated on a lotus, cast in 1952.

name: Khleang Temple
significance: A Theravada temple of the Khmer community in Sóc Trăng, first built in 1533, whose sanctuary holds a 6.8 m image of Gautama Buddha erected in 1916 with funds from the family of Lum Sum. It mixes Corinthian pillars with Khmer ornament and was declared a historic heritage site in 1990.

name: Long Sơn Temple
significance: A Buddhist temple in Nha Trang first erected in 1886 and moved to its present site in 1900 after a cyclone destroyed it, then renovated in 1940 and repaired after damage in 1968. It is dominated by a large white concrete image of the Buddha cast in 1964 and installed the following year.

name: Phaung Daw U Pagoda
significance: A Theravada pagoda at Ywama on Inle Lake in Shan State whose Burmese name means 'principal royal barge pagoda'. It houses gilded Buddha images believed to have been brought to the lake by King Alaungsithu of the Pagan dynasty in the 12th century.
story: On a windy day in the 1960s the barge carrying the images capsized and one image was lost in the lake; when the party returned to the monastery, the missing image was said to be sitting back in its place.

name: Tai Pei Yuen Temple
significance: A Buddhist temple in Singapore's Balestier district, founded in 1938 as the Kuan Yin lodge by Chow Siew Keng, who had come from Guangdong two years earlier, and rebuilt in 1964. Under later abbesses it became known for charitable work, running a free clinic from 1980 and distributing rice dumplings to welfare homes from 1984.

name: Kadadora Vihara
significance: A Buddhist temple in the Kotmale valley whose garbhagriha held the principal Buddha image and whose walls carried paintings of the Buddha's life and the Jataka tales. It was abandoned in 1979 for the building of the Kotmale dam and drowned when the reservoir filled in 1985, one of some 54 religious sites lost with 57 villages.

name: Diệu Đế Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha, flanked by Samantabhadra and Manjushri
significance: A Buddhist pagoda on the Dong Ba Canal in Huế, facing the imperial citadel, built under the Nguyễn emperor Thiệu Trị, who named it for the Four Noble Truths and declared it one of Vietnam's national pagodas. It is known for the four low towers set about its gate and sanctuary.

name: Lankatilaka Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha, with devales to Upulvan, Ganapathi, Saman, Vibhishana, Kataragama and Kumara Bandara
significance: A rock-built temple near Pilimatalawa raised in the reign of Bhuvanekabahu IV and overseen by his chief minister Senalankadhikara, regarded as the finest building of the Gampola period. Designed by the South Indian architect Sathapati Rayar with Pandya sculptors from Tamil Nadu, it sets a Buddha image among six Hindu devales and was declared a protected monument in 1949.

name: Le-myet-hna Temple
deity: Eight seated Buddhas around the central pillar
significance: A four-sided black sandstone shrine at the northwest corner of the Shite-thaung temple in Mrauk U, completed in 1430 for King Min Saw Mon. Doorways on all four sides lead to a central pillar ringed by eight seated Buddhas.

name: Thatta Thattaha Maha Bawdi Pagoda
significance: A 49-metre pagoda in Naypyidaw built by the city's development committee as a full replica of the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya, its principal Buddha image consecrated in May 2014 and the pagoda finished in 2015. The grounds also reproduce the sites of the Buddha's birth, enlightenment, first sermon and passing, for worshippers who cannot make the pilgrimage to India.

name: Chaukhtatgyi Buddha Temple
significance: A Yangon shrine holding one of Myanmar's most venerated reclining Buddha images, 66 metres long. Sir Po Tha paid for the first image in 1899 and it was finished in 1907, but its proportions and stern face were judged wrong; it was pulled down in the 1950s and the replacement, carved under the Dawei master U Thaung with glass eyes made at the Naga Glass Factory, was consecrated in 1973.

name: Wat Chetawan
significance: A Thai Theravada temple in Petaling Jaya founded in 1957 by Phra Kru Palat Vieng and designed by Thailand's Fine Arts Department, its gilded main shrine completed in June 1962 with funds to which King Bhumibol Adulyadej personally contributed. It holds a share of the Buddha relics excavated at Piprahwa in 1898, given by Lord Curzon to King Chulalongkorn of Siam and passed to Malaysia in 2012.

name: Muwangala Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (Sri Pathul Gala footprint slabs)
significance: An archaeological Buddhist temple at Muwangala near Hingurana in the Ampara District, protected as an archaeological site since 26 December 2014. A third-century inscription there records a grant to the temple by a viceroy named Kodini, and the remains include a stupa, a drip-ledged cave, an asanaghara, Buddha-footprint slabs, moonstone fragments, building bases and pillars.

name: Asgiri Maha Viharaya
deity: Gautama Buddha (custodianship of the Sacred Tooth Relic)
significance: The Kandy monastery that heads the Asgiriya chapter of the Siyam Nikaya, one of the two chapters holding custody of the Buddha's Tooth Relic enshrined in the Sri Dalada Maligawa. Commander Siriwardhana founded it on the instructions of Parakramabahu IV of Kurunegala, and it was completed in 1302.
story: By another account the name Asgiri recalls Queen Chandrawathie, mother of King Vikramabahu, who was cremated in the burning ground of Adahana Maluva.

name: Nikasala Aranya Senasanaya
significance: An ancient Buddhist forest hermitage of cave-temple type at Kanduboda-Moragane village near Panduwasnuwara, in the Kurunegala District of Sri Lanka's North Western Province.

name: Aramanapola Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (image house; sacred Bodhi tree)
originNote: site traced to King Devanampiya Tissa (250–210 BCE)
significance: A Buddhist temple at Ganegama near Pelmadulla in the Ratnapura District whose history is traced to King Devanampiya Tissa and which Parakramabahu VI completed as a full temple in honour of his mother Sunethradevi; its name is said to recall monks brought from the Arammana country of Myanmar under Vijayabahu I to restore the order after Chola rule. Its Bodhi tree is held to be one of the thirty-two saplings of the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, and the largest of them.

name: Sri Saddharmagupta Piriven Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (image house and Bodhi tree)
significance: An old piriven vihara — a monastic teaching temple — at Dombawela in Udugampola, Gampaha District, recognised by the government as a protected archaeological monument. Its precinct holds a stupa, image house, Bodhi tree, bell tower, preaching hall, library and monks' dwellings, the old library building having been conserved in 2010.

name: Ibbagala Raja Maha Vihara
significance: An ancient Buddhist cave temple in the mid-valley of the Ethagala rock at Kurunegala, in Sri Lanka's North Western Province. Its title Raja Maha Vihara marks it as one of the temples that historically held royal patronage.

name: Yatala Vehera
deity: Buddha (relic caskets recovered from the stupa)
significance: A stupa at Deberawewa near Tissamaharama in the Hambantota District, dated to roughly the third century BCE and credited either to Yatala Tissa of Ruhuna or to his father Mahanaga. A large number of relic caskets has been recovered from it, and the restoration begun in 1883 took over a century to finish.
story: The stupa is said to have been raised over the place where the prince was born, and by another account to have been offered to Arittha, the first Sinhalese arahant.

name: Pilikuththuwa Raja Maha Vihara
builtDisplay: caves in use by the 2nd–3rd c. BCE
significance: A Buddhist cave temple at Pilikuththuwa in the Gampaha District, on ground inhabited since prehistoric times, whose caves appear to have served monks by the 2nd–3rd century BCE. The complex includes an image house and a dagoba.
story: King Valagamba is said to have sheltered here from time to time during the invasion from South India.

name: Degaldoruwa Raja Maha Vihara
significance: A rock-cut cave temple near Kandy, begun in 1771 during the reign of Kirti Sri Rajasinha and completed by his younger brother Rajadhi Rajasinha after he came to the throne. Behind two roofed ante-chambers the shrine cut into the rock holds a large reclining Buddha, and its walls carry celebrated murals of the Jataka stories and the Buddha's former births.
story: A farmer is said to have found golden sickles in a cleft between the boulders and to have borrowed one each day for his harvest until he tried to keep it, whereupon the guardian sealed the gap — and the king ordered a temple raised on the spot.

name: Magul Maha Viharaya
deity: Gautama Buddha (image shrine, stupa and Bodhi tree)
significance: A Buddhist temple at Lahugala in the Ampara District whose image shrine, stupa and sacred fig all survive in good condition. Tradition assigns its completion to King Kavantissa in the second century BCE, though other accounts credit King Dhatusena of the fifth century CE.
story: Magul means 'wedding' in Sinhala: the site is said to mark where Kavantissa married Viharamahadevi after the sea carried her miraculously ashore, and the foundations of the Magul Maduwa wedding pavilion are still shown there.

name: Samudrasanna Vihara
significance: A Buddhist temple at Mount Lavinia on the coast south of Colombo, completed in 1845. The Sri Lankan government declared it an archaeological protected site on 6 June 2008.

name: Mulkirigala Raja Maha Vihara
builtDisplay: 3rd c. BCE per the Mahavamsa; enlarged 5th and 18th c.
style: cave temple on a 205 m rock
significance: A cave temple cut into a 205-metre rock inland of Tangalle in the Hambantota District, credited by the Mahavamsa to King Saddhatissa and later enlarged under Dhatusena (461–479) and Kirti Sri Rajasinha (1747–1782). Its terraces of caves hold many Buddha images, among them the great reclining Buddha of the Paduma Rahath Vihara, and a Bodhi tree held to be one of the thirty-two saplings of the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi.
story: The rock is linked to the Jataka in which the Buddha, in an earlier birth, gave flesh from his own body to ransom a dove.

name: Lahugala Kiri Vehera
significance: An ancient Buddhist temple with a stupa at Lahugala in the Ampara District, believed to belong to the reign of King Dappula I in the seventh century.

name: Udayagiri Raja Maha Vihara
significance: A Buddhist temple at Udayagiri village in the Ampara District, protected as an archaeological monument since 26 December 2014. A stone pillar inscription records that two generals of King Udaya I exempted the vihara from taxes, and the site is said to go back more than a thousand years.

name: Kande Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (48.8 m seated image in bhumisparsha mudra)
significance: A hilltop Buddhist temple at Aluthgama in the Kalutara District, founded in 1734 by Karapagala Dewamitta Thera. Its precinct holds a stupa built in 1935, a relic chamber, an image house with Kandyan-era frescoes and a Bodhi tree reckoned over three hundred years old, and a seated Buddha 48.8 m high in bhumisparsha mudra, finished in 2007, now dominates the site.

name: Lahugala Kota Vehera
significance: A stupa at Lahugala in the Ampara District, one of only four structures of the Kota Vehera type known in Sri Lanka. Inscriptions at the site, of the first and second centuries CE, name kings including Bhatika Tissa, Kutakanna Tissa and Gajabahu I.

name: Galmaduwa Raja Maha Vihara, Ampara
builtDisplay: trad. King Saddha Tissa, 2nd c. BCE
significance: A Buddhist temple complex with a stupa at Galmaduwa near Hingurana in the Ampara District, believed to have been built during the reign of King Saddha Tissa of Anuradhapura in the second century BCE.

name: Pusulpitiya Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (Dambaran stone image; ancient Bo tree)
significance: A Buddhist temple at Pusulpitiya in the Nuwara Eliya District whose history is traced to the third century BCE or before. It keeps a Bo tree planted in the time of Devanampiya Tissa and one of the four Dambaran Buddha statues said to have been brought from India by Arahat Maliyadeva, and it sheltered the Sacred Tooth Relic on three occasions of political unrest.
story: An Indian brahmin hunting a golden ash pumpkin in the Kotmale country is said to have sacrificed his son to win it, then set it down on a rocky plain where it sank into the stone — giving Pusulpitiya its name.

name: Kshetrarama Maha Vihara
significance: A Buddhist temple at Moratuwa in the Colombo District, established in 1829 by the chief monk Ven. Weligama Sri Sumanatissa Thera. Its old image house holds a seated stone Buddha and the temple keeps ola-leaf volumes of the Tipitaka, while its Seema Malakaya shows architectural features found at no other Buddhist shrine in the country.

name: Kotte Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (reclining image; with a Kataragama devalaya)
style: Two-chamber image house with makara torana and Kandyan-era frescoes
significance: The royal temple of the Kotte kingdom, built beside his palace under the patronage of Parakramabahu VI, ruined in the Dutch period and re-established in 1818 after the site was rediscovered. Its two-chambered image house holds a reclining Buddha under Kandyan-era murals, and part of the old Kataragama devalaya survives alongside the stupa.

name: Ridi Viharaya
deity: Gautama Buddha (9 m recumbent Buddha and a gilded Anuradhapura-era image; also an Avalokiteshvara)
style: Cave temple with a Polonnaruwa-type gedige and Kandyan work
significance: The 'silver temple' of Ridigama, founded in the second century BCE under Dutthagamani at the place where the silver ore that funded the Ruwanwelisaya is said to have been found. Its Rajatha Lena cave holds a nine-metre recumbent Buddha and a gilded Anuradhapura-period image, and the complex was revived in the eighteenth century by Kirti Sri Rajasinha of Kandy.
story: Merchants who had offered jackfruit to arhat monks were led to a seam of silver ore here, which provided the metal Dutthagamani needed to complete the Ruwanwelisaya stupa.

name: Sri Subodharama Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (image-house statues of 1780, a stupa, a Bodhi tree and a Sri Pada footprint shrine)
significance: A low-country temple at Karagampitiya whose vihara was finished in 1795 and its stupa in 1796, with Buddha images dating from 1780 and a Bodhi tree raised from the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi at Anuradhapura. Its murals are valued for bridging the conventional eighteenth-century hill-country manner and the more realistic nineteenth-century low-country style.

name: Neelagiriseya
deity: Gautama Buddha (relic casket enshrined in the stupa)
significance: A large ruined stupa at Lahugala set in a monastic complex of some 36 hectares, credited either to Kavan Tissa or to Bhatikabhaya. Excavation recovered a golden casket whose inscription led archaeologists to identify the contents as relics of the Buddha, and an inscription records a grant by Queen Chula Sivalee.

name: Padiyadora Raja Maha Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha (torso Buddha image, dagoba and Bodhi tree)
significance: An ancient temple in the Ampara District whose construction is attributed to Kavan Tissa, prince of Ruhuna. Its remains include a dagoba and a four-foot Buddha torso, and it is still an active place of local veneration.
story: Its Bodhi tree is venerated as having grown from one of the saplings of the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi at Anuradhapura.

name: Gurdwara Makhdoom Pur Pahoran
deity: Guru Nanak (site of his meeting with Sajjan Thug)
significance: A gurdwara in Khanewal district marking the inn of Sajjan Thug, where Sikh tradition places Guru Nanak's encounter with him; the inn was turned into a shrine to commemorate the meeting. The present building was raised in Samvat 1970 by a descendant of Bhai Jodh Singh.
story: Sajjan is said to have robbed the travellers he sheltered until Guru Nanak sang him a hymn on the worthlessness of a bronze vessel that is bright outside and black within, upon which he confessed and became a follower.

name: Gurdwara Shahid Ganj Singh Singhania
deity: The Sikh martyrs of the eighteenth century, among them Bhai Mani Singh
significance: A memorial gurdwara in the Naulakha quarter of Lahore on a site where large numbers of Sikhs were executed under the Mughal governors of the eighteenth century, including Bhai Mani Singh in 1738. Work began in 1716 and was completed in 1753 after the Sikhs were given control of the ground; the marble building standing today dates from 1935.

name: Gurdwara Sahib Klang
significance: The main gurdwara of Klang and the third home of the town's Sikh congregation, built between 1993 and 1995 with donations from Sikh communities across Malaysia and opened in February 1996. The first Sikh place of worship in Klang was a wooden building put up around 1900 by some fifty Sikhs serving in the Federated Malay States Police.

name: Central Sikh Temple
significance: The oldest Sikh congregation in Singapore, founded in 1912 on Queen Street with support from Sindhi merchants and the Straits Settlements Police and moved to a purpose-built shrine on Towner Road constructed between 1984 and 1986. The Guru Granth Sahib was installed in April 1986 and the building was opened by President Wee Kim Wee that November.

name: Gurdwara Janam Asthan Guru Ram Das
place: Chuna Mandi, Walled City of Lahore
deity: Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru (Guru Granth Sahib read daily)
significance: A gurdwara in the Chuna Mandi quarter of Lahore's walled city standing on the site traditionally held to be the birthplace and childhood home of Guru Ram Das, born in 1534. Construction began in 1801 under Maharaja Ranjit Singh at the request of Maharani Datar Kaur, and the Guru Granth Sahib is read there daily.

name: Gurdwara Chowa Sahib
deity: Guru Nanak (site of the spring he is said to have revealed)
significance: A gurdwara built beside a spring within the walls of Rohtas Fort in Jhelum district, marking a place associated with Guru Nanak's travels. An earlier memorial raised by Charat Singh was replaced by the present building, commissioned by Maharaja Ranjit Singh and finished in 1834.
story: Sikh tradition holds that when Bhai Mardana complained of thirst, Guru Nanak struck the ground with his staff and a spring appeared; Sher Shah Suri's engineers are said to have tried three times, and failed, to move the spring up the hill to serve his new fort.

name: Gurdwara Nanak Shahi
deity: Guru Granth Sahib (commemorating Guru Nanak's visit)
significance: The principal gurdwara of Bangladesh, on Neelkhet Road in Dhaka, marking the place associated with Guru Nanak's visit to Bengal in 1506–1507. A shrine was raised in the first half of the seventeenth century by the Udasi preacher Bhai Almast, the present Indo-Mughal building dates from 1830, and it was renovated in 1988–89.

name: Gurdwara Shaheed Bhai Taru Singh
deity: Bhai Taru Singh, the Sikh martyr
significance: A gurdwara in the Shahidganj area of Lahore commemorating Bhai Taru Singh, executed in 1745 by the Mughal governor Zakariya Khan for refusing to renounce his faith. The shrine was built in 1747–48, in the years when the Sikh misls were taking control of the city.
story: Sikh accounts relate that after ordering Bhai Taru Singh's scalp cut away, Zakariya Khan was struck by unbearable pain and could not pass urine, and found relief only when he had himself struck with the martyr's shoes — dying twenty-two days later all the same.

name: Gurdwara Beri Sahib
significance: A gurdwara in the Babey Beri locality of Sialkot marking a place where Guru Nanak is remembered to have stayed, built by Natha Singh and photographed as early as about 1910. Damaged in the unrest around the Babri Masjid dispute, it was restored in the 2010s and reopened to Sikh pilgrims from India in November 2012.
story: Guru Nanak is said to have rested here under a beri (jujube) tree, still standing, and to have met Hamza Ghaus, a Sufi saint of Sialkot.

name: World Peace Pagoda, Lumbini
significance: A whitewashed stupa at the northern end of the Lumbini Master Plan axis, designed and built by Japanese Buddhists at a cost of roughly a million US dollars and also known as the Nipponzan peace pagoda. Four large gilded Buddha figures face the cardinal directions, and the grave of the Japanese monk Unataka Navatame lies at its base; the wetland north of it shelters the endangered sarus crane.

name: Phra Chedi Klang Nam
deity: Phra Mae Khongkha (goddess of the waters)
significance: A ten-metre bell-shaped chedi on a reddish-brick base at the mouth of the Rayong river, built in 1873 by the provincial administrator Kate Yomjinda in honour of Phra Mae Khongkha and long used by sailors as a landmark for the port. It has become an emblem of Rayong, with an annual festival in the twelfth lunar month and a December rite in which its spire is wrapped in six metres of red cloth.

name: Bhamala Stupa
significance: One of the best preserved Buddhist sites in the Taxila valley, whose main stupa is the largest surviving cruciform example in the Taxila and Gandhara region, with stairways on all four sides and about nineteen smaller votive stupas around it. Excavations begun by John Marshall in 1929 and resumed in 2017 uncovered a Buddha figure roughly 1,700 years old, described as the oldest known image of the Buddha at the moment of enlightenment.

name: Wat Wang Wiwekaram
deity: Gautama Buddha; relics of Luangpho Uttama
significance: A Theravada temple near the Thai-Burmese border at Sangkhla Buri, founded in 1953 by the monk Luangpho Uttama with Mon and Karen settlers and rebuilt on higher ground by 1985 after the Khao Laem Dam flooded its first site. The body of its founder rests here in a glass coffin, while the drowned original is now visited as the Sangkhlaburi underwater temple.

name: Matho Monastery
significance: Founded in 1410 by Lama Dugpa Dorje on the south bank of the Indus about 26 km from Leh, Matho is the only Ladakhi monastery of the Sakya school. Its assembly hall centres on a Shakyamuni Buddha with chapels to Sakya Pandita and other lamas, and an adjoining museum holds thangkas of the 14th and 15th centuries along with festival masks and robes.
story: At the Matho Nagrang festival two monks known as the Rongtsan oracles, chosen every three years after months of seclusion and meditation, are possessed by the monastery guardians and answer questions about the year ahead for Matho and for Ladakh.

name: Wat Chiang Man
deity: Gautama Buddha (Phra Sae Tang Khamani and Phra Sila images)
significance: The oldest temple inside the walls of Chiang Mai, founded in 1297 by King Mangrai as the city was being laid out. Its Chedi Chang Lom is buttressed by fifteen life-size brick-and-stucco elephants, the wihan holds a Buddha image of 1465 said to be the oldest surviving Thai image shown with an alms bowl, and a stone inscription of 1581 in the ubosot records the city’s founding on 12 April 1296.
story: The small quartz Phra Sae Tang Khamani is believed to protect the city, and the stone Phra Sila, carved with the Buddha subduing the elephant Nalagiri, is credited with the power to bring rain.
